en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Saddanīti Treatise (The Garland of Words).
Introduction to the Composition.
Having understood here this sublime Dhamma, which was taught by the Buddha through the method of the wise,
one comes to know the deathless state.
Having bowed down to that Great Hero, the Omniscient One, the Leader of the World;
Having worshipped the Supreme One of Great Compassion, who is pure and the giver of purity,
and having worshipped his True Dhamma— which is pure, peaceful, unconditioned,
beyond the reach of logic, well-expounded, sweet, and auspicious— [one attains the goal].
Having joined his palms in reverence to the Saṅgha— the field of merit,
the Tathāgata who illuminates the pure qualities of virtue, concentration, wisdom, and so forth—
and having performed acts of merit such as paying homage to the Triple Gem;
Having dispelled all obstacles by means of my splendor,
I shall explain the unconfused science of grammar for the sake of the Teaching of the Teacher,
who is skilled in worldly conduct and whose guidance is the true Dhamma.
Through the attainment of the destruction of the taints, there is the perfection of the Dispensation;
and the attainment of the destruction of the taints has the realization of the Truths as its cause.
And that realization of the Truths is considered to be dependent upon practice.
And although that practice may indeed be centered on the scriptures,
for those devoted to the scriptures who have mastered the characteristics of words,
there is no confusion regarding syllables and grammatical cases.
And because, through the state of non-delusion regarding syllables and phrases,
the wise understand the meaning of the Pāḷi in the teaching of the Sugata; through this awakening to the meaning of the Pāḷi,
they apply systematic attention to the Teacher’s instruction.
The wise practice the path, untiring in their application. By practicing methodically,
they reach the supreme, world-transcending Dhamma through the practice of virtue and the other perfections for the sake of purification.
Therefore, those desiring that goal, relying on the method of the wise,
should thoroughly grasp the science of words as it is being expounded by me.
[This includes] roots, the forms derived from roots, and their specific characteristics.
The distinctions of sandhi, nouns, and so forth, as well as the case endings of words,
the methods of the Pāḷi, and other such various modes—
by analyzing these, there will be assistance for the Dispensation.
1. The Analysis of Verbs with Prefixes (Savikaraṇākhyātavibhāga).
In this context, in what sense is it called a "root" (dhātu)? It is called a root because it bears its own meaning (sakattha);

it is called a root because, through connection with an excellence of meaning, it also bears another meaning (parattha); and it is called a root because it is bound by any one of the twenty prefixes as a cause for producing a specific modification of meaning.

It is called a *dhātu* because it "bears" (*dhāreti*) a specific meaning; or, it is called a *dhātu* because it is "borne" (*dhāriyati*) by the wise in many ways, such as: "This is its meaning," "This suffix follows after this [base]," and so forth;

or, it is called a *dhātu* because by means of it the learned "fashion" (*vidahanti*) the production of words, just as one fashions objects made of iron, copper, and other metals from the elements (*dhātu*) of iron, copper, and so on.
Thus, first of all, the meaning of the word *dhātu* should be understood.
In the opinion of the Jina (Buddha), the word *dhātu* is considered feminine when referring to the female sex;
in the treatises (*sattha*), it is masculine when referring to the male sex; and in the opinion of Kaccāyana, it is used in both genders.

Alternatively, in the Jina’s opinion, in the passage “*tato gotamidhātūnī*,” the word *dhātu* occurs with a change of gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*), as in the case of “*pabbatāni*” [where the plural neuter is used for the masculine].
In the phrase "and forests," the word *pabbata* (mountain) serves as an illustration;

however, one should not say here that "the neuter designation is used because it denotes bones," for even when denoting bones, the term *dhātuyo* is seen to be in the feminine gender. Words such as *bhū*, *vā*, etc., are *dhātus*. For example:
*bhū*, *i*, *ku*, *ke*, *takka*, *taka*, *taki*, *suka*, and so forth. According to their classes (*gaṇa*), they are eightfold: the *bhūvādigaṇa*, the *rudhādigaṇa*, and so on.
[The roots are divided into] the *div-ādi* group, the *svā-ādi* group, the *ky-ādi* group, the *guh-ādi* group, the *tan-ādi* group, and the *cur-ādi* group.
Now we shall show the suffixes for these, which are designated as *vikaraṇa*.

For suffixes are manifold, since they occur within nouns (*nāma*), nominal derivatives (*kitanāma*), compounds (*samāsanāma*), secondary derivatives (*taddhitanāma*), and verbs (*ākhyāta*) in their various forms. Briefly, however, the nominal suffixes (*nāmapaccaya*) are of two kinds.

And there is the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta-paccaya*). Therein, the verbal suffixes are twofold, by way of those with vocalic infixes (*vikaraṇa-paccaya*) and those without vocalic infixes (*novikaraṇa-paccaya*).
Among these, the suffixes with vocalic infixes are seventeenfold, beginning with *a*, and fifteenfold when excluding those that include [the root] without being grasped [as an infix].
However, the suffixes without vocalic infixes are manifold, such as *kha*, *cha*, *sa*, and so on. Those which are helpful for the production of the word-form and for the specific meaning...
Whether they be articulate or inarticulate, or whether they be subject to elision or not subject to elision—these sounds are conditions (*paccaya*).
Alternatively, they are called conditions because they go toward their respective causes by way of dependence (*paṭicca*);
or they are called conditions because the production of sound comes from this [dependence].
Since the classification of the nominal suffixes (nāmika-paccayas) will be revealed [later],
we shall not elaborate upon them here in this section on nominal suffixes. However,
that which pertains to the nominal suffixes (no-vikaraṇa) by way of their classification—
Furthermore, this will be explained in detail in the section on verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta-kappa*).
Thus, among the various types of suffixes, one should observe: "These are called vikaraṇa-suffixes. How so? From the *bhū-vādi* class, the suffix *ap* occurs in the sense of the agent;
from the *rudh-ādi* class, the suffixes *ak*, *ar*, *vaṇ*, *ekāra*, and *okāra* occur in the sense of the agent; [and] in the positions of the prefix and the middle...

There is the insertion of *niggahīta* (*-m*), and from the *divādi* class, the suffix *-ya* occurs in the sense of the agent; from the *svādi* class, the suffixes *ṇu*, *ṇā*, and *uṇ* occur in the sense of the agent;
from the *kiyādi* class, the suffix *-nā* occurs in the sense of the agent; from the *gahādi* class, the suffixes *-ppa* and *-ṇha* occur in the sense of the agent;
from the *tanādi* class, the suffixes *-o* and *-ira* occur in the sense of the agent; and from the *curādi* class, the suffixes *-ṇe* and *-ṇaya* occur in the sense of the agent.
The suffixes *aka*, *ivaṇṇa*, *e*, *okāra*, *ya*, *ṇu*, *ṇā*, *uṇā*,
*nā*, *ppa*, *ṇha*, *yira*, *ṇe*, and *ṇaya*— by including those not explicitly mentioned,
fifteen such suffixes are thus indicated.
One should discern that these are suffixes (paccaya) called *vikaraṇa*.
Those eightfold groups of verbal roots (*dhātugaṇa*), which are accompanied by these aforementioned *vikaraṇa*-suffixes as well as others, are of great utility in the Suttantas;
among them, this is the *bhūvādi* group. *Bhū* is in the sense of existence; the root *bhū* is in the sense of being present.
It functions. Among roots that are both transitive and intransitive, this is an intransitive root;
however, it is not transitive like another root *bhū* found in such expressions as "become the Dhamma" (*dhammabhūto*), which expresses the sense of attainment (*patti*).

For this [root] becomes transitive only when joined with prefixes such as *pari* and *abhi*, but not even when joined with prefixes or particles such as *upa*, *parā*, or *patu*. Therefore, the established forms of this [root] are...
Forms are to be known as twofold: intransitive words and transitive words.
Herein, regarding the explanation of pure agentive-verb forms:
there are *bhavati*, *ubbhavati*, *samubbhavati*, *pabhavati*, *parābhavati*, *sambhavati*, and *vibhavati*.
*bhoti*, *sambhoti*, *vibhoti*, *pātubhavati*, *pātubbhavati*, *pātubhoti*—these are intransitive verbs (*akammaka-pada*).

Here, *pātu* is a particle (*nipāta*); like the particles *āvi* and *tiro* in such expressions as *āvibhavati* and *tirobhavati*, it does not qualify the verbal form derived from the root *bhū*, nor does it establish its transitivity (*sakammakatā*). *Ud* and the others are prefixes (*upasagga*).
However, these [prefixes] are qualifiers; they do not establish the transitivity of a verb.

Those words whose meaning is not to be connected with an object are intransitive (*akammaka*). The meaning of intransitive words should be explained according to their respective sense, whether they are transitive (*sakammaka*) or intransitive.
For example: *paribhoti* / *paribhavati*, *abhibhoti* / *abhibhavati*, *adhibhoti* / *adhibhavati*, *atibhoti* / *atibhavati*.
*anubhoti*, *anubhavati*; *samanubhoti*, *samanubhavati*; *abhisambhoti*, *abhisambhavati*—these are transitive verbs (*sakammakapada*).
Here, prefixes such as *pari* and others qualify the verbal forms derived from the root *bhū*, serving both to specify the meaning and to establish their transitivity.
Those words whose meaning is to be connected with an object are [the transitive verbs].
These are transitive verbs. The meaning of transitive words should be explained by way of their transitivity, though in some cases it may also be explained by way of their intransitivity.
Thus there are simple agentive-action verbs. This is the enumeration.
In that context, *bhavati* means "it is," "it exists," "it is discerned," or "it acquires its own form. *Ubbhavati* means "it arises" or "it acquires its own form."
It obtains. "Arises" means it comes into being; it acquires its own form. "Originates" means it comes into existence, it comes to be.
Alternatively, "originates" means it flows from somewhere, it is not cut off, it remains uninterrupted, and it spreads to various places.
"Perishes" means there is ruin, one encounters misfortune, or one reaches a state of non-increase.
*Sambhavati* means it comes into being well; it attains growth, increase, and abundance.
*Vibhavati* means it is cut off, destroyed, or fails; or alternatively, it specifically comes into being or succeeds.
The terms *bhoti*, *sambhoti*, and *vibhoti* are respectively synonymous with *bhavati*, *sambhavati*, and *vibhavati*. *Pātubhavati* means...
It is revealed, seen, made known, and becomes manifest. *Pātubbhavati* and *pātubhoti*—these are explained in the same manner as the term *pātubhavati*.
Thus, the explanation of the meaning of intransitive verbs should be understood according to their respective transitive and intransitive usage.
The same applies hereafter to other intransitive verbs as well.
In the seven dyads beginning with the "Paribhava-duka," two terms in each successive pair have identical meanings;

therefore, we shall explain them by taking only the two terms in each pair. In that context, *paribhoti* (he despises) means *paribhavati* (he treats with contempt), for he harms or oppresses another, or alternatively, he reviles or disregards him.
*Abhibhoti* (he overcomes) means *abhibhavati* (he overpowers), for he overwhelms or crushes another.
*Adhibhoti adhibhavatīti*: Having crushed another, one comes to be; one brings [the other] under one's own control.
*Atibhoti atibhavatīti*: Having surpassed another, one comes to be. *Anubhoti anubhavatīti*: One experiences pleasure and pain; one enjoys them;
one becomes a feeler of pleasure and pain. *Samanubhoti samanubhavatīti*: [One experiences] pleasure and pain...
He feels thoroughly; he enjoys thoroughly; he is one who experiences pleasure and pain thoroughly.

"He overcomes" (*abhisambhoti*) and "he overcomes" (*abhisambhavati*) means he overwhelms and crushes another. Thus, the explanation of the meaning of transitive verbs should be understood by way of their transitivity.
However, in some instances, it is also used in an intransitive sense, as in "he goes" (*gacchati*) or "it proceeds" (*pavattati*).
Likewise, in subsequent instances, other transitive roots—
provided they belong to the *bhūvādi* class and are devoid of suffixes (*apaccaya*)—
are used when expressing an action with a pure agent (*suddhakattukriyākhyāna*), regardless of which verbal root (*dhātu*) they are based upon.
This is the exposition of verbs with a pure agent (suddhakattukriyāpada).
Regarding the exposition of verbs with a causal agent (hetukattukriyāpada):

one causes to develop (bhāveti), causes to manifest (vibhāveti), causes to accumulate (sambhāveti), and causes to refine (paribhāveti); thus there are verbs with a causal agent. Their meaning is the same when considered in terms of having a single object (ekakammaka).

It should be understood [in this way]. However, for the latter, it may also be understood by way of its two objects (*dvikammaka*). One causes to be permeated, one causes to be overcome, one causes to be experienced;
thus there are also causal agentive verbal forms (*hetukattukriyāpada*). This meaning should be understood by way of the two objects.
In this manner, causal agentive verbal forms should be known as being of two kinds; others too should be included.
In this context, "he develops" (*bhāveti*) means that a person develops, cultivates, and repeatedly practices whatever is to be developed;

or alternatively, "he develops" means he increases it. "He develops thoroughly" (*vibhāveti*) means he develops whatever is to be developed in a distinguished manner, or he develops it in various ways, or he cultivates and increases it;
or alternatively, "he develops thoroughly" means he does not develop [it in a limited way], but causes it to disappear [from defilement].
*Sambhāveti* means that one honors, esteems, clearly reveals, and extols the virtue of anyone whatsoever.
*Paribhāveti* means that one cultivates, develops, and increases on all sides whatever is to be cultivated.
Thus the meaning should be understood according to the single object (kamma). Alternatively, *paribhāveti* means that one perfumes a substance that is to be scented.
It perfumes, impregnates, and causes the scent to be taken up. In this way, the meaning should also be understood by way of two objects.

"He causes to be perfumed" means that one person causes another person to perfume or harm an enemy; or alternatively, "he causes to be perfumed" means he causes to be despised or causes to be held in contempt.
"He causes to be overwhelmed" means that one person causes another person to overwhelm or submerge an enemy.
"Anubhāvāpeti" means that one person causes another person to experience or enjoy prosperity.
In the application of the agent, when it is connected with "payutto" (employed), it signifies that while remaining subordinate to the principal factor, it accomplishes the action for this [agent].
This word is an illuminator within the Teaching.
The expression "instrumental case" (karaṇavacana) is seen in most instances;
this was stated with reference to the place where the causative meaning occurs in a verb.
In a noun, there is no place for the causative meaning, as in the case of [the word] "bodhetā" (awakener), and so forth.
A wise person skilled in application, having brought forward such phrases as “they cause them to be eaten even by dogs,” should explain them. Herein,
this instrumental case-ending indicates the sense of the object (kamma), and the locative and genitive cases should also be employed as indicators of that same sense.
How so? "He causes [someone] to be despised" means that one person causes another person who is an enemy to be despised;
likewise, "he is caused to be despised" means that one person causes another person's enemy to be despised. The remaining [forms] should be demonstrated according to this method.

Thus, all these instances of the instrumental, dative, and genitive cases are merely indicators of the objective sense (*kamma-attha*); therefore, the meaning should be understood by way of double object (*dvikamma*).
This is the exposition of the causal agentive verbal forms.
The exposition of the objective verbal forms:
it is brought into being, it is dissolved away, it is despised, it is overcome, it is experienced, it is treated with contempt, it is surpassed.
It is experienced; in this way, there are passive verbal forms (*kammuno kriyāpadāni*) of the verb *bhū*. Furthermore, they are:
*bhaviyyate*, *vibhaviyyate*, *paribhaviyyate*, *abhibhaviyyate*, *anubhaviyyate*, *paribhuyyate*, *abhibhuyyate*, and *anubhuyyate*.
Here, the passive verbal forms of the object (*kammuno kriyāpadāni*) themselves must be construed as the verbal forms of the agent (*kammakattuno kriyāpadāni*). For they are distinct.
Verbal forms do not occur with the agent as the subject.

In that context, "bhaviyata" means that whatever is to be developed (bhāvetabba) by a person—whether it be cultivated, practiced, or frequently performed—or alternatively, "bhaviyata" means that which is increased.
"Vibhaviyata" means that which is to be dispelled (vibhāvetabba)—whatever is dispelled by a person.
"Specifically cultivated" (*visesena bhaviyate*) means it is developed or increased in various ways; or alternatively, "made non-existent" (*abhaviyate*) means it is caused to disappear.
"Despised" (*paribhaviyateti*) means one is treated with contempt or harmed by an enemy person;
or alternatively, "despised" means one is reviled or held in low esteem. "Overpowered" (*abhibhaviyateti*) means one is overcome by an enemy person.
*Ajjhotthariyate* means it is overwhelmed; *abhimaddiyate* means it is crushed. *Anubhaviyate* means prosperity is experienced and enjoyed by the person.
The three terms beginning with *paribhūyate* are explained in the same manner as the three beginning with *paribhaviyate*.
As for the remaining terms, however, whichever word is presented primarily as the action itself is indicated as expressing the objective case (*kamma*).
Therefore, even when the agent is indicated in the singular number, if the object is to be expressed in the plural, the verb for the object is seen ending only in the plural;
but if it is to be expressed in the singular, it ends only in the singular.
Likewise, even when the agent is indicated in the plural, if the object is to be expressed in the singular, it ends only in the singular.
The verb form for the object (*kamma*) is seen [in the passive]. However, if it is to be expressed in the plural, it must be in the plural ending itself.

How so? "The Dhamma is being cultivated by the monk," "The Dhammas are being cultivated by the monk," "The Dhamma is being cultivated by the monks," and "The Dhammas are being cultivated by the monks.
By this method, [the same applies] in all instances regarding the verb forms for the object.

The conventional usage should be applied. However, when there is a verbal form of an action (*kriyāpada*) that indicates the object (*kammattha*), yet there is an imaginative attribution of the status of agent (*kattubhāva*) to that very thing which is the object, that [verbal form] indicates both the object and the agent; it cannot be found separately from the verbal form of the action.
This, then, is the formulation of the application for making the meaning understood here: "One reviles oneself; [this is] ill-spoken."
When it is said that "the fool suffers because of that," even though he is despised by others, he is himself overcome;
for the evildoer is himself overcome in hell by the guardians of hell because he himself committed such karma.
For in this context, just as in expressions such as "he drinks the water himself" or "he makes the mat himself," the sense of being the agent of the action is indeed obtained.
Then there is the state of being the agent of the action.
This is the exposition of the verbal forms of the action of karma. [Now follows] the exposition of the verbal forms of the action of becoming.
"Bhūyate," "bhaviyate," and "ubbhaviyate"—thus are the verbal forms of the abstract noun (bhāva). And otherwise [in the future tense], they are "bhuyyate," "bhaviyyate," and "ubbhaviyyate.

In that regard, just as they accept the explanation of the meaning of the word *ṭhīyate* as "standing" (*ṭhāna*) by way of the abstract noun (*bhāva*), so too for "bhūyate" and the others, the explanation of the meaning as "being" (*bhavana*) and so forth must be accepted by way of the abstract noun. Just as...

They maintain that when there is a connection with nouns ending in the *ki* and *ta* suffixes which denote abstract states (*bhāva*), such as *ṭhānaṃ*, *ṭhiti*, and *bhavanaṃ*, a genitive construction is required;
however, it is not so when there is a connection with verbal forms (*ākhyāta*) denoting abstract states, such as *ṭhīyate* or *bhūyate*.
This is because verbal forms cannot be connected with words already expressing a relationship through the genitive case.

In whatever grammatical operation (*payoga*), when a word expressing the agent (*kattuvācakapada*) is indicated by either the nominative case (*paccattavacana*) or the instrumental case (*karaṇavacana*), while the verb (*kriyāpada*)—which shares the same status as the verbal action of the *kamma* (object)—is indicated without the *kamma*, that [agent-word] there indicates the sense of becoming (*bhāvatthadīpaka*).
For a state of being (*bhāva*) does not proceed in every respect without depending upon an agent. Thus...
Even though "being" (bhāva) exists, it is merely the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*), such as arising, cutting, cooking, and so forth.
However, etymologists employ the instrumental case even in contexts concerning "being," such as in the phrases "it stands" (*ṭhīyate*) or "it exists" (*bhūyate*), as in:
"Surely one who has gone forth must be well-robed, well-covered, and endowed with proper deportment. Therefore...

According to their opinion, it should be construed with an instrumental expression as “it is manifested by that. However, according to the Victor’s (the Buddha’s) opinion, it is done by means of the nominative case itself, as in “that is manifested,” and so forth.
For in the *Saccasaṅkhepa* treatise, the teacher Dhammapāla used the nominative;
in the *Niddesa* scripture, the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) did so; and in the *Dhajagga Sutta*, the Blessed One likewise uttered the abstract noun in accordance with the nominative case.

In the *Saccasaṅkhepa*, it was indeed stated using the first-person singular form that the connection of the word "bhūyate" (it exists) illustrates the sense of becoming (*bhāva*). In the *Niddesa* commentary, it says:
"Rūpaṃ, vibhoti, vibhaviyyati. (Form, it disintegrates, it is disintegrated.)
Thus, from the perspective of its demonstration, the personal pronoun is firm.
Likewise, it is so because of the scriptural evidence found in the *Dhajagga Sutta*, spoken by the Sage himself:
"That will be abandoned. And also because of the presentation of the Pāli text itself.
Through the power of the perfections (pāramitā), just as from the bodies of great queens, there arise the accomplishments of peace;
they are not produced by the words of Sakka and others.
Through the direct vision [of the truth] itself, the application of the three types of persons occurs.
Whether it be in the singular number or even in the plural number, it is our view that [the form] should be constructed in the *parassapada* (active voice) and so forth.
Therefore, [the forms] will be analyzed as: *vibhavissati*, *vibhavissanti*; *vibhavissasi*, *vibhavissatha*.

"I shall cease to exist," "we shall cease to exist," "form will cease to exist," "forms will cease to exist"—such expressions are to be applied in accordance with the words of the Conqueror (the Buddha).
Herein, this is the analysis of the terms: "It will cease to exist" (vibhaviyyati) is identical in form to an object-case (accusative) verb.
There is neither an object-case ending nor an agent-case ending and so forth.
If this were an object-case ending, it would indicate the object;
however, as an instrumental case ending, it indicates the agent.
If this were an agent-noun (kattupada), like the word "is drunk" (pīyate), it would be transitive;
however, he explains that it is not so. If this were an agent-noun, like the word "becomes" (vibhavati), [it would be intransitive].
If it were to stand without the *ya*-suffix, it would not stand in that way.

The *ya*-suffix is taught for the roots beginning with *bhū* in the sense of the agent; however, for the roots beginning with *div*, it is declared [to be used] in the sense of the agent within that very same class (*gaṇa*).
The root *bhū* is not seen among the groups of roots beginning with *div*;
it is seen only in the groups beginning with *bhū* and *cur*.
Therefore, in forms such as *vibhaviyyati*, the suffix *ya* [is applied].
"It should be cultivated"—thus it should be understood by the wise one who knows the proper occasion.
For here, having made it clear, I shall now demonstrate the characteristic of the agent of cultivation; listen to me attentively.
In the phrase "Tisso goes," the agent is the word for the agent;
in the phrase "The Dhamma is taught," the object is the word for the object.
It makes them manifest through their own form; therefore, both are clearly evident.
However, a word expressing a state (bhāva), such as "it will be analyzed" (*vibhaviyyati*),
does not illustrate the agent called "process" (*bhāvanā*) by its own form;
rather, it reveals the agent as a substance (*dabbabhūta*) by its own form.
But when indicating the agent, that abstract state (bhāva), though dependent upon the agent,
is also indicated by the suffix -tva when manifested by a grammatical suffix (paccaya).
And because an abstract state does not exist apart from the nature of the agent.
Since the agent exists in the state of being [the action] by virtue of its nature as an agent,
if that is so, how could there be a designation of "agent" for the action—
as in such expressions as, "There was an assembly of disciples"?
Thus, if the existence [of a thing] depends upon its substrata,
then even when the thing resides in the locus of the agent, the designation of "agent" (kattupaññatti) is established.
Just as in the case of the grammatical factors (kāraka), such as the agent and the object, which depend upon the action (kriyā).
The wise posit that the term *kriyādhāra* (the substratum of action) is that which holds the vessel of the action (*āsana-thālī*).
Likewise, they posit that even when it illuminates the agent who is the support of the action,
the abstract noun (*bhāvapada*) is the designator of the action itself.
Some say that because the state [of being] undomesticated is a single entity,
it belongs to the person who speaks the singular word "bhāveti" alone.
But having reached the canonical text (pāḷi), their statement is not authoritative.
“Those defiled states will be abandoned”—this reading is seen in the ancient word (pāvacana); therefore, let us speak thus:
by means of personal realization alone, the application to the three types of persons [is established].
It is not our preference that [the term] *icchitabba* be joined with two verbal endings;
for a verb in the abstract sense (*bhāve*) is extremely difficult to discern in the Pāḷi.
Therefore, I have stated thus far the means for identifying it.
This is the exposition of the verbal forms of the abstract state (*bhāva*).

Thus, the verbal forms derived from the root *bhū* are fourfold— namely, those of the simple agent (*suddhakattṛ*), those of the causal agent (*hetukattṛ*), those of the object (*kamma*), and those of the abstract state—
or fivefold when including the verbal forms of the object-agent (*kammakattṛ*).

These have been demonstrated in various ways; they are stated separately for the purpose of showing that there is a difference in conventional usage based on the different types of entities among worldly people.
However, in terms of meaning, they are only threefold, according to the three factors of the agent (*kāraka*): the object (*karman*), the agent (*kartṛ*), and the state (*bhāva*).
For the causal agent (*hetu-kartṛ*) is included within the factor termed the "pure agent" (*suddha-kartṛ*), because it is a subordinate part of it; likewise is the object-agent (*karma-kartṛ*).

The agent (*kammakāraka*) [is distinct], but the state (*bhāva*) is entirely alone. For although it is manifold—by way of going, cooking, cutting, and so forth—it is devoid of internal differentiation because its intrinsic nature is that of action (*kriyā*).
Even so, because it depends upon substances (*dabba*), it is divided according to the division of those substances.
Therefore, in the sacred word (*pāvacana*), a word expressing a state is seen even in the plural. The designation "state-agent" (*bhāvakāraka*) applies to verbal roots (*ākhyātika-pada*).

Although one arrives [at this conclusion] by relying on the method of etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*), from the standpoint of actual meaning (*atthato*), the status of being an agent (*kārakatā*) does not apply to the abstract state (*bhāva*).
For it produces nothing, nor is it the cause of an action. Indeed, the definition of an agent (*kāraka*) is precisely the state of being the cause of an action.

Thus, neither in a primary sense nor by way of causality is the status of being an agent found in the abstract state. Nevertheless, because it is merely an instrument (*karaṇamatta*), it is called an agent.
For indeed, *karaṇa* (instrument) is the act (*kāra*), the action; that very thing is the agent (*kāraka*). Thus, the agency of a state (*bhāva*) is to be understood.

Since, however, the characteristic of an agent (*kāraka-lakṣaṇa*) is precisely the state of being the cause of an action, therefore, regarding the characteristic of agents within nominal words, one should set aside the conventional term "agentive state" (*bhāva-kāraka*) and instead employ [the designations] such as "agentive agent" (*kartṛ-kāraka*) and "objective agent" (*kamma-kāraka*) for the six bases, namely: agent, object, instrument, recipient, source, and locus.

Conventional usage is established by grammarians (*veyyākaraṇa*). Thus, based on the method of etymology (*niruttinaya*), what has been stated—namely, the agentive factor (*bhāvakāraka*) and the two factors of object and subject (*kammakattukāraka*)—constitutes a triad of factors (*kārakattaya*).
And the verbal form (*ākhyātikapada*) that illustrates this possesses three factors.
Indeed, it was with reference to this meaning that it was also said by the teachers:
By those who possess the great grammatical expositions and who perceive the methods of etymology:
"That which pertains to the three times, the three persons, expresses action, and possesses three factors of agency;
which has no gender and two numbers—that is called a verb (ākhyāta)."

In this regard, since some grammarians necessarily desire that the *attanopada* (middle voice) endings arise for both the agent (*bhāva*) and the object (*kamma*), we have both listed and explained the verbal forms of the agent and object with *attanopada* endings in order to clarify their views. Furthermore, all these verbal forms consist of three voices;
therefore, for one who desires a garland of verbal forms, they should be understood according to the *parassapada* (active voice) and *attanopada* (middle voice) endings.
These should be applied. For in the Pāḷi and other texts, verbal roots (tikārakas) exist in two ways, according to whether they are *parassapada* (active voice) or *attanopada* (middle voice).

For example: *Bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati.* (The Blessed One dwells at Sāvatthī. *Samādhijjhānakusalā, vandanti lokanāyakaṃ.* (Those skilled in concentration and jhāna, pay homage to the Leader of the World.

*Monaṃ vuccati ñāṇaṃ.* (Wisdom is called "mona. *Atthābhisamayā dhīro, paṇḍitoti pavuccati.* (Through the realization of the meaning, the steadfast one is called "wise. How [are these to be understood]?
For the person who has entered upon the practice, form disappears and is made to vanish; it will be abandoned by him.
Like [an object] placed upon a yellowish-white woolen cloth, it shines and glows. One who offers worship receives worship. Women desiring sons, when they pray, obtain such a son as that.
Such a one is called "the Unattached," equal to Brahmā. Even before the fire-born [Agni], he was already manifest. He may even be abandoned.
"Would not be abandoned"—thus they stand in two ways. Herein, this is the analysis of the textual tradition:
All [the terms] forming the triads are, for the most part, verbal nouns;
they are seen in the three Piṭakas in connection with the parassapada (active) endings.
Indeed, in the prose sections (*cuṇṇiya*), the words associated with the first person are very few,
whereas in the verses (*gāthā*) they are numerous. Furthermore,
in both the verses and the prose sections, [the usage] is otherwise.
"Having become many, they are seen"—thus it should be explained.

Furthermore, the exposition of the case endings (*pada*) such as *nti*, *anti*, and so forth, must be applied according to their respective grammatical forms. In this way, the verbal roots (*kriyāpada*) belonging to the third person singular (*tikāraka*) are to be understood by way of their phonetic form, their definition, and their exposition.
Now, we shall state the analysis of the root *bhavati* according to its status as being without prefixes (*nopasagga*) and without an object (*akammika*), etc.
Those without prefixes and without objects, those with prefixes and without objects,
and those with prefixes and with objects— thus has the state of being (bhūti) been analyzed.
But this statement [is made] in such contexts as "having become one who has become the Dhamma" and so forth.
This has been stated by me for the purpose of experiencing the meaning, having set aside [other considerations]. However, in this sense,
it should be specifically understood that when combined with prefixes, it becomes fourfold, provided it is not transitive.

The roots that are without prefixes and without objects, as well as those with prefixes that are without objects, become single-objected when the *kārita* (causative) suffix is applied to the *bhū* root. For example:
“He develops wholesome states” (*bhāveti kusaladhammam*) and “He makes them disappear” (*vibhāveti*). Thus it is said here.
These [verbs] should be demonstrated by the wise who understand the teaching within the Dispensation.
When there is a causative suffix (*kārita-paccaya*),
how is it to be known by the wise that they possess two objects— namely, when they have both a prefix (*upasagga*) and their own [inherent] object (*sakamma*)?
"Men overcome other men, those of the animal species;
a man overcomes another man through prosperity.
This is called transitive, and this is intransitive.
"How are we to know? Speak to us in detail.
"What need is there to speak at length? I am able to say only a portion;
I shall explain it with care—listen to me as I speak."
A verbal noun (ākhyātika-pada) is declared to be of two kinds:
that which has an object and that which is without an object; thus should the wise discern.
In that regard, when an action is performed by an agent through the employment of a word—
That which is accomplished without an action is not "transitive" (sakammaka).
For when it is said, "he cooks," it is understood that some kind of object—
whether boiled rice or something else— is being prepared by some person or other.
Furthermore, when an action in its application is devoid of an object (kamma), this is understood as the meaning of the word; one should determine that it is "intransitive" (akammaka).
When it is said by some person, "Devadatta stands," [the verb is intransitive].
A locus (*ṭhāna*) is indeed within the scope of the intellect, but nothing that has become an object of action (*kamma*) is so.
In this context, a transitive verb reveals both the agent and the object as appropriate; thus should the wise discern it.
“A person cooks rice; the rice is cooked by itself.

From such examples this principle is to be known: even when not explicitly stated, there is the category of intransitive verbs (*akammakapada*), which [express] either the agent (*kattā*) or the action itself (*bhāva*).
He explains according to what is appropriate; thus should the wise one discern it.
Here, the word "stands" indicates the agent who is called "cultivation";
and here, the word "is established"—this same method applies even where it is not explicitly stated.
Having thus understood the distinction between transitive and intransitive verbs, the wise person should apply this knowledge;
they should also recognize the triad of transitive verbs when there is both an agent and a causal agent, as in:
"A man causes gold to be made into a bracelet" and "He causes a man [to do something]."
And also: “A man drives a chariot to a village for another man.
Here, this method is not applicable to the verbal root *bhū*;
therefore, it is explained here that this word takes only two objects.
This method is indeed traditional, yet it is not seen in the Pāḷi;
it has been explained by me in this way solely according to the opinion of certain [teachers].
And here: "Then the king, with various forms of torture..."
Regarding the reading "kārāpetī," one should explain it thoroughly in the Niddesa.
Having supplied the word "manussehi" (by men) as a textual ellipsis,
the wise [commentator] sees that the reading must be completed with the words, "they have them eaten even by dogs."
Having understood this method, one should apply it according to the sequence of the recitation:
"A man has a gold bracelet made by a goldsmith.
Here, the suffixes of the vikaraṇa type are stated in their own form.
And in order to illustrate the usage of those [suffixes] within their respective groups (sagaṇa), it is for the sake of making them known to others—
so that they may understand, "In this group, this root occurs"—
that they are explained by means of other suffixes. It is not [for the sake of] mere notification.
For indeed, whatever grammatical relation (paccaya) is prescribed for the active and passive voices functions throughout the eightfold group of roots.
This is for the sake of preventing confusion among listeners regarding the forms derived from the root *bhū*.
Thus, various methods have been explained by me here.

Those who are unskilled in the world regarding the diverse formations of verbal roots and verbs—even the wise—remain possessed of doubt once they encounter the terminology of verbs; therefore, [this has been clarified].
The wise person, who delights solely in the welfare of both self and others and possesses firm affection for the Teaching,
should apply himself with even more acute intelligence to their practice,

aspiring toward proficiency in the modes of expression found within the Three Baskets along with the Eightfold Commentary. Thus, regarding the movements of expression in the nine-limbed Tipiṭaka together with the commentaries...
The First Chapter, titled "The Analysis of Verbs with Suffixes," in the work *Saddanīti*, composed for the benefit of the wise.
2. Analysis of the Series of Verbal Forms of the Root *bhū* (Bhavati-kriyā-padamālā-vibhāga) Henceforth,

I shall explain that which is called the "Sequence of Verbal Forms" (*kriyāpadakkama*), which illuminates the case endings and other grammatical features, and which increases the intelligence of those who hear it.

In that regard, for verbal roots (*ākhyātika*), the case endings beginning with *ti* indicate the characteristic of action; they are eightfold, according to the tenses of the present, fifth (imperative), seventh (optative), past (*parokkhā*), conditional (*hiyyattanī*), future (*ajjatanī*), future-in-the-making (*bhavissantī*), and the past conditional (*kālatipatti*).
Among these: *ti*, *anti*, *si*, *tha*, *mi*, *ma*, *te*, *ante*, *se*, *vhe*, *e*, and *mhe* are called the present case endings.
*Tu*, *antu*, *hi*, *tha*, *mi*, *ma*, *taṃ*, *antaṃ*, *su*, *vho*, *e*, and *āmase* are called the fifth case endings.
*Eyya*, *eyyuṃ*, *eyyāsi*, *eyyātha*, *eyyāmi*, *eyyāma*, *etha*, *eraṃ*, *etho*, *eyyāvho*, *eyyaṃ*, *eyyāmhe*—these are called the seventh case endings (*sattamī-vibhattiyo*).
*A*, *u*, *e*, *ttha*, *aṃ*, *mha*, *ttha*, *re*, *ttho*, *vho*, *iṃ*, *mhe*—these are called the past tense endings (*parokkhā-vibhattiyo*).
*Ā*, *ū*, *o*, *ttha*, *aṃ*, *mhā*, *ttha*, *tthuṃ*, *se*, *vhaṃ*, *iṃ*, *mhase*—these are called the past day endings (*hiyyattanī-vibhattiyo*).
*Ī uṃ*, *o ttha*, *iṃ mhā*, *ā ū*, *se vhaṃ*, *aṃ mhe*—these are called the present tense endings (*ajjatanīvibhattiyo*).
*Ssati ssanti*, *ssasi ssatha*, *ssāmi ssāma*, *ssate ssante*, *ssase ssavhe*, *ssaṃ ssāmhe*—these are called the future tense endings (*bhavissantīvibhattiyo*).
*Ssā ssaṃsu*, *sse ssatha*, *ssaṃ ssāmhā*, *ssatha ssisu*, *ssase ssavhe*, *ssiṃ ssāmhase*—these are called the past conditional tense endings (*kālātipattivibhattiyo*).
Of all these verbal endings (*vibhatti*), whichever are the first six sets of endings are called *parassapada* (active endings).
However, whichever are the latter six sets of endings are called *attanopada* (middle endings).

Among them, the *parassapada* consist of the present tense (*vattamānā*) six, the fifth tense (*pañcami*) six, the seventh tense (*sattami*) six, the past tense (*parokkhā*) six, the remote past (*hiyyattani*) six, and the recent past (*ajjatani*) six.
There are six future [forms], six [forms] for what will come to be, and six instances of the lapse of time; thus they are of forty-eight kinds. Likewise for the others.
All of these combined amount to ninety-six kinds.

As for the *parassapada* (active voice) and *attanopada* (middle voice), there are two forms each for the first, middle, and third persons. These four each in the present tense and so forth, according to the eight case-inflections, total thirty-two; such is their combined measure.
In each pair of locations, the first is the singular and the second is the plural.
Among those, for the present tense endings, *anti*, *si*, *tha*, *mi*, and *ma* are the *parassapada* (active voice) endings;

*te*, *ante*, *se*, *vhe*, *e*, and *mhe* are the *attanopada* (middle voice) endings. Thus, among the *parassapada* and *attanopada* endings, *anti* and so forth constitute the third person (*paṭhamapurisa*).
*sitha* is the second person (*majjhimapurisa*); *mi* and *ma* are the first person (*uttamapurisa*); *te* and *ante* are the third person (*paṭhamapurisa*);
*se* and *vhe* are the second person; *e* and *mhe* are the first person.
Within the first, second, and first persons as well, *ti* is the singular (*ekavacana*) and *anti* is the plural (*bahuvacana*); thus are the singular and plural forms.

The knowable [forms] are to be understood according to their order. In this way, the remaining case-endings (*vibhatti*)—namely, the third person, second person, and first person; the active voice (*parassapada*), the middle voice (*attanopada*); and the singular, dual, and plural numbers—are to be understood.

In that context, in what sense is it called a "case-ending" (*vibhatti*)? It is called a case-ending because it divides (*vibhajati*) the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) according to time and other factors.

Furthermore, by means of the nominal case-endings beginning with *si*, it encompasses all meanings in their entirety through the distinctions of self-referential (*sakattha*), other-referential (*parattha*), and so forth.
It is called *vibhatti* because it divides; or, it is called *vibhatti* because it divides the factors of action (*kāraka*) and so forth according to the singular and plural numbers;
or, it is called *vibhatti* because it is that which is to be divided by knowledge; or, it is called *vibhatti* because they divide the meaning by means of it;
or else, even though there is a presentation of grammatical forms without case-endings in the teaching of the Conqueror, since the meaning cannot be indicated in its entirety without case-endings.
The wise also analyze [the term] as "they resort to" or "they serve him" in various or specific ways.

Regarding that, we shall state the characteristics of the uninflected description (avibhattikaniddesa), together with examples of usage and so forth. The uninflected description is found in nominal stems (nāmika).
This should be understood as the illustration here for those [teachings] not explicitly stated:
"Like a great banyan tree, the Elder is supreme among speakers;
his teaching is the Buddha’s dispensation alone, neither deficient nor redundant."

In that context, "thera" is a designation without a case ending (*avibhattika*). [The compound] *theravāda* means "the doctrine of the elders" (*therānam ayam*); one should understand its meaning to be that this doctrine is the most excellent among all other doctrines.
One who knows the method should also recognize the use of the nominative case without a case ending in such passages as "kāyo te sabba sovaṇṇo" (your body is entirely golden).
"Is it not seen that the description of the absence of case endings (*avibhattikaniddesa*) also occurs in verbal forms?
For instance, in the phrase 'O sir, eat, drink,' whoever might be the one who speaks [is so addressed].
If, according to his view, there were to be an absence of case endings in such a case,"
“‘Bhikkhu, O man,’ and so forth—this word is not [to be understood] in that way.
‘Bhikkhu, O man,’ and so forth, is spoken by means of elision (*lopa*);
for likewise, words such as ‘khādā’ are spoken by means of elision.”
Thus, this designation without case endings (*avibhattikaniddesa*) is not found among verbs; it is found only among nouns (*nāma*).

Even there, in the phrase "And the eight persons who saw the Dhamma," the shortening of *puggala* to *puggala* should be understood as occurring by way of metrical license (*chandavasena*), and not as a designation without case endings like *kakusandha* in the phrase "Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa."

The explanation of the uninflected form (*avibhattikaniddesa*) is to be understood. In the passage, “When a woman is sitting near a monk who is sitting, or lying down near him,” the word *bhikkhu*—because it has the sense of what ought to be said as “towards a monk” (*bhikkhumhi*)—can appropriately be called both a nominative in the locative case and an uninflected explanation of a case ending that was not seen [in the original].
In that instance, however, it is formed according to the speaker’s intention (*chandavasena*).
It is not appropriate to say that those *pada*s also belong to the category of being taught without case endings (*avibhattikaniddesa*).

In this context, "third-person forms" (*parassapadāni*) means those *pada*s whose referent is another (*parassa atthabhūtāni*). Here, even though the highest persons (*uttamapurisa*) have their own referents (*attano atthesu*), the designation "first-person forms" (*attanopada*) is not applied.
For although they are one's own referents, these persons are called "highest."
Nevertheless, because the others are more prevalent, the designation of those [others] has been applied to these by the ancients.

"Attanopadāni" means words that have one's own self as their referent (attha); thus, they are "attanopadāni. Furthermore, in this context, even though the first and middle persons have a third-person sense, the technical term "third person" (parassapada) is not employed for them.
These first two are for one's own benefit and for the benefit of others respectively;
yet they are also [considered] true because the conventional designation for the other two is established through their association with them.
Furthermore, this [designation] and these [others] possess the status of being prior designations.
Likewise, for the purpose of removing the fault of confusion,
this designation "itself" (attanō) has certainly been superimposed upon these [terms].
Here, there are many designations such as the term "another's word" (parassa-pada) and so forth.
Because it was established by the ancients, the designation "ancient" (porāṇikā) is recognized.

Therefore, we do not seek the etymological meaning of the three persons, such as the first person and so forth, here. For, according to conventional usage (rūḷhi), the designation of "person" was assigned to the [suffixes] *ty* and so on by the ancients.
Regarding the singular and plural numbers: the expression of a single meaning is the singular; the expression of many meanings is the plural.

The plural number. Alternatively, even when there is plurality, the expression of a single meaning—whether that meaning has been unified by the mind through a collective (*samudāya*) or a generic (*jāti*) perspective—is called the singular;

likewise, the expression of what is one as if it were the support (*nissaya*), because it is spoken by way of its support for a plurality, is also called the singular. This is because many meanings possess the characteristic of unity.
The singular number (*ekavacana*) is so called because it expresses a single thing, just like the word "one.

Even when there is no plurality, the plural number (*bahuvacana*) is so called because it expresses a single meaning—as if there were many—by way of self-respect, delimitation, matrix, connection, method, question, similarity, the conjunction of various states of consciousness, and various objects.
Likewise, even when there is only one meaning—such as "dwelling therein" or "son"—the plural number is used by way of conventional usage (*rūḷhi*), as if there were many.
The plural number (*bahuvacana*) is so called because, although there is only a single meaning, it is spoken of as if there were many by way of expressing that one meaning through another sense;
or, although there is only a single meaning, it is spoken of as if there were many by way of its dependence [on multiple factors];
or, although there is only a single meaning, it is spoken of as if there were many by way of the diversity of its objects and the diversity of its functions. Thus, by these modes...
It should be understood that when something is to be expressed in the singular, the singular number is used as if it were being expressed in the singular;

and when something is to be expressed in the plural, the plural number is used as if it were being expressed in the plural. "The plural" (*puthuvacana*) and "the manifold" (*anekavacana*) are synonyms for this very term.
This is the meaning of "number" (*vacana*) with respect to nouns, verbs, and case-endings.
It is to be understood according to its function by one who seeks the meaning of the Teaching.
Therefore, for the purpose of making that meaning known, we shall here explain the usage of verbs together with the usage of nouns—
such as "the king comes," "my friend comes," and "one mind"— which are singular-number usages for a single referent.
“Kings are coming,” “my companions are coming,” “neither of my two sons is to be given away,” “two or three”—
such are the uses of the plural for many objects.
“That army was great,” “you are well-disposed toward many people,” “let all that folk exert themselves,” “of the group of women.”
"Pavara, I gave a pair of robes to the Buddha; I shall teach you two things, O monks:

great love for the Triple Gem and the necessity for a person to cultivate confidence—[namely] the Saṅgha of monks, the army, the host of gods, and the assembly of the Noble Ones"—such examples as these, along with "the dyad" and "the triad," are instances of the singular number being used for plural referents by way of collective reference (*samudāyavasena*).
In some such instances, however, plural constructions are also seen.

For example, such usages as “honored by the circles of kinsmen,” “the hosts of deities assembled,” “all these classes of deities,” “two assemblies of deities,” “three pairs,” and “four novelties” are found.
These [expressions] refer to a collective that should be expressed in the singular, but are used in terms of a plurality of constituents.

The application of the plural number should be understood as follows: when things are being grouped together, they enter into the category of the plural for the sake of multiplicity either collectively or individually;
therefore, it should be known that the name "plural" refers to a case where there is regard for a plurality of entities.

Expressions such as “One should not kill a living being” (pāṇaṃ na hane) and “The crop prospers” (sasso sampajjati) are applications of the singular number for things that are multiple by way of genus (jāti); it is also appropriate to say that these are applications of the singular number for things that are multiple by virtue of their commonality of state (tabbhāvasāmaññena).

“*Nāgaṃ raṭṭhassa pūjitaṃ, Sāvatthī saddhā ahosi pasannā*” (The Naga honored by the kingdom; Sāvatthī was faithful and confident)—such expressions are singular grammatical usages applied by way of metonymy (*nissaya-vohāra*) to things that actually function through their basis.
“The three characteristics (*tilakkhaṇa*); the wholesome and unwholesome; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases;
the Dhamma and Vinaya; the Gandhabba who is the army of the mind; when there is no inclination (*nati*), there is no coming and going; in the absence of coming and going...”

Expressions such as “when there is no [existence], there is no passing away and rebirth” are instances of using the singular number for many referents (*bavhatthāna*) when the characteristic is unity (*ekattalakkhaṇa*).
Expressions such as “Thus we grasp it; our nature, our exertion—how could we say this, Meghiya? are instances of using the plural number for a single referent by way of the self (*attavasena*).

Expressions such as “Those people said this to that bhikkhu: ‘Eat, venerable sir’; among humans, being human, I gave a seat to those who had arrived” are instances of using the plural number for a single referent by way of showing respect (*garukāravasena*).

Expressions such as “states that are without conditions” (*appaccayā dhammā*) and “unconditioned states” (*asaṅkhatā dhammā*) are uses of the plural number either because they do not delimit a single referent, or because they employ the plural by way of an unrestricted number.
Some, however, say that these plural usages occur due to the clarity of the tradition of the teaching; but that should not be accepted.
For the Tathāgata does not teach the Dhamma while lacking mindfulness and clear comprehension, nor is any logical justification seen for it in the *Mātikā*.

"In the question, in the answer, and thus in all three places, while teaching phenomena such as 'without conditions' (appaccaya), the Teacher repeatedly teaches the Dhamma by means of the plural number, having entered the stream of instruction.
Expressions in the plural number, such as "Which phenomena are without conditions? and so forth, follow the method of connecting the matrix (mātikā) for the sake of a single meaning.
“‘These phenomena are without conditions’—such expressions employ the plural number according to the method of a question’s sequence regarding a single referent.

‘Which phenomena are not perversions? With the exception of those phenomena, all remaining wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena’—such expressions employ the plural number by way of similarity to the nature of the question regarding a single referent.
‘There are, monks, other phenomena that are profound, difficult to see, difficult to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of logic...’”
“Subtle and to be realized by the wise, which the Tathāgata, having personally realized through direct knowledge, proclaims”—
this use of the plural number is on account of the conjunction of many minds and many objects for a single meaning.
“At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Mahāvana.”
"There are sons of the Videhas, Dīghāvu the increaser of the realm;
they shall exercise sovereignty in Mithilā, O lady"— such words as these,
though many, are used in the plural by way of conventional usage (*rūḷhi*) for a single referent designated as "sons" because of their residing therein.
“He addressed Sāriputta and Moggallāna: ‘Go, Sāriputtas, having gone to Kīṭāgiri, perform an act of banishment against the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka from Kīṭāgiri; these are your co-residents.
And such expressions as “Is it well with you, sons of good family? Come, tigers! Turn back! are examples of using one meaning [to convey] another meaning.
The use of the plural number by way of a single designation refers to cases such as,
"The beds cry out," where the plural is employed based on the support for a single referent.
The expression "the four foundations of mindfulness" is the use of the plural for a single referent by way of the diversity of its objects.
“Four right endeavors” (*cattāro sammappadhānā*) is an application of the plural number for a single referent according to the distinction of function.

In this regard, the singular number is fivefold: the singular referring to a single entity, the singular referring to a collection, the singular referring to a genus, the singular referring to that which supports it, and the singular referring to a single characteristic.
Here, however, it is the singular referring to a genus.
In terms of meaning, it should be understood that these are singular forms referring to commonality.

There is the plural used for a plurality of meanings, the plural used for a plurality of collections, the plural used for oneself, the plural used as a mark of respect, the plural used to indicate indefiniteness,
the plural used according to the method of connecting the headings (mātikā), and the plural used according to the method of connecting the questions.
The plural number is fifteenfold: the plural used for questions of similar nature; the plural used for various mental associations and various objects;
the plural used for their inhabitants; the plural used for their sons; the plural used for a single designation; the plural used for those dependent on or related to them;
the plural used for a diversity of objects; and the plural used for a diversity of functions. Thus, all [these] together are twentyfold.
The singular and plural numbers are thus subsumed. Herein, this is the determination of the textual tradition (pāḷi):
The singular number occurs when there is a single referent, or when it is used for the sake of brevity, or even for the sake of emphasis;
and there is also the singular number characterized by a collective unity or a generic unity.
In the Piṭaka together with its commentaries, these forms are generally seen in the texts.
However, while the plural number occurs only a few times in the heavy (canonical) texts,
it is rare in the Pāḷi itself but frequent in the Aṭṭhakathās and Ṭīkās.
For indeed, in the Canon, the plural is used in the singular form;
when there is a plurality of venerable ones, this is the illustration here:
“Homage to you, O noble steed among men! Homage to you, O supreme among men!”
"Relying upon your teaching, I have attained the deathless state.
A wise person who examines the syllables should understand that such readings as these are found in many ways within the Jina’s dispensation.
Since even for the Great Seers, who deserve exceptional reverence,
a description is seen occurring through the use of the singular number,
therefore one skilled in conventional usage should employ it according to the requirements of the sense.
Whether it be a singular construction or otherwise,
for the most part, the wise [term] remains in the plural within that residence;
its sons are few, and even the singular [form] is used in dependence upon them.
In the *Mātikā-sandhi-ādi* [sections] concerning the non-delimitation of various states of mind (*puthucittāpariccheda*), one should explain both the plural and the singular.
This is due to the single designation, the function, and likewise the objective domain.
Having understood these two types of grammatical number— the plural and that which depends on what is supported by it— as being few, and having thus recognized their proper application,
the learned one should employ conventional usage according to the canonical text.

Now we shall explain the occurrence of the verb (*ākhyāta*) by way of time and other factors: the verbal form is characterized by action and indicates time, grammatical relation (*kāraka*), and person (*purisa*).
Therein, "time" refers to three times—past, future, and present—or six times when including the past, future, present, indefinite, and conditional times;
each of these is further divided into three persons.
In the times previously described—that is, from which [time] it proceeds—it is verbal (ākhyātika);
therefore, its function is considered to be the illumination of time.

"Kāraka" refers to the object (*karman*), the agent (*kartṛ*), and the state (*bhāva*). For these perform and cause performing, both by way of metaphorical usage and primary nature; thus they are called "kārakas. They should be understood, respectively, as the cause of action, the accomplisher of that [action], and the very nature of that [action].
Action, the agent, and the state—thus are the factors of action threefold.
Herein, the case-endings and suffixes are stated according to their true nature, and not otherwise.
Words such as "paribhaviyyati" (is despised) and so forth are established as the object among the factors of action.
“Sambhavati” and so forth are formed with the *sijjhar* (present tense) suffixes in the agentive (*kattukāraka*) case.
“Vibhaviyyati” and so forth are formed with the *sijjhar* suffixes in the impersonal (*bhāva*) case.
Thus, among these three types [of cases], the case-suffixes (*vibhatti-paccaya*) are considered [to apply].
There is no verbal form whatsoever that is entirely devoid of the threefold agency;
therefore, even when it is used merely to illustrate that [agency], it is still called a verb.
Even if the agency of the action itself has not been explicitly mentioned;
In the definition of a kāraka, there is no accomplishment of action through that [kāraka], nor through its state or condition;
thus, it does not exist even according to logical reasoning. Likewise, in the case of verbal forms (ākhyātika), its designation as such exists only by way of conventional linguistic usage (nirutti).
"Or the method of establishment (*patiṭṭhitanaya*)," we have explained, having reflected upon it.
"Person" (*purisa*) refers to the singular and plural numbers, as well as the first, middle, and third persons.

Therein, the first person consists of those forms of the nominative case that share the same grammatical core (*sādhāraṇa-adhikaraṇa*) with the verb, which express either the agent or the object, excluding the words *tumha* and *amha*.

The suffix occurs after all verbal roots (dhātu), whether it is employed—as in such instances as "the resolve succeeds in the name" (*nāmamhi abhinīhāro samijjhati*) and "awakening (*bodhi*) is said to be knowledge in the four paths"—or even when not employed, provided there is a corresponding referent—as in such instances as "he speaks or acts;
he is known by the wise as 'Pīḷiyakkha'; thus it is called speech" (*bhāsati vā karoti vā, pīḷiyakkhoti maṃ vidū, vuccatīti vacanaṃ*).
However, in certain passages of the Canon, because the word "name" (*nāma*) is not employed [in the context], [the suffix does not occur].
The meaning of the construction in the first person is difficult to understand, as in: "I shall cause you to feel pain; let both my feet comfort me therein.
For here, the word "feet" (*pādā*) is to be supplied as a textual ellipsis; it means:
"Let both feet of the King comfort me, who am wearying from the inability to speak while announcing this painful instruction; speak freely."
And there is the intention: "Speak to me. This intention is very difficult to understand because it exists within the Pāḷi;
therefore, O knower of the weighty, grasp the weighty [meaning] as it presents itself.
In this context, because the earth element (*bhūdhātu*) is the governing topic, there are these illustrative phrases by way of the earth element:
*so paribhavati*, *te paribhavanti*, *paribhavati*, *paribhavanti*; *sapatto abhibhaviyate*, *sabbā viya anubhūyate*, *abhibhaviyate*, *anubhūyateti*.
Wherein, although the noun (*nāman*) possesses the capacity to denote the agent, because it lacks the nominative case ending, it is [construed] with a verb (*ākhyātapada*).

Co-referentiality (*tulyādhikaraṇatā*) is not obtained; in that case, depending on a co-referential word that expresses the object (*kamma*) and is in the nominative case (*paccattavacana*), the three persons beginning with the first person are obtained. How so? For example:

*paribhaviyyate puriso devadattena* (the man is being despised by Devadatta), *paribhaviyyase tvaṃ devadattena* (you are being despised by Devadatta), *paribhaviyyamhe mayaṃ akusalehi dhammehi* (we are being despised by unwholesome states). Herein—

Furthermore, this statement—that "in cases such as *nindanti tuṇhimāsinaṃ*, although the noun functions as the object (*kamma*), because it is not in the nominative case (*apaccattavacanattā*), it cannot share the same grammatical core (*tulyādhikaraṇatā*) with the verb, and thus the first person (*paṭhamapurisa*) should not arise"—is not tenable. Why?
Because in phrases such as *nindanti tuṇhimāsinaṃ*, the word "people" (*janā*) must be supplied (*ajjhāharitabbassa*).
Because it is desired that the name denoting the agent (*sādhaka*) stand in grammatical coreferentiality (*tulyādhikaraṇabhāva*) with the verbal form.
This same method applies to the subsequent cases as well.
When there is coreferentiality with the verbal form, the second person (*majjhimapurisa*) occurs in the nominative case (*paccattavacana*), whether it denotes the agent or the object (*kamma*).
Even when the word *tumha* is employed, and even when it is not employed provided its referent (*taṭṭhāniya*) exists, [the suffix] follows after all verbal roots (*sabbadhātu*).
For example: *tvaṃ atibhavasi*, *tumhe atibhavatha*; *atibhavasi*, *atibhavatha*.
Where, although the word *tumha* expresses the agent (*sādhaka*), because it is not a nominative case (*apaccattavacanattā*), [it takes the suffix].
Co-referentiality with the verbal form is not obtained; therefore, the second person (*majjhimapurisa*) does not occur there.
Rather, the other two [persons] occur in dependence upon a co-referential word that is a direct object (*kamma*) expressed in the accusative case (*paccattavacana*). How so?
"The enemy is overcome by you" (*tayā abhibhaviyate sapatto*), and "I am overcome by you" (*tayā abhibhaviye ahaṃ*).

The word *uttamapuriso* (the supreme person) occurs after all verbal roots (*sabbadhātūhi*), whether the word *amha*—which denotes the agent or the object and functions as a nominative case ending—is employed in grammatical coreferentiality (*tulyādhikaraṇe*) with a verb, or even when it is not employed because its position is already occupied. [Examples:
*ahaṃ paribhavāmi*, *mayaṃ paribhavāma*; *paribhavāmi*, *paribhavāma*; *ahaṃ paribhaviyyāmi*.
"By unwholesome states, we shall be despised; [I] shall be despised; [we] shall be despised.

Where, although the word *amha* expresses the agent (*sādhaka*), because it is not in the nominative case (*paccattavacana*), coreferentiality with the verb is not obtained, there the first person (*uttamapurisa*) does not occur.
However, the other two [persons] do occur, as the word expressing the object (*kamma*) is in the nominative case.
[This occurs] depending on a word that has a common substratum (*tulyādhikaraṇa*). How so? "Prosperity is to be experienced by me;

you are to be overcome by me. Thus, wherever nouns and the like—whether expressing the agent (*sādhaka*) or the object (*karman*)—which exist in the nominative case, obtain a common substratum with a verbal form, there the first person and so forth are obtained.

Therefore, the state of having a common substratum (*tulyādhikaraṇabhāva*) for the personal endings (*paccattavacana*) of nouns and so forth is indeed the cause for the arising of the first person and the others.
When two or three persons are expressed by a single [word], the "other" person (*paro puriso*) should be understood as the [highest] person.

Here, "single expression" (*ekābhidhāna*) means expression together (*ekato abhidhāna*) and expression at the same time (*ekakālābhidhāna*). And that occurs only when the particle *ca* is employed; it does not occur when the particle *vā* is employed.
Because when there is a designation of different times, there is no inclusion of that [other time]. Examples of such usage include: “May you be skilled in the goal;
may we be skilled in the goal,” and so forth. In this regard, regarding the expression “May you be skilled in the goal”:
[it implies] “He is skilled in the goal, and you are skilled in the goal; thus, ‘may you be skilled in the goal.’”
In this way, when two people are expressed by a single term, another person should be understood [as the referent].
However, regarding the phrase "We are skilled in the goal," it should be understood as either:
"He is skilled in the goal and I am skilled in the goal—thus we are skilled in the goal," or "You are skilled in the goal and I am skilled in the goal—thus we are skilled in the goal."
Or likewise, when two are expressed by a single term, another person should be understood [as implied].
For example: “He is skilled in meaning, you are skilled in meaning, and I am skilled in meaning;
we are skilled in meaning,” or “He is skilled in meaning, they are skilled in meaning, and you are skilled in meaning; you [plural]...”
Or, when three people speak with a single utterance, such as: "May you both be skilled in what is beneficial; may I also be skilled in what is beneficial;
may we all be skilled in what is beneficial," another person should be understood [as being included].
Another method regarding the meaning is stated: "You are skilled in what is beneficial, and he is also skilled in what is beneficial..."
"May you be skilled in what is beneficial," or "I am skilled in what is beneficial, and he is skilled in what is beneficial;
we are both skilled in what is beneficial"—in this manner, the method of meaning (*atthanaya*) is manifold.

Likewise, in the remaining case-endings, such as the fifth and seventh cases and so forth, the third person should be understood as referring to another person. And in all verbal forms expressing plurality:
[This applies] to plural endings, but not to verbal expressions that denote a single entity even when ending in the plural, nor to those that denote a single significant meaning.
Here are these verses for the purpose of illustrating the objection:
"In the expression 'And you are he,' and so forth..."
"How could there be the second person in such expressions as 'You be' and so forth?
And how could there be the first person in such utterances as 'I am' and 'He is,' or 'We are' and so forth?"
And here it is said:
"The 'other' (para) is called that which is mentioned later, according to the sequence of the grammatical designation;
however, it should be understood in this way as having the name 'other-man' (paropurisa)."
After the first, there is what is called "the middle" and also "the superior";
after the middle, there is what is called "the superior person.
Thus, however, this classification here is in accordance with conventional usage.
There is no fault in grasping that which conforms to it.
Since the reading "And you, Bhaddā, may you be happy, and so too this great deer" has been seen, therefore we should speak thus.
"You two are happy"— this is the meaning seen there;
even though this method has been stated thus according to my own judgment,
although my own judgment may be spoken of as being very weak indeed.
Nevertheless, because it was spoken according to principle, it was not offensive:
"They banished me from the kingdom while I was ruling righteously;
you, along with the country folk and the assembled townspeople."
“Both I and Queen Maddi, Jālī and Kaṇhājinā too—
removing each other’s grief— we then dwelt in that hermitage.
These verses also serve to establish this meaning.
In those [verses], the meaning will be clearly manifest by the very method already stated;
thus it should be understood by the wise—what is the use of much speaking?
By whatever manner of speaking that is pleasing, [the meaning is conveyed].
If the meaning is not contradicted, that is the authority for the wise.
This [person] called "another person" does not exist separately from the three persons, because it is included within them.
For the sake of the listeners' proficiency regarding all conventional meanings, even though it is not found separately [in the grammatical rules], it has been extracted as if it were found.

Here, the activity of persons should be characterized in brief as follows: "In the sense of the first person pronoun (*amha-vacana*), it is the highest; in the sense of the second person pronoun (*tumha-vacana*), it is the middle; in the sense of the third person pronoun (*añña-vacana*), it is the first."
Since the designation "masculine" (purisa) has been stated for *tya* and the others,
it should be understood that this [suffix] is called *tabbanta-ākhyātika* (a verbal derivative ending in *tabba*) and indicates the masculine gender.
Thus, in every respect, the indication of tense, grammatical function, and gender for the verb (*ākhyātika*) has been explained.
Regarding "the characteristic of action" (*kriyālakkhaṇa*): how is it to be understood that a verb possesses the characteristic of action?
It is characterized by action, or action is its characteristic;
thus is the characteristic of action to be understood, and for this reason as well.
Having heard such words as "gacchati" (he goes), which indicate action,
those wise ones who know the verb have designated them as "ākhyātaka" (verbal).
Just as the state of denoting a sentient being is the characteristic of a noun, so too is this the case for the verb.
Thus, the very denotation of action (*kriyā*) is the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) of the verb (*ākhyāta*) itself.
However, in terms of its meaning,
it should be understood by those who know characteristics that its characteristic here is "the state of expressing action," as it is characterized by such experts.
When asked, "What are you doing?", by means of the reply "I am cooking" and so forth,
the status of being expressive of action is recognized through the giving of such an answer.
In this way, the characteristic of action belonging to a verb (ākhyātika) should be understood.
Now, the occurrence of case endings according to the tenses should be understood as follows:
In the present tense, the *vattamāna* (present) ending occurs;
in the sense of benediction (*āsiṭṭha*), location (*ṭhāna*), and purpose (*attha*), the fifth case (*pañcamī*) occurs in the present tense.
The seventh case (locative) is used for the present tense, for hypotheticals, and for the sense of consent;
the sixth case (aorist) occurs when the past is not witnessed by the speaker.
Regarding time starting from yesterday, it occurs in the past tense.
Whether it be perceptible or imperceptible, the term *hiyyattanī* is the linguistic designation for the past.
From today onwards, in the time that has passed, the term *ajjatanī*—
whether referring to what is perceptible or imperceptible— is used for the proximate past.
"In the future tense, it occurs when time is proceeding;
in the case of the 'past beyond' (kriyātipanna), it is the past beyond time (atītakālātipatti);
and it also occurs in the future—so it has been stated by those who know grammar."

Having thus understood the occurrence of case endings according to time, those who desire proficiency in the various applications seen in the Suttantas—which are the domain of a clear, vast, and sharp intellect—should observe the series of verbal forms expressed through the sequence beginning with *ty-*, etc.:
*bhavati*, *bhavanti*; *bhavasi*, *bhavatha*; *bhavāmi*, *bhavāma*; *bhavate*, *bhavante*; *bhavase*.
*bhavatha*, *bhavanti*. *bhave*, *bhavāmhe*. This is the series of verb forms (*kriyāpadamālā*) devoid of other suffixes (*aññayoga*) and so forth.
And in the Suttantas, verb forms devoid of other suffixes and so forth are seen even when there is a need for meaning (*atthasambhave*). For example:
"When one sees with wisdom that 'all conditioned phenomena are impermanent'"; "O charioteer, what you say to me"; "another *sepaṇṇi*."
The series of verbal forms beginning with “I go” (gacchāmi) serves to illustrate this meaning.
Here, there are three types of connection among the verbal forms: *tayoga* (the first person plural), *mayoga* (the first person singular), and *aññayoga* (other persons).

Among these, the second persons (*majjhimapurisa*) are to be understood by way of *tayoga*; the first persons (*uttamapurisa*), by way of *mayoga*; and the third persons (*paṭhamapurisa*), by way of *aññayoga*.
Herein, this is the summary verse for *tya* and the others in their respective order:
The first is by means of *añña*; the middle one, however, is by means of *ta*;
the last ones are by means of *ma*; they should be grasped by one who is discerning.
To ensure proficiency in the various applications [of these forms], we shall state another series of verbs accompanied by other persons and so forth:
*so bhavati*, *te bhavanti*; *tvaṃ bhavasi*, *tumhe bhavatha*;
*ahaṃ bhavāmi*, *mayaṃ bhavāma*. *So bhavate*, *te bhavante*; *tvaṃ bhavase*, *tumhe bhavavhe*; *ahaṃ bhave*, *mayaṃ bhavāmhe*.
This is a series of verbs accompanied by various conjunctions and so forth.
Furthermore, verbs accompanied by various conjunctions and so forth are seen in the Suttantas. For example:
“And as for this, O King, that the prince has well-placed feet—this too is a mark of a Great Man belonging to this Great Man.”
For him, there are these seven jewels. "He who hastens when it is time to hasten, and who delays when it is time to delay—you are my teacher;
I too desire to see you; my father has come here"—such is the series of verbs for the purpose of illustrating this meaning.
That word which occurs in a sense expressible by the word *tumha*, yet does not itself express the meaning of *tumha*,
does not establish the connection of the verb with the third person (*taya*), but rather establishes its connection with another [person].
And that word which occurs in a sense expressible by the word *amha*, yet does not itself express the meaning of *amha*, that word likewise [does not establish the connection with the first person].
It establishes that the verb is connected with *mā*, and not at all that it is connected with anything else.
