In this regard, concerning the sense expressed by the word *tumha* (you), [examples are]: "Your Honor does not go for the sake of merit, to see King Sivi";
"May you not strive for the schism of the harmonious Saṅgha"; and "Venerable sir, let the Blessed One wash his rag-robe here."
These and others are such applications. However, regarding the meaning expressible by the word *amha*, there are applications such as: “Upāli, O Great Hero, pays homage at the feet of the Teacher;
your disciple, O Great Hero, Saraṇa, pays homage to the Teacher. This is what should be noted here:
that [the forms] *tvaṃ*, *tumhe*, *ahaṃ*, and *mayaṃ* are distinct from the suffixes *-ta* and *-ma* which indicate the same meanings.
The term *aññayoga* refers simply to a construction (*payoga*) that indicates something else;
in that case, the first person occurs. If this is so, how is it in instances such as: "Having grasped an iron peak of excessive size, you stand in the sky;
having heard this, I have confidence in your words, O best of seers"? For in these cases, there is indeed the occurrence of the second and third persons.
Is it not seen that [the pronoun] does not arise from the first person? It is said:

because in such passages as “Taking up an iron hammer of excessive size, you stand in the sky,” we observe that the personal pronouns beginning with “you” (tumhe) and “we” (amhe)—such as the word “you” (so) and others—function as substitutes for finite verb forms ending in case-suffixes like “stand” (tiṭṭhasi), since they share the same grammatical core (samānādhikaraṇa) when fully extracted and are subordinate to the meaning of those verbs.

And the state of being born as a person of middle or superior capacity is to be attained. In such applications, even words such as "you" (*tvaṃ*) and "I" (*ahaṃ*), though not explicitly present, must be supplied by virtue of observing the forms ending in *syāt* (the optative);
for example, "sātvaṃ vaṅkamanuppattā, kathaṃ maddi karissasi" (O Maddi, having reached this crooked path, what will you do?
and "so ahaṃ vicarissāmi" (Thus I shall wander). In some instances, however, they are seen in their complete form.
In such examples as “village after village,” “city after city,” and so forth—

since a verb is characterized by action and is devoid of gender distinctions— we shall state another series of verbs for the purpose of illustrating the commonality of the state of being across the three genders:
“the man becomes,” “the maiden becomes,” “the mind becomes,” “the men become,” “the maidens become.”
[There are] minds. "O man, you are"; "O maiden, you are"; "O mind, you are. "Sirs, you men are"; "Ladies, you maidens are";
"Sirs, you minds are. "I am a man," "I am a maiden," "I am a mind."
“We are men,” “we are maidens,” “we are minds. This same method applies to the forms in the *attanopada* (middle voice), as well as to all forms in the remaining case endings (*vibhatti*).
This is indeed a series of verbal forms (*kriyāpadamālā*) that illustrates the commonality of the three genders for verbs (*ākhyātika*).
For it is said in the *Niruttipiṭaka*: “The characteristic of a verb is that it is independent of gender distinctions (*aliṅgabhedam*). In this context, "independent of gender distinctions" means:
What is the meaning? The term "aliṅgabhedam" (without distinction of gender) refers to a meaning that is common to the feminine, masculine, and neuter genders. For example:
"puriso gacchati" (the man goes), "kaññā gacchati" (the girl goes), and "cittaṃ gacchati" (the mind goes).

Among the four types of verbal bases taught, by taking the final word ending in the vowel *a*—as in "bhavatī" (he/she/it is)—one forms the entire series of verbal forms in every way, such as "bhavati, bhavanti, bhavasī," and so forth.

In this same way, having taken the words ending in the suffix *-ant* that follow the vowel *a*, such as "ubbhavati" and so forth, the entire series of verbal forms should be constructed in every respect as follows:

"ubbhavati, ubbhavanti, ubbhavasī," and so on. Furthermore, having taken the words ending in the suffix *-ant* that follow the vowel *o*, such as "bhoti" and "sambhoti," as well as those ending in the suffix *-ant* that follow the vowel *e*, such as "bhāveti" and "vibhāveti," one should proceed according to the method of the Pāli text itself.

A series of verbal forms (*kriyāpadamālā*) should be constructed; it is not here according to the method already stated. For in such instances, the progression of the verbal form is difficult to discern.

Therefore, the series of verbal forms should be constructed according to what is available. Indeed, not all worldly people in the world speak by joining every single verbal root (*dhātu*) with all ninety-six case-endings (*vacana*);
yet, even though they do not speak in this manner, their speech is not incomplete.
Since there is no such name, one should avoid the points that ought to be avoided and construct the series of words (*padamālā*) as far as possible.
This applies likewise to the fifth and subsequent case-endings (*vibhatti*). This concludes the exposition of the series of verbal forms according to the present tense (*vattamāna-vibhatti*).
From here on, however, by successively transforming the very words already mentioned, [the series] serves as the framework (*mātikā*) for the fifth case-endings and so forth.

These are to be understood. Now, however, we shall present two sets of verbal paradigms according to whether they are accompanied by the three *yaks* (personal endings) or not, including certain alternative forms (*rūpantara*) that have arisen through phonetic substitution (*ādesa*), for the sake of easy memorization by listeners and to prevent confusion regarding masculine usage:
*bhavatu*, *bhavantu*; *bhavāhi*, *bhava*, *bhavatha*; *bhavāmi*, *bhavāma*; *bhavataṃ*, *bhavantaṃ*.
May he be, may they be. May I be, may we be. Let him be, let them be. May you be, may you (plural) be.
I am, we are. Let him be, let them be. May you be, may you (plural) be. May I be, may we be.
This is the exposition of the series of verbal forms according to the fifth case ending (*pañcamīvibhatti*).
*bhaveyya*, *bhave*, *bhaveyyuṃ*; *bhaveyyāsi*, *bhaveyyātha*; *bhaveyyāmi*, *bhaveyyāma*, *bhavemu*;
*bhavetha*, *bhaveraṃ*; *bhavetho*, *bhaveyyāvho*; *bhaveyyaṃ*, *bhaveyyāmhe*—or [in other words]:
he would be, he would be, they would be; you would be, you (plural) would be; I would be, we would be.
May we be. He may be; they may be. You two may be; you all may be. I may be; we may be—thus [it is].
This is the exposition of the series of verbal forms according to the seventh case ending (the optative). He was; they were. He was; they were. I was; we were. They were; they were.
*Babhūvittha*, *babhūvivho*. *Babhūviṃ*, *babhūvimhe*—or alternatively, *so babhūva*, *te babhūvu*;
*tvaṃ babhūve*, *tumhe babhūvittha*; *ahaṃ babhūvaṃ*, *mayaṃ babhūvimha*. *So babhūvittha*, *te babhūvire*;
*tvaṃ babhūvittho*, *tumhe babhūvivho*; *ahaṃ babhūviṃ*, *mayaṃ babhūvimhe*—or alternatively. This [is the form].
The exposition of the series of verbal forms by way of the remote (parokkhā) case endings:
abhavā, abhavū; abhavo, abhavattha; abhavaṃ, abhavamhā; abhavattha, abhavatthuṃ;
abhavase, abhavavhaṃ; abhaviṃ, abhavamhase—or else: *so abhavā*, *te abhavū*; *tvaṃ abhavo*.
You were (*abhavattha*). I was (*aham abhavam*), we were (*mayam abhavamhā*). He was (*so abhavattha*), they were (*te abhavatthuṃ*).

You were (*tvam abhavase*), you all were (*tumhe abhavavhaṃ*). I was (*aham abhaviṃ*), or "we were" (*mayam abhavamhase*). This is the exposition of the series of verbal forms according to the past tense (*hiyyattani*) inflection.

He was, they were. He was, he was (you). I was, we were. You were, you were (plural). Or: "I was," or "we were. Thus: he was, they were. You were, you were (plural). I was, we were. He was, they were. You were, you were (plural). You were (singular), you were (plural). I was, we were. He was, they were. You were, you were (plural). You were (singular), you were (plural). 3. Determination of Miscellaneous Matters (Pakiṇṇakavinicchaya) Henceforth I shall explain the determination of miscellaneous matters,
for the sake of proficiency among the wise in meanings that involve various applications.
In this regard, the exposition should be understood as ninefold: the extraction of the meaning; reflection on the word "meaning" (attha); the application of the excellence of the meaning;
the inclusion of verbal forms according to whether they are identical or non-identical; the inclusion of verbal forms according to the characteristics of the traditional texts (āgama);

the inclusion of verbal forms according to tense; the inclusion of tenses; the correlation with the treatise (pakaraṇa); and the elucidation of the meaning of the words such as the present tense and so forth.
First, in the extraction of meanings (*atthuddhāra*), we shall perform the extraction of the meanings of words that share the same phonetic form (*samānasutika*).
Here, the meaning of the words *bhoti* and *bhaveti*, which are designated as verbal forms (*ākhyātapada*), must be extracted.

For these two, although they have the same phonetic form as other words designated as nominal forms (*nāmikapada*)—namely, the words *bhoti* and *bhaveti*—they are both different in meaning and different in case-ending (*vibhatti*).

For in the Dispensation, certain words are similar in sound to one another, yet they may be identical in form while having different meanings, different bases for their application, different grammatical genders, different case endings, different numbers, different tenses, different times, and different word-origins. Regarding their difference in meaning:
"All that which depends on the body decays; this man of little learning is like a bullock... (Dhp 102).
“*Jīrati*, *santo*, *tasito*, *pahu santo na bharati*, *santo ācikkhate muni*, *santo sappurisā loke*, *santo saṃvijjamānā lokasmin*” — such are the applications [of these terms].

Here, it should be understood that the two instances of the word *jīrati* denote, as appropriate, the departure from youth and the process of increasing [in age]. The five instances of the word *santo* should be seen as denoting, as appropriate, one who has reached exhaustion, one who is similar [to others], one who is pacified, and one who is found existing.

However, regarding the state of having different bases for their occurrence, examples include such terms as *akataññū* (ungrateful) and *mittadubbhī* (treacherous to friends), as well as *assaddho akataññū ca*.

In this context, it should be understood that the two occurrences of the word *akataññū* have different bases for their occurrence because they arise in dependence upon different bases: one based on the knowledge of what has been done and the other based on the lack of knowledge thereof.
Regarding the case of different genders (*asamānaliṅgatta*): [examples include] “May Sakka, lord of the gods, be happy, Pañcasikha; and you too, Bhaddā, be happy.
Wherever she is established, my mother exists—she is to be supported by me.
In this context, it should be understood that the two words *sukhī* and the two words *sā* differ in gender according to the masculine and feminine genders respectively.

Regarding the case of different grammatical cases (*asamānavibhattikatta*), there are examples such as: “From food, from the stomach; from which he understands phenomena with their causes. Here, it should be understood that the two instances of the word *yato* have different cases because they are accompanied by the first and fifth case endings respectively. Regarding the case of different numbers (*asamānavacanakkatta*), these are the applications:
“The person who, supported by his mother, surveys this world...”
In such passages as, “The ordinary person, when angry, slays even one who gives him life and provides peace,” the word *hanti* is in the singular number. Also:
“Surely these hunters in the forest [slay] the herds of deer... [and so forth].
"Having surrounded them with snares and immediately cast them into a pit, they tear them apart with fierce [teeth] and kill the best among them.
In such passages, however, the plural number is used. "The virtuous one, endowed with conduct. Come, venerable sirs, be virtuous. In these cases, it is the plural.
In such passages as, "The saint, the tamed, the self-controlled, the celibate; indeed, the saint is proclaimed by the virtuous;
he is a glorious Great King—the Four Great Kings," the words *sīlavā* (virtuous) and others appear both in the singular and the plural.
However, when they are not identical, there occurs either a difference in case-ending (*vibhatti*) or a difference in number (*vacana*) among those that are heard to be identical.
Or it is perceived. Those very same applications [apply here]. How so? “The virtuous, the clearly comprehending; the Dhamma of the virtuous; the peaceful, the tamed;
the peaceful, the true persons”—such passages as these. Regarding the difference in time:
“Have you not heard, brahmin, while the discourse was being recited: ‘The gods do not envy the prowess of man’?”
"Those people will cross over the realm of Death, so difficult to cross"—such passages as these are examples.

Here, the two words *issanti* (present tense) and *issanti* (future tense) should be understood as being of different times due to their respective temporal values of present and future. Furthermore, they are also of different grammatical moods (*vibhatti*) by virtue of being in the present and future tenses.
In the case of words that are not of the same grammatical class (*asamānapadajātika*), there are examples such as: “*Sayaṃ samāhito nāgo, sayaṃ abhiññāya kamuddiseyyaṃ.
Pathe dhāvantiyā pati, ekaṃsaṃ ajinaṃ katvā, pādesu sirasā pati. Giriṃ caṇḍoraṇaṃ patī*.

Here, it should be understood that the two instances of the word *sayaṃ* are nouns and indeclinables, while the three instances of the word *pati* are nouns, verbs, and prefixes respectively; thus, they are not of the same grammatical class.
In this manner, it should be elaborated in all instances.

Thus, within the Dispensation (*sāsana*), there are certain words that, while being identical in sound (*samānasutika*) and identical [to one another], are nevertheless not identical in meaning (*asamānattha*), not identical in the basis for their application (*asamānapavattinimitta*), not identical in gender (*asamānaliṅga*), not identical in case-ending (*asamānavibhattika*), not identical in number (*asamānavacanaka*), not identical in suffix (*asamānantā*), not identical in tense (*asamānakālika*), and not identical in the class of word (*asamānapadajātika*). Among such words, whichever possesses the status of a verb (*kriyāpada*)—
That which manifests the nature of a noun does not possess the nature of a verb; and that which manifests the nature of a verb does not possess the nature of a noun.
Nevertheless, because they are grasped as a unity due to their commonality of sound (*suti*), the extraction of meaning (*atthuddhāra*) must be performed.
Therefore, we shall state the extraction of the meaning for the words *bhoti* and *bhaveti*, which share the same sound with the aforementioned verbs through their identical phonetic form.
How so? The word *bho* is a verb when used in connection with an agent, and a noun when used in connection with an action; therefore, it functions in two senses: as a verb and as a noun.
Therein, in the sense of a verb, it occurs by way of being in the present tense; in the sense of a noun, however, it occurs by way of address.
As for its occurrence in the sense of a verb: "One person is" (*eko bhoti*). In the sense of a noun: "Do not lament, O sir" (*mā bho paridevesi*). Regarding this, it is said:
The word *bho* occurs in these two senses: as a noun-base (*nāmapadattha*) and as a form of address (*ālapanavisesita*).
Furthermore, the word *bhava* also occurs in the sense of this very term when it is connected with the present tense, as in "I am" (*bhavāmi*).
The word *bhavāmi*, when joined with the fifth case-ending (*pañcamīvibhatti*), functions in the senses of commanding and requesting.
The word *bhaveyyāmi*, when accompanied by the seventh case-ending (*sattamīvibhatti*), functions in the senses of assenting and supposing.
Herein, this is the direct statement that establishes its first sense:
“I shall be superior to the gods, I shall become a lord of men;
endowed with beauty and the marks [of a great man], may I be peerless in wisdom.
This, moreover, is our composition of verses which establishes all those points:
“May he be happy, and may I also be happy; may he be happy, and may I also be happy. Through this worship of the Buddha, may all beings become happy.”
"May I also attain happiness here, together with my ministers and kinsmen.
May he too be happy, and may I also be happy;
if he should be happy, then may I also be happy."
Thus, in this way—
the word *bhava* occurs in these three places: in the present fifth case ending and in the seventh case ending.
When the present tense occurs in one way,
and in two ways each in the fifth and seventh tenses, it illustrates five meanings;
or alternatively, when the present tense occurs in two ways, it expresses the first person.
The meaning of the word "bhava" can also be applied as "bhavati" (it comes to be).
Now, however, I shall cite a passage from the Pāḷi that establishes the meaning already stated; listen to me.
Who are you that, seeing no shore, struggle in the midst of the ocean?
Having perceived what purpose, do you exert yourself so intensely?
O deity, having reflected upon the nature of the world and the nature of exertion—
Therefore, in the midst of the great ocean, not seeing the shore,
I strove. For in the previous verse,
the meaning of the word "āyuhe" should be understood by the discerning as "he strives" (āyūhati).
This [term] is explained by way of a variation in case-ending,
as "the seventh [case] occurs in the present tense," or by way of the *tissēkār* (the particle *e* following *tissa*).
Furthermore, in the latter verse, regarding the word "āyuhe":
One who knows the meaning of words should discern that the meaning of "āyūhāmi" is "I am bringing about.
Likewise, regarding the word "bhave," which is in the present tense,
one should discern its fourfold meaning as "bhavati" (he/it is), "bhavasi" (you are), "bhavāmi" (I am), and "bhavāma" (we are).
In other such readings as well, this method should be applied by one who perceives the underlying logic within the teaching that is an ocean of methods.
Thus, this word *bhava* functions in five or six meanings of verbal roots. Likewise, regarding a nominal word ending in the seventh case (locative) suffix:

It also refers to meanings designated as growth (*vuddhi*), the round of existence (*saṃsāra*), kamma-existence (*kammabhava*), and rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*). For instance, in such passages as “He delights in non-existence (*abhave*), he does not delight in existence (*bhave*)”, it refers to growth. In “Wandering in existence (*bhave*)”, it refers to the round of existence.
In “When there is existence, birth comes to be; with birth as condition, aging and death arise”, it refers to kamma-existence. In “While existence thus exists”, it refers to... [rebirth-existence].

It should be understood as "rebirth-existence" (upapattibhava). In this manner, the meanings of other verbs derived from the root *bhū* should also be extracted according to their respective possibilities.
These meanings are derived from the sense of the verb (ākhyāta); they should never be taken [directly] from the [nominal] suffixes.
Since these have been extracted by way of extracting the meaning (*atthuddhāra*), they are thus listed by name.
This is, in brief, the demonstration of the method for extracting the meaning here.
Furthermore, in the investigation of the word "meaning" (*attha*), it should be observed as follows: [the forms] *bhavante*, *parābhavante*, *parābhave*, and so forth.

Words such as *gacchati* (he goes), *gacchaṃ* (going), and *gacchato* (of one going) are particular words (*visesa-sadda*), like [the word] "goer," and not general words (*sāmañña-sadda*) like the word *nātha*, which expresses meanings such as "begging" or "afflicting," nor like the word *deva*, which expresses [meanings such as] "king" or "deity.
Furthermore, those among these that are particular words remain particular words at all times; and those that are general words likewise remain general words at all times.
In this regard, the specific nature of terms such as "gacchati" (he goes) should be understood as follows: *gacchati* is one noun-phrase (*nāmapada*) and one verb (*ākhyāta*).
Likewise, *gacchanti* is one noun-phrase and one verb. *Gacchato* is one genitive form ending in *-to*, while the other is a conventional term (*rūḷhisadda*).
Even though they possess specific meanings, because they are similar and share a common phonetic form (*suti-sāmañña*), they direct the intellect toward their respective objects.
It does not arise [as a case-ending] without the connection to another word, whether it be a noun (*attha*), a particle (*pakaraṇa*), or another word (*saddantara*).

For instance, when "gacchati patiṭṭhitaṃ" (he goes, established) is said with the connection to another word, it is understood as a noun-word ending in the locative case; however, when "gacchati tisso" (Tissa goes) is said, it is understood as a verb.
Likewise, when "sa gacchaṃ na nivattati" (he, going, does not turn back) is said, it is understood as a noun-word ending in the nominative case.

It is understood as a verb when it is said, "He goes, [he is] a bringer of news for his son. It is understood as a gerund (absolutive) when it is said, "He fell while going or while being carried away.
It is understood as a conventional term (rūḷhisadda) denoting a tree when it is said, "Leaves and flowers fall from the one who is going.

Thus, regarding specific words that are either verbs or nouns and which share the same phonetic form with nouns or verbs, [the distinction is made] through the connection of their meanings and so forth.

Any connection that makes known a specific meaning must necessarily be sought. Thus, the quality of being a "specific word" (*visesa-sadda*) should be understood in the case of verbs such as "he goes" (*gacchati*), which, though standing individually as either a verb or a noun and expressing a single meaning, possess this specific character.

However, in the case of verbs and nouns such as "the god rules" (*nāthati devo*), which do not share the same phonetic form with other nouns or verbs and express multiple meanings, [the distinction is different].
It should be understood as being merely a common word (*sāmañña-sadda*).

For when "he rules" (*nāthati*) is stated without any specific connection among the various possible relations—such as meaning "he begs," "he torments," "he exercises sovereignty," or "he prays"—the sense [of these meanings] presents itself;
likewise, when "god" (*deva*) is stated, [the senses of] "cloud," "sky," "king," or "deity" present themselves.
Or rather, the meaning "Visuddhideva" (the deity of purity) presents itself.
But when it is stated as "he desires right practice" (*nāthati suppaṭipattiṃ*) through connection with another word, then the meaning of the verb *nāthati* is understood as "he entreats.
When it is stated "he desires all defilements" (*nāthati sabbakilese*), the meaning is understood as "he torments. [And] "he desires in his own mind" (*nāthati sakacitte*).
When it is said, "He exercises sovereignty," the meaning "he rules" is understood. When it is said, "He protects the welfare of the world," the meaning "he wishes for [it]" is understood.
Likewise, when it is said, "The god thunders," the meaning of the name-word "god" is understood as "cloud.
When it is said, "The cloud has been pierced and is free from mist," the meaning "the sky" is understood. "Let him drink..."

When it is said, “The deity [has sent] water,” the meaning understood is “the king. When it is said, “The deity falls from the divine realm due to the exhaustion of his lifespan,” the meaning understood is “a deva.
When it is said, “The god beyond gods, possessing the hundred marks of merit,” the meaning understood is “the pure deity.
In this manner, other general terms should also be understood.
Having understood all this according to the meaning of the sound, and how the sound is not contradicted by the meaning, so should the meanings and sounds be reflected upon.

Herein, this is merely an illustration for the purpose of reflection: when it is said, "May you be well-meaning" (*atthakusalā bhavante*) or "May you perform your duties" (*kiccāni bhavante*), this word *bhavante* is a verbal form identical in meaning to *bhavanti*.
In this way, both the meaning and the word must be considered. When it is said, "I see you, sir," or "I desire you, sir," there are two noun-words possessing the sense of the accusative case;

thus, both the meaning and the word must be considered. When it is said, "He praises people, sir," or "He desires people, sir," there are two noun-words possessing the senses of the nominative and the accusative cases respectively; thus, both the meaning and the word must be considered.
When it is said, “Thieves are ruined,” the word “are ruined” (*parābhavante*) is a verbal form (*ākhyātika-pada*) having the same meaning as the feminine noun “ruined ones” (*parābhavantī*);

thus both the meaning and the sound must be considered. When it is said, “People desire those who are ruined for their enemies,” the words “are ruined” (*parābhavante*) are two nouns (*nāma-pada*) possessing the sense of the accusative and the nominative cases; thus both the meaning and the sound must be considered.
When it is said, “*eso parābhave*,” one should consider both the meaning and the word thus: “*parābhave*” is a verb (*ākhyātapada*) having the same sense as the future form “*parābhaveyya*.
When it is said, “*ete parābhave loke, paṇḍito samavekkhiyā*,” one should consider both the meaning and the word thus:
“*parābhave*” is a noun (*nāmapada*) in the accusative case (*upayogattha*), plural number.

When it is said, “*parābhave sati*,” one should consider both the meaning and the word as a noun-phrase (*nāmapada*) in the locative case, singular number, used to characterize a state (*bhāvalakkhaṇa*).
When it is said, “*tumhe me pasādā sambhave*,” this word “*sambhave*” is a verb-phrase (*ākhyātapada*) having the same meaning as “*sambhavatha*”;
thus, both the meaning and the word should be considered. [And when it is said,] “*ehi tvaṃ sambhavavhe*.”

When it is said, “*Sambhavavhe*,” this should be considered as a noun-word (*nāmikapada*) in the feminine gender, expressing the name of a woman called Sambhavā, and thus both its meaning and its sound must be reflected upon.

When it is said, “*Ehi tvaṃ sambhavavhe patiṭṭhitan*,” this should be considered as a noun-word in the masculine gender, expressing the name of a man called Sambhava, and being in the locative case; thus both its meaning and its sound must be reflected upon.
“Varuṇa and Brahmadeva were the chief disciples;
the attendant of the Great Seer Revata was named Sambhava”—such is the canonical text (pāḷi).
When it is said, “when phenomena appear,” this word “appearing” (pātubhavante) is [to be understood] as “appearing” (pātubhavanti) [in the plural].
When it is said, "The verb (*ākhyātapada*) has the same meaning as the noun (*sanipāta*)," both the meaning and the sound must be considered in this way.
When it is said, "May you protect the people," the verb, the *tinta*-suffix, and the pronoun are words that express the meaning "may your honor protect those people";
thus, both the meaning and the sound must be considered. When it is said, "You manifest through your virtues," regarding the word "you manifest" (*pātubhavase*):
This [term] "pātubhavasī" is a verbal form (*ākhyāta-pada*) having the same meaning as "pātubhavasi"; thus both the meaning and the word should be considered.
When it is said, "O you who manifest your qualities," the words "pātubhavāhi," "attano guṇahetu," "tvaṃ," and so forth are respectively a verb, a noun, a particle, and a pronoun;
thus both the meaning and the word should be considered. When it is said, "I manifest by means of my own qualities," the term "pātubhave" [is to be understood].
This [term] "pātubhavāmi" is a verb (*ākhyāta-pada*) synonymous with "sanipāta"; thus, both the meaning and the sound must be considered.

When it is said, "May this meritorious deed manifest for me," the verb and noun phrases expressing the sense "may this meritorious deed protect me in *saṃsāra*" must likewise have their meaning and sound considered. By this method, it should be applied in all cases.

The meanings of words should be considered according to what is appropriate. In this regard, there is a specific mode of pronunciation for certain words that are homophonous, as seen in such instances as:
“They do not store them in a granary; one should not pass between them”; “I shall teach you, O Licchavis, the seven principles of non-decline”;
and “These are your seven [treasures], O King, and you are the supreme treasure. In these cases, despite the words being identical in sound, there is a distinction in their pronunciation.

It is desirable. For when there is a specific pronunciation, the words become distinct; when the words are distinct, the meaning becomes distinct, and for those who grasp the meaning, the attainment of that meaning is not difficult, like seeing a reflection on the surface of a perfectly polished mirror.
And that [meaning] belongs to one who has previously grasped the convention regarding any one of the relations between meanings and so forth.
It occurs only when [the meaning] is already known, not otherwise. For this was said by the ancients:
“Sounds that have not yet attained the status of being objects do not convey meaning;
they do not reveal meanings from the mere words alone unless they are already known.”

Regarding what we have stated here— that "a specific mode of pronunciation is required"— the following verse serves as an illustration of that specific pronunciation, in accordance with the method of explaining by means of the hand-gesture (*sahatthappakāsana-naya*) used in the verse on giving:
"In the reading 'na te saṃ koṭṭhe openti,' the wise one,
having split the word 'na te,' should indeed read it as 'na te saṃ koṭṭhe.'"
“Those monks do not open their storehouses”—thus one should understand the meaning.
This same method applies to these and other readings as well.
Now, as for what was said, “of some,” for what purpose is that? [It is to show: “It goes when it is established; it goes...”
In such passages as "I see three, sirs; you are experts in the meaning, sirs;

when one speaks, the other, though having heard the same, replies," this is for the purpose of showing that no distinction in the utterance of those who have heard the same thing is obtained. Therefore, this should be observed here:
where a distinction in the utterance of those who have heard the same thing is obtained, there is also a distinction in the meaning by way of the division of the words.
Or by way of non-distinction; therein, in the application [of the recitation], one should utter certain words having split them where they share the same sound.
For example: “The cause is a condition, by way of the root-condition, for states associated with the root and for the material phenomena originated thereby.
He speaks together with that; he is carried away by the ear. He praises people who are becoming; becoming...”
"Passāmi," and so forth, are such applications [of the text]. Here, having slightly paused after "hetū" (causes), one should recite "hetusampayuttānaṃ" (associated with causes).
Likewise, having paused after "so" (he), one should recite "tena saddhiṃ" (together with that).
Having paused after "bhavaṃ" (sir), one should recite "te jane" (those people).
The remainder, however, should not be recited by making an interruption where there is a common phonetic sequence (*samānasutika*).

For when one reads with an interruption at a place where there should be no interruption, the meaning becomes corrupted. Thus, the distinction in the pronunciation of the meaning for those with a common phonetic sequence should be understood according to whether there is a division or non-division of words.
For here, in cases such as "so tenā," the grasping of two word-meanings is a division (*vibhāga*), while the grasping of a single word-meaning is a non-division (*avibhāga*).

This is what is intended. And here, the conceptualization of a state of having identical phonemes (*samānasutika*) by grouping together those that are separately determined and do not have identical phonemes is for the purpose of indicating a difference in meaning and for the purpose of showing a distinction in pronunciation.
For these [words] do not have identical phonemes with respect to one and the same referent (*attha*), as is the case with "sappo, sappo" and so forth.
Nevertheless, by virtue of being treated together in a single context, there is a semblance of having identical phonemes (*samānasutilesa*) that is obtained.
They are stated as "having the same vowel" (*samānasutikāni*) for the purpose of indicating a different meaning and to show a specific mode of pronunciation.
This same method applies elsewhere in similar instances. This is what should be observed here:
wherever among the eighteen modes of vowels a specific meaning is obtained through any one of those modes, [the term is applied].
However, when making an elision (vicchinditvā) before pronouncing [the word], there is no aesthetic beauty of sound, or the meaning becomes corrupted;
therefore, in such applications, words that are phonetically identical should not be pronounced by making an elision. In that regard, by what mode is the attainment of a specific meaning achieved?
Either by means of the division of words or by means of their non-division, through the proximity of syllables.
Or by way of the proximity of words, or by way of the proximity of the syllables of a word, or by way of a hiatus, or by way of a verbal expression of action,
or by way of stuttering speech arising from fear, anger, and so forth, or by way of the doubling of a word expressing a quality,
or by way of the doubling of a verb, or by way of the division of a compound word, or by way of illustrating grounds for disrespect.
In these eighteen ways— namely, by way of indicating uninterruptedness, by way of indicating non-uninterruptedness,
by way of indicating the sense of "again and again," by way of the word *iva* used as a comparative particle,
by way of indicating the meaning of the denotation of the word-meaning based on the word *iti*, and by way of indicating the mind proceeding in such a manner— or, in detail, in twenty-six ways.
From among those modes or even more than that, by whichever mode there is the attainment of a specific meaning.
Herein, first, regarding words—whether by way of division or non-division—that have identical phonetic forms, when there is the attainment of a specific meaning, [it is said]:
"That association protects him; progress is seen in them. Do not slay us, O King; do not [slay] me."
"...is not found"—such are the applications [of these terms].
However, when a specific meaning is obtained through the proximity of syllables, as in: "Honored by the peaceful, he is beneficial;

freed from attachments, the victor in battle—him I call a brahmin. Like one who formerly thought himself a fang-bearer among fang-bearers, leaping upon them... and "The Conqueror of All... and so forth.
"I bow with my head to the headless one. "From the earth up to the Brahma-world, it spreads through the world of the Radiant One, burning with fire"—such are the applications.
When a specific meaning is obtained by virtue of the proximity of words, as in:
"Water has reached the state of water," or "Kings, royal ministers, and so forth, [are] the happiness of the world."

"I bow to the Buddha, the benefactor of the world, the opener of the eye of wisdom, who inclines toward the state free from affliction, whose refuge is infinite knowledge and compassion, who is well-composed, stainless, and beneficial.
I bow to the Dhamma, the excellent restraint from existence, and to the Saṅgha, the mine of virtues, who are free from defilement.
Such are the applications [of these verses].

Regarding the attainment of specific meanings through the proximity of words (*padakkharasannidhāna*), there are such applications as: “The benefit is immeasurable; Siddhattha is the one whose every purpose is accomplished;
he is the benefactor honored by the three worlds. Having approached, the Fully Awakened One spoke these words.
In this regard, here are verses that clarify the intended meaning (*adhippāya*) concerning the proximity of syllables and so forth:
If the letter *m* is separated from the sound *mahito iti*, the sound here is meaningless;
the wise one should call it a "syllable" (*akkhara*). By means of the conjunction of syllables, they are to be known.
In such instances as "santehi mahito hito" (honored by the peaceful for their welfare),
there is a distinction in meaning despite the words being identical in form.
Prefixes, particles, and whatever else illuminates meaning—
even if it consists of a single syllable— is designated as a "word" (pada) by the wise. Furthermore,
the collocation of words and the syllables within those words [constitute the basis of expression].
I have spoken thus with reference to what is obtainable in a compound (*samāsa*).

By way of distributive repetition (*vicchā*), when a specific meaning is obtained, there are such usages as “a hundred jars in every village” (*gāme gāme sataṃ kumbhā*) or “every village is delightful” (*gāmo gāmo ramaṇīyo*); for here, by way of distributive repetition, all villages are encompassed.
But that which expresses various substrates (*adhikaraṇa*) simultaneously—
The desire to pervade is *icchā*; that is designated as *vicchā*.

When a specific meaning is obtained through the use of karmapravacanīyas, there are such applications as: “The moon shines upon every tree (*rukkhaṃ rukkhaṃ pati vijjotate cando*); the moon shines around every tree (*rukkhaṃ rukkhaṃ pari vijjotate cando*); the meaning is that it shines above and above the trees.
However, when a specific meaning is obtained through the use of words uttered as repetitions (*kathitāmeḍita-vacana*) when fear, anger, and so forth have arisen, these are the applications:
— First, in fear: such expressions as “Thief! Thief! and “Snake! Snake!”; in anger: such expressions as “Outcaste!
Outcaste! Cāṇḍāla! Cāṇḍāla! Pierce! Pierce! Strike! Strike!”; in praise: such expressions as “Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta!
and “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir!”; in haste: “Come forward, Vāseṭṭha! Come forward, Vāseṭṭha! and so forth.
“Go, go! Cut it down, cut it down! and so forth [expresses] urgency. “Come, come! and so forth [expresses] curiosity. “Oh, the Buddha! Oh, the Buddha!
and so forth [expresses] wonder. “Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness! Oh, how delightful! Oh, how delightful! and so forth [expresses] laughter.
“Where, my only son? Where, my only son? and so forth [expresses] sorrow. “The Vajjis will flourish, the Vajjis will flourish! and so forth [expresses] confidence.
“Vajjī,” and so forth. Thus, when fear, anger, and the like have arisen, a specific meaning is obtained through the use of speech that is stuttered or repeated.
Here, however, even in the absence of a different literal meaning, the very fact that the words illuminate the sense by way of reinforcement constitutes the acquisition of a specific meaning.
[This occurs] in cases of fear, anger, and praise.
A wise person should employ repetition (āmreḍita) in cases of haste, curiosity, joy, grief, and faith.
The word *ca* has the sense of an unexpressed conjunction (*avutta-samuccaya*); therefore, its inclusion of censure (*garahā*), disrespect (*asammāna*), and so forth, should be understood.

For instance, in expressions such as “a wicked person, a wicked person,” it is used in the sense of censure; in “a handsome one, a handsome one,” it is used in the sense of disrespect; and in “where is this weakling?

and similar phrases, the repetition (*āmeḍita*) should be seen as expressing intensity. When a specific meaning is obtained through the doubling of a word denoting a quality, as in “Kaṇho... [the same principle applies].
“Kaṇho ca ghoro ca,” and so forth. For the meaning of “kaṇho kaṇho” is “extremely black.
When a specific meaning is obtained through the doubling of a verb, there are examples such as “dhame dhame nātidhame. Therein, “dhame dhame” means one should blow, but not not blow;
“nātidhame” means, however, one should not blow beyond measure. This is by way of the division of words in *saṃhitā*.

Regarding the attainment of specific benefits, there are such expressions as: "men and non-men, gods and asuras," and "remorse occurring in the form of regret concerning what has been done and not done, whether wholesome or unwholesome.
Here, however, we shall compose a verse in order to generate supreme skill in the minds of the wise:
"By your power, O Conqueror, [you have shown] the beneficial and the harmful, the beneficial within the harmful."
Having discarded what is inferior and having attained the superior, they say, "May we be free from illness.
Regarding the attainment of a specific meaning by way of illustrating the basis for lack of respect: "You and you [engage in] slander, quarreling, strife, and dispute," and so forth.
Regarding the attainment of a specific meaning by way of illustrating the sense of continuity: "He enjoys it day after day."
Such are these examples. When a specific meaning is obtained by way of illustrating uninterruptedness (*anirantara*), there are cases such as: “Rapture arises moment by moment (*khaṇe khaṇe*)”;
when a specific meaning is obtained by way of illustrating repetition (*punappuna*), there are cases such as: “He causes the princes to fear again and again (*muhuṃ muhuṃ*”).
When a specific meaning is obtained by way of the particle *iva* used in the sense of a comparison (*upamāna*), [there is]: “May the King protect according to Dhamma...”
In cases where a specific meaning is obtained by way of indicating the denotation of the word-meaning based on the word *iti*, there are such examples as:
“‘Buddho, buddho,’ thus speaking, he manifested joy,” and so forth.
In cases where a specific meaning is obtained by way of indicating the state of mind occurring in that manner, there is: “Thinking ‘Buddho, buddho,’ [he attained] the path... and so forth.
“...then I shall purify it,” and so forth. In such applications as these, a word that shares the same vowel sound (*samānasutika*) must not be pronounced with a break.
For if it is pronounced with a break, there is no aesthetic refinement of sound (*saddavilāsa*).
However, in certain cases—such as in the phrase “the sphere of what is done and not done, wholesome and unwholesome”—if it is pronounced with a break, the meaning becomes corrupted.
Therefore, it should not be recited by breaking it up; rather, it should be recited as a single connected whole.
Thus, the determination regarding those with identical suttas has been presented, adorned with twenty-six modes and more.
Furthermore, since the determination regarding those with identical suttas has been shown, the determination regarding those with non-identical suttas must also be shown.

Since it exists, we shall also demonstrate that: where a reading is found in which there is the elision of a following consonant after a *niggahīta*, and also the separation of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogabyañjana*).
In those applications, the word containing the *niggahīta* should be pronounced as a single unit together with the immediately following word.
Which are they? “Sace bhutto bhaveyyāhaṃ-sā’jīvo” (If I were to eat, he would live).
“...it was censured by me. This flower has arisen. It is merely exhaustion, not Nibbāna, because of its description as 'profound' and so forth"—such passages as these.

For here, by means of the immediately following words, there is—as if a single recitation of two synonymous *sutika* words that have become internalized within the two subsequent verse-quarters without interruption, such as "if I were to eat"...—the non-interruption of the sequence.
It should be recited by way of being pronounced as a single connected unit, such as: “Sace bhutto bhaveyyāhaṃ—sājīvo garahito mama,” and so forth.
For it is precisely this kind of specific mode of recitation that is approved and employed by all the wise ancients, because it is appropriate for conveying the intended meaning in such ways as:
“His livelihood was censured by me; it arose for him; it was spoken of as deep,” and so on.

However, in whatever manner of pronunciation the meaning becomes clear, in those applications where there is a connection with words such as *ca* (and) or *pana* (but), the word should be pronounced with a slight pause.
For example: “*Vāḷā ca lapasakkharā. Accantasantā pana yā, ayaṃ nibbānasampadā, ‘idaṃ dukkhan’ti*.
(And the harsh, gravelly sounds; but that which is utterly peaceful, this is the attainment of Nibbāna: “This is suffering.”)
“Does knowledge that ‘this is suffering’ arise for one speaking the words? “Yes. “In that case, does knowledge arise for ‘iti,’ ‘ca,’ ‘danti,’ ‘ca,’ ‘duti,’ ‘ca,’ ‘khanti,’ ‘ca’?
“One should not say so. Such are the applications [of the argument].
For in these, in the first application, one should read “vāḷā cā” by slightly separating it as “vāḷā-cā,” and then pronounce “lapasakkharā.”
In this context, *lapasakkharā* means words that are sweet like sugar. However, in the *Jātakaṭṭhakathā*, it is stated:
"They are sweet like sugar because they are devoid of useless speech. Therefore, the compound should be understood in two ways by way of the *bahubbīhi* and *tappurisa* types:
either "those whose sweetness is like sugar" (*lapā sakkharā viya yāsaṃ tā lapasakkharā*), or "sweetness by means of words, as if by sugar" (*lapehi vā sakkharā viyāti lapasakkharā*).

In the second formulation, one should recite “accantasantā pana yā,” having slightly separated [the words] as “accantasantā pana” and then uttering “yā. For the meaning is: “but this attainment of Nibbāna which is absolutely peaceful (accantasantā).

In the third formulation, in these four places—*iti*, *ca*, *danti*, and *khanti*—one should utter the syllables *i*, *daṃ*, *du*, and *khaṃ* after having slightly separated them, and immediately thereafter the word *ti*.
For if they were uttered here without separation, the meaning would become faulty because it would be understood otherwise. How so?
In such instances, if the recitation were not interrupted, the word *iti* would be a particle expressing the meaning "thus" (*evam*);
however, by way of euphonic combination (*sandhi*), it would not be a conventional term (*rūḷhisadda*) expressing the sense of the vowel *i*. The word *danti* would mean "taming" (*damana*);
it would not be a term expressing the syllable *daṃ*. The word *duti* would be meaningless; it would not be a term expressing the syllable *du*. The word *khanti*...

It may have the sense of "forgiveness" (*khamaṇa*), but it is not a designation for the syllable *khaṃ*. Therefore, the vowels *i*, *daṃ*, *du*, and *khaṃ* should be slightly separated [from the following consonants].
For here, the division of the compound word (*saṃhitā-pada-ccheda*) should be understood as *i iti*, *daṃ iti*, *du iti*, *khaṃ iti*, and so forth;
and there is the elision (*lopa*) of the vowel *i* that follows. However, one should not say here: "In the case of similar vowels (*sarūpa-sara*), when another similar vowel follows..."
There is no elision [of the entire compound], but rather only the elision of the preceding vowel, just as in the case of *tatrāyanti*.
This is because the elision of the preceding vowel is demonstrated in the canonical text (*pāḷi*) in the passage: “Unwearying, digging for water on the path, they found mud there in the courtyard.
For thus has the meaning been glossed by the masters of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathācariya*): “*Papaṃ* means increased water (*pavaddhaṃ āpaṃ*). Therefore, "thus..."
In the phrase "cā"ti, one should also make the elision of the following *i*-sound after dividing it as "iti cā"ti; [the elision] is not of the preceding one.
For if the preceding *i*-sound—which expresses the word *iti*—were lost, the meaning designated by the *i*-sound would not be understood through the particle *iti*;
however, even if the *i*-sound of the particle *iti* were lost, that meaning is indeed still understood.
In the phrase “*Devadatto ti me sutaṃ*,” it is like the referent (*padattha*) of the word *Devadatta*.
Therefore, when the letter *i* follows the word *iti*, the elision (*lopa*) must be applied only to that subsequent *i*, not to the preceding *i* which expresses the sound *i*.

However, in the *Kaccāyana*, with reference to the general rule of common usage (*yebhuyyappavatti*), it is stated that there is elision of a dissimilar vowel (*asarūpasarassa*) following a dissimilar vowel, but not of a similar vowel (*sarūpasarassa*) following a similar vowel.
Regarding *sarūpa-sarassa*: it should be understood that the elision (*lopa*) of a preceding form (*sarūpa*) followed by a subsequent form (*parasara*) is stated in the *Mahāpadesa Sutta*.

However, in cases such as “*antarā ca Rājagahaṃ antarā ca Nāḷandaṃ*,” even when there is the connection of words beginning with *ca*, one should not utter the phrase after making a pause (*vicchinditvā*).
And in those applications where augment letters (*āgama-kkharādi*) and so forth are seen, the preceding words [are treated accordingly].
They should not be pronounced separately; they should be pronounced only together with subsequent words that possess phonemes from the traditional scriptures (*āgama*).
For example: “*Nakkhattarājāriva tārakānaṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca*” and so forth.
Wherever a distinct connection between them is observed and the meaning is appropriate, there they [should be joined] according to the sense.
They should be recited by making a break [in the compound]. For example: “He made an effort regarding the bath;
he also made an effort regarding the rice gruel, the hard food, and the meal. In this case, one should recite it as:
“He made an effort regarding the bath,” making a break there, and then “he also made an effort regarding the rice gruel, the hard food, and the meal. For it is thus...
When "api" (also/even) is present, it does not mean that the bhikkhu merely made an effort regarding bathing;

rather, he also made an effort regarding rice gruel, solid food, and the meal—thus it is capable of clarifying the meaning. In this context, the word "api" denotes a conjunction used in the sense of "and.
However, where a connection with one or both of the preceding words is observed, either individually or as a pair, [the particle functions accordingly].
According to the logic of the sense, those [words] should be uttered there after being appropriately divided as required. For example:
“He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end;
he proclaims the holy life, both in its meaning and its phrasing, which is entirely complete and pure. ‘Dependent origination, monks, to you...’”
"I shall teach it; listen to that and attend to it well: 'internal confidence and singleness of mind,'" and so forth—these are the applications.
In this regard, there are these verses that clarify the intended meaning:
"Whether by the word *dhamma* or by the word *brahmacariya*, the path..."
Having joined [the words], the wise one should utter: "It is meaningful and well-phrased"—this is what is meant.
The word "carefully" (*sādhuka*) may be joined with the word "listen" (*suṇātha*), or likewise with the word "attend to it" (*manasikarotha*), as it has been stated.
Having raised [the words] and joined them by means of both feet,
one should understand that a connection— whether with each one individually or with both—
is seen through the proper application of the meaning of the words.
This meaning has been stated here by me according to my own judgment;
it was spoken by me relying on the method of the lions among former teachers.
This same principle applies to other such readings as well.
One who seeks the goal of the Teaching should be led by one skilled in method.
Having reflected upon the word according to its meaning, and the meaning according to the word,
the wise person should speak accordingly, and not otherwise.
This is the consideration of the word *attha* here.

It should be characterized as follows when joined with the excellence of meaning (*atthātisaya*): from its connection with the excellence of the meaning of the element *bhū*, it is seen in the sense of "increasing" [in the phrase]:
"Seated to one side, Mahānāma the Licchavi uttered this inspired utterance: 'The Vajjis will flourish...'"

In the section on expansion (*vaḍḍhana*), [the forms] are seen as follows: either "O Vajjis," or "I alone am the corrupter, the destroyer of beings, for King Mahāpatāpa," or "The Vedas do not provide protection for that man who betrays his friends and destroys beings," or "A slaughter of beings has been committed by me.

In the compendium of verbal forms (*vacanasaṅgaha*), it should be noted thus: the third person plural of the present tense is similar to the third person plural of the fifth [case] in the third person. [The form is] *tumhe bhavatha*.

In the *parassapada* (active voice), the singular of the four persons of the first person in the present fifth tense (*vattamānapañcamī*) is identical to the singular [of the corresponding tenses], and the plural is also identical to the plural. "I am" (*ahaṃ bhavāmi*), "we are" (*mayaṃ bhavāma*).

In the *attanopada* (middle voice), the singular of the second person in the present tense is similar to the two singulars of the second person in the past (*hiyyattanī*) and future (*ajjatanī*) *attanopada*s;
in some instances, there is a slight distinction based on the combination of phonemes.

Having excluded [the previous case], this same method should be applied to what follows as well. *Tvaṃ bhavase*: this is the form of the present tense (*vattamānā*). *Tvaṃ abhavase*: this is the form of the past day (*hiyyattanī*) and the day before yesterday (*ajjatanī*).
The third person singular of the middle voice (*attanopada*) in the present tense is identical to the third person singular of the middle voice in the fifth [tense, the future] (*pañcamī*).
And it is similar to two forms: the third person singular of the *parokkhā* (aorist) and the third person plural of the *majjhima-purisa* (middle voice).
"Ahaṃ bhave" is the form for the present tense (*vattamānā*) and the fifth tense (*pañcamī*). "Tvaṃ babhūve" is the form for the *parokkhā*.

The third person plural of the *uttama-purisa* (first person) in the *attanopada* (middle voice) of the present tense is [identical] to the two *attanopada* forms of the *parokkhā* and the *ajjatanī* (imperfect).
It is similar to the third person plural forms. *Mayaṃ bhavāmhe*—this is the form for the present tense (*vattamāna*).
*Mayaṃ babhūvimhe*—this is the form for the aorist (*parokkhā*). *Mayaṃ abhavimhe*—this is the form for the recent past (*ajjatani*).
The fifth mood (*pañcamī*) in the *attanopada*, third person plural, is identical to the aorist (*parokkhā*) in the *attanopada*, third person plural.
It is similar. *tumhe bhavatho*—this is the form for the fifth tense (present).
*tumhe babhūvitho*—this is the form for the remote past (*parokkhā*). Indeed, the third person plural of the remote past in the *parassapada* voice is similar to two forms:
the third person plural of the remote past in the *parassapada* voice and the third person plural of the present (*ajjatanī*) in the *attanopada* voice.
*Te babhūvu*: this is the form for the aorist (*parokkhā*). *Te abhavu*:
this is the form for the past day (*hiyyatta*) and the current day (*ajjata*). For the aorist, the third person plural of the *parassapada* is used with the first person singular of the *attanopada*;
for the past day, the third person plural of the *parassapada* is used with the first person singular of the *attanopada*.
And it is similar to the four forms: *tumhe babhūvittha* (you all were), *so babhūvittha* (he was)—these are the forms of the remote past (*parokkhā*);
*tumhe abhavattha* (you all were), *so abhavattha* (he was)—these are the forms of the recent past (*hiyyattani*);
and *tumhe abhavittha* (you all were)—this is the form of the current day (*ajjatani*).

The third person singular form of the *parokkhā* tense is similar to two other forms: the third person singular of the third person active (*parassapada*) in the past tense (*hiyyattani*), and the third person singular of the third person middle (*attanopada*) in the present tense (*ajjatani*).
"Ahaṃ babhūvaṃ" is the form for the *parokkhā*; "ahaṃ abhavaṃ" is the form for both the past and the present tenses.
The third person plural *parassapada* of the *parokkhā* tense is similar to the third person plural *parassapada* of the past (*hiyyattanī*) tense.
"Mayaṃ babhūvimha" is the form for the *parokkhā*; "mayaṃ abhavamha" is the form for the past (*hiyyattanī*).
The first person singular *attanopada* of the *parokkhā* tense is [similar] to the first person singular *attanopada* of the past (*hiyyattanī*) tense.

And it is similar to two forms: the third person singular of the *parassapada* (active voice) for the *ajjatani* (present) tense, and the first person singular of the *attanopada* (middle voice) for the *ajjatani* tense.
"Ahaṃ babhūviṃ" is the form for the *parokkhā* (aorist) tense. "Ahaṃ abhaviṃ" is the form for the *hiyyattani* (past) and *ajjatani* tenses.
The third person singular *parassapada* of the *hiyyattani* is similar to the first person singular *attanopada* of the *ajjatani*. "So abhavā."
The third person singular *parassapada* form of the past tense (*hiyyattanī*) is similar to the third person singular *parassapada* form of the present tense (*ajjatanī*). You were (*tvaṃ abhavo*).
The second person plural *parassapada* form of the future tense (*bhavissanti*) [is similar] to the second person plural *parassapada* form of the past tense (*kālātipatti*), as well as to two forms:
the second person plural *attanopada* and the first person singular *parassapada*.

It is similar. "Tumhe bhavissatha" (you will be) is the form for the future tense (*bhavissati*). "Tumhe abhavissatha," "so abhavissatha" (you/that person would have been)—these are forms for the past conditional (*kālātipatti*).
The third-person singular middle voice (*attanopada*) of the future tense is [replaced] by the third-person singular middle voice of the past conditional.
It is similar. "Tvaṃ bhavissase" is the form for the future; "idaṃ bhavissantiyā rūpaṃ. "Tvaṃ abhavissase" is the form for the past tense (kālātipatti);
"idaṃ kālātipattiyā rūpaṃ. The second person plural middle voice (attanopada) of the future is similar to the second person plural middle voice of the past tense:
"tumhe bhavissavhe" is the form for the future; "idaṃ bhavissantiyā rūpaṃ. "Tumhe abhavissavhe" is the form for the past tense; "idaṃ kālātipattiyā rūpaṃ."

The third person singular form of the future tense (*bhavissanti*) in the *attanopada* (middle voice) is similar to the third person singular form of the past conditional (*kālātipatti*) in the *parassapada* (active voice).
"I shall be" (*ahaṃ bhavissaṃ*) is a form of the future tense; "I would have been" (*ahaṃ abhavissaṃ*) is a form of the past conditional.
It should be understood that all other forms for the various cases and numbers are dissimilar from one another. On this point, there are these verses:
In the present tense and the fifth (imperative), two forms ending in *tha* are proclaimed;
for example, in the case of "tumhe bhavatha," there are two types of illustrations.
In those same tenses, two forms ending in *mi* and two forms ending in *ma* are likewise stated in each case.
“Bhavāmi” (I am) and “bhavāma” (we are)—here one should point out the forms.
In the present tense (*vattamāna*), the future (*hiyyatta*), and the periphrastic future (*najjatani*) case endings, this set [of forms] occurs:
“bhavase tvam” (you are), derived from the present tense case ending.
The form “abhavase” is derived from the past (hyastana) and recent (adyatana) tenses.
This [form] has been explained there in relation to the present (vartamāna),
fifth (pañcamī), and remote (parokṣā) tenses, by way of the first two [suffixes].
One should know that the forms *aham* (“I”) and *tvam* (“you”) are used for the future (*bhave*),
the remote past (*babhūve*), and the three tenses— the present, the non-remote past, and the day-past (*ajjatani*)— as they are designated by the suffixes *-mi*,
*-si*, *-ti*, *-ma*, *-tha*, *-nti*, *-mha*, *-tha*, *-nta*. The form *mhettayam* follows in sequence, distinguished by the word *mayaṃ* (“we”).
One should indicate [the past] by saying: “sambhavāmhe,” “babhūvimhe,” and “abhavimhe.
For in the fifth person (pañcamī) and the present (aparokkhā), the form here consists of two syllables, *ho*;
thus, “bhavavho” and “babhūvivho” are the forms specifically modified by the word “tumhe” (you).
In the case of the remote past (*parokkha*) and the past tenses of yesterday (*hiyyatta*) and today (*ajjatani*),
one should know that from the remote past the form is *uttayam* and *te babhūvu*;
from yesterday and today, one should know it is *te abhavu*.
In the case of the remote past tense (*parokkha*), as well as in the past and present tenses (*hyattana* and *najjatani*),
one should designate the fivefold group of verbal roots (*saddita*) together with their respective suffixes (*tatha-saṃyoga*).
Among those, one should know that the two forms *babhūva* and *ittha* are the forms born of the remote past tense.
The forms called "middle" and "first" are stated according to plurality and singularity;
they should be known as the two bases for non-existence (*abhava*) arising from the past tense suffixes (*hiyyattanī-vibhatti*);
these are the middle and the first, stated according to plurality and singularity.
“Abhavittha”—this is a verbal form derived from the suffix of the present day (*ajjatanī*).
Furthermore, it should be construed with the word *tumhe* (you) when there are multiple agents;
it is prescribed for the aorist (*parokkhā*), the benedictive (*āvha*), the conditional (*hiyyattanī*), and the present day (*ajjatanī*).
In that context, the form *ādim* is stated as having been "babhūva";
one should join the form *abhavam* of the two [verbs] with the word *aham*.
According to the rules for the remote past (*parokkhā*) and the first person plural (*kāhiyyattanī*), *mhadukam* becomes *mayaṃ*.
"Babhūvimha" and "abhavimha"— these two forms are used respectively in the past tense (parokkhā),
the benedictive (hiyyattanī), and the present tense (najjatanī) case endings.
However, the form "babhūvi" is the one produced by the past tense (parokkhā).
But for the others, [the form] is *abhavim*, accompanied by the word *aham* (I),
in its entirety. Indeed, in this context, the opinion is that up to the second person (*ādvayaṃ*) in the past,
present, and future tenses, the form *abhavā* is the first-person singular (*ekatte*) form.
In the cases of the past and the future, however, "odvayaṃ" (the dual ending) is stated here;
in the sense of non-existence (*abhava*) when there is singularity, the form is the middle person.
Regarding the two acquisitions of the future time, it is spoken [as follows].
In the plural, the singular, with conjunctions, and in the three persons:
“you will be” (tumhe bhavissatha) is considered [the second person] from the perspective of the future;
likewise, “you will not be” (abhavissatha tumhe) and “he will not be” (abhavissatha so).
This pair of expressions is stated by way of the lapse of time (kālātipatti).
It is uttered in cases of the lapse of future time;
in the place of the second person, it consists of the pair *ss* and *se*, together with the conjunctive suffix.
"Bhavissase tvaṃ" and "Tvaṃ abhavissase"—
these are the grammatical applications (payoga) that a wise person should explain therein.
There are two forms ending in "ssavhe," joined with "sena," and four forms ending in "ssaṃ."
This too has been explained in two ways, according to the analysis of the literal sounds:
"bhavissavhe" is used for plurality and belongs to the future tense (bhavissantika) with the middle person;
"abhavissavhe" is used for plurality and belongs to the past tense (kālātipatti) with the middle person.
“Bhavissaṃ” (I shall be) is the preeminent future tense in the singular;
“abhavissaṃ” (I would have been) is the preeminent past conditional in the singular.
Thus, through these stated words, there is a correspondence with those already mentioned.
"Whatever exists among those [factors], all that is established in forty-one ways.
The remaining fifty-five are entirely dissimilar.
Having grasped this method, declare what is possible in every case."
This is the summary of the numbers [of verbal suffixes] here, according to whether they are identical or non-identical.
Regarding the summary of case-number and verbal number by way of the characteristics of the traditional texts (āgama), it should be noted as follows:
In the future tense, the remote past, today, the present, and the past tenses;
In some instances it is permanent, in others it is impermanent; there occurs the addition of the letter *i*.
Indeed, that addition of the letter *i* occurs in the *parokkhā* (aorist) case-ending:
in the plural number at the middle position, and in the plural number at the highest (first person) position.
This statement was uttered with reference to the parassapada (third person) endings.
Furthermore, it should be understood that even the singular form of the third person does not function as an ātmanepada (first person) ending; this applies entirely to all future forms.
Furthermore, in the cases of *hiyyattan*, *ajjattan*, and *kālātipatti*, there is the addition of the letter *a* in its entirety; this is how one should observe it.
In the present tense (*ajjatanimhi*), when there is plurality, as well as in the middle and the highest [persons], [the same applies].
In the case of *bavhattha*, there is the insertion of the vowel *i*.
The insertion of *i* occurs invariably in the sense of "passing beyond time" (*kālātipatti*);
however, the insertion of *a* in that same context is said to be non-universal (*anekantika*).
The addition of the vowel *a* indeed indicates the past tense (*hyattanya*);
in the remote future (*parokkhā*), only the vowel *i* is seen.
There is both the addition of the vowel *a* and the addition of the vowel *i*.
However, [the particle] *ajja* is seen in the forms *ajjatanika*, *kāla*, and *atīta*.
Among the three remaining case endings, the triad of *nā* (namely, *na*, *ne*, *nā*) is not prescribed;
this applies entirely to the present tense (*vattamānā*), the fifth case (*pañcamī*), and the seventh case (*sattamī*).
Accompanied by the vowel *i* alone, there are two case endings (*vibhatti*);
one should observe that there are seven and twelve number forms (*vacana*) therein.
Accompanied by the vowel *a* alone, however, there is only one case ending.
One should observe that there are twelve declensions here.
When combined with the suffixes *aka* and *ika*, there are only two case endings;
in this context, there are four and twelve declensions respectively.
But when freed from the three modes (ākāra), there are only three case-endings (vibhatti);
one should explain that there are thirty-six words (vacana) here.
In the past (parokkhā) and present (ajjatanī) tenses, there are five and eight [words] respectively.
"Words become liberated from the letter *i*.
Thus, herein, the inclusion of the case-endings (*vibhatti*) and the ninety-six types of words (*vacana*) should be understood by the discerning.
This is the summary of case-terminations and numbers according to the characteristics of the scriptures (*āgama*).
However, in the summary of case-terminations and numbers according to time, there is a twofold summary: the summary by way of the three times and the summary by way of the six times.

Among these, the present tense (*vattamāna*), the fifth (optative), and the seventh (imperative) terminations belong to the present time; those ending in the present tense, the fifth, and the seventh terminations—
Words are expressions pertaining to the present. The *parokkhā*, *hiyyattanī*, and *ajjatani* case-endings are past-tense;
words ending in the *parokkhā*, *hiyyattanī*, and *ajjatani* case-endings are expressions of the past. The *bhavissanti* case-ending is future-tense;
words ending in the *bhavissanti* case-ending are expressions of the future. The *kālātipatti* case-ending, however, is sometimes past-tense and sometimes future-tense.
Therefore, words ending in those [suffixes] can express both the past and the future. This is the summary of case-suffix expressions according to the three times.
Furthermore, this is the summary of case-suffix expressions according to the six times—the *parokkhā*, *hiyyattanī*, and *ajjatanī* suffixes.
Words ending in past tense suffixes (*atītakālika*), as well as those ending in the remote past (*parokkha*), the conditional (*hiyyattan*), and the present (*ajjatanī*), are expressions of the past.
The future tense suffix (*bhavissanti*) is of the future time; words ending in the future tense suffix are expressions of the future.
The present tense suffix (*vattamāna*) is of the present time; words ending in the present tense suffix are expressions of the present. The fifth case suffix (*pañcamīvibhatti*)...

The fifth case-ending (*pañcamīvibhatti*) is the time of command; words ending in the fifth case-ending are expressions of command. The seventh case-ending (*sattamīvibhatti*) is the time of supposition;

words ending in the seventh case-ending are expressions of supposition. Here, however, the terms "expressions of command" and "expressions of supposition" are used merely as conventional designations, because the fifth and other case-endings are seen to occur in instances such as injunctions (*āsiṭṭha*) and permissions (*anumati*).
[This concludes] the section on the tense of past non-occurrence (*kālātipatti-vibhatti*).

The *kālātipatti* tense is that which expresses the lapse of time; the words ending in the terminations of the *kālātipatti* tense are called *kālātipattivacanāni*. Thus, the compendium of case-terminations and verbal moods should be understood by way of the sixfold division of time (*kālachakka*).
Within the compendium of time, there is a threefold compendium of time: the compendium of the three times, the compendium of the fourfold time, and the compendium of the sixfold time.
The present tense occurs in the fifth and seventh cases;
the past tense, including the remote past and so forth, occurs with the lapse of time (*kālātipatti*);
the future tense occurs in the sixth case, or optionally with the lapse of time.
Thus should the three times be understood, as explained by that which elucidates them.
Is it not stated in the Kaccāyana treatise that time is fourfold:
the past, the future, and the time expressed by the present?
The time expressed as "truth" (sacca) is intended as the present;
however, it is also called the "proximate time" because of the possibility of its meaning [applying to other times].
For thus it has been stated by the teachers: "That which is the three times..."
Nothing whatsoever is seen that is declared to be devoid of time.
Yet, even when the time is not explicitly stated, the meaning therein is appropriate;
for thus, sixfold time is elucidated in the *Nirutti*.
The past, the future, the present, the imperative, the conditional, and the lapse of time—thus it is sixfold.
Among these, there are two moods: the imperative and the conditional.
Even though the grammarians have explained [the forms] *gacchatu* and *gaccheyya*, when such words are uttered,
the action does not reach completion; it is neither yet to come nor already past.
Words involving the lapse of time (kālātipatti) refer to both the past and the future;
thus they are described by the learned in grammar.
Those formed with the fifth and seventh case endings express commands and possibilities.
"They occur in the present" is not how it was stated there. Therefore,
in the Kaccāyana treatise, regarding the word "anuttakāle," its meaning should be understood here as "at a time when [something] has not been stated."
Even though this is indeed so, a wise person who understands the underlying method should regard even the present as being subject to both commands and hypothetical constructions. Why?
Because both the issuing of a command and a hypothetical construction are real.
"Since these purposes are seen to be accomplished in the present,
the phrase 'at a time not past' indicates this meaning; or rather,
it is so called because it expresses a time proximate [to the present]."
The accomplishment of actions such as going and so forth is not seen at the very time when [the verb] "let him go" or "he went" is uttered; therefore,
the case endings indicated at that time are those which point to the time [of the action] when it was not yet being uttered.
"Or 'the time' means the stated time"—it is thus that [time] is understood here.
In the recitation concerning the purification of the offering (*dakkhiṇāsuddhi*), this third [case ending] has indeed been employed;
for it is only in this way that their function as indicators of time is appropriate, and not otherwise.
In order to clarify two meanings within the treatise known as Kaccāyana,
the Elder Kaccāyana spoke the phrase "nutta-kāle.
Thus, the compendium of tenses is stated in three ways and also in four ways.
Now, the compendium of the four tenses is set forth.
The parokkhā (aorist) and the past tense endings—
namely, the hyastanī and the adyatani— these three are declared for the past.
Those [optatives] used for the future are designated as *bhavissanti*;
those used for the present are *vattamāna*. Thus, they are made fivefold across the three times.
Those ending in the fifth and seventh [case endings] are prescriptive (*āṇatti*) and hypothetical (*parikappika*).
When they are being combined, they go into combination with the present tense.
Because it is identical to the fifth [case] by virtue of its status as that which is currently occurring,
it is therefore considered the fifth case.
Although the seventh [tense] is indeed similar to those [other tenses] as a seventh, it is nevertheless called the "seventh" because it occurs after them; such is our opinion.
If, on account of the lapse of time (*kālātipatti*) and so forth, it were thus a present tense (*vattamānika*), [then...]
The sixth [case] would be that which expresses the past time that has already elapsed.
Is it not the case that the fifth [case] is identical to the sixth in terms of its position?
Through those seven case-endings, there may be a seventh and an eighth.
If anyone should say this, one should reject it with "no," because of the possibility of the lapse of time regarding both the past and the future.
For thus has this been stated separately in the *Cūḷanirutti*.
One should explain [the rule] as "past" for both the lapse of time (*kālātipatti*) and the future.
Why, then, is it stated in the *Kaccāyana* that it is "past" only when there is a lapse of action (*kriyātipanna*)?
Furthermore, if one were to say this, one should clarify it by adding the word "mostly" (*pāyena*).
For in the world, usage for the most part proceeds with reference to the past, connected with the lapse of time; such is the characteristic to be observed.
Herein, this expression for the past due to the lapse of time is as follows: "If, monks, this king [should have] his righteous father, a righteous monarch..."
“You shall not deprive him of life; rather, even on this very seat, the dustless, stainless Eye of Dhamma will arise within him.
“Behold, Ānanda, this son of a great treasurer, who has squandered eighty-two crores of wealth right here in this city, and having taken a wife, is now wandering for alms.
For if he had not squandered his wealth during his youth, he would have [established] his enterprises...”
If he applies himself to his business in this very city, he will become the foremost merchant.
But if he goes forth and renounces the world, he will attain arahantship, and his wife will be established in the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala).

If, in his middle age, he does not squander his wealth but applies himself to his enterprises, he will become the second-most prominent merchant. One who goes forth and renounces the world [in that case] becomes a non-returner (anāgāmī).

“...he would have become a third merchant; had he gone forth and renounced the world, he would have become a once-returner, and his wife too would have been established in the fruit of stream-entry. Or: “If the Teacher were to live as a householder...”

“He would have been a wheel-turning monarch; the novice Rāhula would have been the counselor-treasure, the Elder Nun the woman-treasure, and the sovereignty over the entire world-system would have belonged to them alone.
In this way, there is a statement in the past tense due to the lapse of time.
How is there a statement in the future tense due to the lapse of time? “He would have remained food for a long time, if he had not...”
“We are disputing: ‘A jackal carries off a rohita fish that has no head and no thumb,’ or:
‘If, Ānanda, women had not obtained the going-forth from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, the holy life, Ānanda, would have lasted long,’ or:
‘This is the mother of Aṅgulimāla, thinking, “I will bring back Aṅgulimāla.”’”
"He goes; if he meets [him], Aṅgulimāla will kill his mother, thinking, 'I shall complete my thousand fingers.
If I do not go, there will be a great loss. In this way, there is a statement regarding the future due to the lapse of time (*kālātipatti*).
However, in the *Kaccāyana*, for the most part, it refers to past occurrence (*atītappavatti*) by means of the tense of the lapse of time.
It should be understood that "belonging to the past" (atītakālikatā) has been stated [in this context].
However, in the *Kaccāyana* as well, this same meaning is seen:
"it also occurs in the future," whereas [the term] *kālātipatti* refers to the past.
"In the case of what is not directly perceived, the past tense is used for the remote [past]—such is the characteristic.
Even though it exists, the mention of the 'past' here is made without regard for that [rule].

Because it speaks of the lapse of time, there is the drawing forward of what is yet to come;

[This is expressed] by means of the tenses pertaining to the past, future, and present.
The seventh [case] remains as the seventh itself and does not become the eighth.
