It should be understood by the discerning that [the term] is stated for the purpose of including it within the present tense (paccuppanna-vibhatti) under the fifth case-ending (pañcamī). However,
starting from the fifth case-ending, it is included within the seventh case-ending (sattamī).
There must be a sixth [case], yet it is not called "the sixth";
rather, taking the sixth as a reference point, it is called "the seventh.
Even when speaking in this manner, one does not explicitly show the sixth in between.
One should discern the underlying intention [of the author] when it is stated that [the term] was spoken for the purpose of inclusion within the seventh case-ending (locative) and the present tense.
For this is the inherent nature of things regarding their own profound meanings.
The making known of one's intention by whatever means possible.
If this is so, then after explaining the case-endings (*vibhatti*) for the past and the future first, the case-endings for the present should be taught thereafter.
Why were they not spoken thus in the treatise called *Kaccāyana*;
why were only the present case-endings spoken at the beginning?
Because they say that these [endings] alone are sufficient for the path of worldly discourse.
Therefore, these case endings possess manifold applications.
According to the established method, their manifold application must first be explained;
it is held that the case endings arise from the present tense onwards.
Having spoken of the past and the future, thereafter [he speaks] of the present;
for when this is stated, there is elegance of expression in the world.
Therefore, in speaking with elegance, one should take into account the past and so forth.
The fifth and seventh [cases] are taught for the purpose of including [the present tense] immediately following the present tense within the case endings of the present. For here,
just as when "mother and father" is said, there is a smooth expression, yet in that very same statement, the reverse [of the singular] occurs.
When one says "father-mothers" (*pitāmātaro*) by way of a compound, it does not constitute elegant speech; therefore, such a verbal construction is not worthy of honor.
However, the reading "may my father and mother give" (*pitā mātā ca me dajjuṃ*) is worthy of honor because, being expressed by way of analysis, it allows for the desired application [of the terms].
In exactly the same way, when one says "past, future, and present" (*atītānāgatapaccuppanna*), it constitutes elegant speech, whereas "past, present, and future" (*atītapaccuppannānāgata*) does not.
When stated in such a manner, the expression is not smooth; therefore, such a verbal construction would be unworthy of honor.

However, the statement, “Having past objects, it ranges over the present and the future,” is indeed worthy of honor because it is intended for the ease of metrical composition and allows for the application of words as desired.
This is the canonical text (pāḷi) to be understood here:
“Whatever form there is—past, future, or present,” and:
“The one who sees the end of birth follows the single path;
the compassionate one understands the way.”
"By this path those of old have crossed, and those who will cross and those who are crossing the flood," and:
"Those Perfectly Enlightened Ones who have passed away, and those Buddhas yet to come..."
“Those who are fully enlightened now, the destroyers of the sorrow of many—
all of them, honoring the true Dhamma, have lived, do live,
and likewise will live; this is the natural law of the Buddhas.”

Thus, among these various applications of grammatical terms, here, by way of the application as desired, three present-tense case-endings (*vibhatti*) have been stated at the beginning out of the eight case-endings belonging to the past, future, and present times.
And that statement was made for the purpose of making known their great utility, since they mostly occur in the path of common usage. Of those [three], however, two...
The technical designations "fifth" and "seventh" for the case endings should be stated in their proper sequence when there is a desire for elegant expression;
they are established with reference to the past and future tenses.
Thus, by means of such desired application, the present case endings [are distinguished].
Having divided [the subject] into three parts, it was proclaimed by Kaccāyana at the beginning.

Regarding the verbal root *bhū* in the sense of "being," its form designated as a verb (ākhyāta) is spoken of in various ways without confusion, ending in suffixes such as *ti* and so forth.
Now, its form known as a noun (nāmika), ending in suffixes such as *si* and so forth, is likewise explained.
I shall speak upon the meanings of words so that listeners may attain proficiency.
Those wise ones have declared that which bends (*namati*) toward its own meaning or toward the meanings of others is called "name" (*nāma*).
In this context, "name" (nāma) and "nominal" (nāmika) are one and the same;
thus, that which is nominal should be understood as possessing gender and case-endings.
Gender (liṅga) refers to the designation of sentient beings, namely: feminine, masculine, and neuter.
In this context, there are seven case endings (vibhatti), and among them, four are specifically mentioned:
the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh; thus, there are seven case endings.
In the sense of gender (liṅga), the first case (paṭhamā) is feminine (sāyaṃ), divided into two as "si" and "yo";
in the sense of object (kamma), the second case (dutiyā) is also [feminine], divided into two as "aṃ" and "yo".
In the sense of instrument (karaṇa), the third case (tatiyā) is also [feminine], divided into two as "nā" and "hi".
The fourth case (catutthī) is used for the recipient (sampadāna); it is divided into two types: *sa* and *naṃ*.
The fifth case (pañcamī) is used for the source (apādāna); it is divided into two types: *smā* and *hi*.
The sixth case (chaṭṭhī) is used for the possessor (sāmī); it is also divided into two types: *sa* and *naṃ*.
The locative case is seventh; it is also divided into two types: "smin" and "su.
The vocative is eighth; with "siyā" and "eva," there are fourteen.
Each of these case endings is connected to two forms.
"Being" (satva) is to be understood here as the meaning designated by the term "substance" (dabba).
That which acts is the agent (kattā), or that which it performs is the action (kamma);
or else, that by means of which one acts, such as a shuttle, is designated as the instrument (karaṇa).
That which one gives to, or which finds pleasure in, is considered the recipient (sampadāna);
that from which fear arises is proclaimed as the source (apādāna).
That over which a group has authority is indeed taught as the possessor (sāmī).
That in which one performs an action is termed the "occasion" (*okāsa*).
That which one addresses is the "subject matter" (*vatthu*), and it is declared to be an "addressing" (*āmantana*).
It is the act of making someone present by means of sound, whether that person is actually present or not.

It should be understood that, except for the purpose of address (*ālapanattha*), the arising of the nominative and other case endings in the sense of gender (*liṅgattha*) and so forth is stated by way of illustration.
Herein, this is to be seen as the characteristic of grammatical derivation (*niruttilakkhaṇa*): the nominative case ending occurs in the sense of the direct object (*paccattavacana*);

the accusative case ending occurs in the sense of the objective case (*upayogavacana*); the instrumental case ending occurs in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇavacana*); the dative case ending occurs in the sense of the recipient (*sampadānavacana*).
The fourth case ending occurs; in the sense of departure, the fifth case ending occurs; in the sense of possession, the sixth case ending occurs;
in the sense of location, the seventh case ending occurs; in the sense of address, the eighth case ending occurs.

The direct (paccatta), the instrumental (upayoga), the agentive (karaṇa), the dative (sampadāniya);
the ablative (nissakka), the genitive (sāmivacana), the locative (bhummam), and the vocative (ālapana) as the eighth.

Among these, the direct case (paccattavacana) refers to that which serves to express the individual nature of the three genders—feminine, masculine, and neuter—as established by their respective characteristics.

The term "instrumental case" (upayoga-vacana) signifies the purpose of indicating that which is employed by whoever performs an action. The term "agentive case" (karaṇa-vacana) signifies the purpose of indicating that which brings about the production of the result.
The term "dative case" (sampadāna-vacana) signifies the purpose of indicating the act of giving that [result] to someone.

The term "ablative case" (nissakka-vacana) signifies the purpose of indicating departure from or separation from something. The term "genitive case" (sāmī-vacana) signifies the purpose of indicating the owner or possessor of something.

The term *bhummavacanaṃ* (locative case) has the purpose of indicating the locus of that [action]. The term *āmantanavacanaṃ* (vocative case) has the purpose of indicating the addressing of that [person].

How so? [In the forms] *bhūtā*, *parābhūtā*, *sambhūtā*—all of this should be taken in detail—as well as *anubhontī*, *samanubhontī*, and so forth.
Having excluded nine words—those being joined by way of the vowel *ī*—these [remaining] are included among those of fixed gender (*niyataliṅga*).
Thus, the fourfold feminine genders derived from the root *bhū* have been illustrated by way of the vowels *ā* and so forth. This is the illustrative list according to the feminine gender:
*bhūtaṃ*, *mahābhūtaṃ*, *bhavittaṃ*, *bhūnaṃ*, *bhavanaṃ*, *parābhavanaṃ*, *sambhavanaṃ*, *vibhavanaṃ*.

Manifestation, appearance, disappearance, separation, well-being, contempt, overcoming, surpassing, experiencing, experiencing together, and experiencing in succession—these are neuter nouns with a final nasalized vowel (*niggahīta*).
Examples include *atthavibhāvi* (one who discerns the meaning) and *dhammavibhāvi* (one who discerns the Dhamma).
These are neuter nouns ending in the vowel *i*.
Gotrabhū, cittasahabhū, nacittasahabhū. These are neuter nouns ending in the vowel *u*.
All of these should be understood as being neuter by their very nature.

Here, it should also be understood that the word *bhūta* itself, when denoting the primary elements (*bhūtarūpa*), is necessarily neuter. In this context as well, *bhūta* and *parābhūta* are of indefinite gender.
The forms beginning with *sambhūta* are appropriate in the neuter gender.
How so? *Bhūtaṃ*, *parābhūtaṃ*, *sambhūtaṃ*, *vibhūtaṃ*. [This is] the abbreviated series (*peyyāla*).
*Samanubhavamānaṃ*, *paccanubhavamānaṃ*, *anubhontaṃ*, *anubhavantaṃ*, *samanubhontaṃ*, *samanubhavantaṃ*, *paccanubhontaṃ*, *paccanubhavantaṃ*.
Arising, coming into being, fully arising, fully coming into being, manifesting, becoming manifest,
prevailing, prevailing over, overcoming, overcoming beyond, cultivating, causing to arise together,
causing to distinguish, causing to prevail over, being caused to prevail over, being enjoyed, being used.
The elision follows. *Paccanubhaviyamānaṃ* and *paccanubhuyyamānaṃ*—these are forms whose gender has been inserted among the fixed neuter nouns.
Thus, the three types of neuter genders derived from the root *bhū*, beginning with those ending in the nasal stop (*niggahīta*), have been illustrated.
This is the presentation of examples by way of the neuter gender; in this manner, the three genders derived from the root *bhū*, beginning with the masculine, have been pointed out.
"Whatever sounds have been explained here as not well-established by me,
those should be sought out within the sections of the Canon by one who is discerning.
[The vowels] o, ā, the nasal dot (bindu), i, ī, u, and ū are situated at the end in seven ways."
The distinctions of gender are thus described by those learned in etymology:
the five endings beginning with *ā*, *i*,
and *u* vowels are to be understood as feminine distinctions, or alternatively, all six [vowel endings] ending in *o*.
The vowels *i*, *u*, and *bindu* (m) are to be known as the three endings by one who discerns;
they are described by those learned in etymology as the distinctions of the neuter gender.
In the masculine gender there are seven endings, while in the feminine there are five or six.
In the neuter gender there are likewise three; thus, with five [genders], they are sixfold.

However, since words such as "bhūta" (being) and so forth—when spoken by way of etymology, denotation, explanation of meaning, establishment of the word's function, synonyms, and extraction of the intended sense—become clear and easy to understand, we shall explain their etymologies and so on as far as possible.
It is for the purpose of generating satisfaction in the wise and for the sake of the listeners obtaining a more acute intelligence regarding the meanings.
In this context, "existent" (*bhūta*) means that which comes into being through the manifestation of the aggregates; this, first of all, is the etymological derivation (*nibbacana*).

"Existent" is said to refer to a being (*satta*) by way of including everything; this is the statement of the referent (*abhidheyyakathana*). [As it is said: "And whatever being has come to devour time, they shall all alike lay down [their bodies]."
And the phrase “the collection of elements in the world” is the supporting statement for this meaning.
Alternatively, *bhūta* refers to a specific class of beings belonging to the non-human race (amanussajāti) who bear that name; this is the statement of the literal referent (*abhidheyyakathana*).

And the phrases “one skilled in spirits,” “a physician of spirits,” and “seized by a spirit” are supporting statements for this same meaning. Furthermore, regarding the terms “being,” “mortal,” and “creature,” and so forth, therein—
The term that has come down there is a synonym for the word *bhūta*, which expresses the meaning "a being.
Furthermore, what appears in the Niddesa Pāḷi as “*maccu*, *satto*, *naro*, *mānavo*, *poso*, *puggalo*, *jīvo*, *jagu*, *jantu*, *hindagu*, *manujo*,” this too is merely a synonym.
All of these, taken together, are stated as follows:
A being, a mortal, a person, a creature, a living soul, an individual;
a progeny, a life-force, a wanderer, a spirit, a breathing thing, an embodied one, and likewise a Tathāgata.
A sentient being, a mother-creature, the world, a human, a youth, and a man.

The word *sarīra* is masculine when meaning "body" (*puma*), neuter when meaning "a being" (*bhūta*), and feminine when used for "progeny" (*pajāti*); this is according to gender, not according to meaning.
Thus, words denoting existing beings possess all three genders.
That being which crawls on its shanks is here called a *jaṅghala*;
the name "being" (*satta*) has been elaborated through the terms "living creature" (*pāṇa*) and "designation" (*abhidhāna*).
In this treatise, the terms "synonymous expression" (*pariyāyavacana*), "designation" (*abhidhāna*), and "conceptualization" (*saṅkhā*), among others, are synonymous.

These are intended [here]. However, by way of extracting the meaning, the word *bhūta* is seen in the sense of the five aggregates, humans, elements, eternal things, existing things, those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), sentient beings, trees, and so forth;
its application will be made manifest later in the analysis of the triad of "being" (*atthattika*).

"Bhāvaka" means one who develops (*bhāveti*), thus "bhāvaka. This is the etymological derivation (*nibbacana*). One who performs the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is a "bhāvaka. This is the statement of the referent (*abhidheyyakathana*). "The bhāvaka..."

“Clever and wise”—this is the statement that establishes this meaning. “A developer, intent on development, devoted to development, perfected in development”—this is a figurative expression (*pariyāya-vacana*).
These two phrases, “one who has become [so]” (*bhūto*) and “a developer” (*bhāvako*), are stated by way of the simple agent and the causal agent respectively.
Beyond this, because they are easy to understand by following the method of exposition, [the author] does not state “this is the etymological derivation” (*nibbacana*) and so forth.
In some instances, we shall present, as appropriate, statements that establish the meaning, figurative expressions, and summaries of the meaning.
For if all of these were presented in every case, there would be excessive prolixity in the text;
therefore, for those words whose meaning is already evident, we shall not state their referents, but shall provide only their etymological analysis (*nibbacana*). However, for those...
The meaning is profound; we shall explain their referent.
*Bhava* means becoming (*bhavana*); *bhava* is said to mean growth (*vuddhi*).

Because the root *bhū* is seen to be used in the sense of increase due to its connection with excellence, taking *bhavana* to mean "growing," [the term is explained]. In the phrase, "The king’s prosperity and the king’s adversity," this refers to the sense of growth.
This is the corroborating statement for the meaning. Alternatively, "existence" (*bhava*) refers to eternalism (*sassata*).

For the view that occurs by way of eternalism—namely, "the self and the world are eternal"—is the "eternalist view" (*sassatadiṭṭhi*); therefore, it is called "the view of existence" (*bhavadiṭṭhi*). This is the corroborating statement for this meaning.
Likewise, "existence" (*bhava*) refers to the "view of existence" (*bhavadiṭṭhi*), because it functions [with the thought] that "existence is eternal; it persists."

The eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*) is called the "existence-view" (*bhavadiṭṭhi*). Indeed, by eliding the latter member of the compound, *bhavadiṭṭhi* is referred to simply as "existence" (*bhava*).
The statement, "They declare liberation from existence through existence," is a scriptural passage that establishes this meaning. Herein is the meaning of the canonical text:
certain recluses or brahmins, through the existence-view, or through [the pursuit of] existence such as sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) and so forth, [seek] from all existence...

They spoke of liberation, which is the purification from the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). Alternatively, according to the meaning "that by which beings come into being (*bhavanti*) and increase," *bhava* refers to the merits that constitute success;
thus it is said: "Thus he has transcended both existence and non-existence. This statement serves as proof for this meaning.
Here, however, is the explanation of the Pāli words: *bhava* means success (*sampatti*).

“Non-existence” (*abhava*) means failure. Likewise, “existence” (*bhava*) means growth, while “non-existence” means decline. “Existence” means eternalism (*sassata*), while “non-existence” means annihilationism (*uccheda*).
“Existence” means merit (*puñña*), while “non-existence” means evil (*pāpa*); he has transcended all of that.

Furthermore, the aggregates (*khandha*) together with their spheres are also “existence. Passages such as “sense-sphere existence” (*kāmabhava*) and “form-sphere existence” (*rūpabhava*) serve to establish this meaning.

[This is] the statement. Herein, however, the aggregates (khandhā) are called "existence" (bhava) in the sense that "whatever is discerned obtains its own form," or in the sense that "it comes into being, it arises continuously from the origination of ignorance, craving, and so forth.

Space (okāsa), on the other hand, is "existence" in the sense that "beings and the phenomena of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) come into being and are born therein. Furthermore, both kamma-existence (kammabhava) and rebirth-existence (upapattibhava) are existence.
“Becoming. Regarding the statement, “With clinging as condition there is becoming; it is twofold: there is kamma-becoming and there is rebirth-becoming,” this is the supporting word for this meaning.
Therein, kamma itself is becoming, thus it is kamma-becoming. Likewise, rebirth itself is becoming, thus it is rebirth-becoming.

Here, it is called “becoming” because rebirth comes into being (*bhavati*); however, kamma is [also] called “becoming” because, as a cause of happiness, it is said, “The arising of Buddhas is a happiness.”

Thus it has been said. Because it is the cause of existence (*bhava*), it should be understood as "existence" by way of the designation for its fruit. Alternatively, because its characteristic is the act of bringing forth (*bhāvanā*), it brings forth;
thus it is "existence" (*bhava*). What does it bring forth? Rebirth (*upapatti*). Therefore, because it brings forth rebirth, it is called "existence.
Regarding the term "brings forth," the meaning is "produces" in the sense of an agentive cause. Alternatively, [it refers to the formula]: "With existence as condition, birth arises."
Because one comes into being by means of this, it is called "becoming" (*bhava*); thus, kamma-becoming is what is meant.
Furthermore: "The uninterrupted succession of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases as they proceed is called *saṃsāra*."

Saṃsāra is also existence (bhava) according to the definition already stated. The phrases, “Suffering in existence is the suffering of existence,” and “wandering in existence,” are statements that establish this meaning.

In that regard, in what sense is saṃsāra called existence? It is in the sense that the conventional designation for beings occurs therein—that is, in the mass of phenomena (dhamma-puñja) consisting of the succession of aggregates and so forth.
This is the explanation of the meaning of the word *bhava* by way of its functions as a noun (*bhāva*), an agent (*kattā*), an instrument (*karaṇa*), and a locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
Here we shall state the extraction of the meanings of the word *bhava*:
growth, excellence, merits, the aggregates, sorrow, and that which is designated as "non-existence";
cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) and eternalism—this is what is signified by the word *bhava*.
Craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*), the view of existence (*bhavadiṭṭhi*), rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*), and kamma-existence (*kammabhava*)—
all these are designated by the term "existence" (*bhava*). In certain passages of the Canon, there is a dyad consisting of craving for existence and the view of existence.
By the elision of the final member of the compound, it is expressed by the word *bhava*.
"Non-existence" (*abhava*) means that which is not existence.
It is fourfold: misfortune, loss, annihilation, and evil.
In the Teaching, these meanings are expressed by the word *abhāva*.
*Bhāva* refers to intention (*ajjhāsaya*), which is also called "purport" (*adhippāya*). Passages such as: "The state of mind (*thīnabhāva*) is difficult to discern;
a wise man should manifest his state toward the king’s wives; he reveals the state that has entered his heart"—these serve to establish this meaning.
...the word. Furthermore, the state of a thing (*vatthudhamma*) is also a *bhāva*. The statement, “Of those established by convention as *bhāva*,” is a supporting word for this meaning;
consciousness (*citta*) is also a *bhāva*. The statement, “You perform harmful and cruel deeds, and in your *bhāva* there is no skill whatsoever,” is a supporting word for this meaning.
Activity (*kriyā*) is also a *bhāva*. [The phrase] “characteristic of *bhāva*”...

And the statement, “the seventh case [is used] for existence” (*bhāvasattamī*), is a word that establishes this meaning. Furthermore, they say that “existence” (*bhāva*) is a synonym for “being” (*satta*);
or else, it is a designation for the root (*dhātu*). In that context, intention, the objective phenomenon, consciousness, and being—these are what “come to be,” thus they are “existence” (*bhāva*).
Likewise, it is “existence” because one “develops” (*bhāveti*) it; however, as an action, it is “existence” (*bhāva*) because it is the process of becoming (*bhavana*).

And that [existence] is of many kinds, according to birth, going to a state of being, maturation, and so forth. Furthermore, existence in the sense of a state is also "bhāva," which is called female-nature (*itthibhāva*), male-nature (*pumbhāva*), and the female faculty (*itthindriya*). Herein, this is the etymological meaning:
it is "bhāva" because by means of this, the mind and the designation become "a woman" or "a man."
This etymological derivation of *nattanomati* has been cited here based on the opinion of the lion-like ancient teachers, and not merely fabricated by me.
For this was said by the ancients: "The state of a woman is *itthibhāva*; or, by means of this, the mind and the designation become 'woman' (*itthī*)."

Regarding the term “itthibhāva,” likewise, in the case of *pumbhāva*, the analysis should be understood as follows: either *pumbhāvo* is “the state (*bhāva*) of a male (*puṃsa*),” or it is “that by which the mind and the designation come to be (*bhavati*) as ‘male’ (*pumā*),” thus it is called *pumbhāva*.
This is an explanation of the meaning of the word *bhāva* according to its functions as an agent, a state, or an instrument.

"Non-existence" (*abhāva*) means that which is not existence; what is it? It is emptiness (*suññatā*), the state of non-being. "Intrinsic nature" (*sabhāva*) means the being of itself (*attano bhāvo*);
the meaning is simply its own original state (*pakati*). Alternatively, "intrinsic nature" refers to whatever form is obtained by phenomena when their existence is possible;
it is the state known as the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), such as the modes of bending, deformation, hardness, touching, and so forth.
Such is the meaning. “Commonality or intrinsic nature is considered the characteristic of phenomena”—this is the statement that establishes this meaning.

Furthermore, *sabhāva* (intrinsic nature) is a phenomenon of ultimate reality (*paramattha-dhamma*) possessing its own characteristic. In what sense? In the sense of being "with" (*sa-*) "nature" (*bhāva*).
*Sabbhāva* means the nature of the good; it is the quality of the virtuous—such is the meaning. Alternatively, [it refers to] one's own...

Existence (*bhāva*) is the state of being (*sabbhāva*). The statement, "They cause [one] to grasp the state of being," is a word that establishes this meaning. Or, existence that is actually found is the state of being (*sabbhāva*).
The statement, "Such is the state of being of grasping," is a word that establishes this meaning.
This is an explanation of the meaning of the terms *sabhāva* and *sabbhāva* by way of establishing them as abstract nouns (*bhāvasādhana*).
*Sambhava* means arising (*sambhavana*), the act of arising, or logical consistency (*yutti*).
For logical consistency is called "arising" in such passages as, "Arising is the cause of grasping. Alternatively, it is *sambhava* because things arise from it;
for that from which anything arises is the source (*sambhava*). *Pabhava* means originating (*pabhavana*), continuity, or that which originates (*pabhavati*).
Or, it is the source (*pabhava*) of this. For that from which anything originates is the source.
Furthermore, it should be understood that these two terms, *sambhava* and *pabhava*, have the same meaning in some instances, but different meanings in others. How so?
The term *sambhava* denotes the act of arising, logical connection, designation, the nature of origination, and the sense of a condition; however, the term *pabhava* denotes the act of arising...

It expresses both the sense of origin and the sense of condition; therefore, setting aside the sense of condition, it should be understood as having a distinct meaning [from "cause"], yet it should also be understood as having a meaning identical to the sense of condition.
For it has been said: "Condition (paccaya), cause (hetu), source (nidāna), reason (kāraṇa), origin (sambhava), and originator (pabhava)—these are one in meaning, though different in phrasing."
“Root, cause, and source, likewise origin and birthplace;
origination, nutriment, and object—these are synonyms for ‘condition’ and ‘arising.

This verse also supports this meaning. This is an explanation of the meanings of the terms *sambhava* (origin) and *pabhava* (birthplace) by way of the grammatical functions of the abstract noun (*bhāva*) and the ablative case (*apādāna*).
Thus, in this context, six factors of accomplishment (sādhana) are explained by way of the agent, the object, the instrument, the point of departure, and the locus.

These become sevenfold when the recipient (sampadāna) is added as a factor of accomplishment; that [recipient] will be clarified further on in such passages as, "Dhanabhūtī is so called because wealth (dhana) became his (bhava).
In this manner, all factors of accomplishment are sevenfold according to the types of action performed.
These are what are also called "factors of action" (*kāraka*); there is no means of accomplishment other than these.
Here, the term "means of accomplishment" (*sādhana*) is explained for the sake of the proficiency of the wise regarding grammatical applications and the meanings [of words].

For indeed, verbal expressions joined with words whose means of accomplishment are poorly arranged have meanings that are difficult to understand, whereas those joined with words whose means of accomplishment are well-arranged have meanings that are easy to understand.
Therefore, [the meaning] is rooted in the accomplishment of the application (*payoga*), and the purpose (*attha*) is rooted in that application. For those wise ones who possess sharper intelligence,
being accustomed to explaining the purpose by performing it correctly in accordance with the application— such as in the case of passages like "He mostly uses robes that have been requested,
and only rarely those not requested"— they are indeed capable of grasping the meanings that must be understood through the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) among various other meanings.
It should be understood that they are, in every respect, upholders of the Blessed One’s dispensation of the scriptures (*pariyatti-sāsana*).
Hereafter, because it is easy to understand by following the method (*naya*), we shall not state, "This is the specific proof (*sādhana*).

We shall do so merely for the purpose of inspiring great respect among the wise regarding the words of the Supreme Victor, which possess various meanings and essences within their diverse and manifold textual formulations (*pāḷigatika*).

For the purpose of expanding the intelligence of those who hear, we shall bring forth and present, as appropriate from here and there among the Sutta, Geyya, Vyākaraṇa, Gāthā, and other divisions, only those words that accomplish the intended meaning.
"Pabhāva" (power) means that which comes into being (*bhavati*) through its own nature (*pakārato*); it is simply majesty (*ānubhāva*). "I do not see your power... [and so forth].
"By which you [shall go] to Mithilā"—this is the statement that establishes this meaning. "Experience" (*anubhava*) means the act of experiencing;
what is that? It is the act of enjoying. "Majesty" (*ānubhāva*) refers to power, energy, spells, splendor, and strength.

"One who has great majesty (*mahānubhāva*) is so called because he possesses a great majesty consisting of energy, or consisting of power, energy, spells, splendor, and strength"—this is the statement that establishes this meaning.
Radiance, energy, power, majesty, and strength— these five are called *ānubhāva* (majesty),
and you may also call them *pabhāva* (splendor). However, regarding the word *ānubhāva*,
it denotes meanings such as radiance (*teja*) and so forth.
The wise one should explain the etymology of the word *attha* according to its occurrence.

Alternatively, *ānubhāva* means that which is to be experienced as a fruit (*anubhavitabba-phala*). The statement, "He is of great power (*mahānubhāva*) because of the greatness of the fruit to be experienced," is the supporting word for this meaning.
*Parābhava* means perishing (*parābhavana*); alternatively, it is so called because one perishes (*parābhavati*).

“Failure. The statement, “Failure is easy to recognize,” is a word that establishes this meaning. Furthermore, according to the reading “*dhammadessī parābhavo*,” the etymology should also be understood from the perspective of the future tense:
“he will fail (*parābhavissati*), therefore it is failure (*parābhavo*). Alternatively, it is called “failure” because by means of it people fail (*parābhavanti*);
what is that? It is the state of being one who points out the Dhamma improperly, and so forth. “The first...”

“This is that ruin”—this statement establishes the meaning of this [term]. *Vibhava* means Nibbāna. For it is called *vibhava* because it has departed from existence (*bhava*), as in “it has departed from existence”;
and it is called *vibhava* because existence has departed from it due to its being the cause for such departure.
Furthermore, the great thieves of the defilements, which oppose the noble treasures, are called *vibhava* because they are cut off, destroyed, and eliminated from here.

“Cessation” (*vibhava*). Regarding the word “cessation” (*vibhava*) as a designation for *nibbāna*, the statement, “While existence (*bhava*) thus exists, cessation is to be sought,” is the proof for this point.
Furthermore, these are synonyms for *nibbāna*:
*Nibbāna*, cessation (*vibhava*), liberation (*mokkha*), cessation (*nirodha*), the deathless (*amata*), and the equal (*sama*);
The cessation of formations is the stilling of suffering, deathless and undecaying.
It is the turning away, the unconditioned goal, the state of peace, the unformed.
It is the further shore, the destruction of craving, the destruction of suffering, and the destruction of the fetters.
The security from bondage, dispassion,
the end of the world, the destruction of becoming,
liberation, and the cessation of formations.
Purity and complete purification by the virtuous;
liberation through deliverance, release, and the waning [of defilements]; Nibbāna, the exhaustion of acquisitions;
the peaceful unconditioned element, and the radiance shining in all directions.
The names [of the Buddhas] mentioned here are devoid of specific epithets;
a wise person should observe that they are designations for Nibbāna.
For terms such as "refuge" and "shelter" are indeed used in a relative sense.
Regarding the "Special Verses," one should explain these here:
The refuge, the shelter, the formless, the peaceful, the true, the unattached;
The very hard-to-see sanctuary, the ultimate resort, and the state beyond affliction.
Taintless, stable, eternal, consciousness that is non-manifesting;
Harmless, auspicious, secure, subtle, and supramundane.
Infinite, imperishable, an island, the ultimate, absolute state.
"Exquisite and deathless"—thus it should be analyzed in many ways.
However, by the teachers who explain the meaning of the term *gotrabhū*, it is said that "lineage" (*gotta*) refers to Nibbāna; thus it is spoken of as "lineage."
"Vibhava" refers to views such as destruction, annihilation, non-existence, and severance. In this context, "vibhava" has the sense of "destruction," "dissolution," "severance," and "perishing.

The statement, "Some proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and dissolution of an existing being; such is 'vibhava' for all phenomena," is a scriptural passage that establishes this meaning. [The term] "sampatti" [means attainment].

But specifically, it is called *vibhava* because it exists (*bhavati*) in a distinguished manner (*vi-*). The statement, “Those desiring to see the king’s glorious wealth (*siri-vibhava*),” is a word that establishes this meaning.
Furthermore, wealth is called *vibhava* because beings exist (*bhavanti*), increase, and attain growth, development, and abundance by means of it.
The statement, “He was reborn as the son of a brahmin possessing eighty million in wealth (*asīti-koṭi-vibhava*),” [establishes] this meaning.
This is the definitive statement. However, this is a figurative expression:
Wealth, property, substance, possessions, belongings, assets, goods, merchandise, one’s own, and purpose—these are the terms denoting wealth.

The view of annihilation (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), however, is called "non-becoming" (*vibhava*) because it is destroyed; it is "non-becoming" due to the grasping [of the idea]: "Both self and the world do not arise again after death.
The statement "craving for non-becoming" (*vibhavataṇhā*) is the word that establishes this meaning.
For "craving for non-becoming" is the name for craving accompanied by the view of annihilation. Herein, the analysis of the meaning is stated:
The views of annihilationism and nihilism regarding wealth, Nibbāna, and attainment are expressed by the term *vibhava*;
thus the wise should understand it.
"Manifestation" (*pātubhāva*) means the act of becoming manifest, a manifestation. "Appearance" (*āvibhāva*) means the act of appearing, an appearance; these two are [synonymous].
The meaning is simply "manifestness. "Disappearance" (*tirobhāva*) means the act of disappearing; it is concealment.
"Absence" (*vinābhāva*) means the act of being apart; it is separation. "Safety" (*sotthibhāva*) means the state of being safe; it is the state of well-being, the existence of happiness.
In its essential sense, however, it is simply fearlessness and the absence of calamity. "Existence" (*atthibhāva*) means the state of being present.

*Vijjamānatā* (the state of being present) is non-separation. *Natthibhāvo* (the state of non-existence) is non-existence, non-presence, separation, emptiness, vanity, and voidness. This concludes the section on masculine nouns ending in long vowels (*okāra*).
One who overcomes is a conqueror (*abhibhavitā*), anyone who overcomes another. Likewise, one who treats with contempt is a despiser; one who experiences is an experiencer (*anubhavatīti*).

The experiencer (*anubhavitā*) is anyone who experiences pleasure, pain, or neither-pleasure-nor-pain. Such is the one who experiences thoroughly (*samanubhavitā*). Regarding the term "one who experiences in succession" (*paccanubhavitā*):

here, just as in such expressions as "the giver of the Deathless" (*amatassa dātā*) or "the arouser of the unarisen Path" (*anuppannassa maggassa uppādetā*), the words "giver" (*dātā*) and so forth—which denote the agent—are construed with words like "of the Deathless" (*amatassa*) and so forth, which denote the object and end in the genitive case.

A construction (*yojanā*) is seen together [with these]; likewise, for these words as well, a construction such as "the conqueror of the enemy" (*paccāmittassa abhibhavitā*) and so forth should be made.
The same applies to other words of this kind. The Description of Masculine Nouns Ending in *ā*:
"He exists," thus he is "Bhavaṃ" (a venerable one). Or, "he will exist," thus he is "Bhavaṃ"—a person who is increasing. "He is easy to recognize, O Bhavaṃ."
“Defeat is easy to recognize: one who desires the Dhamma is a victor; one who rejects the Dhamma is defeated.
This statement serves as proof for this meaning. Alternatively, the person with whom one speaks may be addressed as “bhavaṃ” (sir/master), as in:
“Bhavaṃ Kaccāyana,” “Bhavaṃ Ānanda,” or “I imagine that bhavaṃ longs for the king’s wife as his consort,” and so forth. In these instances—
However, no regard should be paid to the etymological meaning (*dhātuttha*); regard should be paid only to the conventional meaning (*sammutiattha*), because of the statement:
"Conventional speech is true; it is the cause of worldly convention. For within the sphere of common usage, worldly convention alone is primary and not to be transgressed.

"He perishes" (*parābhavati*) means "perishing" (*parābhava*). Likewise: "contempt" (*paribhava*), "overpowering" (*abhibhava*), "experience" (*anubhava*). "He originates" (*pabhavati*) means "he arises" (*pahoti*).
“*Pabhavaṃ*” means that which can be produced; it refers to anyone who is capable. “*Appabhavaṃ*” means not being able to produce. This term *appabhava* is seen in the Jātaka:
“Like a cloud torn by the wind, I, weeping, approached a tree;
there, being unable to produce [any other support], I grasped a branch with my hands.”
In this regard, the following is an illustrative statement. This is the section on the masculine gender ending in *niggahīta*. Regarding "Dhanabhūti":
it means "may wealth (*dhana*) be his," thus he is Dhanabhūti. Regarding "Siribhūti": this is a designation for both splendor (*sobhā*) and wisdom and merit (*paññā-puñña*);
"may that be his" thus he is Siribhūti. Likewise, Sotthibhūti, Suvatthibhūti. This is the section on the masculine gender ending in *i*.
"Bhāvī" means one who has the habit of becoming (*bhavana-sīla*), one who is subject to becoming (*bhavana-dhamma*), or one who is proficient in becoming (*sādhukārī*); thus is "vibhāvī.
"Sambhāvī" and "paribhāvī" are likewise. In that context, "vibhāvī" refers to a wise person capable of discerning the meaning (*attha-vibhāvana*).
Here, such terms as "vidvā" (learned), "vijjāgata" (possessed of knowledge), and "ñāṇī" (possessed of wisdom) should be understood as synonymous expressions. On this point, there are these verses:
The learned one, one who has attained true knowledge, the knower, the one who has discerned, the wise, the sagacious;
the awakened one, the confident, the cognizant, the one who knows faults, the perceptive, the one who sees clearly;
the one with insight, the eloquent, the intelligent, the prudent, the poet.
Skilled, discerning, wise, possessed of a [sure] course, and possessed of insight;
having eyes, having ears, capable, steadfast, vast, and far-sighted;
endowed with wisdom, intelligent, and sagacious—such are their names, for they are illuminators.
The Exposition of Masculine Nouns Ending in *Ī*.

“Self-born” (*sayambhū*): he who comes into being by himself is self-born. Who is he? He is the Blessed One, the Sage of the Sakyans, who, without the instruction of another, personally penetrated all knowable phenomena and attained omniscience. For this was said by the Blessed One:
“I have no teacher; there exists no one equal to me.”
"In the world with its devas, there is no one who is my equal.
For I am the Arahant in the world; I am the unsurpassed Teacher;
I alone am the Perfectly Enlightened One; I have become cool and attained Nibbāna."

In terms of its essential meaning, however, the "Self-Become One" (*sayambhū*) is the continuum of aggregates (*khandhasantāna*) that has been refined by the perfections (*pāramitā*), which—along with self-originated knowledge (*sayambhūñāṇa*)—is free from all defilements (*kilesa*) together with their residual impressions (*vāsanā*). It is the substratum for an immeasurable multitude of qualities such as great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
Such a continuum of aggregates is called the "Foremost Person in the World. For this was said by the Blessed One: "Bhikkhus, there is one person..."
"A marvelous person arises in the world as he appears; what is that one person? It is the Tathāgata, monks, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

That one person is now well-known by names acquired through his qualities as they truly are, such as "the Omniscient One" and "the Sugata," and is also well-known by his clan as "Gotama" and "Kinsman of the Sun," and as "Son of the Sakyans," "Sakyan," and "Sakyamuni."
He is renowned by his lineage as the Lion of the Śākyas and the Bull among the Śākyas; he is renowned by his parents as the son of King Suddhodana and Queen Māyā;
and he is renowned by the name he assumed as Siddhattha. Regarding this, there are these verses:
"He who was that one person, the Buddha, the best among those who speak;..."
He is named Gotama, and likewise the Kinsman of the Sun.
Because he was born in the Śākya clan, he is renowned as the Son of the Śākyas (Śākyaputra);
he is addressed as Sakka, and likewise as the Sage of the Śākyas (Śākyamuni).
Because of his preeminence everywhere and because of his excellence among the Śākyas,
he was honored as "Sakyasīha" (Lion of the Śākyas) and "Sakya-puṅgava" (Bull among the Śākyas).
By his father, he was known as "Suddhodana," renowned like the moon in the sky.
Known even by his maternal kin as the son of Queen Māyā;
the All-Knowing One, the Sugata, the Buddha, the King of Dharma, the Tathāgata;
the Samantabhadra, the Blessed One, the Victor, the Ten-Powered Sage.
The Teacher, the Leader, the Protector,
the Lord of Sages, the Guide of the World;
the Bull among Men, the Conqueror of the World.
The Fully Enlightened One, supreme among bipeds;
the God of gods, honored by the world; the Lord of Dhamma, the Great Sage;
the All-Seeing One, charioteer of men to be tamed, conqueror of Māra.
The Lord of Dhamma, whose speech is free from duplicity, the Caravan Leader;
the Pure God, the God of Gods, the Sovereign of Recluses.
He of vast wisdom, the Unsurpassed One, the Lion among Men, the Possessor of Vision.
The sage among sages, the best of men, renowned among people as one possessing the six supernormal powers;
the son of Aṅgīrasa, king of ascetics, kinsman of the world, untiring;
the speaker, the promoter, the turner of the wheel of the True Dhamma, the lord of ascetics.
The island of the world, the treasury of glory, the lord of recluses, the supreme among men;
the knower of the three worlds, the lamp of the world, the highest of persons;
the seer of truth, endowed with the marks of a hundred merits, he who is truly named.
Unequaled and peerless in eloquence, the supreme person among the five-eyed;
the conqueror of all, the knower of all, whose name is Truth, the one who has gone beyond;
the preeminent man, the seer of all, the charioteer of humanity.
He is praised as the Fully Enlightened One, known as the Supreme among Beings,
the Such-like One, the Proponent of Analysis, and the Greatly Compassionate One;
he is extolled as the Embodiment of Vision, the Embodiment of Dhamma, and the Embodiment of Knowledge.
He is praised as "Brahmabhūta" and "Purisājañña";
as the "Foremost in the World," the "Self-Become One," the "Great Seer," and the "Crusher of Māra.
He is the "One of Unfailing Speech," the "Dhammakāya," and the "Conqueror of Māra."
The names of the Great Seer, based on his qualities, are incalculable.
Who, even among the wise, could describe them all?
For there, names such as "Omniscient" and others would be common [to him].
For all Buddhas, [the name] is not "Gotama" and so forth.
In the Teaching, both a Buddha and a Paccekabuddha are called "Self-Become" (*sayambhū*).
Some say "Brahmā is the Self-Become," but that is not within the scope of the Teaching.
The words “Buddho,” “Tathāgato,” “Satthā,” and “Bhagavā” circulate frequently throughout a thousand worlds.
Among these, however, these are the first and the last words.
"One should move even from a single [point]," thus the confident one should discern.
However, the words of distinction and the words of dependence—these words may be of two kinds: those that depend and those that do not depend.

For instance, such designating terms as "caravan leader" (*satthavāha*) and "supreme man" (*naravara*), or "one possessed of the six direct knowledges" (*chaḷabhiñña*), depend upon qualifying attributes.
How so? "The disciples, who have mastered the threefold knowledge and have overcome death, attend upon the unsurpassed caravan leader who has thus conquered the battle."
That which the world worships,
and which the world-protectors always revere—
this is the sublime teaching of that [Buddha].

“By the Knower, the Knowable is to be known by the Best of Men,” and “The Teaching of the One Possessed of the Sixfold Higher Knowledge”—such [terms] are dependent upon qualifying words. However, it should be understood that such forms as “Buddha,” “Jina,” and “Bhagavā” are not dependent upon qualifiers.
Some, however, might say here: “Muninda, Samaṇinda, Samaṇissara, Yatissara, Ādiccabandhu...”
"Because there is no difference in meaning among such designations as 'the kinsman of the sun' mentioned here, there is the fault of tautology. That is not so;
for designations are seen to be twofold: those that are constructed and those that are not constructed, depending on whether they are subject to mental formation (*abhisaṅkharaṇīya*) or not.
For instance, in some places, certain [beings] are called "the lion of the Sakyas."
Depending on the designation "Lion of the Sakyas," "Lord of the Deer of the Sakyas," and so forth, they construct various and manifold designations;
for even in the Pāvacana (the Word), the reading "Dviduggama-vara-hanutta-malatthā" is seen.
Likewise, some, depending on the designation "Dhamma King," construct such terms as "Dhamma Disampati. The designation "Omniscient One" (Sabbaññū)...
Based on the designation "all-seeing, all-seer," they construct such terms as these;
based on the designation "thousand-eyed," they construct such terms as "one with a thousand eyes.
Based on the designation "kinsman of the sun," they construct such terms as "kinsman of the companion of the lotus. Based on the designation "lotus-born," [they construct] "dustless" (*nīraja*).

They construct such names as "kuñja" and so forth. For even in the Pāli Canon, considering that whatever is a lotus is by definition "born in water," the reading "Jalajuttaranāmino" (He whose name is Jalajuttara) is found in place of what should have been "Padumuttaranāmino" (He whose name is Padumuttara), spoken by Noble Ones who have attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) by way of the elegance of their teaching.
Thus, such constructed designations are seen.
Furthermore, the designations such as “Buddha, the Blessed One” are unconditioned designations. For this has been said by the Dhamma-General, the Venerable Sāriputta:

“‘Buddha’—this name was not made by a mother, nor made by a father, nor made by a sister, nor made by kinsmen and blood-relations, nor made by deities; it is a designation pertaining to liberation belonging to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.”
“‘Buddha’ is a designation based on realization, namely, that which occurs together with the attainment of omniscient knowledge at the foot of the Bodhi tree”;
likewise, “‘Bhagavā’—this name was not given by his mother... [and so forth] ...it is a designation based on realization, namely, ‘Bhagavā’.
Thus, the designations “Buddha” and “Bhagavā” are unconditioned designations; for those designations do not [arise from causes].
Furthermore, names such as “Teacher,” “Sugata,” and “Conqueror” (Jina) are not constructed in dependence upon other designations,

nor are other designations seen to be constructed in dependence upon these. For instance, in dependence upon the designation “Buddha,” one does not construct further nominal designations such as “Awakened One,” “One who Awakens others,” or “The Awakener.”

Likewise, based on the designations of names such as "Bhagavā," "Satthā," and "Sugato," they do not further construct designations of names such as "one possessed of fortune," "instructor," or "one of beautiful speech. Thus, in order to demonstrate this distinction,
there is no tautology in the sequence beginning with "Munindo, Samaṇindo, Samaṇissaro, Yatissaro, Ādiccabandhu, Ravibandhu," and so forth.
It should be understood as "done by us. In this way, the method should be applied elsewhere as well. Regarding this, it is said:
"The name that is conditioned, and the name that is unconditioned— The Buddha is the one who has crossed over the two difficult paths; thus the name would be twofold."
One who is "pabhū" is a lord (issara), meaning one who exists having overcome others by force.

The statement, "This hunter is the master (pabhū) of the forest," is an expression that establishes this meaning. One who is "abhibhū" is one who overcomes; thus he is an "abhibhū," such as an unconscious being (asaññasatta).
What does he overcome? The four formless aggregates (arūpa-khandhā). Thus, because he overcomes the four formless aggregates, he is an "abhibhū. And furthermore—

Because of its constant state of intentionality, even in the absence of the act of overcoming prior to the arising of non-perception, at the time of attaining the jhāna, one develops the fifth jhāna already reached by means of the fading away of perception (*saññāvirāga*).
By causing the four formless aggregates (*arūpakkhandha*) not to occur within the state of non-perception (*asaññibhava*), one begins to overcome them;

since the task of overcoming them is now accomplished, it is said that "one overcomes" (*abhibhavati*), thus being called an "overcomer" (*abhibhū*). Furthermore, by virtue of its constant state of intentionality—

Even though the activity of overcoming is absent [in the present], because it possessed activity during its previous conscious state, it is entirely appropriate to speak of that which is now eternally unconscious as being "active" by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), just as one speaks of that which was conscious.

For in the world and in the Teaching (*sāsana*), we see instances where even that which is unconscious is spoken of as being active through metaphorical designation, just like that which is conscious. How so? In the world, for example: "The bank wishes to fall. But in the Teaching: [as follows]—
“Seeing the child rolling about, the vast trees, filled with anxiety, bent down of their own accord and approached the child”;
and “Now the trees are like glowing coals, O Blessed One, casting off their foliage in search of fruit”; and “The fruit satisfies the farmer.”

And so forth. Regarding the word *abhibhū* (the conqueror) denoting the non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*), the statement “he thinks he has conquered the conqueror” (*abhibhuṃ abhibhuto maññati*) is the proof for this meaning here.
Alternatively, one who conquers is a *abhibhū*; that is, anyone who is a conqueror of others.
Specifically, however, only the Tathāgata is the *abhibhū*. For this was said by the Blessed One: “Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata is the conqueror, unconquered.”
“...the one who sees all other things, the wielder of power. However, some say that “Abhibhū is the name for the Sahassa Brahmā.

He is called *vibhū* because he has become distinguished (*visesabhūta*). This meaning is supported by the following scriptural passage: “If the Buddha were the stream of existence, he would have crossed it; he is the one who has reached the end of the world, the *vibhū*.
Here, the meaning is that he has become distinguished by the excellence of both his physical body and his Dhamma-body. And it is said:
“Even when visible, his form-body is inconceivable;
what need is there to speak of the Dhamma-body, which is the domain of uncommon knowledge?
One who overcomes is an *adhibhū*; that is, a lord (*issara*).
“Then, scorched by the heat of my asceticism, the lord of the three worlds,
assuming the appearance of a brahmin, approached me for alms”—
this is the statement that establishes this meaning. *Patibhū* means one who has become a counterpart (*patibhūto*), as in “a counterpart of a bull.”

This is the statement that establishes the meaning of this term. One is called a *gotrabhū* because one has "become" (*bhūto*) by taking as an object the Deathless Great Nibbāna, which is designated as the lineage (*gotra*).
It refers to a person endowed with a mind of powerful insight that has reached its culmination through the immediate condition (*anantarapaccaya*) of the stream-entry path.
For this was said by the Blessed One: "And what kind of person is a *gotrabhū*? Those phenomena..."
“Immediately after [this], there is the descent of the noble Dhamma; a person endowed with those qualities is a ‘gotrabhū’”—this alone is the statement here that establishes the meaning.
Furthermore, one who merely experiences the lineage of a recluse—even a recluse with a yellow robe around his neck—is a *gotrabhū*.
For he experiences and finds the mere lineage of being a "recluse," but not the qualities of a recluse within himself.
Because it does not exist, it is called "the lineage" (*gotrabhū*). This statement serves as proof for this meaning:
"In the future, Ānanda, there will be those of the lineage who wear the saffron robes around their necks, yet are immoral and of evil character.
*Vatrabhū* is Sakka; for he, having attained the status of Sakka through the seven duties such as supporting his parents and so forth, [surpassed] others...

He overcomes by means of his duty (*vatta*), thus he is *Vatrabhū*. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, having also taken the sense of "attaining" (*patti*) which is obtainable from the verbal root *bhū*, it is stated:
"Having overcome others by means of his duty, he attained divine sovereignty, thus he is *Vatrabhū*"; and also:
"Or, because he overcomes the asura named Vatra, he is *Vatrabhū*"; and: "*Vatrabhū*, the father of the conquerors."
This is the statement that establishes the meaning of this word. For here, *vatrabhū* means the conqueror (*abhibhavitā*) of the asura named Vatra.
*Jayataṃ pitā* means the father of those who are victorious. Terms such as "Sakka, Indra, Purindada," and so forth, are synonymous expressions;
however, we shall explain these under the section on the Creator (Dhātā). *Parābhibhū* means one who overcomes others (*paramabhibhavati*). The same applies to *rūpābhibhū* and other such terms.
"Sabbābhibhū" means one who overcomes everything that is to be overcome; thus, he is "Sabbābhibhū.
And this name "Sabbābhibhū" is appropriate for the Tathāgata alone. For this was said by the Blessed One:
"I am the conqueror of all, the knower of all."
“Unstained by any phenomena, having abandoned everything,
liberated through the destruction of craving—
having realized this for himself, whom would he point to as his teacher?”
The exposition of masculine nouns ending in *ū*. This is the exposition of nouns with fixed gender.
Now, the exposition of words such as *bhūta*, *parābhūta*, and *sambhūta*—which have indeterminate genders but are included among those of fixed gender—is stated.
In that context, *bhūta* means "he has come into being" (*abhavī*) by means of his own conditions; thus, *bhūta* means "born," "fully born."
"Born," "fully born," or "manifested"—or else "become" (*bhūta*) means whatever has acquired its own form, whether conscious or unconscious.
Alternatively, it is "become" because it exists in such a manner; thus "become" means real, true, not false, and not perverted—whatever it may be.
Here, the word *bhūta* has the sense of truth; the phrase "the meaning of 'become'" (*bhūtaṭṭha*) is the statement that establishes this point.
*Parābhūto*: one who has fallen away (*parābhavī*) is *parābhūta*. *Sambhūto*: well-become (*suṭṭhu bhūto*). *Vibhūto*: specifically become (*visesena bhūto*).
Or, *vibhūto* means "renownedly become" (*vissuto bhūto*); the phrase "an object that has become manifest" (*vibhūtārammaṇaṃ*) is a statement that supports this meaning.

Alternatively, *vibhūto* means "one who has come into being" (*vibhavī*), which signifies "perished" (*vinaṭṭho*); the phrase "when form has become manifest, contacts do not touch" (*rūpe vibhūte na phusanti phassā*) is [the scriptural support] for this meaning.

A word that establishes [a meaning] is a *sādhaka-vacana*. "Manifested" (*pākaṭo*) means become apparent (*pātubhūto*). "Becomes visible" (*āvi bhavatīti*) means made manifest (*āvibhūto*). "Disappeared" (*tirobhūto*) is likewise. "Separated" (*vinābhūto*) is likewise.
"Capable" (*bhabbo*) means fit to come into being (*bhavitumanucchaviko*). "Despised" (*paribhūto*) means one who is treated with contempt; whoever is oppressed or reviled by anyone is "despised.
"One who acts as he pleases" (*yathākāmacārī*) has the sense of being "going" (*gamyamāna*). "Overcome" (*abhibhūto*) means one who is overcome (*abhibhaviyyate so*).
"Overcome" (*abhibhūto*): he is overcome, thus "overcome. Likewise, "half-become" (*addhabhūto*). Here, the word *addha* has the same meaning as the word *adhi*.
The statement, "Bhikkhus, the eye is half-become; forms are half-become; eye-consciousness is half-become," is the scriptural proof for this meaning. Similarly:
"In this case, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu does not [regard] that which is not yet half-become..."

And even the phrase “he does not develop himself. Therein, *anaddhabhūtaṃ* means not overcome by suffering. That which is called a human existence not overcome by suffering is what he does not develop—that is, he does not master it; such is the meaning of the sutta passage. It is experienced (*anubhūto*) by him; thus it is thoroughly experienced (*samanubhūto*), repeatedly experienced (*paccanubhūto*), and developed (*bhāvito*). Here, “developed” (*bhāvito*)— [The remainder of the text follows: ...is that which has been cultivated, brought to growth, made much of, and perfected. He who develops himself in this way, developing himself, masters himself. Just as a well-bred thoroughbred horse masters its rider, so too one who develops himself masters himself. Having mastered himself, he dwells at ease, having attained the goal, with a mind at peace. This is the fruit of developing oneself. Furthermore, there is this verse: “One who develops himself, developing himself, masters himself; like a well-bred thoroughbred, he masters his rider. Thus it was said. And herein, “mastering himself” means overcoming himself. One who masters himself is called a master of self. Mastering himself, he dwells at ease, having attained the goal, with a mind at peace. This is the fruit of mastering oneself. Furthermore, there is this verse: “One who masters himself, mastering himself, dwells at ease, having attained the goal, with a mind at peace. Thus it was said. And herein, “dwelling at ease” means dwelling happily. One who dwells at ease is called one who dwells happily. Dwelling at ease, having attained the goal, with a mind at peace, he experiences the bliss of liberation. This is the fruit of dwelling at ease. Furthermore, there is this verse: “One who dwells at ease, dwelling happily, experiences the bliss of liberation, having attained the goal, with a mind at peace. Thus it was said. And herein, “experiencing the bliss of liberation” means experiencing the bliss of Nibbāna. One who experiences the bliss of liberation is called one who experiences the bliss of Nibbāna. Experiencing the bliss of liberation, having attained the goal, with a mind at peace, he is called one who has reached the ultimate end. This is the fruit of experiencing the bliss of liberation. Furthermore, there is this verse: “One who experiences the bliss of liberation, experiencing the bliss of Nibbāna, has reached the ultimate end, having attained the goal, with a mind at peace. Thus it was said. And herein, “having reached the ultimate end” means having reached the final limit. One who has reached the ultimate end is called one who has reached the final limit. Having reached the ultimate end, having attained the goal, with a mind at peace, he is called a Tathāgata. This is the fruit of reaching the ultimate end. Furthermore, there is this verse: “One who has reached the ultimate end, having reached the final limit, is a Tathāgata, having attained the goal, with a mind at peace. Thus it was said. And herein, “Tathāgata” means one who has come thus, one who has gone thus, one who has acted thus, one who has lived thus, one who has realized thus. This is the fruit of being a Tathāgata. Furthermore, there is this verse: “One who is a Tathāgata, having come thus, having gone thus, having acted thus, having lived thus, having realized thus, is called a Tathāgata. Thus it was said. And herein, “called a Tathāgata” means designated as a Tathāgata, described as a Tathāgata, made known as a Tathāgata, manifested as a Tathāgata, revealed as a Tathāgata. This is the fruit of being designated as a Tathāgata. Furthermore, there is this verse: “One who is designated as a Tathāgata, described as a Tathāgata, made known as a Tathāgata, manifested as a Tathāgata, revealed as a Tathāgata, is called a Tathāgata. Thus it was said. And herein, “called a Tathāgata” means one who is praised, extolled, lauded, and celebrated by the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, by this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. This is the fruit of being praised. Furthermore, there is this verse: “One who is praised, extolled, lauded, and celebrated by the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, by this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, is called a Tathāgata. Thus it was said. And herein, “praised” means commended. One who is praised is called one who is commended. Being commended, being extolled, being lauded, being celebrated, he is called a Tathāgata. This is the fruit of being commended. Furthermore, there is this verse: “One who is commended, being extolled, being lauded, being celebrated, is called a Tathāgata. Thus it was said. And herein, “extolled” means praised. One who is extolled is called one who is praised. Being praised, being lauded, being celebrated, he is called a Tathāgata. This is the fruit of being praised. Furthermore, there is this verse: “One who is praised, being lauded, being celebrated, is called a Tathāgata. Thus it was said. And herein, “lauded” means glorified. One who is lauded is called one who is glorified. Being glorified, being celebrated, he is called a Tathāgata. This is the fruit of being glorified. Furthermore, there is this verse: “One who is glorified, being celebrated, is called a Tathāgata. Thus it was said. And herein, “celebrated” means honored. One who is celebrated is called one who is honored. Being honored, he is called a Tathāgata. This is the fruit of being honored. Furthermore, there is this verse: “One who is honored is called a Tathāgata. Thus it was said. And herein, “honored” means revered. One who is honored is called one who is revered. Being revered, he is called a Tathāgata. This is the fruit of being revered. Furthermore, there is this verse: “One who is revered is called a Tathāgata. Thus it was said. And herein, “revered” means respected. One who is revered is called one who is respected. Being respected, he is called a Tathāgata. This is the fruit of being respected. Furthermore, there is this verse: “One who is respected is called a Tathāgata. Thus it was said. And herein, “respected” means esteemed. One who is respected is called one who is esteemed. Being esteemed, he is called a Tathāgata. This is the fruit of being esteemed. Furthermore, there is this verse: “One who is esteemed is called a Tathāgata. Thus it was said. And herein, “esteemed” means highly regarded. One who is esteemed is called one who is highly regarded. Being highly regarded, he is called a Tathāgata. This is the fruit of being highly regarded. Furthermore, there is this verse: “One who is highly regarded is called a Tathāgata. Thus it was said. And herein, “highly regarded” means held in high esteem. One who is highly regarded is called one held in high esteem. Being held in high esteem, he is called a Tathāgata. This is the fruit of being held in high esteem. Furthermore, there is this verse: “One who is held in high esteem is called a Tathāgata. Thus it was said. And herein, “held in high esteem” means venerated. One who is held in high esteem is called one who is venerated. Being venerated, he is called a Tathāgata. This is the fruit of being venerated. Furthermore, there is this verse: “One who is venerated is called a Tathāgata. Thus it was said. And herein, “venerated” means worshipped. One who is venerated is called one who is worshipped. Being worshipped, he is called a Tathāgata. This is the fruit of being worshipped. Furthermore, there is this verse: “One who is worshipped is called a Tathāgata. Thus it was said. And herein, “worshipped” means adored. One who is worshipped is called one who is adored. Being adored, he is called a Tathāgata. This is the fruit of being adored. Furthermore, there is this verse: “One who is adored is called a Tathāgata. Thus it was said. And herein, “adored” means honored. One who is adored is called one who is honored. Being honored, he is called a Tathāgata. This is the fruit of being honored. Furthermore
In this context, in such passages as “The enlightenment factor of mindfulness, Kassapa, has been rightly expounded by me;

it has been developed,” one should understand that the primary term denoting the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*) is used in the Dispensation. However, in the systems of the non-Buddhist sects (*titthiya*), the term “developed” refers to the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*).
For this is stated in the Canon: “He did not long for what was not developed. Therein, the five strands of sensual pleasure are called “developed.”
"He does not desire them, he does not cultivate them"—this is the meaning of the sutta passage. He is "esteemed" (*sambhāvito*) because he is honored;

likewise, "discerned" (*vibhāvito*), "perfumed" (*paribhāvito*), and "overwhelmed" (*anuparibhūto*). Regarding "one who has overwhelmed the mind" (*manaṃparibhūto*): he is one by whom the mind has been overwhelmed, thus he is "one who has overwhelmed the mind.
Here, "one who has overwhelmed the mind" refers to one who has slightly failed to overcome [the mind]. For "mind" (*manaṃ*) is a particle (*nipātapada*).
“By my exceedingly wise son, Devadatta, I have been offended—both by his own lack of Buddhahood and by his absence of patience, loving-kindness, and so forth;
the Elder Kumārakassapa and the Elder Nun have also caused me offense;
I have been provoked,” and in such passages as these, its usage should be understood. Herein, we shall state some grammatical justification for the word *manaṃ*.
The word *mana* is divided into two types: as a noun (*nāma*) and as a derivative (*nepātika*).
"His mind is calm" means he is one who has become tranquil within his own mind.
"To be despised" (*paribhavitabbo*) means capable of being despised by another; thus, he is to be treated with contempt.
*Paribhavanīyo*. For in the place of the suffix *-tabba*, the construction with the word *sakkuṇeyya* (capable of being done) is seen:
"The object not yet obtained is to be obtained, is obtainable, or can be obtained. Alternatively, that which deserves to be despised (*paribhavituṃ*) is *paribhavitabbo*.
Thus, it is to be treated with contempt (*paribhottabbo*), hence *paribhavanīyo*. For likewise, in the place of the suffix *-tabba*, the construction with the word *arahati* (deserves) is seen.
“‘That which is to be obtained’ means that which deserves to be acquired. Here, however, the presence of the word *paribhottabbo* (to be enjoyed/used) is illustrated by the canonical passage:
“A khattiya, O Great King, though he be young, is not to be despised nor to be disregarded (*na paribhottabbo*).
The verbal roots preceded by *abhi-* and *adhi-* have the same meaning. The remaining pairs of terms should be understood according to the method [of analysis].
"Bhamāno" means "one who exists" (*bhavati*); here, the elision of the letter *v* in the middle should be understood. Regarding this, it must be said:
"Is that 'bhamāno' Saccaka?"—in this passage of the Pāḷi, however, the form of the root *bhavati* appears precisely through the elision of *v*.
Here is the canonical text (*pāḷi*): “Who is this Saccaka, son of the Nigaṇṭhas, who would dare to challenge the Blessed One’s doctrine?
*Vibhavamāno*: he is called *vibhavamāno* because he “disappears” (*vibhavati*). This applies similarly in cases such as *paribhavamāno*.

In that context, “*abhisambhonto*” means performing it, bringing it to completion; its meaning is the same as in the verse: “Performing all [tasks], let him dwell in the king’s service. This is the meaning of this term.

The statement is effective. However, since these words such as "bhavamāno" (being) and so forth are incomplete personal pronouns, they must be construed by supplying complete subsequent verbs, just as in the examples:
"saramāno rodati" (remembering, he weeps), "gacchanto gaṇhāti" (going, he takes), or "gacchanto so Bhāradvājo addasa accutam isiṃ" (going, that Bhāradvāja saw the immortal sage).
Thus, one should connect them as follows: "rājā bhavamāno sampattiṃ anubhavati" (the king, being, experiences prosperity), and so on.
For expressions such as “saramāno gacchanto” (going while remembering) are not identical to expressions such as “yāto gato patto” (gone, gone, arrived);
rather, they depend upon a subsequent verbal action, just like words ending in the suffix *tvā*.
“Paribhaviyamāno” means “he is being despised,” thus [the term] “paribhaviyamāno. The same applies to “paribhuyyamāno” and so forth.
These are also instances of incomplete personal (accusative) constructions; therefore, they should be construed by supplying the full subsequent verbs, as in:
"The thief, being led away by the king’s men, thought thus," or "Wealth, being experienced by a person, goes to destruction," and so forth. Thus it is in all such cases.
These [terms] are to be applied among those whose verbal forms are incomplete.

This is the exposition of the words *bhūta*, *parābhūta*, and *sambhūta*—which belong to the indeterminate genders but have been placed among the determinate genders. Thus, the exposition of masculine nouns derived from the root *bhū* has been clarified according to their respective etymologies and other characteristics.
Now the description of the feminine gender is stated: therein, "bhāvikā" means she who develops (*bhāveti*), thus she is a "developing one" (*bhāvikā*).
She who performs development (*bhāvanā*) is a developing one. Development (*bhāvanā*) means increasing, expanding, bringing to excellence, repeated practice, and frequent cultivation.
"Vibhāvanā" means making manifest, showing clearly. Alternatively, "vibhāvanā" means non-development, causing to disappear. "Sambhāvanā" means exalting.
*Thomanā* (praise). *Paribhāvanā* means habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*), or increasing on all sides. This is a description of the feminine gender ending in *-ā*. *Bhūmi* (ground):
It is called *bhūmi* because beings (*sattā*) exist (*bhavanti*) therein; or else, it is called *bhūmi* because stable and moving things are born (*bhavanti*), arise, and grow (*vaḍḍhanti*) there.
*Bhūmi* is said to be the earth (*pathavī*). As in the passage beginning, "For the attainment of the first ground," and so forth.
However, the supramundane path is called "the ground" (*bhūmi*). As for that earth which is known by the blind, ignorant masses, it has these designations:
"Earth, Medinī, Bhūmi, Bhūrī, Bhū, Puthuvī, Mahī, Chamā, Vasumatī, Ubbī, Avanī, Ku, Vasundharā."
"Jagatī, khiti, vasudhā, dharaṇī, go, dharā"—
if it is asked where it has been seen before that the words *bhū*, *ku*, and *go* function in the sense of the word "earth," [it is said]:
"In the words *vidvā*, *bhūpāla*, *kumuda*, *gorakkha*, and so forth."
One should discern that *bhū* with the suffix *ku* means "earth" (*pathavī*).

*Bhūti* is the state of becoming (*bhavana*); *vibhūti* is destruction, or specifically a state of being (*visesato bhavana*). Alternatively, it is called *vibhūti* because beings come into existence through it in a distinguished way;
thus, it is simply excellence (*sampatti*), as in "the king's *vibhūti*" or "desirable excellences."
And this is the statement that establishes the meaning of this term.

This is the section on feminine nouns ending in *ī*. *Bhūri* means the earth (*pathavī*). For it is called *bhūri* because beings (*bhava*) exist therein; or it is *bhūri* because it exists, is perceived, or increases;
or alternatively, it is *bhūri* because beings—both those who have come into being and those yet to be—are delighted in what depends upon it. [It refers to] those dependent on the earth.
For beings indeed delight in the earth; therefore, for this reason as well, it is called *bhūrī*.

Regarding the word *bhūrī* when used to denote the earth, the statement "one of vast wisdom" (*bhūripañño*) establishes its meaning. Furthermore, it is called *bhūrī* because it is like the earth (*bhūrī viyā*);
thus *bhūrī* is the name for wisdom that is extensive, equal to the earth. As it is said: "From application (*yoga*), indeed, *bhūrī* is born; from non-application, the destruction of *bhūrī*."
Here, the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) supports this meaning. Alternatively, it is called *bhūrī* because it delights in the true object (*bhūte atthe ramati*);
this is the name for wisdom (*paññā*), and the commentary on the passage "vast wisdom, the guide" (*bhūrī medhā pariṇāyikā*) supports this meaning.
Or else, it is *bhūrī* because wisdom itself overcomes states such as lust; it also [means] that it overcomes the enemies, namely lust and the rest.
"Vast" (*bhūrī*). For it has been stated by the Venerable Sāriputta in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*: "It is called 'vast' (*bhūrī*) because it overcomes lust;
it is wisdom. [It overcomes] hatred and delusion... Lust is an enemy (*ari*); because it crushes that enemy, it is 'vast,' namely wisdom.
Hatred... Delusion... All kamma leading to existence is an enemy; because it crushes that enemy, it is 'vast,' namely wisdom. In this context, however, "change-of-lineage" (*gotrabhū*)—
It should be understood that although it ought to be called "aribhū," the word *bhū* has been placed first and pronounced as the compound word *bhūrī* by way of euphonic combination (*sandhi*).

Furthermore, it should be understood that in such nominal words, meanings such as "overpowering" are indeed obtainable even without a prefix, whereas this is not the case for verbal roots. This, moreover, is a synonym for wisdom (*paññā*).
Wisdom is understanding, reflection, investigation, discernment, and thorough examination;
it is sagacity, the investigation of phenomena,
close observation, skillfulness, vastness, and precise scrutiny.
Non-merit and perplexity, intelligence that investigates,
clear comprehension, and the faculty of wisdom;
the power of wisdom, non-delusion, and right view.
And from the Abhidhamma, these have been taken by me as a goad:
knowledge, understanding, penetration, the sword, the stream, and view;
wisdom, awakening, intelligence, the awakened, and inspired eloquence—these are "awakening."
Dhamma, science, course, wisdom, discernment, insight, intelligence, liberation;
investigation, the source, the cleanser, sagacity, and sagacity itself;
knowledge, proficiency, and medical science as well.
Regarding what was stated as “soto bodhī,” these are two names for knowledge;
they flourish even in the case of Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples.
Furthermore, the two names “abhisambodhi” and “sambodhi”—
It thrives only for Paccekabuddhas and Omniscient Buddhas.
Furthermore, the supreme designation of "Abhisambodhi" (Perfect Enlightenment),
which is a designation for knowledge, thrives only for the Omniscient Sambuddha.
The designation "Buddha" refers either to the state of supreme enlightenment known as *sammāsambodhi*, or to the designation for knowledge that grows forth from omniscience itself.
That which is called "omniscience" (*sabbaññutā*) is indeed the knowledge belonging only to the Omniscient One.
But the remaining [terms] are applicable throughout all [the verses],
as they are designations for knowledge (*ñāṇa*). However, although the state of knowledge exists [in them],
