I have not demonstrated [them here] because there is no other specific purpose [for doing so], such as the "eye of the Dhamma" (*dhammacakkhu*) and so forth.
*Bhūtī* is the wife of *Bhūta*. For just as the wife of a *peta* is called a *petī*, so too the wife of *Bhūta* is called *Bhūtī*.
*Bhotī* refers to the woman with whom one speaks; she is to be addressed as "madam" (*bhotī*).
Therefore, it should be understood that by this term, a woman is designated. For just as when speaking with a man...
A man is addressed as "Sir" (*bhavaṃ*); in the same way, when speaking with a woman, the woman is addressed as "Madam" (*bhotī*).
An illustration of this is: "From where has Sir Bhāradvāja brought these children?
and "I shall attend upon Madam; let Madam not be angry. Alternatively, here a certain being [is designated] by way of the female gender.

One who has received a name should be addressed as "bhotī" (lady); therefore, by this term, it should be understood that even a woman whose name is received in the feminine gender may be addressed as such, and likewise one who is not a woman.
For instance, even a son of the gods (*devaputta*) is addressed as "bhotī" in reference to the word *devatā* (goddess), because he is to be addressed in the feminine gender;
how much more so, then, the case of a daughter of the gods (*devadhītā*). Likewise...

For in the passage, "Lady, you surely know; tell me that when asked," the feminine designation "lady" (*bhoto*) is employed here with reference to the word *devatā*. Herein, this is the meaning of the words of the sutta:
"If that fraudulent ascetic, seeking wealth, does not know, does the lady—the deity—know? Furthermore—
“You are one who desires my welfare, O yakkha; you are one who desires my benefit, O deity.

I shall do according to your word, for you are my teacher.”—In this passage from the *Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī* story, the term “desirous of welfare” (*atthakāmo*) is used in the masculine gender in consideration of the masculine sound of the word *yakkha*.
And because of the word "deity" (*devatā*), which is feminine in gender, Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī, though a man, was addressed in the feminine form as "one who desires our welfare.
Elsewhere too, because of the word "deity," a son of the gods (*devaputta*) was addressed in the feminine form:
"O foolish woman, you do not understand the word of the Arahants."
“You are one who desires my welfare, mother; you are one who desires my benefit, O deity.
In this context, however, in the passage “Come, foolish woman, ask forgiveness from the mighty King Kusarāja,” it is the female alone that is expressed by means of the feminine gender.
Therefore, in some cases, regardless of the actual referent consisting of a female or male person, [the form is used] depending solely on the grammatical gender.
The forms *bhotī*, *devatā*, *silā*, *jambū*, and *bhotiṃ*—meaning "deity," "stone," "rose-apple tree," and "deity" respectively—should be joined with the nominative singular and other case endings.

However, in some instances, having regard for both gender and meaning, they should be joined as in "bhotī itthī" (she is a woman) or "bhotiṃ devaṃ" (he is a deity), and so forth. Regarding *vibhāvinī*:
she makes manifest (*vibhāveti*) is *vibhāvinī*. The same applies to *paribhāvinī* and others. This is the section on feminine nouns ending in the vowel *ī*.

*Bhū* means that which exists as being (*sattāyamānā*) and thus comes to be (*bhavati*). Alternatively, *bhū* refers to the formative factors of beings (*sattasaṅkhāra*) because they come into existence (*bhavanti*), are born (*jāyanti*), and increase (*vaḍḍhanti*) therein.
*Bhū* is called "earth" (*pathavī*). *Abhū* is speech devoid of growth (*vaḍḍhi-virahita*); or, it is "that which has not been before," thus *abhū*, meaning "speech that has not occurred before.

Or, it is "that which has not come to be," thus *abhū*, meaning "unreal speech. [The Buddha said: "How can you speak such a thing to me? It is indeed evil!"* *Abhuṃ me kathaṃ nu bhaṇasi, pāpakaṃ vata...*
"You speak"—this is the statement that establishes the meaning of these points. This is the exposition of feminine nouns ending in the vowel *ū*. This is the exposition of fixed feminine nouns.

However, the exposition of words such as *bhūta*, *parābhūta*, and *sambhūta*—which have indefinite genders but are included among the fixed feminine nouns—is easily understood by following the method [of the treatise].
Thus, in this way, for feminine nouns derived from the root *bhū*, according to their respective [rules]...
The exposition by way of etymology and so forth has been clarified.
Now, the exposition of the neuter gender is stated: therein, "the primary" (*bhūta*) refers to the fourfold great primary materiality, beginning with the earth element.
For that exists as a support for others, thus it is "primary" (*bhūta*); or else, it exists (*bhavati*) therein.
It is called "derived matter" (*upādārūpa*) because it exists dependent upon that [primary matter]. Alternatively, "matter" (*bhūta*) means a being, or one named "being.
For the word *bhūta* in the neuter gender refers to any being whatsoever, and in this sense it is also used for beings such as *yakkhas* and the like: "Time devours all beings, including oneself;
having rebuked the beings who have gathered here from that place... [and so forth].

In such passages as "apakkamī," the neuter usage should be understood. If it is argued that this is a change of gender (liṅgavipallāsa) for the sake of the ease of verse composition (gāthābandha), that is not so; for even in the prose arrangement of the *Cūḷaniddesa*, the neuter gender of the word *bhūta* is demonstrated in the passage:
"The great elements, such as the yakkhas and others, which seize [something], neither an internal nor an external location for them is perceived.
Thus, the neuter gender of the word *bhūta* is established.
It should be understood as follows. "Great primary element" (*mahābhūta*) refers to the fourfold materiality of the great primary elements as previously described.
Its status as a "great primary element" is to be known by such reasons as its "great manifestation. How so? It is a "great primary element" because it is a "greatly become" (*mahantaṃ bhūtaṃ*);

it is also called a "great primary element" because it is similar to the "great primary element" known as a magician; it is also called a "great primary element" because it is similar to the "great primary elements" that are *yakkhas* and so forth; [and] because of their greatness...
That which has come to be through conditions such as food and clothing is also called a "great primary" (*mahābhūta*); that which has become a great modification is also called a "great primary.
Thus, the state of being a great primary should be understood by way of reasons such as its great manifestation. Here, this should be clearly observed:
the word *bhūta* occurs with both masculine and neuter genders.
In the case of designations (*paṇṇatti*), [the suffix] *guṇa* is used for both the quality and the possessor of the quality, while *itthi* and *liṅga* denote the feminine gender.

Regarding the method beginning with the words *bhūta* and *sambhūta*, those which express designations should be applied according to the three genders; this is to be understood as the specific distinction.
“The being stands, O beings, these beings stand; this one is a recluse.
Now the being, the minds, the beings are indeed stainless.
This bride is a barren being”—these are the examples cited.
One who seeks the true meaning of the Teaching should carefully examine what has been stated.

"Bhavitta" means a place of growth. For it is called "bhavitta" because beings (*bhava*) grow (*bhavanti*) therein; the statement, "My birthplace, my place of growth—thus he sank in the mud," is a word that establishes this meaning.
Both "bhavittaṃ" and "bhāvittaṃ" are readings found by me in two ways.
In the *Bhaggava Jātaka*, it is seen [as such] by virtue of its shortness and length.

"Bhūna" means existence (*bhavana*); "bhūna" means growth (*vaddhi*). The statements, "I alone am the defiler, destroyed by my own growth (*bhūnahatā*), of the king of great majesty," and "A destruction of growth (*bhūnahacca*) has been committed by me," are words that establish this meaning.
"Bhavana" means the act of existing. Alternatively, beings exist—that is, they grow—there through sons, daughters, and various prosperities.
"Bhavana" is called a dwelling or a house; the statement, "My paternal dwelling," is a word that supports this meaning.
"House, home, abode, dwelling, and residence"—these are synonymous terms. "Parābhavana" means falling into decline.
"Sambhavana" means flourishing well. "Vibhavana" means annihilation or destruction.
*Pātubhavanaṃ* means manifestation; its meaning is simply becoming visible or attaining a distinct form. *Āvibhavanaṃ* means coming into the range of direct perception.
*Tirobhavanaṃ* means being concealed or hidden. *Vinābhavanaṃ* means separation or absence. *Sotthibhavanaṃ* means well-being or security.
*Paribhavanaṃ* means oppression or contempt. *Abhibhavanaṃ* means dispelling or overcoming. *Adhibhavanaṃ* means overwhelming or surpassing. *Anubhavanaṃ*...
*Paribhuñjanaṃ*: enjoying. *Samanubhavanaṃ*: enjoying thoroughly. *Paccanubhavanaṃ*: enjoying thoroughly even by way of predominance.
This is the description of the neuter gender ending in a nasalized vowel (*niggahīta*). *Atthavibhāvī*:

that which has the nature of making the meaning manifest—whether it be the mind, knowledge, or a family—is called "meaning-manifesting" (*atthavibhāvī*). Likewise for "dhamma-manifesting" (*dhammavibhāvī*). This is the description of the neuter gender ending in the vowel *i*.
The change-of-lineage consciousness has either a concept as its object or a sublime (mahaggata) state as its object.
For it overcomes the lineage of the sense-sphere and develops and brings about the lineage of the sublime; thus it is called "change-of-lineage" (*gotrabhū*).

Furthermore, "change-of-lineage" refers either to the knowledge of change-of-lineage occurring in the cognitive process of the Path with Nibbāna as its object, or to that occurring in the cognitive process of the attainment of fruition with conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) as its object.

This is the knowledge of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū-ñāṇa*) that has arisen. For among these, the first overcomes the lineage of the worldlings (*puthujjana-gotta*) and develops the lineage of the noble ones (*ariya-gotta*);
and because it takes Nibbāna as its object by way of making it its cognitive support—thus being designated by the term "lineage"—it is called "change-of-lineage.
The second, however, although it likewise has formations as its object, [serves] as a condition of repetition for the resultant consciousnesses together with their associated mental factors.
Because one develops [the path] toward Nibbāna, which is called the "clan" (gotra), one is called a "change-of-lineage person" (gotrabhū).
This is the analysis of the textual tradition: the word spoken as "gotrabhu" by way of its short vowel should be understood as neuter, as it refers to knowledge, consciousness, and so forth.
The term “gotrabhū,” however, is spoken with a long vowel;
it should be understood as masculine, referring to a person (puggala) and so forth.
But when stated with a long vowel [as in *gotrabhū*], one should not say it is neuter.
The other varieties, ending in *bindu* (anusvāra), are said to be threefold.
In the Teaching, those ending in *ī* and *ū* undergo shortening;
having attained the neuter gender, they move swiftly together.
That which exists together with the mind is *cittasahabhu*; that which does not exist together with the mind is *nacittasahabhu*, [referring to] matter (*rūpa*).

This is the exposition of neuter nouns ending in the vowel *u*. This is the exposition of those neuter nouns whose gender is fixed. The exposition of words such as *bhūta* and *parābhūta*, whose genders are not fixed but are included among the fixed neuter nouns, is easily understood by following the method [of the rules].
Thus, in this way, regarding neuter nouns derived from the root *bhū*, [the treatment has been given] according to their respective etymologies and so forth.
The exposition has been clarified. Thus, in every respect, the exposition of the three genders is complete.
This triad of genders, consisting of words derived from the verbal root *bhū*, has been stated through various methods of indication.
Having embraced his most beloved son, who was well-endowed with auspicious marks,
the man performed the rites for the discernment of signs as he desired.
Thus, regarding the movements of expression among the wise in the Three Piṭakas together with the commentaries, which consist of nine divisions.
In the Saddanīti treatise composed for the sake of proficiency,
the fourth chapter is the analysis of nominal forms derived from the verbal root *bhū* that possess three genders.
5. The Nominal Paradigm Series for Masculine Nouns Ending in -o.
From this point forward, I shall explain the garland of nouns derived from the verbal root *bhū*, as well as other series of nouns.
When this is thus stated, there will be no scattered discourse here;
the classification of the garlands of names will indeed become complete.
Therefore, the doctrine heard from the lions among former teachers has been included here.
Having performed the purification of conduct, I shall speak with full determination.
Puriso, purisā (nominative singular and plural). Purisaṃ, purise (accusative singular and plural). Purisena, purisehi, purisebhi (instrumental singular and plural).

Purisassa, purisānaṃ (genitive singular and plural). Purisā, purisasmā, purisamhā, purisehi, purisebhi (ablative singular and plural). Purisassa, purisānaṃ (genitive singular and plural). Purise (locative singular).
*purisasmim*, *purisamhi*, *purisesu*. *Bho purisa*, *bhavanto purisā*.

This is the method for the nominal declension (*nāmikapadamālā*) of the base form *purisa*, extracted from the *Niruttipiṭaka* composed by the Venerable Mahākaccāna, who had mastered the analytical knowledges (*pabhinnapaṭisambhida*).
Therein, [it is shown] in the singular and plural numbers of the masculine gender (*purisavacana*).
The nominative case endings and so forth occur. For example: *puriso tiṭṭhati* (the man stands), *purisā tiṭṭhanti* (the men stand).
In that context, *puriso* is the nominative singular in the masculine gender; *purisā* is the nominative plural in the masculine gender.

One sees a man (*purisaṃ*), one sees men (*purise*). In that context, *purisaṃ* is the accusative singular form in the masculine gender; *purise* is the accusative plural form in the masculine gender.
"Done by a man" (*purisena kataṃ*), "done by men" (*purisehi kataṃ*), "done by men" (*purisebhi kataṃ*).
In that context, *purisena* is the instrumental singular form in the masculine gender; *purisehi*, *purisebhi* are the instrumental plural forms in the masculine gender.

It is given to a man (*purisassa*), it is given to men (*purisānaṃ*). Therein, *purisassa* is the dative case in the singular number of the masculine gender; *purisānaṃ* is the dative case in the plural number of the masculine gender.
Freed from a man (*purisā nissaṭaṃ*), freed from a man (*purisasmā nissaṭaṃ*), freed from a man (*purisamhā nissaṭaṃ*), freed from men (*purisehi nissaṭaṃ*), freed from men (*purisebhi nissaṭaṃ*).
Therein, *purisā* is the ablative case in the singular number of the masculine gender. *Purisasmā*... [and so on].
*Purisasmā* means that in the singular number of the masculine gender, the ablative case occurs;
*purisehi*, *purisebhi* means that in the plural number of the masculine gender, the ablative case occurs.

*Purisassa pariggaho*, *purisānaṃ pariggaho*. Therein, *purisassa* means that in the singular number of the masculine gender, the genitive case occurs; *purisānaṃ* means that in the plural number of the masculine gender, the genitive case occurs.
[It is] established in a man, established in a man, established in a man, established in men.
In this context, "purise" is the locative case in the singular number of the masculine gender; "purisamhi" … [etc. … "purisasmim" … [etc.
… "purisesu" is the locative case in the plural number of the masculine gender.

"O man, stop! Sirs, you men, stop!"—here, "O man" (*bho purisa*) is an address in the singular number of the masculine gender, and "Sirs, you men" (*bhavanto purisā*) is an address in the plural number of the masculine gender;
by this method, the principle is to be expanded in all instances.
In the *Cūḷanirutti* composed by the Great Elder Yamaka, after stating the singular vocative form for addressing someone as "bho purisa" (O man) using the short vowel,
the plural vocative form for addressing many is stated as "bho purisā" (O men) using the long vowel. Although such a method does not exist in the *Niruttipiṭaka*,
nevertheless, regarding the context of addressing many, there are plural vocatives such as "bho yakkhā" (O yakkhas), and so forth.
Since this is seen in the *Jātakaṭṭhakathā* and other texts, it is more highly esteemed and serves as an authority for the wise;

therefore, following the opinion of the Great Thera Yamaka as well, one should apply the paradigmatic series of noun forms (*nāmikapadamālā*) for the vocative case by stating "puriso, purisā, purisaṃ" and so forth, as in:
"bho purisa, bho purisā, bhavanto purisā."
In this context: *puriso* is the nominative singular; *purisā* is the nominative plural. *Purisaṃ* is the accusative singular;
*purise* is the accusative plural. *Purisena* is the instrumental singular; *purisehi* and *purisebhi* are two forms of the instrumental plural.
*Purisassa* is the dative-locative singular; *purisānaṃ* is the dative-locative plural. *Purisā*, *purisasmā*, and *purisamhā* [are the ablative forms].
Three are the nominative singular forms: *purise*, *purisā*, and *puriso*. Two are the instrumental plural forms: *purisehi* and *purisebhi*. One is the genitive singular form:
*purisassa*. One is the genitive plural form: *purisānaṃ*. Three are the locative singular forms: *purise*, *purisasmiṃ*, and *purisamhi*. One is the locative plural form: *purisesu*.
One is the vocative singular form: *bho purisa*. [Two are the vocative plural forms: *bho purisā*...
"Bhavanto" and "purisā" are two plural forms.
Furthermore, among these, "purisā" is identical for the nominative, ablative, and vocative cases; "purise" is identical for the accusative and locative cases;
"purisehi" and "purisebhi" are identical for the instrumental and ablative cases; and "purisānaṃ" is identical for the dative and genitive cases.
Nevertheless, the state of non-confusion should be understood by way of meaning. How so? By such expressions as “A man stands, men stand;
he sees a man, he sees men,” and so forth.
And herein, *bho* is a particle used in the sense of addressing. It is not only a singular form; rather, it is also—
The phrase "there is also the plural" includes the usage of the plural form "bho purisā.
However, since "bhavanto" is exclusively plural, it should be understood that the word "purisā" is stated again [in the commentary] for that reason.
Thus, after the Great Thera Yamaka had stated the singular vocative address as "bho purisa" using the short vowel, he stated the plural vocative address as "bho purisā" using the long vowel.

It has been stated thus. For indeed, in the Pāḷi and in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), the particle *bho* is divided into two types according to the singular and plural numbers. Here are these illustrative passages:
“Now, would the threefold-knowledge (*tevijja*) Brahmins who possess wives meet and coincide with Brahmā, who is without a wife? Certainly not, Master Gotama.”
"Marvelous, Master Ānanda! Extraordinary, Master Ānanda! Come, Master Recluse!
Come, Master Wanderer!"—such passages from the Canon and the Commentaries illustrate the usage of the word *bho* in the singular number. [And as it is said:
"In that case, Master, listen also to me. Just as we alone are worthy to approach the venerable Gotama for a visit, so am I not..."
"Friends, I do not applaud the well-spoken words of the ascetic Gotama as being well-spoken;
look at this son of good family! Friends, O *yakkhas*, I would divide him up among you and give it to you.
However, friends rogues, I am not pure, and your deed does not please me. He said to those men: "Friends, do not kill me!"
"Show [him] to the king and then kill him"—this and other such examples from the Pāḷi and the Aṭṭhakathā illustrate the usage of the term *bho* when employed in the plural.
However, in the Kaccāyana-pakaraṇa, the two phrases "bho purisa" and "bho purisā" are stated as forms of the singular vocative for addressing.
This should be understood in a way that does not contradict the Āgamas.

Some, however, maintain that when addressing someone standing nearby, the singular form of address is "bho purisa" with a short vowel, whereas when addressing someone standing at a distance, the singular form of address is "bho purisā" with a long vowel.
They say nothing regarding the address of men or women whether they are standing near or far. The same applies to those standing near or far [when addressing women].
And when they are addressed by a woman, they should be asked: "How should one speak when addressing men who are nearby and those who are far away?
Certainly, when questioned in this way, they will not be able to say anything further.
Even if they were to say: "Sirs, 'men' is precisely how one addresses both those nearby and those far away."
[If it is argued that] one says, "Sir," then they should be asked:

"If the word 'bhavanto' (sirs) is used as an address for men standing both near and far through this undivided expression, then since that is the case, one should also use the short form 'bho purisa' (O man) to address a man standing far away.
Why, then, instead of saying that, do you use [the long form] only when addressing one who is not far away?"
Do you desire the singular form of address as "bho purisa" with a short vowel,
and for what purpose do you desire the plural form of address as "bho purisā" with a long vowel when addressing someone standing at a distance?
Is it not the case that in such passages as "Taggha bhagavā bojjhaṅgā, taggha sugata bojjhaṅgā," [the term] serves as a word of address?
The long form “Bhagavā” is indeed fit to be an address for the Buddha whether he is standing nearby or at a distance;
likewise, the short form “Sugata,” which serves as an address, is also [fit].
However, among these, while no shortening of the address “Bhagavā” is seen anywhere, [such a shortening] of the address “Sugatā”...
Furthermore, since no long vowel is seen anywhere [in this context], one should disregard the distinction between long and short vowels;
thus, the word "purisa," spoken in its short form, becomes a term of address for a person standing nearby when addressed according to its natural tone (*pakatisara*),
whereas it becomes a term of address for a person standing at a distance when addressed according to its drawn-out tone (*āyata-sara*).

It should be understood that it *becomes* [so]. Likewise, addressive plural expressions spoken with a long vowel—such as "bhavanto purisā" (O sirs, men), "bho yakkhā" (O spirits), "bho dhuttā" (O rogues), and so forth—become addressive words for persons standing nearby when used with a natural tone (*pakati-sara*), serving as addressive terms for those not far away;
whereas, when used with a drawn-out tone (*āyata-sara*) at the time of addressing persons standing at a distance, they become addressive words for those far away.
The words of address for those standing at a distance should be understood as follows:

for in certain places, whether at short or long intervals, the Brahmins recite the Veda with a drawn-out tone, a medium-drawn tone, and an extremely drawn tone, like a song that is impossible to write down. Thus, even among all the vowels, [they use] the drawn-out [tone].
The pronunciation of the plural suffix (*sarenuccāraṇa*) would indeed be obtained, yet it is impossible to write [it all];
therefore, without entering into such a path, by the expression "O man" (*bho purisa*), there is an addressing of a person whether standing far away or not far away;
and by the expressions "O men" (*bho purisā*) and "Sirs, O men" (*bhavanto purisā*), there is an addressing of persons whether they are standing far away or not far away.
It should be observed: thus, for one standing at a distance, the measure is simply the addressing with a long-drawn-out voice, not the distinction between long and short duration;
therefore: "O Teacher! O King! O Goer! O Sage!
O Staff-bearer! O Bhikkhu! O Self-awakened One! O Lady! O Daughter! O Woman! O Gruel! O Lady! etc.
Addressing someone who is nearby and addressing someone who is at a distance occurs through such words as "O bride," "O sir," "O clan-member," "O bone," and "O eye.
It should also be understood that addressing someone nearby occurs through such words as "Sirs, Teacher," "Teachers," "Ladies, maiden," and "Maidens."
This, then, is the conclusion here:
Having heard those words of his, they saw the king’s son;
and the son, seeing his father from afar, spoke out aloud.
"Come, gatekeepers armed with swords,
let the followers of Kāśyapa kill me, O lord of men!
Answer me when asked about this matter."
"What fault indeed could there be for me today?"—
thus [he thought] when the King of the True Dharma,
skilled in discourse and all-seeing, had well-expounded the *Somanassa-jātaka*.
The short vowel is seen even when standing at a distance, as in the word "janinda";
it is never seen as long anywhere—this is the rule I maintain.
Here, this must also be addressed: "From where, indeed, has this come—the idea that 'addressing one who stands far away' is the same as 'addressing one who stands not far away'?"
From the Science of Grammar (*Saddasattha*). The science of grammar is not of assistance to the Buddha’s word in its entirety; rather, it is so in one part.
In this treatise, "plural" (*bahuvacana*), "manyfold" (*puthuvacana*), or "multiple" (*anekavacana*) are identical in meaning;
there is only a difference in expression. Therefore, in all instances, [one may use] either "plural" or "manyfold."

Alternatively, the term “plural” (*anekavacana*) may be used; however, this usage of “plural” as meaning “many words” (*puthuvacana*) is the convention among those learned in grammar (*niruttaññū*) within the Dispensation (*sāsana*), whereas the other is the convention of those who know the science of linguistics (*saddasatthavidū*).
But why is the dual number (*dvivacana*) not mentioned in this treatise? It is because the dual number does not exist in the word of the Buddha (*buddhavacana*).
There is no such name; therefore, it was not stated. But is it not the case that there are three numbers in the Buddha’s word?
For instance, "āyasmā" is the singular, "āyasmantā" is the dual, and "āyasmanto" is the plural? That is not so;
for if the expression "āyasmantā" were a dual number, then [in cases like] "puriso, purisā," etc.,...
Which [form] would you call the dual number? Therefore, there is no such thing as a dual number in the Buddha’s word (*buddhavacana*).
For it is for this very reason that, by means of rules such as *si*, *yo*, *aṃ*, *yo*, *nā*, and *hi*, only the singular and plural numbers are shown.
But is it not the case, sir, that [the following is said]: "Let the venerable ones listen to me; today is the Uposatha of the fifteenth day. If it is the right time for the venerable ones..."?
In the passage, "Let us perform the Uposatha of mutual purity," the term "Venerable Sirs" (*āyasmantā*) is used referring to two individuals;
however, in Pāli passages such as, "Venerable Sirs, the four Pārājika rules have been recited," it is used referring to many.
One cannot say that it was stated "just so and not otherwise," for this is also the case when announcing one's *parivāsa* (probation) and other matters.

Is it because it was stated by the authors of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathācariya*), who understood the intention of the Sugata, that "one announcing [the offense] to two should say, 'May the Venerable Ones bear this in mind,' and one announcing it to three should say, 'May the Venerable Ones bear this in mind'? This is indeed what was stated;

however, it was stated according to the conventional terminology of the Vinaya. Is it not the case that the Vinaya is the word of the Buddha (*buddhavacana*)? Why then [is it called the terminology of the Vinaya]?
"Do you say that there is no such thing as a dual number? It is true that the Vinaya is the word of the Buddha;
nevertheless, because it is spoken by way of a formal act of the Vinaya (*vinayakamma*), it is merely a specific designation and is not included within the general category of plural forms.
For if "āyasmantā" were a dual number, then the verbs used in connection with it would also have to be duals; yet such [verbs] exist.

There are no dual-number verbal forms. For even one skilled in the arrangement of syllables, though possessing meditative absorption and seeing with the divine eye, would not perceive even a single dual-number verbal form in the Buddha’s word for a hundred or a thousand years;
thus, because of the absence of the dual number among verbal forms, there is no dual number among nominal forms. And because of its absence among nominal forms as well—

The absence of that [dual number] should be understood in the case of verbal forms (*kriyāpada*). In the Sanskrit language, dual endings exist for both [nouns and verbs], but in the Māgadhī language, they do not.
Furthermore, the grammatical term "plural" (*puthuvacana*) also indicates this same point: that "there is no dual number in the Buddha’s word.
For that [term] refers to a form of speech that is distinct from both the dual and the plural as they are stated in the Sanskrit language.
In this context, the expression of a meaning that is distinct from those meanings already stated is called a "plural expression" (*puthuvacana*). If it is asked:
how is this an expression distinct from the dual and plural forms as used in the Sanskrit language?
It is because there is no conventional usage of the term "plural expression" in the Sanskrit language; therefore, this [term] is [used] in contrast to those [Sanskrit usages].
It is called a "word" (*vacana*) because it expresses a meaning that has become distinct from those [meanings] expressed by dual and plural forms.
And how, in the Pāli language, is there a "plural word" (*puthuvacana*) expressing a meaning distinct from what is expressed [by duals]?
Because in the Pāli language, a "dual" (*dvivacana*) is stated with reference to two [entities], and not with reference to many such as three, four, five, and so forth.
However, the plural number is used when referring to many [objects], not when referring to two; this is the distinction in the Sanskrit language.
In the Māgadhī language, the plural number is used when referring to many—such as two, three, four, five, and so on.
Therefore, it is called the "plural" (*puthuvacana*) because it is an expression for a meaning that has become distinct from the meanings expressed in the Sanskrit language.

This is the distinction in the Magadha language. Therefore, the meaning should be understood here as “a word for many,” that is, a statement concerning a manifold or diverse object (*puthubhūta* or *puthuna*).

Now, based on the method extracted from the *Nirutti-piṭaka* regarding “puriso, purisā, purisan,” the nominal declension (*nāmikapadamālā*) of the word *bhūta*—which serves as its base form—is stated:
Bhūto, bhūtā. Bhūtaṃ, bhūtāni. Bhūtena, bhūtehi, bhūtebhi. Bhūtassa, bhūtānaṃ.
Bhūtā, bhūtasmā, bhūtamhā, bhūtehi, bhūtebhi. Bhūtassa, bhūtānaṃ. Bhūte, bhūtasmiṃ, bhūtamhi, bhūtesu.
Bho bhūta, bhavanto bhūtā.
Alternatively, the plural form "bho bhūtā" should be understood.

Just as the noun paradigm for the base form *bhūta* has been applied here according to the masculine pattern, so too should the noun paradigms for the abstract nouns (*bhāva*) and other similar terms be applied according to the masculine pattern.
In this context, other similar bases for words such as *buddho* include *buddha* and so forth.
Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha, Magga;
Khaṇḍha, Kāya, Kāma, Kappa;
Māsa, Pakkha, Yakkha, Bhakkha.
Nāga, megha, bhoga, yāga; rāga,
dosa, moha, māna, makkha,
thambha, kodha, lobha.
Laughing is indeed burning, heat;
desire is coughing, asthma, and disease.
Assa, sassa, issa, and sissa—
Lion, tiger, tree, mountain;
Indra, Sakka, god, village;
moon, sun, flood, island.
Passo, yañño, cāgo, vādo, hattho,
patto, soso, gedho, somo,
yodho, gaccho, accho.
House, palace, watchtower, hall;
man, mountain, deer, hare;
dog, crane, goat, bird.
Horse, elephant, donkey, and snake;
tree, palm, cloth, and banner;
serpent, winged insect, bird, and boa constrictor.
Kharabha, Sarabha, Pasada, Gavaja;
Mahisa, Vasabha, Asura, Garuḷa;
Taruṇa, Varuṇa, Balisa, Paligha.
The sāla, the dhava, and the khadira,
the godhuma, the saṭṭhika, and the barley;
the kaḷāya and the kulattha.
The sesame seed, the mung bean, and the rice grain;
the kshatriya, the brahmin, and the vaishya;
the shudra, the rogue, and the pukkasa.
A Caṇḍāla husband, a nobleman,
a human, a charioteer, and a chariot;
a renunciant and a householder.
The ox, the camel, and the donkey;
women and female attendants— these and other such [terms] one should discern.
And here they might say: "But surely, sir, from seeing the reading 'oroohā ca kumārā ca' (concubines and princes), the word *orodha* must be feminine?
That is not so; for in that context, "oroohā" is indeed a masculine noun ending in *-o*, not a feminine noun ending in *-ā*.
You speak thus only because you imagine it to be a feminine noun ending in *-ā*, but it is not a feminine noun ending in *-ā*.
Rather, it is stated in the plural number like the word *mātugāmā*, and thus it is a word ending in the vowel -ā.
But surely, sir, the feminine gender of the word *orodha* is evident in the *Sammohavinodanī* and other works; how so? [It is said:
“The deity dwelling in the tree, being angry with the Elder, first tempted his mind, saying: ‘Seven days from now, your attendant—’”
“‘The king will die,’ she announced in her dream. Having heard those words, the Elder informed the king’s concubines (*orodha*).

At that very moment, they all let out a great cry together. Here, one might argue: “Since the word ‘orodhānaṃ’ (of the concubines) was used and then followed by ‘tā’ (they), the feminine gender of the word *orodha* is made clear.
This is not so, because the meaning has been misunderstood. For here, [the meaning] is wrongly grasped...

This is for your benefit. Here, however, because the word *orodha* (harem-women) expresses the referent of the feminine gender, and since the word "they" (*tā*) was used with reference to that feminine referent, the meaning is precisely "those women.
But as for you, because you were not raised by a mother and father and did not live in the household of a teacher, you do not understand this subtle matter and say whatever comes to your lips.
"One should not say that the mouth exists for the purpose of eating or for the purpose of speaking;
rather, a wise person is one who speaks whatever has entered the mouth.
"Venerable sir, we do not speak whatever has entered the mouth; rather, we speak only by taking the words of the masters of the Aṭṭhakathā."
"We say: 'The commentaries alone are our refuge; we do not believe you.
Whether you believe us or not, do not misrepresent the teachers of the commentaries by saying, "We speak only by taking the word of the commentators of the Aṭṭhakathā.
For the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā did not state that "the word *orodha* is feminine."
There is indeed such a place mentioned; therefore, you have slandered the commentator as well.
It is not proper to slander venerable ones such as the Buddha, for it leads to the acquisition of great harm. For this was said by the Blessed One:
"By his own misapprehension, he slanders us and generates much demerit; thereby he ruins himself."
Having thus shown the impropriety and blameworthiness of such misrepresentation, they should further be addressed as follows:
"There is also an example similar to the one you have cited in the *Jātaka-ṭṭhakathā*; listen to it. For in the commentary on the *Kosiya-jātaka*, it is said:
'While the Teacher was dwelling at Jetavana, he spoke concerning a certain woman in Sāvatthī. It seems she [belonged] to a certain man..."
The reading "the wife of a faithful, devoted lay follower (upāsaka) who is a brahmin is unvirtuous and of evil character" is seen [in the text].
For here, having stated "he spoke concerning women," the word "she" (sā) is used; therefore, according to your view, the word *mātugāma* would have to be exclusively feminine and not masculine.
Do you not see even this word of the Aṭṭhakathā? That very [text]...
But look at the words of the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Is that very *Aṭṭhakathā* your refuge, and nothing else?
If you desire the feminine gender for the word *orodha* by depending on the word *tā*, then here too you must desire the feminine gender for the word *mātugāma* by depending on the word *sā*.
Thus addressed, they were left without an answer, speechless, and overcome with embarrassment.
With their shoulders drooping and their faces cast down, they would brood.

Here too, since the word *mātugāma* (woman) expresses the referent of the feminine gender, and since the pronoun "she" (*sā*) is used with reference to that feminine referent, the meaning is precisely this: "that woman.

For in some instances, because a quality-word (*guṇasadda*) that stands in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with a primary term expressed in the masculine or neuter gender follows the gender of its own denotation (*abhidheyyaliṅga*), it is here rendered according to the masculine gender.
Even when something ought to be demonstrated according to the neuter gender, the designation of the feminine gender is seen by disregarding the gender and attending only to the feminine referent.

For example: "In this case, Visākhā, a woman is well-organized in her work, has her attendants under control, conducts herself agreeably to her husband, and protects the household wealth"; and: "Who indeed..."
"What, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the condition, why some woman here is ugly, misshapen, and unpleasant to look at;
and is poor, destitute, lacking in wealth, and of little influence?
Here, Mallikā, some woman is prone to anger, full of distress, and when spoken to even slightly, she becomes resentful, angry, and ill-tempered."
“...he manifests anger, hatred, and resentment,” and “Now, monks,
that jewel of a woman rises before the wheel-turning monarch and retires after him, being ever obedient to his every command”— these are the applications [of the term].

However, in some instances, because the word *guṇa* (quality), which stands in grammatical apposition with a neuter noun expressing the primary subject, follows the gender of its own denoted meaning (*abhidheyyaliṅgānuvatti*), [the quality is expressed in the feminine].
Even though it ought to be demonstrated according to the neuter gender, the masculine designation is seen here regardless of the gender and with reference only to the masculine referent. How so?
"Five hundred paccekabuddhas were long-time residents on this Isigili mountain. And that minister-treasure of the wheel-turning monarch was known among his kinsmen..."

"One who causes [others] to enter and one who restrains those unknown. In some instances, a description is seen that conforms to the gender of the expressed meaning (*abhidheyyalinga*) of the word for quality (*guṇasadda*), which stands in grammatical apposition with a term expressing striving (*padhānavācaka*) in all three genders. How is this so?
That woman is "virtuous and of beautiful character. O Nakulamātā, "endowed with eight qualities, a woman, upon the breakup of the body..."
After death, one is reborn in companionship with the gods of the Manāpakāya realm.
A person endowed with faith, a family endowed with faith, and a mind that is tamed bring happiness.

As for the word *seyyo*, it generally remains in its vowel-ending form (*okārantabhāva*) and conforms to all three genders because it exists in a single form. How so? "A friend endowed with wisdom is better"; "This very veneration is better"; "One day of life is better."
“Non-gain that is in accordance with the Dhamma,
and gain that is contrary to the Dhamma—
gain in accordance with the Dhamma is better.”
Between gain that is unrighteous and the fame of those lacking wisdom,
as well as the ill-repute of the wise—
the ill-repute of the wise is better than the fame of those lacking wisdom.
Praise from fools and blame from the wise— of these two,
blame from the wise is better than praise from fools.
Pleasure consisting of sensual desires and the suffering born of solitude— [the latter is better].
Solitude is better, even if it involves suffering, than the pleasure consisting of sensual desires;
and between life lived unrighteously and death lived righteously,
death through righteous conduct is better than a life lived unrighteously.
Thus, this word *seyyā*, by remaining in its vowel-ending state (*okārantabhāva*), conforms to all three genders.
However, in some instances, it is seen conforming to the feminine gender by remaining in its long-vowel ending state (*ākārantabhāva*), as in: “For even a woman, O lord of men, is better than a man.
But when it takes the nasalized ending (*niggahītanto*), it conforms to the neuter gender; such a form, however, is not established. In cases of this kind...
"Do you not see the application [of the rule]? When addressed thus, they will be left without an answer.

Even if they were to say this: "In various passages of the Suttas and in the Aṭṭhakathās and other works, because the word *mātugāma* is seen in the form of a masculine noun ending in *-o*, such as *mātugāmo* or *mātugāmena*, it must be of the masculine gender."
“We accept that the word *itthī* (woman) is connected with the word *sā* (she),
taking into account only the referent of the feminine gender while disregarding the sound of the word *mātugāma*. However, we do not accept the former point stated by you,
because we do not see the word *orodha* standing in the form of a masculine noun ending in *-o*, such as ‘*orodho*’ or ‘*orodhena*’.”
Then these words found in the Vinaya Piṭaka should be shown to them: “Now at that time King Udena was sporting in the pleasure garden together with his harem; then the harem spoke thus to King Udena.
Having thus shown these Sutta passages, [the passage] from the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā beginning with “Rāmo... [should be cited].
Having shown the statement, "King Nāma was afflicted with leprosy and felt disgust for his harem and dancers," they should be dismissed with the words: "Go,
you, having approached the family of the Teacher, learn thoroughly the words and syllables of the Blessed One’s true Dhamma for the sake of its long endurance."
Now, we shall state some analysis regarding the words *mātugāma* (woman), and so forth:
although the words *mātugāma*, *orodha* (female attendant), and *dāra* (wife) are all denoters of feminine referents, they are invariably masculine in gender.
Among these, those learned in the science of grammar maintain that even when the word *dāra* refers to a single individual, it must take the plural ending.

It does not have a singular number as its grammatical function. We, however, allow that the word *dāra* has a singular number when it refers to a single object, but for the most part we allow it to have a plural number; there is no need to speak further regarding its use in the plural sense.
For in the Pāḷi, the word *dāra* is for the most part plural, while its singular usage is rare. In this regard, here are some examples:
“Male and female slaves, dependents,
sons, wives, and we ourselves— all of us— should practice the Dhamma for the sake of the next world.”
"Therefore, indeed, our young do not die," and:
"He who behaves toward the wives of his kinsmen or friends with impetuosity and passion—
one should know him as a 'basest man' (avasala)."
“There is one who, dissatisfied with his own wife, is seen among courtesans;
he is seen among the wives of others—that is a gateway to ruin”;

and separately, “the longing for children and wives,” but in compound, there are many such uses of the plural, such as “children and wives are the western quarter” and “through children and wives [he harms] himself.”

However, instances of the singular number are few. For example: “Even if one should live as a gleaner among the wives of elders, he who gives food to his wife and dependents even from a small amount...”;
and, “Those householders who perform merit, who are virtuous lay followers, and who support their wives in accordance with the Dhamma—to them I pay homage, Mātali.”
“I shall not go to another’s wife; I shall be devoted to my own wife,” and:
“Whatever man desires to be born again and again in birth after birth, he should avoid another’s wife as one who has washed his feet avoids the mud.”
Usages of this word in the singular number, such as these, are few.
However, by virtue of its characteristic as a collective compound (*samāhāra*), this word *dāra* sometimes occurs in the neuter gender and in the singular number, as in the examples cited here:
"taking wife and children" (*ādāya puttadāraṃ*) and "the gathering of wife and children" (*puttadārassa saṅgaho*). Thus, both the grammatical gender and the meaning are as stated in these instances.

Having observed this, noble sons endowed with faith should develop proficiency for the sake of the endurance of the True Dhamma regarding the nominal declensions of all words ending in -o that are composed of the *bhū*-root— such as "bhūto," "bhāvako," and "bhavo"— as well as other such words, by relying on the pattern of the word "purisa" as it occurs in the forms "puriso" and "purisā."
But have all words ending in the vowel *o* entered the masculine gender (*purisanaya*) in every respect, being exactly identical in all their forms?
They have not so entered. For some words ending in *o* have entered the masculine gender in every way, while others have entered it only partially;
and some words ending in *o* have entered the masculine gender only partially.

There are some vowel-final words (*okārantapada*) that are included in the masculine gender (*purisanaya*) both entirely and partially, while some vowel-final words are not included in the masculine gender at all.
Among these, which are the vowel-final words that are included in the masculine gender both entirely and partially?
They are such as "saro," "vayo," and "ceto. For this word *saro* denotes the word *usu* (arrow), the act of hearing (*saravana*), and vowels beginning with *a*.
If the term *ce* (if) signifies "in every way," it is included in the category of persons (*purisana*).

If it signifies "a lake," it is included in the category of persons only partially, because it belongs to the class of mind-terms (*manogaṇa*). If the word *vayo* signifies "decline," it is included in the category of persons in every way.
If it signifies "the source of life-span" (*āyukoṭṭhāsa*), it is included in the category of persons only partially, because it belongs to the class of mind-terms. *Ceto*—if...
If sound (*sadda*) denotes a conventional designation (*paṇṇatti*), it is entirely included within the category of persons (*purisapuggala-naya*).

But if it denotes consciousness (*citta*), because it belongs to the class of mind (*manogaṇa*), it is partially included within the category of persons. And what is called the "class of mind" is as follows:
mind, speech, vital heat, and fire.
Tapo, ceto, tamo, yaso; Ayo,
payo, siro, chando,
Saro, uro, raho, aho.
These are the sixteen.
Now, in order to clarify what has been stated, we shall explain the nominal declension of the words *manas* and so forth:
Mano, manā. Manaṃ, mano, mane. Manasā, manena, manehi, manebhi. Manaso, manassa.
*Manānaṃ*. [The forms are: *mana*, *manasmā*, *manamhā*, *mane-hi*, *mane-bhi*. *Manaso*, *manassa*, *manānaṃ*.
*Manasi*, *mane*, *manasmiṃ*, *manamhi*, *manesu*. *Bho mana*, *bhavanto manā*.
Or alternatively, it should be understood that the plural form *bho manā* is also used. Thus: *vaco*, *vacā*; *vacaṃ*, *vaco*, *vace*; *vacasā*, and so forth.
The nominal paradigm should be applied [to the word *aha*]. However, in place of the singular locative case of the word *aha*, one should apply:
*ahasi*, *ahe*, *ahasmiṃ*, *ahanhi*, *ahu*, *ahanī*.

Now, for the purpose of showing the distinctions between other forms, we shall state the nominal paradigm of the neuter gender word *mana* as well; it should not be objected that this has been stated in an inappropriate place.
Manaṃ, manāni, manā. Manaṃ, manāni, mane. Manena, manehi, manebhi. Manassa, manaso, manānaṃ.
Manā, manasmā, manamhā, manehi, manebhi. Manassa, manaso, manānaṃ. Mane, manasmiṃ, manamhi, manesu. Bho mana, bhavanto manā.
Or alternatively, "bho manāni, bho manā" is also [correct].
The plural number is to be understood. This same method applies to what follows as well.

In this context, regarding the masculine noun *mano*, having set aside the forms *mano*, *manasā*, *manaso*, and *manasi*—which correspond to the nominative, instrumental, dative, genitive, and locative cases—whatever remains [is the plural]. And regarding the neuter noun *mano*:
The nominative singular forms “mano” and “manāni,” as well as the two forms “mano” and “manāni” used in the eighth (instrumental) case, are set aside;
all the remaining forms are equal in number according to their respective order.
Some say that the word *mano* ending in *-o* is neuter gender; they should be told: if it were neuter gender, [the following would apply].
It might be argued that because of such expressions as *tassadisehi vaco vaya* and so forth, these words should also be of the neuter gender (*napuṃsakaliṅga*).
However, the Teachers do not say, "These are neuter genders"; rather, they say, "They are masculine genders" (*pulliṅga*). And because in the Pāḷi it is said, "The body is impermanent;
the mind is impermanent," and "The body is suffering; the mind is suffering," and [the question] "Is it permanent or impermanent? [the answer is] "Impermanent."
Many such masculine applications have been seen, beginning with "bhante. By this it is known that the word *mano* is exclusively masculine.
If, however, it were neuter, then hundreds of words in grammatical apposition with it—such as "anicca" and "dukkha"—would also have to be neuter; yet they are not neuter, but rather...
The genders of the words to be expressed follow the gender of the referent (*abhidheyya*). Thus, it should be understood that the word *mano* possesses the masculine gender.
[Objection: If the word *mano* is not neuter, how is the neuter form "manāni" seen?
[Response: It is true that "manāni" is indeed neuter; nevertheless, this refers to the vowel-ending (*okāra*) which is taken as the primary member in the *manogaṇa* (the group beginning with *mano*).

The form of the word *manasa* does not exist. If one asks, "Then what is it?"—it is the form of the word *mana* itself, which belongs to the *manas*-group, has the same gender as the word *citta*, and shares the same suffix, yet is not included within the *manas*-group and ends in a nasal stop (*niggahīta*).

For the word *mana* is divided into two ways according to its masculine and neuter genders—as in "mano, manaṃ"—just as [the word] *ajjava* is [divided] as "ajjavo, ajjavaṃ. "If the mind is not corrupted... "Peaceful..."
For the text reads: "tassa mano hotī" (he has a mind). And if that word *mano* were not neuter in gender, [the following would be impossible]:
"Garu cetiyapabbatavattaniyā, pamadā pamadā pamadā vimadaṃ."
Regarding the verse: "Having well understood the ascetic, he did not smile;
the mind of the Sage had fallen upon the foul," why is the word "fallen" (*patitaṃ*), which is in grammatical apposition with the word "mind" (*mano*), presented here in the neuter gender?

And because the word in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇapada*) is present in the neuter gender, does it follow that the word *mano* is known to be neuter by virtue of the proximity of the other word?
That is not so, because a word in apposition does not indicate a specific gender in all instances.
For if a word in apposition were to indicate a specific gender in every case, then [in the phrase] "the four faculties" (*cattāro indriyāni*), [the gender would have been indicated].
Here too, the word "four" (*cattāro*) would cause the term *indriya* to take the masculine gender, yet it cannot do so;

for the word *indriya* is invariably neuter. If you desire the word *mano* to take the neuter gender by relying on the coreferential term "fallen" (*patita*), then [you must also accept that] in the phrase "four faculties" (*cattāro indriyāni*), the word "four" (*cattāro*) [would likewise require the neuter].
"Based on the word *samānādhikaraṇa* (co-referential), you maintain that the word *indriya* must be masculine.
"No, sir, we do not maintain that the word *indriya* is masculine; rather, we maintain that it is neuter.
Because the word 'four' (*cattāro*) stands there by way of a shift in gender, we take it as 'four' (*cattārī*); therefore, [the phrase is] 'the four faculties' (*cattāri indriyāni*)."

"Regarding 'atthaṃ dhārema' (let us hold to the meaning): if that is so, then in the case of the phrase 'patitaṃ asubhesu munissa mano' (the Sage’s mind has fallen upon the unattractive) as well, one might think that the word 'patitaṃ' stands by way of a change of gender (liṅgavipallāsa), and thus hold the meaning to be 'fallen' (patito).
We do not hold this, because a change of gender is not intended here. For if the word *mano* were masculine, then the word in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with it..."
"One might say it should be called *patito*. Why did the teacher not know how to say this? It is not that he knew and yet did not say *patito*;
rather, he said *patitam*, by which it is understood that 'the word *mano* is neuter.
Do not speak thus; for a term in grammatical apposition sometimes follows the gender of the principal word, and sometimes..."
It does not follow [the gender of the other term]; therefore, it is not absolutely authoritative for indicating a specific gender.
In cases such as “Friend Visākha, womenfolk,” “the harem,” or “Come, Visākha, bones, mind,” it is only the specific form [of the word] that serves as the authority.
If the specific gender were to be understood only through words in grammatical apposition, then in instances such as “the four great elements,” and so forth...
There would be no determination of gender. However, since the determination of gender does indeed occur even in such instances as these, how so?

"Four" is masculine, while "great elements" (mahābhūtā) is neuter; therefore, even here in the phrase "the sage’s mind fell upon the foul," there is a determination of gender: "fell" is neuter and "mind" (mano) is masculine.
Having heard this, they will remain silent. Then, to those who have become silent, this should be said:

"Since words occurring in the *manogaṇa* group must in some instances be joined with their coreferential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) words in the neuter gender, therefore the word *mano*, which is preeminent in the *manogaṇa* group, must also in some instances have its coreferential words joined in the neuter gender."

Thus they have been joined together. For indeed, the former teachers [have composed] poetic compositions such as: "The darkness in the hearts of those beings to be trained perishes in an instant, struck down by the splendor of the True Dhamma";
"One whose speech is difficult is called 'dubbaca'"; "One whose head is bowed is 'avaṃsiro'";
and "Those in whose eye of wisdom there is little dust of passion and the like are 'apparajakkhā'. And so forth.

They [the commentators] have so explained it; however, they did not compose such a grammatical arrangement in order to demonstrate that words such as *vaca*, *sira*, and *rajas* possess a neuter gender (*napuṃsakaliṅgatta*).

Rather, they did so because even for words like *sira* and *mana*, which belong to the *manogaṇa* and are masculine (*pulliṅga*), there are instances where they appear with such a shift in gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*) while functioning as coreferential terms (*samānādhikaraṇapada*) with others.
This has been composed out of compassion, with the intention of making [the matter] known.

Here too, according to your own opinion, if the word *mano* were neuter, then words such as *vaco* and *sira* would also fall into the neuter gender, because they are indicated as being in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with a neuter term. But do you actually desire that these [other words] also be neuter?
"Certainly, having heard this, they will remain silent, unable to unravel it. Even though they see no other reason for taking [the opposite side], they might say:
'Sir, if the word *mano* is not neuter, why do the grammarians say that the word *mano* is neuter?
They should be told: 'If you accept the opinion of the grammarians...'"

If you would accept that the word *mano* has a neuter gender, consider this: is not the Blessed One himself peerless in the world, a great grammarian, a Great Man, confident, and a crusher of the doctrines of others?

For neither the reciters of the *padakas*, nor the grammarians, nor the brahmins such as Ambaṭṭha, Māṇava, Pokkharasāti, and Soṇadaṇḍa, nor the wanderers such as Saccaka and the Nigaṇṭhas, were able to equal the Blessed One in debate; on the contrary—
The Blessed One himself, like a maned lion amidst a herd of rutting elephants, crushed their various arguments without fear and established them in great truths;
for it was by such a Blessed One, skilled in conventional usage (*vohārakusala*),
that the word "mind" (*manas*) was spoken in such ways as "the body is impermanent" and "the body is suffering," as well as "the mind is impermanent" and "the mind is suffering."
Many Pāli passages are seen that indicate the masculine gender; therefore, it should be understood as the essential point that the word *mano* is indeed masculine.
Thus addressed, they will remain speechless, without a reply, abashed, with shoulders drooping and heads cast down, brooding in silence.
Now, the nominal declension of the words *sara*, etc., is specifically stated:
Saro, sarā. Saraṃ, sare. Sarena, sarehi, sarebhi. Sarassa, sarānaṃ.
Sarā, sarasmā, saramhā, sarehi, sarebhi. Sarassa, sarānaṃ. Sare, sarasmiṃ, saramhi, saresu.
Bho sara, bhavanto sarā.

This is the nominal declension of the word *sara* when it signifies sound (*sadda*)—specifically the sound of an arrow (*usu-sadda*) or sounds beginning with the vowel *a*—and thus belongs entirely within the masculine gender (*purisaliṅga*).
However, this is the nominal declension of the word *sara* when it signifies a lake (*rahada*) and belongs to the *manogaṇa* class, entering the masculine gender only partially:
*Saro*, *sarā*. *Saraṃ*, *saro*, *sare*. *Sarasā*, *sarena*, *sarehi*, *sarebhi*. *Saraso*, *sarassa*, [sarehi, sarebhi].
*Sarānaṃ*. [The forms are: *sarā*, *sarasmā*, *saramhā*, *sarehi*, *sarebhi*; *saraso*, *sarassa*, *sarānaṃ*; *sarasi*, *sare*, *sarasmiṃ*, *saramhi*, *saresu*.
*Bho sara*, *bhavanto sarā*, or *bho sarā*. *Vayo*, *vayā*. *Vayaṃ*, *vaye*.

*Vayena*, *vayehi*, *vayebhi*—these should be understood according to the masculine paradigm (*purisanaya*). This is the nominal declension (*nāmikapadamālā*) of the word *vaya*, which enters entirely into the masculine paradigm and denotes decline.

Now, the nominal declension (*nāmikapadamālā*) of the word *vaya*, which denotes a portion of life and belongs to the class of mind-objects (*manogaṇa*) included in part within the masculine gender (*purisanaya*), is as follows:
*vayo*, *vayā*; *vayaṃ*, *vayo*, *vaye*; *vayasā*, *vayena*, *vayehi*, *vayebhi*. This is to be understood according to the method of mental application (*mananaya*).
"He whose mind consented, who roams the forest like a hunter; they struck him down, he who was to be pierced. (*Tassa ceto paṭissosi, araññe luddagocaro. Cetā haniṃsu vedabbaṃ.*)

*Ceto*, *cetā*; *cetaṃ*, *cete*; *cetenā*, *cetehi*, *cetebhi*—this should be understood according to the masculine paradigm. This is the nominal declension of the word *cetas* when it denotes a conventional designation (*paṇṇatti*) that enters entirely into the masculine paradigm.
However, this is the nominal declension of the word *cetas* when it denotes the mind (*citta*) and enters into the masculine paradigm only in part:
*ceto*, *cetā*; *cetaṃ*, *ceto*, *cete*; *cetasā*, *cetenā*, *cetehi*, *cetebhi*—this should be understood according to the neuter paradigm.

*Yaso*, *kulaputto*, *yasaṃ kulaputtaṃ*, and *yasena kulaputtena* should be construed according to the masculine paradigm in the singular number, or alternatively, in both the singular and plural numbers.
Thus, certain words ending in *-o* enter the masculine paradigm entirely, while others enter it only partially;
by this method, all such words should be understood with the eye of wisdom.

Having investigated, the distinction must be understood. For those who perceive no distinction, not knowing such classifications as these, misrepresent the intended meaning by attributing this or that phrasing [to the wrong context];
therefore, this classification explained by us here should be carefully mastered by sons of noble family endowed with faith. Which ones?
Are there certain words ending in *-o* that have entered partially into the masculine paradigm and partially not?
These are *mano*, *vaco*, *tejo*, *sadda*, and so forth, as well as the word *ayya*. Regarding these, the nominal declension (*nāmikapadamālā*) for *mana* and the others has been explained below.
However, regarding the nominal declension of the word *ayya*, one should state it according to the masculine paradigm as follows: "ayyo, ayyā; ayyaṃ, ayye."
In the context of address, two singular forms—“bho ayya” and “bho ayyo”—and two plural forms—“bhavanto ayyā” and “bhavanto ayyo”—should be employed.
Here, the word *ayyo* is a singular form when functioning as a nominative case, but it is both singular and plural when functioning as a vocative case.
Regarding this, the following is an example of usage: “Ayyo kira Sāgato... (It is said that Master Sāgata...).

“‘He has been made to engage in combat with the Ambatitthika Nāga; let the noble Sāgata drink the Kapotika broth, O Venerable One’”—such are examples of the singular vocative usage of the word *ayya*. “Then that woman said this to the man:
‘That bhikkhu did not force me; rather, I myself am going with that bhikkhu.’”
“He is not the doer; go and ask for his forgiveness”—such are the uses of the singular form of address with the word *ayya* (sir).

“Come, sir, to the royal residence; having sat down, listen to me. Come, sir, let us go forth among the recluses, the sons of the Sakyan”—such are the uses of the plural form of address with the word *ayya*. And on this point there is [this verse]:
The word *ayya* is a term for the singular when used as a proximate designation (*paccatteka-vaca*);
it may be plural when used in address (*ālapan*), and it may also be singular.
Thus, certain words ending in *-a* enter into the masculine gender category only partially, while others do not enter into it at all.
Which are some words ending in the vowel *o* that do not enter into the masculine gender at all?

Only the word *go*. For this is the nominal paradigm (*nāmikapadamālā*) of the word *go*: Nominative: *go*, *gāvo*, *gavo*. Accusative: *gāvuṃ*, *gāvaṃ*, *gavaṃ*, *gāvo*, *gavo*. Instrumental: *gāvena*, *gavena*, *gohi*, *gobhi*. Dative:
*gāvassa*, *gavassa*, *gavaṃ*, *gunnaṃ*, *gonaṃ*. Ablative: *gāvā*, *gāvasmā*, *gāvamhā*, *gavā*, *gavasmā*, *gavamhā*, *gohi*.
*Gobhi*: *gāvassa*, *gavassa*, *gavaṃ*, *gunnaṃ*, *gonaṃ*. *Gāve*, *gāvasmiṃ*, *gāvamhi*, *gave*, *gavasmiṃ*, *gavamhi*, *gāvesu*, *gavesu*, *gosu*.
*Bho go*, *bhavanto gāvo*, *gavo*. This is the nominal paradigm of the word *go* (cow), which has not entered into the masculine system (*purisanaya*) in every respect.

"But surely, sir, the word *go* (cow), by way of the sequence of words beginning with *goṇa* (bull) produced from itself, has entered into the category of persons (*purisana*) both partially and not partially?

True. Although the word *goṇa* is produced by means of the word *go*, according to the statement, "The application of words follows the speaker's intention," we have taken it separately from the word *go* and inserted it into the category of persons. Of that—
For a justification for separate inclusion is seen in the case of the *sy*-suffixes and so forth, because they remain in a single form;

therefore, disregarding the word *goṇa* even though it is derived from the word *go*, and taking only the pure word *go*, it is stated that the word *go* has not entered into the masculine mode at all.
But surely, sir, the word *go*, being in the nominative case, is similar to the word *purisa* (man) in its masculine mode?

Is it entered by way of a single part? That is not so; for the word *go* always ends in *-o*, and unlike words such as *purisa*, it does not first remain in the state of ending in *-a* and only later acquire the meaning of ending in *-o*.
For this very reason, it remains exactly as *go* even in the place of the nominative case and in the place of the vocative case.
If, depending on its status as a nominative... [the word *go*]... of the word *go*...
Partial inclusion within the masculine gender must be accepted; otherwise, the discussion regarding words ending in *-o* mentioned as "certain words ending in *-o*" would illuminate what purpose?
That discussion would be entirely fruitless. Therefore, the venerable ones should attend to the method exactly as stated by us.
In this way, the word *go* (cow) is to be seen as not included at all within the masculine gender.
And here they might ask thus: “We know that the word *go* does not enter into the masculine paradigm at all—in the manner of ‘go, gāvo, gavo;
gāvuṃ, gāvaṃ, gavaṃ,’ and so on—but where do words such as *jaraggava* and *puṅgava* enter?
To them it should be explained thus: “Words such as *jaraggava* and *puṅgava* [enter] in every respect...”
“...have entered into the system of persons. For such is the distinction between these two words from the term *go*: *jaranto ca so go cāti jaraggavo* (“an old one and he is a cow, thus an old ox”).

Here, due to the nature of the compound word, there is the elision of the letter *na*, and the letter *ta* becomes *ga*; furthermore, in a compound, when followed by a feminine suffix (*simhi*), the substitution of *o* for the vowel *o* of the word *go* occurs.
Therefore, in the Pāḷi text it says: “*visāṇena jaraggavo*” (with the horn of an old ox).
The singular form is seen. For elsewhere, because there is no accompanying word (*upapada*), only the plural form *gavo* is seen.
But here, because there is an accompanying word, by virtue of its status as a compound word, only the singular form *jaraggavo* is seen.
For in the case of *jaraggavo*, it is analyzed as "those who are old and they are oxen" (*jarantā ca te gavo ca*), thus according to the plural number.
The state of being etymologically derivable (*nibbacanīyatā*) is not obtained because [the term] is established in a single conventional sense according to worldly usage.
Thus, the nominal declension should be applied according to the masculine pattern: “*jaraggavo*, *jaraggavā*; *jaraggavaṃ*, *jaraggave*; *jaraggavenā*.
This same method applies to such terms as *puṅgavo* and *Sakyapuṅgavo*.
In this context, *puṅgava* refers to a bull known as the leader or chief (*nisabha*) of a herd of cattle. This is the term used in the canonical text in such passages as:
"Just as a lord of cattle, immediately after birth, touches the earth with his even feet," and "If among cattle running along, the bull goes straight.
However, in such instances, some explain it as "one who is both male (*puma*) and a cow (*go*), thus a *puṅgava*."

They state the etymological meaning [of the word]. We, however, do not state an etymological meaning on the grounds that this term is conventionally established (*nirūḷha*) in the sense of "exertion" (*padhāna*).

For it is not possible for this term to possess the capacity to manifest merely the male gender, in the same way that words such as *puṅkokila* (male cuckoo) have the capacity to manifest the male nature of the cuckoo and so forth;
rather, it possesses the capacity to manifest its status as the primary factor (*padhānabhāva*).

It is possible. Therefore, in such cases as "Sakyapuṅgava" (the bull among the Sakyas), the meaning of the compound should be understood as follows: he is like a bull (*puṅgava*) designated as a leader (*nisabha*);
thus, he is a bull among the Sakyas, or a bull within the Sakyas—hence "Sakyapuṅgava.

Alternatively, because words such as "lion," "tiger," and "elephant" standing as the final members of a compound denote excellence, terms such as "Sakyapuṅgava" may be understood as "Sakyaseṭṭha" (the best of the Sakyas), and so forth.

The meaning must be grasped. Thus, because they function within the mode of persons in every respect, the dissimilarity of the word-sequences of terms such as *jaraggava* (old bull) and *puṅgava* (bull) from the word-sequence of the term *go* (cow) must be established.
Furthermore, the fact that the term *go* does not enter into the mode of persons in any way whatsoever must also be established.

Regarding the word *āpasadda*, there exists a difference of opinion among teachers concerning its gender and number; therefore, according to that [latter] opinion, it does not enter into the masculine derivation at all.
In the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) on the Pāḷi passage “*Aṅguttarāpesu*,” it is stated:
“the water (*āpo*) to the north of the Mahī river”; however, in the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*), having referred back to that, it says: “the water (*āpo*) of the Mahī river, for him...”
It is said: "Because they are to the north of the country, and because the country is not far from them, that country is called 'Uttarāpa'.
Thus, the teachers maintain that the word *āpa* is exclusively feminine and plural;
in their opinion, when the form *āpo* occurs as the nominative plural feminine, the forms for the second, third, fifth, and seventh case plurals are as follows: [āpā, āpehi, āpānaṃ, āpesu].

What would they be like? For instance, just as there are forms such as *purise*, *purisehi*, *purisebhi*, and *purisesu* for the masculine gender ending in *-a*, no forms of the feminine gender ending in *-ā* joined with the case endings beginning with *kā* (the nominative) are seen anywhere in the same way.
Therefore, according to their view, the method of the paradigm (*padamālā*) is exceedingly difficult to establish.
Those who respect the system of grammar have declared that the word *āpa* possesses plurality and a feminine gender. Thus,
it should be understood that the status of *āpa* as having a feminine gender and a plural ending is accepted based on the opinion of the grammarians.
In the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, however, an example of the word *āpo* used in the neuter gender and singular number is seen:
“But the deficient water became subject to the predominant earth. In the *Jātakapāḷi*, on the other hand, its singular ending is also seen;
for instance: “Pure and fragrant water, there the *āpo* flows down. In this passage—
The word *āpo* is seen standing in the singular number. Here some might say: "The word *salila*—meaning water that has become pure and fragrant—is what flows there;
thus, the use of the singular number is made by way of the word *salila*, not by way of the noun (*nāma*) itself.
For the word *āpa* is exclusively feminine in gender and ends in the plural number. Likewise...

"For although the application of the plural number—'the waters flow there together'—should have been stated, it is taught by way of a change of grammatical number for the sake of preserving the meter. This is not correct;

for it would have been possible to say, "the waters flow there together," just as in the case of the plural usage in the phrase "those [bones] are seen today. Since it was not stated thus, and because...
In the Pāli, the singular usage “water is obtained, fire is obtained, air is obtained” is seen;
therefore, the fact that the word “āpo” (water) ends in the singular number is directly perceived.
Now, they might further argue: “Is not its plural ending also directly perceived in the Pāli itself, as in ‘āpo’?”
And [the question: "Did the gods and the earth, fire and wind come then?"—that too is not so.
For here, with reference to the word "gods," the plural form "came" (*āgamuṃ*) is employed, but not with reference to the word "water.
If the plural form were employed with reference to the word "water," then it would also have to be employed in the plural with reference to the words "earth," "fire," and "wind."
It would have to be so. If that were the case, then earth, fire, and air would also attain the status of plural forms; however, they do not. These are not plural;
rather, they are singular. They function by way of conventional usage (*rūḷhi*), because they do not apply to meanings such as "water" in its primary sense (*pakati*).
For instance, they are produced after performing the preliminary practice (*parikamma*) upon the water-kasina and so forth.
The deities receive the names "water" and so forth by way of their objective referents (*ārammaṇa*). Even though they have been addressed in this way, they might say:
"But, sir, is not the plural form *aṅguttarāpesu* seen in the Pāli? They should be told: "You have not entered the path of correctness;
for you do not understand the occurrence of words. As for the plural form *aṅguttarāpesu*, it refers to [the people] 'among the Aṅgas and the Uttaras'."
Expressions such as "among the Aṅgas, among the Magadhas," though plural, are stated by way of conventional usage (*rūḷhi*) even for a single country;

they do not intend the meaning of "waters" (*āpa*). For in the phrase "among the Aṅguttarāpas," the meaning of "waters" is subordinate, whereas that which is expressed by the masculine plural—the meaning of "country"—is the primary sense.

In the phrase “the monastery has been entered by a recluse” (*āgatasamaṇo saṅghārāmo*), just as the meaning designated as “monastery” (*saṅghārāma*) is understood from the word *āgatasamaṇa*—which functions by making the meaning designated as “recluse” (*samaṇa*) subordinate—one should understand the meaning as follows:
having taken the meaning designated as “Aṅguttarāpa,” it refers to the country named Aṅguttarāpa; thus, the meaning is “in the country among the Aṅguttarāpas. Likewise...
For the Pāḷi text is seen as follows: “He dwells among the Aṅguttarāpas; there is a market town of the Aṅgas called Āpaṇa.
In this context, those who have water (āpo) to the north (uttara) of the Mahāmahī River are the Uttarāpas; those who are both Aṅgas and Uttarāpas are the Aṅguttarāpas—among them, the Aṅguttarāpas.
Thus, the plural number is used for a single country, not for the sense of the word *āpa* itself; therefore, in the Commentary...
It is said: “In that district of Aṅguttarāpa. Thus spoken, they will be left without reply.
Nevertheless, those who say, “The word *āpa* is feminine in gender and plural in number,” should be asked:
“On what basis do you, venerable sirs, say that the word *āpa* is feminine in gender and plural in number?”
Being thus questioned, they would reply: "That very country is Aṅga;
however, because the waters of the Mahī River lie to the north [of it], and because of their proximity, it is called Uttarāpatha"; and also:
"The waters of the Mahī River lie to the north of that country, and because of their proximity, that country is called Uttarāpatha. Thus [it was taught] by the ancient teachers.
"A specific grammatical construction is seen here; therefore, we say it is feminine and plural.
This is true that it is seen, but it was constructed by adopting the opinion of the grammarians (veyyākaraṇa) in the science of grammar (saddasattha).
Furthermore, the science of grammar does not assist the word of the Buddha (buddhavacana) in every respect, but only in part. Therefore—

In the *Kaccāyanappakaraṇa*, the characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) were stated in order to perform the inclusion and exclusion of desired and undesired forms, according to the principle: "For the gender appropriate to the word of the Victor (*jinavacana*) is produced.
Now, if the word *āpa* is feminine and plural, how is the form *āpo* established? [It is established] from the word *āpa*.
Having applied the first *āp* suffix and having applied the substitution of *o* for the final vowel of that [word], the form *āpo* is established, just like the word *gāvo*.
This illustration is incorrect; for the word *gāvo* is derived from the word *go*, which invariably ends in the vowel *o*.
Thus, when the suffix *ām* follows, the final vowel of the word *go* is replaced by *āv*, and subsequently, the *ām* is replaced by *o*, whereby the form *gāvo* is produced.

Furthermore, there are no two alternative readings for the word *āpa*. For when it reached the Buddha’s word (*buddhavacana*), the word *āpa* became one whose stem ends in the vowel *a*, and not otherwise.

Even though they were told this, those who harbor the thought "this alone is the truth, nothing else," and who are characterized by stubbornness, grasping, and an inability to relinquish, [remain as they are].
Standing on the point that "well-spoken words are not easily understood by those who take pleasure in opposition," they might say:
"Just as the word *gāvo* [is masculine], why should the word *āpo* not be feminine and plural?
Then, these Sutta passages should be shown to them. Namely: "Water..."

Having shown the scriptural passages: “One perceives water; having perceived water as water, one conceives of water, one conceives in water, one conceives ‘water is mine,’ and one delights in water,” one should ask: “In this context, what is the word ‘water’ (āpo)?
Certainly, desiring that the word *āpo* be in the plural, they will say: “It is the second case plural.”
They should be asked: "Is it not the case that the word *yu* is not heard? They might reply:
"The word *yu* is not heard because it has undergone the substitution of *kata*. Whatever the venerable ones desire, they say is present in the mouth [of the speaker].
But as for this term "*āpato*," what do the venerable ones say it is? This too is "a plural form ending in the suffix *-to*."
We say this because the suffix *to* occurs both in the singular sense and in the plural sense.
Thus, while you yourself desire that it be plural, you state that "the word *āpo* ends in the plural"; yet you also state that "from *āpa*" (*āpato*) is likewise "ending in the plural suffix *to*.
However, in the phrase "he conceives [it] in water" (*āpasmiṃ maññati*), of what case-ending is "in water" (*āpasmiṃ*) composed, and by what substitution?
