"Is it produced?"—surely, when questioned thus, they will be left without an answer. Likewise, those who hold the view that "the word *āpa* is feminine and plural" should be asked:

"Regarding what was stated by the teachers, adopting the opinion of the grammarians, as 'that which is water' (*yā āpo*) and 'of them' (*tāsām*), in that context, regarding the expression 'of them' (*tāsām*), [is it] 'of waters' (*āpānam')?"
“Should the meaning be stated by bringing forward the word *pada*, or rather [by bringing forward] *āpa*?
If it is said, “The meaning should be stated by bringing forward the word *āpā*,” then in that case one should say “*yā āpā*” (which waters), just like the phrase “the maiden who stands.
If, on the other hand, it is argued that there is no such thing as the word *āpā* and that the word *āpo* itself is the plural form, then in that case, regarding the word “*tāsām*” here as well—
The meaning should be understood by bringing in the word “āpassa. Why?
Because, according to your view, since the singular form “āpo” would have to become plural, the word “āpassa” would also have to be treated as plural and joined with the word “tāsaṃ”;
such would be the logical construction. If that were the case, there ought to be no word at all for “āpānaṃ,” just as [in the following example].
However, just as there are singular and plural forms such as *puriso*, *purisā*; *purisaṃ*, *purise*;
and *go*, *gāvo*, *gavo*, *gāvuṃ*, so too there ought to be singular and plural forms for *āpo* such as *āpo*, *āpā*; *āpaṃ*, *āpe*.
And this being the case, it should not be said that "the word *āpa* is exclusively plural."
The words of those who speak thus are faulty and difficult to maintain, because we see the singular-number readings in the *Mūlapariyāya Sutta*:
“He conceives of water as water,” and because we see the etymological explanations given in the singular number in the *Visuddhimagga* and other works:
“It is called ‘water’ (*āpo*) because it flows (*āpnoti*) to various places by way of its trickling nature,” and so forth.
However, whereas in the Pāḷi the word *go* (cow), though included in the feminine gender,

is seen used in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with both pronouns and non-pronouns that indicate plurality— such as in the phrases "he should drive those cows here and there with a staff" (*tā gāvo tato tato daṇḍena ākoṭeyya*) and "these are givers of food and givers of strength" (*annadā baladā cetā*)—
it is not so [used] in the Pāḷi with words indicating plurality.
The word *āpa-* is seen used in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with either feminine gendered nouns or non-feminine nouns.

For if the word *āpa-* were feminine, there would have to be either the suffix *-āp-* after the word *āpa-*—just as there is the suffix *-āp-* after the word *kañña*—or the suffix *-ī-* after the word *āpa-*—just as there is the suffix *-ī-* after the word *nada*; yet neither of these occurs.
Because both [the suffix and the feminine marker] are absent, every rule stated for the feminine gender does not apply there;

by this it is known that "the word *āpa* is not of the feminine gender. But, sir, is it not the case that the suffix *-āp* is also absent from the word *go*, and because of its absence, the rules stated for the feminine gender do not apply?
This being so, why is only that [word *go*] feminine, and not this word *āpa*?
To this it is replied: the word *go* is not necessarily feminine; rather, it is masculine.
However, even if the suffix *ā* does not occur there due to the feminine gender, the suffix *ī* occurs optionally, and other rules prescribed for the feminine gender may also apply.
For that [word] stands as having a nature always ending in a vowel, and thus produces its own feminine forms such as *go* and *gāvī*.
Because it is the cause of production, that [word] possesses the feminine gender. However, in the case of the word *āpa*, suffixes such as *īp* are not applicable;

therefore, it cannot be said to possess the feminine gender. Or, just as the status of the feminine gender arises for the word *go* based on its conventional usage in the sense of a non-masculine form, it is not so for the word *āpa*. For the word *āpa* consists merely of a non-turbid form.
The conventional usage of the form *avisadā* is not seen, by which this word could possess the feminine gender. When addressed in this way, they will be left without an answer.
Likewise, those who think, "The word *āpa* is always feminine and plural," should be told:
just as in the case of the word *kaññā*, which is feminine and is established in the nominative singular in its short-vowel form as *kaññā*.
The *smiṃ* suffix following the *ā* case-ending does not remain in its own form;
rather, it remains as both *yaṃ*-ness and *yā*-ness, as in "kaññāyaṃ" and "kaññāyā.

It is not so with the word *āpo*, which you have classified as feminine (*itthiliṅga*) and established with a short vowel as "āpa," where the subsequent *smiṃ* suffix remains as both *yaṃ*-ness and *yā*-ness.
Rather, the word *āpo* remains in its own form [as a masculine noun] when one thinks "in water" (*āpasmiṃ*).

If, however, the word *āpa* were feminine, the locative suffix *-smin* would not remain in its own form. Since the locative suffix *-smin* does remain in its own form, the word *āpa* is therefore not feminine.
For indeed, among the hundreds of thousands of millions of categories included within the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dhamma, [the word *āpa* is never used as feminine].

In certain passages of the Canon, the *smiṃ* case-ending remains in its original form after feminine nouns that are established in the nominative singular as ending in the vowel *a*. If this is stated, they will be left without an answer.
However, some might say here: "The word *āpa* is neuter; for instance, in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, [it says] ‘omattaṃ’..."
"But [you might ask: 'Why are the words in grammatical apposition with it (the water) indicated in the neuter gender, as in the statement: "But the water has become predominantly earth-natured"?

That is not so; for just as with words such as *tama* (darkness), *vacī* (speech), and *siras* (head) which occur in the *manogaṇa* class, words in apposition with the word *āpa* (water) must in some instances be indicated in the neuter gender. For the ancient teachers..."

In poetic compositions (*saddaracanā*), in the passage: "The darkness in the hearts of those beings to be trained (*veneyyasatta*) goes to destruction in an instant, struck down by the splendor of the True Dhamma," the neuter gender form "vihataṃ" (struck down) is seen as being in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the word "tamo" (darkness). Likewise, in the passage:
"One who has harsh speech toward this person who is disagreeable and unpleasant is called 'dubbaca' (one of bad speech)," [the term *dubbaco* is derived] from the word "vaco" (speech).

The term *dukkha* is neuter when it stands in grammatical apposition; for example, in the phrase “one whose head is bent is ‘bent-headed’” (*avanatasiro*), the word *avanata* is neuter because it stands in apposition with the word *sira*.
Similarly, in the phrase “those in whose eye of wisdom there is little dust of passion and so forth are ‘few-dusted’” (*apparajakkhā*), [the term *appa*] stands in apposition with the word *raja*.

The neuter gender (*napuṃsakaliṅga*) is seen in the word *appa*. Those teachers did not compose such a verbal construction merely to indicate that words like *taṃ* and *rasa* possess the neuter gender when used in apposition with those [other] words;

rather, it is because even when masculine forms occurring in the *manogaṇa* (the group beginning with *mano*) are employed, they may also function as neuter—as in the case of "he whose mind is beautiful is *sumano*" (*sobhanaṃ mano tassāti sumano*).
They composed [the text] to show that there are instances where words stand in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*).
Just as the verbal construction beginning with "vihataṃ" was not made for the purpose of indicating the neuter gender of the words *tama* and *vacasira*,
likewise the verbal constructions "omattaṃ" and "adhimattapathavīgatikaṃ jātaṃ" were also not made for the purpose of indicating the neuter gender of the word *āpa*.

It was not so made. However, because the word *āpa* (water) shares a common grammatical status (*samānagatika*) in part with the words *mano* (mind), etc., which occur in the group of neuter nouns (*manogaṇa*), its coordination (*samānādhikaraṇatā*) with a neuter noun is appropriate;
therefore, in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, coordination with the neuter word *āpa* was established in the passage: "But the minor water has become subject to the predominant earth."
Nevertheless, because the word *āpa* (water) follows the same grammatical course as *mana* (mind) and other terms in part,
and because we see its usage in compound words such as "āpokasiṇaṃ" and "āpogataṃ" where the medial *kāra* [is elided],
one should not take the statement "omattaṃ" and so forth to mean that it is intended to indicate the neuter gender of the word *āpa*. Rather, it is due to a change in gender.
It should be understood that this was stated for the purpose of making it known that in some instances there is such a grammatical derivation of the word.
Furthermore, the gender must be changed in the cases of "omatto" and "adhimattapathavīgatiko jāto.
For if the word *āpa* were neuter, its nominative and accusative forms with the suffix *-san* would be found in the Buddha's words and other texts; however, no such forms exist. Moreover, ...
—There is no neuter gender ending in the vowel *o* anywhere; for neuter genders are only threefold, namely those ending in the *niggahīta* (anusvāra), *i*, and *u*.
Therefore, the neuter gender of the word *āpa* is not established.
When they are thus addressed, they will be left without an answer. Thus, the feminine gender of the word *āpa*, which was taken as ending in *o*...

Furthermore, there is no absolute absence of the neuter gender; however, for that which is taken by way of the *niggahīta* [anusvāra], the neuter gender may occur in some instances, as seen in the following usage:
"Venerable Nāgasena, it is said 'the ocean, the ocean. For what reason is water (*āpa*) called 'the ocean'?
Regarding this, some might say: "If, sir, by way of the vowel ending..."
"The word *āpa* that has been cited does not possess both genders by virtue of being feminine and neuter;
rather, of what gender is the word *āpa* ending in *-o*? "We say it is masculine.
"If, sir, the word *āpa* is masculine, then let its masculinity be made evident through its suitability for contemplation (*nijjhānakkhamatā*)."
"And it should be so; bring a sutta accordingly. "We shall bring the sutta; we have no burden in bringing a sutta.
Having spoken thus, these words of the sutta should be shown to them. For example: "Is water apprehended? Yes.
Is an agent or a maker of water apprehended? It should not be said so. [Regarding] the past..."
“Is there water? “Yes. “Does it perform the function of water by means of that water? One should not say this. For these words from the Sutta state:
“It conceives of water; it conceives in water.
And here, by the phrase “it is found,” etc., the singular number of the word *āpa* (water) is established; once that is established, its plural number is also established.
It is indeed established. For in the grammatical treatises (*saddasattha*), only the singular number is prohibited, not the plural;
therefore, by the form “āpenā,” the disappearance of the feminine gender of the word *āpa* is established, because there is no substitution of *enā* in the feminine.

Likewise, by the forms “āpassa” and “āpasmiṃ,” there is likewise the disappearance of the feminine gender, because in the feminine, the nominative-accusative singular (*nā*) and the dative-locative singular (*smā*, *smiṃ*) do not exist in their own form.
By the word “past” (*atīta*), there is the disappearance of the feminine gender and the neuter gender, because of the absence of a neuter noun ending in *-o*,
and because of the absence of a feminine noun ending in *-o* that functions as a quality-name (*guṇanāma*).
Furthermore, this is because in the Buddha’s word and other texts, one does not see forms with the suffix *-san* such as *cittāni* or *rūpāni*.
The disappearance of the neuter gender from that which was grasped as having an *okāra* ending is extremely evident. Furthermore, something else should be said here:

regarding the statement, "Is there past water? Yes," the word "past" (*atīta*)—by means of this *okāra*-ending term which indicates the designation of water in its clear form—indicates the absence of its designation in an unclear form and the absence of its designation in a form free from both.
It is established. Since its status as being expressed in a non-feminine form is absent, its feminine gender is even further removed.
And since its status as being expressed in a form free from both [feminine and masculine] genders is absent, its neuter gender is likewise even further removed.
Thus, the word *āpa*, when apprehended in its diphthongal ending (*okāra*), is neither feminine nor neuter. However, in the *Milindapañha*, by way of the nasalized vowel (*niggahīta*):
It should be understood that [the word *āpa*] has arrived as a neuter gender; nor should it be said here that the words "past" (*atīta*) and "by him" (*tena*) are stated by way of a change of gender.

This is because there is an absence of feminine and neuter gender forms for the word *āpa*, which follows the gender of its expressed referent (*abhidheyya-liṅga*)—unlike [words such as] *kaññāya cittāni* and so forth. Furthermore:
The Tathāgatas and the disciples of the Tathāgata are skilled in conventional usage;

therefore, because these supreme persons who are skilled in conventional usage have spoken [of water] as "past water" and so forth, one should not think that the terms "past" (*atīto*) and "by that" (*tena*) are stated here by way of a change in grammatical gender.

Consequently, the word *āpa* (water), which shares the same grammatical core (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with those terms, is understood as having a long vowel ending (*okārantabhāvena*) and is singular in number.
It should be understood that this word is masculine and takes both the singular and plural endings according to usage, because it must be applied in such forms as “āpo, āpā;

āpaṃ, āpe,” and so forth. Having heard these scriptural passages thus stated along with their analysis, those who maintain that the word *āpa* is feminine and plural will certainly be left without an answer.
Here someone might say: "Was the masculine gender and the singular number in the Pāḷi not seen by the masters of the Aṭṭhakathās and Ṭīkās, who describe the word *āpa* as being feminine and plural?
It is not that they did not see it; they certainly saw that grammatical method.
However, it is because they were proficient not only in the Buddha-word consisting of the Three Piṭakas together with the Aṭṭhakathās, but also [in other fields].
Furthermore, those who are proficient in the entire science of grammar (saddasattha) have no fault in taking recourse to the methods of that science to demonstrate their own scholarly expertise,
to clarify that "such a rule is stated in the science of grammar," and to describe the feminine gender and plural number of the word *āpa*.
For instance, in the commentary (*ṭīkā*) on the *Mūlapariyāya Sutta*:

By those very [authorities], it was stated—indicating that the word *āpa* is used in the masculine singular—that "water is fourfold by way of characteristic, constituent, object, and conventional designation;
among these," and so forth. Therefore, there is no fault on their part. For those venerable ones are worthy of honor;
we pay homage to them alone, and their words are not a vessel for censure. As for those who speak in direct opposition and are indeed stubborn...
They claim that the word *āpasadda* possesses a feminine gender and plural number; their statement alone is the basis for the objection.

However, since we establish both the masculine and neuter genders of the word *āpasadda*—which possesses two meanings—in accordance with the method of the Pāḷi, anyone who is able to crush this argument and establish another will succeed.

This possibility does not exist; however, this matter is a great thicket in the sense that it is difficult to penetrate, and it is extremely subtle because it is to be realized by wise ones possessing extremely subtle knowledge through the accumulation of wisdom.
Indeed, all these statements are intended to generate supreme skill in listeners regarding the grasping of both the meaning and the phrasing in various contexts within the Dispensation.

This was stated for the purpose of preventing the laxity and heedless conduct of those who pass their time according to the opinions of grammarians without showing respect, and to demonstrate the exceedingly great importance of the Dispensation;
it is not for the purpose of self-exaltation or disparaging others.
According to this principle, sons of good family endowed with faith should apply themselves for the sake of the long endurance of the Blessed One’s Dispensation.

However, since there is no such thing as a commentary that possesses greater authority than the canonical text (pāḷi), we shall apply the declensional paradigm of the word *āpa* strictly in accordance with the method of the canon, for the sake of the listeners' non-confusion; what need is there here for the methods of grammatical science (*saddasattha*)?
Here is the relevant passage from the Udāna: "What would one do with a well, if there were water everywhere?"

Āpo, āpā. Āpaṃ, āpe. Āpena, āpehi, āpebhi. Āpassa, āpānaṃ. Āpā, āpasmā, āpamhā, āpehi, āpebhi. Āpassa, āpānaṃ. Āpe, āpasmiṃ, āpamhi, āpesu. Bho āpa, bhavanto āpā. We shall also apply this to pronouns and other words: *yo āpo*, *ye āpā*; *yaṃ āpaṃ*, *ye āpe*;
*yena āpena*—the rest should be understood accordingly: *so āpo*, *te āpā*; *atīto āpo*, *atītā āpā*. The rest should be understood accordingly. Thus it is said:
"The word *āpa* and others are considered in every respect to be identical to [the paradigm of] the masculine."
The word *go* (cow) is not considered identical to the word *purisa* (man) in every respect.
Words such as *mana* (mind) are considered identical to *purisa* in one respect;
words such as *sara* (arrow) are considered identical either in one respect or in every respect.

But as for those words here that are called "the group of mind" (*manogaṇa*), how is their status as the "group of mind" to be observed? It is said: the reason for observing their status as the "group of mind" is this:
"The group of mind consists of the 'group of mind' and so forth, as well as the 'not-group-of-mind'."
Thus, words are to be known as threefold in the exposition of the class of nouns (*manogaṇa*):
those that [denote] a person, a thing, and an object.
And they become [words] ending in -sā, -so, and -syantā;
for when they are compounds or end in taddhita suffixes, they indeed have -m, -o, and -kāra in the middle.
And the applications of the words *soka*, *āra*, and *anta* are seen in the context of *kriyāyoga*;
such words as these should be understood as belonging to the "class of mind" (*manogaṇa*).
Herein, we shall demonstrate the applications that establish this meaning by drawing them from the Teaching and from common usage as appropriate.
If one speaks or acts with a pure mind, [one is dear to me]. Pay close attention. Mental phenomena are preceded by the mind.
With a mind-made body, through psychic power, he approached [him] who was delightful to the mind.
He who, having said "I shall give," sets his mind on not giving. [These things] are cultivated by speech; they are rooted in speech, established in speech.
He awakened this lotus of those to be trained with the rays of his speech;
the Buddha-moon is pure, free from the stain of passion.
Having heard the words of Kassapa, Alāta spoke as follows:
Having heard the words of the Sage, I have gained even greater confidence.
You are my companion and friend, Sīvaka; being well-trained, carry out my word well. Subhadda, I am twenty-nine years of age.
In life, O life, one grows old; the qualities of youth are gradually abandoned, like a fire burning with its brilliance.
Skilled in heat, in heat, in the element of heat; the kasiṇa of heat. Supreme through austerity, of austerity, in austerity, possessing the wealth of austerity, having loathing for austerity.
Why does your reverence dwell in the uninhabited forest, practicing austerity here for the sake of attaining the state of a Brahmā?
He knew it with his mind; thus a reflection arose in his mind; having kept this matter in mind, having known the reflection in the mind.
The knowledge of the minds of others (*cetopariyañāṇa*): he discerns the mind; with his own mind he discerns the minds of other beings and other persons.
He is one who dispels darkness, one from darkness, one in darkness, the dispeller of darkness, the remover of darkness. I give this to you with glory.
O glorious one, O you who possess glory, one endowed with glory and wealth. Indeed, our wealth is obtained through glory. [There is] Queen Yasodharā, glory...
Having obtained [wealth], one should not become intoxicated. It is like rust arising from iron itself—iron, O iron-man, bounded by an iron fence, covered over with iron.
Better it is to eat an iron ball, an iron bowl, made of iron; "iron-lover" (*ayokanta*) means that which grinds iron.
Eat with ghee or with milk; indeed, drinking milk is excellent, O Yaññadatta; in milk there is nourishment (*ojā*).

*Payodharā*, *payonidhi*. He received [it] with his head, he who has a thousand eyes. "From the head": having placed the hands together in reverence at the head, one should worship the source of the sages' power.
"Hair of the head," "he cuts off the head. He who avoids sensual pleasures as one avoids the foot of a venomous snake.
"Having caused your head to be struck. "Lake," *saraso*: three kinds of lotuses in that lake.
O Brahmin, [the verse] *Saroruhaṃ*: "Those whom they serve, whether with poetic meter (*chandas*) or with wealth—Sāvitrī is the mouth of poetic meter.

[Examples: *chandasi*, *chandoviciti*, *chandobhaṅgo*; "I shall push away with my chest (*uras*)," *uraso*, "born from the chest" (*urasi jāyati*), *urasiloma*, "pierced in the middle of the chest" (*uromajjhe vijjhi*).
[Examples: *rahasā*, *rahaso*, *rahasi*, "having sat down in secret" (*rahogato nisīditvā*), "thus I thought then."
Examples [of the nominative] are: *ahasā*, *ahasi*. Examples [of the locative] are: *jāyanti tattha pārohā*, *ahorattānam accaye*.

And here, examples such as “*manena*, *manassa*, *mane*, *manasmiṃ*, *manamhi*,” as well as “*mana-āyatanaṃ*, *tamaparāyano*, *ayapatto*, *chandahānī*,” and “*na manaṃ aññāsi. Yasaṃ laddhāna dummedho. Siraṃ chindatī*” and so forth.
And forms are not shown [here] because they do not manifest as mental aggregates, not because they are unobtainable;
therefore, from the beginning, there are these verses that clarify the nature of the mental aggregates:
"By the mind, of the mind, in the mind..."
Those beginning with *iti* and ending with *so*, which consist of the forms of words,
are called the "manogaṇa" (the group of particles).
The mind-element is the ray of speech;
the quality of asceticism is the matured wind;
the fire-element is the destruction of darkness.
Endowed with fame and wealth;
reflections in the mind; iron ladles and breasts;
hair like a lotus; in the midst of the chest, gone into seclusion.
The violation of meter lasts for a day and night;
"mind-made" and "iron-made"—such is the distinction found at the end of the characteristics within the *manogana*.
Having heard the words, "cut off the head," and "iron cuts," thus [it is said].
The successful accomplishment of the application [of grammatical rules] depends on the characteristics found within the group of nouns ending in *-man*.
The method explained for the group of nouns ending in *-man* does not apply to feminine gender nouns;
however, it certainly applies to masculine and neuter gender nouns as appropriate.
Thus, in every respect:
those forms which are the ends [of the senses] appear in the collection of the mind;
and the forms within the middle and the interior are employed for the removal of sorrow.
This is the characteristic of the group of consonants (manogaṇa). Thus has the characteristic of the group of consonants been set forth—unconfused, unobscured, and free from tangles.
Now we shall explain the characteristics of the group of consonants and so forth:
those which are in this domain...
That [suffix] is elided after a word ending in *sā*, *so*, or *syantā* according to what is appropriate; however,
the vowel *o* does not occur at the end of compounds or words ending in *taddhita* suffixes.
And those [words] used in the sense of "sorrow" (soka) do not occur in the application of the verb *kri*;
all such words are merely sounds.
The *manogaṇa* and so forth are considered [to be used]. For example: “*bilaṃ*, *padaṃ*, *mukhaṃ*,” and so on. Their forms are:
*bilasā*, *bilaso*, *bilasi*, *bilagato*, *bilaṃ pāvisi*. He went by foot (*padasā*), three steps (*padavārāni*), do not make [noise] with the mouth (*mākāsi mukhasā*).
Evil is expelled like food gone astray from the mouth. Tamed by truth and endowed with self-control, he drinks the supreme taste, the essence consisting of flavor.
This is the characteristic of the mental aggregate and so forth.
Furthermore, there is this:
But in the case of compounds and so forth, they indeed become medial vowels;
however, in that specific domain, they do not remain as final vowels.
And there is the application of the term *sokāra*.
They do not exist in the context of *kriyāyoga*;
such sounds as these are considered to belong to the class of the mind (*manogaṇa*).
For example: “Water, wind, autumn,” and so forth. Their forms are as follows:
*āpodhātu*, *vāyodhātu*, *āpokasiṇaṃ*, *vāyokasiṇaṃ*, *āpomayaṃ*, *vāyomayaṃ*, *jīva tvaṃ saradosataṃ*, *saradakālo*.
[The cases are: *āpena*, *āpassa*, *āpe*, *āpasmiṃ*, *āpamhi*; *vāyena*, *vāyassa*, *vāye*, *vāyasmiṃ*, *vāyamhi*; *saradena*.
*saradassa*, *sarade*, *saradasmiṃ*, *saradamhi*. One perceives water as water; one perceives wind as wind. One longs for autumn;
the river is delightful in autumn. However, some might say here:
"Should not the word *vāya*—just like the word *vāya* [meaning 'crow']—be desired in the *manogaṇa* and other such groups? To this it is replied:
Among these [terms], such as "vāyu vāyo," only the latter is intended.
In the case of the "manogaṇa" group and others, the "nādi" (the nasal sound) is included here by virtue of being the first member of the series.
For indeed, there are phrases such as "manodhātu vāyodhātu."
By means of the vowel *a* alone, those words with medial *o* are established.
When the word "wind" (*vāyu*) is included here by way of including the initial [term],
the form "air element" (*vāyodhātu*)— with its middle syllable elided— will not exist.
For just as the form of the word *āyu* is seen with its grammatical augment—
as in the phrase "with life, my only son"— and as in the words beginning with *manasa*,
the form of the word *vāyu* is not seen with its augment in that same way.
Therefore, in the list beginning with "the group of mind" (manogaṇa), there is no room for that [term].
For thus do the teachers say: "It blows, therefore it is wind (vāyo)";
such is the meaning of the word "wind-element" (vāyodhātu) in various places.

Where earth and water, fire and air find no footing—herein lies the sound-triad beginning with *āpādi* within the group of words beginning with *manogaṇa*. This too is the characteristic of the group of words beginning with *manogaṇa*.

Here, those beginning with *manogaṇa* are divided into two types: those beginning with *bila* and those beginning with *āpa*. Thus has the characteristic of the group of words beginning with *manogaṇa* been taught clearly, without confusion, without obscurity, and without entanglement.
Now we shall explain the characteristics of the group of unpleasant sounds: Those sounds which are not within the range of the ear, and those which, though within range, might be so—
sounds of such a nature are designated as the group of unpleasant sounds.
Which are they? They are the words for meaning (*attha*), phrasing (*byañjana*), syllables (*akkhara*), sound (*sadda*), and so forth, as well as the long forms of the word *orasa*.

For among these, in place of the nominative case endings for the words beginning with "meaning" (*attha*), there occur forms such as *atthaso*, *byañjanaso*, *akkharaso*, *suttaso*, *upāyaso*, *sabbaso*, and *ṭhānaso*.
However, in place of the nominative case endings for the long forms of the word *orasa*, there occur the forms *dīghaso* and *oraso*.
These are the forms. This is the characteristic of the group of non-mental [factors].
Furthermore, there is another:
those which are entirely liberated from the states of "it," "he," "she," and so forth.
Such are these sounds designated as the "group of non-man" (*amanogaṇa*).

What are they? They are words such as *purisa-kaññā-citta* and so forth. This too is the characteristic of the group of non-man. Thus has the characteristic of the group of non-man been declared clearly, without confusion, without obscurity, and without entanglement.

When the characteristics of the group of man and so forth have thus been demonstrated, someone might say: "As for this which was stated by you, 'those [words] which, in the state of being compounds (*samāsa*) and so forth...'"

By such [rules] as "majjhokārāva honti tū," which define the characteristics of the *manogaṇa* (the group beginning with *man*) and so forth, does it follow that in expressions such as "parosataṃ gomayaṃ godhano" (a cowherd with more than a hundred cows), the words *gopa*, *rasa*, and others would also attain the status of belonging to the *manogaṇa* and so on? They do not. Why is that? Because:
"In this context, the *manogaṇa* and other groups depend upon the final vowel (*anta-sotta*)."
The expression “majjhokārā” is a conventional statement, not derived from the Āgamas or other such sources.
In cases such as “more than a hundred cow-dung [cakes],” the preceding word belongs to the class of unpleasant sounds;
this is due to its being dropped and because of its impermanence.

Therefore, they do not incur [an offense]. Thus, the definition of the group of non-mental [terms] has been shown in its entirety in every respect. In this way, regarding the analysis of the group of mental [terms], the division should be understood as threefold:

the group of mental [terms], the group beginning with the mental [terms], and the group of non-mental [terms]. Therein, when words included in the group of mental [terms] enter into a compound, their forms may also become otherwise according to the three genders, as in:
"a person of unagitated mind," "a family of steadfast heart," and "a female lay follower whose speech is trustworthy."

In this regard, however, some say: "When the word *mano* does not remain in its own sense, but is used in another sense—such as 'he whose mind is undistracted is one of undistracted mind' (*abyaggamanaso*), or 'he whose mind is unattached is one of unattached mind' (*alīnamanaso*)—then the series of nominal derivatives is obtained according to the pattern of the word *purisa*, and not according to the pattern of the word *mano*. That should not be accepted.
Because both [positions] are appropriate according to the circumstances. For instance, in the *Visuddhimagga*, with reference to the individual, the method of counting by mind is seen in the passage:

“Having accepted the request of one whose mind is adorned with qualities such as patience, gentleness, and loving-kindness. In its commentary (*Ṭīkā*) as well, the method of counting by mind is seen in the phrase:
“Requested by the Elder Daṭhānāga, who possessed a steadfast mind. Therefore, the word of those who speak thus should not be accepted. Speaking in this way...
And they, having reflected with a distracted mind on the fact that words such as *abyaggamanasa* and *sadḍa* should be established in their base-form ending in the letter *s*—
namely, as *abyaggamanasaiccādi*— consider that [the forms] should be joined with all case-endings (*vibhatti*) and two numbers according to the method of *purisa*.
And this being so, [they would derive] the sixth, fourth, and third case forms as *guṇabhūsitacetaso*, *thiracetasā*, and so forth.
There might be other forms that are not intended; since there are such, one should not grasp it in this way, but rather grasp this distinction:
for in cases where, by virtue of a compound, the word *manas* and words such as *cetas* do not function in their own primary sense (*sakatthe*) but function in another sense (*aññatthe*).

In this regard, the nominal paradigm (*nāmikapadamālā*) of words that undergo the addition of the suffix *sakāra* is obtained as appropriate according to the "man" pattern (*purisanaya*) and the "manana" pattern within the *man*-group;
however, for those that do not undergo the addition of *sakāra*, it is obtained only by the "man" pattern.

Furthermore, where words such as *mana* and others function in their own sense (*sakatthe*) only within the scope of compounds (*samāsa*), there the nominal paradigm of those that do not undergo the addition of *sakāra* is [obtained] by the "man" pattern.
And it is obtained through the mental group (manogaṇa) and by means of the process of reflecting (mananayena).

Now, for the purpose of clarifying this meaning and for the purpose of producing skill in the paths of words among the wise, we shall demonstrate the sequence of the aforementioned words by dividing them into three ways:
"He whose mind is attached is one whose mind is attached (byāsattamanaso)."
Regarding the word “man” (*naro*) as being thus absolutely dependent upon a person:
A man with a distracted mind; men with distracted minds. A man with a distracted mind; men with distracted minds.
By a man with a distracted mind; by men with distracted minds. Of a man with a distracted mind.
Of a man with distracted mind, of men with distracted minds. From those with distracted minds, from him with a distracted mind, from those men with distracted minds;
by those with distracted minds, by those men with distracted minds. Of one with a distracted mind, of a man with distracted mind, of men with distracted minds.
In one with a distracted mind, in [a man] with a distracted mind, in [a man] with a distracted mind.
In *byāsattamanamhi nare*, *byāsattamanesu naresu*. O man of distracted mind, "you, sirs, are men of distracted minds"—this is the series of noun cases (*nāmikapadamālā*).
In this way, the occurrence or non-occurrence of the augment *sakāra* (the letter *s*) must be determined. For here, [it is absent] in the first and second case endings.

In the place of the singular and plural [cases], there is an augment (sāgama) appropriate to the third, fourth, sixth, and seventh cases in their singular forms, due to the following of a substitute vowel (ādesa-sara), a case-ending (vibhatti-sara), or another suffix (para).
This method is subtle and should be carefully attended to.
Another method: "He whose mind is distracted is 'one with a distracted mind' (byāsattamanas)"—thus it is also used in reference to a person (puggala).
The nominal series for this word follows the masculine pattern alone, as in: “*byāsattamano naro*, *byāsattamanā narā*, *byāsattamanaṃ naraṃ*,” and so forth.
In all these cases here, however, there is no insertion of the letter *s*. There is also another method:
“*byāsatto ca so mano cāti byāsattamano*”; thus, even though this word depends on the mind (*citta*), [it is formed in this way].

“*Byāsattamano*, *byāsattamanā*; *byāsattamanaṃ*, *byāsattamane*; *byāsattamanasā*, *byāsattamanenā*”—in this manner, according to the method of inflection for the mind (*mano*), there is a nominal paradigm within the group of mind-derivatives.

However, in this case, the augment *s* occurs only in place of the singular forms of the third, fourth, sixth, and seventh cases, because of the following of the substitute vowel *sa*. And just as it is here, so too [is it] in the case of *alīnamanasaḥ*.
This threefold method should also be understood in the case of "naro" and so forth.
However, when expressing it in the neuter gender, the series of nominal forms (nāmikapadamālā) should be constructed as follows:
"byāsattamanasaṃ kulaṃ, byāsattamanāni kulāni; byāsattamanasaṃ kulaṃ, byāsattamanāni kulāni; byāsattamanasā kulenā," and so on.

Furthermore, here, in the place of the singular number for the first, second, third, fourth, sixth, and seventh [cases], the augment *s* occurs as appropriate because of the following substitute vowel (*ādesa-sara*) and case-ending (*vibhatti-sara*).
This method is also subtle and should be carefully attended to.
However, when expressing the feminine gender, in the place of the nominative singular alone, [one says] "a woman with a distracted mind" (*byāsattamanasā itthī*).

Having spoken with reference to the *āgama*, one should then apply the feminine suffix *-ī* according to the rule for young girls (*kaññā-naya*) as follows: “a man with distracted mind, women with distracted minds, a woman with a distracted mind.
Likewise: “a female lay follower (*upāsikā*) whose word is trustworthy, female lay followers whose words are trustworthy, a female lay follower whose word is trustworthy,” and so forth.
Also: “a family with distracted minds, a woman with a distracted mind,” and so on.
However, it should be applied according to the method of the "Cittakaññā" (The Maiden of Consciousness). In this instance, however, there is no insertion of the vowel *ā* in any case.
For the purpose of generating a variety of knowledge in those who hear, we shall present another series of nominal derivatives along with their etymologies:
*mano* itself is *mānasaṃ*; one whose mind (*mānasaṃ*) is uplifted is *samussāhitamānaso*. "One whose mind is uplifted..."
“*Samussāhitamānasā*, *samussāhitamānasaṃ*, *samussāhitamānase*, *samussāhitamānasenā*” should be applied according to the masculine paradigm.
One who possesses beautiful wisdom (*medhā*) is “*sumedhaso*. “*Sumedhaso*, *sumedhasā*; *sumedhasaṃ*, *sumedhase*;
*sumedhasenā*” is according to the masculine paradigm; likewise for “*bhūrimedhaso*” and so forth. Here are the applications:
“Regarding those whom they call ‘Sumedha,’ the one of vast wisdom, the wise Sumedha—why indeed have you been separated from him, even for a moment, O Piṅgiya?
The Gotamas possess vast insight; the Gotamas possess vast wisdom.”
“O Brahmin, I do not dwell apart from them even for a moment—those Gotamas of vast wisdom, those Gotamas of vast intelligence.
When referring to the feminine gender, the forms are “samussāhitamānasā sumedhasā”; when referring to the neuter gender, [the form is] “samussāhitamānasaṃ.”
"Of the wise one": this refers to forms (*rūpa*). The sequence of words for these [forms] should be applied according to the method for feminine nouns.

This determination of feminine gender and so forth in place of the masculine gender ending in *-o* has been made for the purpose of illustrating the method; for specifically, it is the discussion of those ending in *-o* that is intended here.
Moreover, in the world, a system of rules (*nīti*) shines only when explained in its various aspects, and this is a system of rules within the Dispensation (*sāsana*); therefore—
"Thus have they been explained in various ways.
All these words ending in long vowels are thus stated according to their grammatical method as masculine nouns for the sake of the Teaching by the Great Sage.
Regarding those [verses], whatever specific distinction appears in the Canon (pāḷi) at the place where the nominative case occurs,
I shall now set that forth. For, according to the method beginning with "Just as the tops of forest thickets are in full bloom," etc.;
The forms of the masculine gender ending in *kattha* and *codanta* might be otherwise;
one should explain that form as being only in the nominative singular (*paccattavacana*).
Some authorities state: "The locative case is used in the sense of identity (*paccatta*)."
In this regard, we shall present some scriptural passages: "There is no personal effort, there is no effort by another, there is no human effort;
saṃsāra is limited; the soul is the seventh [factor]; one should not speak thus;
both fools and the wise, having run on and wandered through [saṃsāra], will make an end of suffering. These are to be understood in two ways, according to the singular and plural numbers.
The substitution of *ekāra* for both the singular and plural nominative cases should be understood.
As for those who say, "In the phrase *vanappagumbe*, there is a designation of the locative case for the nominative case," they should be told:
"If *vanappagumbe* is a designation of the locative case for the nominative case, then in that case, [the form] *thāliyaṃ*..."
“Just as in the case of ‘he cooks rice,’ because the possibility of a locative construction exists here, what meaning does this expression ‘in the first month of summer, in the summer’ illuminate?
They might reply: “Sir, we do not say that ‘in the forest grove’ is a locative expression;
rather, we say it is a locative designation for a nominative expression. Even so, there is still a fault.

Is it not the case for you that even in the expression “Give to the Saṅgha, Gotamī,” although it is stated that the locative case is used for the dative, the word “in the Saṅgha” (saṅghe) is indeed both a locative hearing and a figurative assumption of a locus, because the Saṅgha serves as the locus for the act of giving?
For it is impossible to prevent such a mental process; therefore...
In this regard, however, the following distinction must be understood: "In some instances, even the nominative case takes the form of the locative case.
For when it is understood in this way, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

Indeed, in such cases, the Blessed One—who is skilled in the varieties of grammar and compassionate toward the world—did not teach in this manner [using the nominative] when he ought to have demonstrated it by means of the nominative case; rather, he taught it for the sake of the world.

How could it provide an exposition of the locative case while appearing to produce confusion? Therefore, one should not say "an exposition of the locative case" by merely grasping the commonality of the term.

If you accept an exposition of the locative case by grasping the commonality of the word, then one would also have to accept "an exposition of the accusative plural for the singular [of] the personal pronoun."

Furthermore, in that same way, if there were a locative case-noun indication for the singular noun “attakāre,” then because a substratum would be heard [implied], the unintended meaning—“there is no object whatsoever in self-agitation”—might result, rather than the intended meaning: “self-agitation does not exist.
Even if one takes it as a dative plural case-noun indication, because the sense of the dative is negated by the word “natthi” (does not exist),...

Because it would be improper to speak [in that way], there would indeed be a fault; however, since the word "not" (*natthi*)—just like the words "is" (*atthi*) and so on—is joined with the nominative case, it is understood that "attakāre" is a nominative singular form.

Even in the passage, "Fools and the wise, having run on and wandered through [saṃsāra], will make an end of suffering," the term "the designation of the locative case" refers to the nominative singular.
Or, if there were an apprehension that it was a "designation by way of usage" (*upayogavacananiddesa*), there would be the fault of not knowing how to say even as much as "fools and wise men.
However, because of its connection with the word "will do" (*karissantī*), it is understood that "fools and... and so forth is indeed the nominative case (*paccattavacana*).
Just as, for instance, when the word "the eye arose" (*cakkhuṃ udapādī*) is pronounced according to the elision of the *niggahīta* [anusvāra], [it is understood as the nominative].

In the phrase “Give me an eye, as I have been asked,” although there is equality [of status] due to the usage of the accusative case, it is the meaning of the nominative case alone that presents itself to the listener, because it is expressed by the verb “arose” (*udapādi*).

It is not the meaning of the accusative case, which would constitute a shift in grammatical number (vibhatti-vipallāsa), because that meaning cannot be expressed by the verb “arose”; for the Blessed One said, “An eye arose.”
At the time of speaking, who explains the meaning by changing the word "the eye arose" (*cakkhuṃ udapādi*) [into its nominative form]? Likewise,

even though the singular case-forms such as "a fool" (*bāle*) and "a wise man" (*paṇḍite*) are identical in sound to other forms such as the locative and accusative "in a fool" (*bāle*) and "a wise man" (*paṇḍite*),
only the meaning of the singular case-form appears to the listener, not the meaning of the other case-forms.

Because the meaning must be understood according to its application. Thus, in such passages as “O fool, in the forest thickets,” and so forth, one should understand that these are simply words in the nominative singular case (*suddhapaccattavacana*), and not words in the locative or instrumental cases merely because they share a common sound with those cases.
As for what was stated by the Teacher in the *Jātakaṭṭhakathā*—
“I desire the three regions between the mountains:
Pañcāla, Kuru, and Kekaka; even more than that, O Brahmin, do I desire.”
In the commentary on this *Kāmanīta-jātaka*, regarding the phrase “*Tikiccha maṃ brāhmaṇa kāmanītan*,” it is stated: “*Kekake cā* is the accusative case used in the sense of apposition;
by that, he indicates the kingdom of Kekaka. And speaking thus, he says: “He sees men; he is established among men.”
In such passages as “I see people in the world with wealth,” since for the most part words like “purise” (men), “loke” (in the world), “sadhane” (with wealth),
and “manusse” (people) appear in the form of the accusative plural, the locative singular, and so forth, while the nominative singular and plural forms are not evident,
he speaks— assuming that this [present case] is exactly like those— referring to their predominant usage.
I think so. For teachers sometimes explain things differently according to their own preference.

But this is our own preference: that *kekake* is indeed a nominative singular, just like the co-occurring terms *Pañcālā* and *Kuru*, yet it is expressed in the plural because it denotes a kingdom, just like the term *Kurū*. For the Blessed One did not say, "a khattiya... [and so on].

Just as in expressions such as "a brahmin," "a merchant," and so forth, where things are indicated by identical case endings, one might indicate the latter among co-occurring locations by means of the accusative case;
however, no logical justification is seen for stating "the Pañcālas" and "the Kurus" in the nominative case while stating "in Kekaya" in the accusative.
Therefore, this term "Kekake" is indeed in the nominative case.
For indeed, the Master who composed the *Sandhivisodhana* (The Purification of Sandhi), while clarifying that such words are in the nominative case, stated in his own treatise:
“*vanappagumbo vanappagumbe, sukhaṃ dukkhaṃ jīvo, sukhe dukkhe jīve*”;
and in the commentary (*ṭīkā*) as well, while clarifying their status as nominative cases, he says: “*vanappagumbo*...”

Having established the forms *sukhaṃ*, *dukkhaṃ*, and *jīvo* as the bases to be proven, he states the derivation of the forms *vanappagumbe*, *sukhe*, *dukkhe*, and *jīve* by means of the elision of the nasal (*niggahītalopa*) and the substitution of the vowel *e* (*ekārādesa*). This is in accordance with the method of the Pāḷi.
The teacher Kaccāyana also, relying on the method of the Pāḷi, [formulated] the nominative plural ending according to the rule "dvipade tulyādhikaraṇe."
Thus it was said. Therefore, he stated in the *Vutti*: “The two words have a common substratum (*tulyādhikaraṇa*).
Furthermore, this expression “*dvipade tulyādhikaraṇe*” should be understood as being spoken in the same way as the word “*aṭṭha nāgāvāsasate*” is used when one ought to say “*aṭṭha nāgāvāsasatāni*.
Some, however, maintain that these [two words] are in the singular locative case. In that regard, if “*vanappagumbe*” is taken as a descriptive adjective (*paccatte*),...
“Bhummavacanaṃ” (the locative case) and “kekake” (in the sense of the nominative) are in the accusative case;
as for “esese eke ekaṭṭhe,” here “esese” may be either locative cases in the sense of the nominative or accusative cases in the sense of the nominative.
Just as these [words] are not of such a nature [but are] purely nominative cases, so too are “vanappagumbe,” “kekake,” and so forth.
They do not become such [forms], but remain purely singular personal pronouns. Thus, in every respect,
in cases such as “*vanappagumbe*, *bāle*, *paṇḍite*, *kekake*,” and “*viratte kosiyāyane*, *aṭṭha nāgāvāsasate*, *ke purise*, *esese*,” and so forth—
[these examples] being numerous according to the masculine gender, feminine gender, neuter gender, all nouns, the singular number, and the plural number—

It must necessarily be accepted that for those standing in the excellent dispensation (*sāsana*), the realization of the forms of the singular and plural nominative cases occurs solely through the substitution of the vowel *e*.
Thus, the status of words such as *vanappagumbe*, *bāle*, and *paṇḍite* as pure nominative singular forms is exceedingly subtle and difficult to discern;
it can only be understood by a faithful son of good family who has attended upon a teacher.
Having carefully received that instruction, it should be understood.

For within the Buddha’s word, various methods of the Pāḷi are seen which cause the eye of knowledge of those who contemplate words to be obscured, both in respect of the phrasing (*sadda*), the meaning (*attha*), and the underlying intention (*adhippāya*).
Among these, first, this is a point of obscuration regarding the phrasing: where one should say "Virattā Kosiyāyanī," [it is said] "viratte."

In the phrase “kosiyāyane,” the nominative singular feminine form is seen; where one would say “ko puriso” (who is the man?), the nominative plural masculine form of the pronoun is seen as “ke purise”;
and where one would say “kinnāmo te upajjhāyo” (what is the name of your preceptor?), the compound word “konāmo te upajjhāyo” is seen referring to the masculine gender.
For indeed, “konāmo” means “kiṃ nāmaṃ etassa” (what is the name of this?).
This is a compound. By this, the following method should also be understood: “What is the name of the woman? What is the name of the family?
When one should say, “Where is your strength, O Great King? [one says] “What is your strength, O Great King?”;

here, by means of the word *kva*, the locative case-ending (*-su*) of the word *ko* is seen to have a slightly similar sound, for *kva* and *ko* are mutually slightly similar in sound. Likewise, “here... [and so forth].

"In the winter and summer seasons," here meaning "in these winter and summer seasons"; "he did not bind himself to that purpose, they did not bind themselves to that purpose"—other [verses] should also be applied accordingly.
In terms of its meaning, however, this is a point of confusion: "that which is not even two-feathered gold, gone into blind darkness."
Here, the negative particle *na* should be connected with the word "done" (*kata*). The meaning is: "not done" means "as if done.
For in this context, the negative particle functions as a comparison, not as a negation. [As in:
"One who lacks faith and is ungrateful..."
The man who has severed the connection,
who has destroyed the opportunity and vomited out his hopes—
he is indeed the supreme person.”
Other such [passages] should also be applied accordingly.

From the intended meaning (*adhippāya*), this is a point of confusion: although it should have been stated thus—"Having destroyed craving, the conceit 'I am,' the views of eternalism and annihilationism, that which is based on the twelve sense-bases, and delight-and-lust, the brahmin goes untroubled"—instead of saying that, it takes up that very same meaning and expresses it by another method.
“Having slain mother and father, and two kshatriya kings,
and having destroyed the kingdom together with its subjects— the brahmin goes forth free from affliction.
Thus it was said.
“Cut down the forest, not the tree; from the forest fear is born.
Having cut down both the forest and the undergrowth, become forest-free, O bhikkhus.

Other passages such as these should also be applied accordingly. Thus, various methods of the Pāli canon are seen which cause the eye of knowledge of those who contemplate syllables to become confused, both in terms of the words, the meaning, and the underlying intention. As it has been said:
“Even those who know the entire science of grammar are deluded regarding the sequence of recitation;
for, in most cases, methods found in the texts are inconsistent with worldly usage.
Therefore, a wise person, having set aside even that external scholarship, should apply himself to this very [work].”
“One should train to cross the ocean of the stainless Dhamma and reach the landing-place of Nibbāna.

Because the method of the canonical texts (pāḷi-naya) is thus difficult to discern, one should understand the essential meaning of such passages as “in the forest thickets,” “the foolish,” and “the wise” as being in the nominative singular case alone;

one should not assume they are in the locative or accusative cases merely because of the commonality of the phonetic ending, nor should one interpret them as locative or accusative forms on the basis of such endings.
Even though they are produced by the same vocal organs, they are indicators of specific meanings because they are individual indicators (*paccatta-jotaka*).
For even words produced by the same vocal organs become indicators of specific meanings through their connection with context, grammatical gender, other related words, and so forth. How so?
When it is said, “The lion sings,” the meaning understood is “a man of such a name. But when it is said, “The lion wags its tail,” the meaning understood is “the king of beasts. Thus...

By way of context (*atthavasena*), there occurs the illumination of a specific meaning for words that are phonetically identical. For instance, when one standing in a battle cries out, "Bring *sindhava*," it is understood to mean "a horse.
However, when one says, "Bring *sindhava*," in a sick ward, it is understood to mean "salt.

Thus, by way of context (*pakaraṇavasena*), there occurs the illumination of a specific meaning for words that are phonetically identical. When "issā" is said, [it refers to] a woman of such a name...

It is understood as "of a virtuous nature. But when "isso" (this) is said, it is understood as "the deer named Accha. Thus, by means of gender (*liṅga*), there occurs the illumination of a specific meaning for those [words] that share a common sound in part.

However, although in cases such as "Call Devadatta, the water-pot bearer, the staff bearer," etc., the water-pot, the staff, and so forth are also genders, nevertheless, because this is under the heading of "those sharing a common sound," [only the former are intended].
That [meaning] is not intended here.

However, when it is said, "Envy arises," and "Envy followed the man," there occurs an illumination of the specific meaning as stated above—namely, that those who hear the same thing together [understand it differently]—by means of the connection with other words (*saddantara*). Likewise: "O monks, a lion..."
When it is said, “The king of beasts comes out from his lair in the evening,” it is understood that this refers to the maned lion, the lord of beasts.
But when it is said, “Sīha is a novice monk; Sīha is a general,” it is understood that this refers to a novice named Sīha and a general named Sīha.
Thus, by means of connection with other words, a distinction in meaning is revealed even for those [words] that are phonetically identical.
It occurs thus: “The group-of-six bhikkhus saw the group-of-seventeen bhikkhus repairing the dwelling.
In this way, through the connection between the words, there is the manifestation of a specific meaning—the sense of the accusative and dative cases—among those who hear it together.
Likewise: “Bhikkhu, bail out this boat,” [where] a certain bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One.

In this way, even for those words that are phonetically identical, there occurs an indication of specific meanings—such as the sense of address (*ālapanattha*), the sense of the nominative (*paccattattha*), or the sense of the abstract noun (*saṅkhātattha*)—by means of their connection with other words (*saddantarābhisambandhavasena*).

Therefore, expressions such as “*vanappagumbe yatha phussitagge*” (like the tops of trees in a forest when they have blossomed), although they share similarity with the locative and instrumental cases, must be understood as pure nominative singular forms by virtue of their connection with other words.
For it is only in the case of the singular and plural nominative endings that [the distinction] occurs through the substitution of the vowel *e*.
"Such forms as these are words used for the instrumental case of the base *bhūm*. Now, one might ask:
"Since such forms are seen in the Canon (*pāḷi*), should it not be said that 'there exists a masculine gender with a single vowel [ending]'? It should not be so said;

for those forms are specific types of words whose status as having a long vowel ending is inherent. Indeed, because they are established by way of substitution (*ādesa*), there is no separate masculine gender with a single vowel ending.
There is no such [separate] name; therefore, only the sevenfold classification of masculine nouns as previously stated should be accepted.

However, some might say: "In that grammatical series of noun-inflections for all words ending in the vowel *o*—analyzed by adopting the method of the word *purisa* (man) as 'bhūto, bhūtā, bhūtaṃ,' and so forth—the singular dative case includes the substitution of *ā*."
"Why are the forms [of the suffix] not stated?"—it is for the purpose of showing the distinctions.
For when such forms in the singular fourth case (dative) are examined according to the method of the Canon and the method of the ancient commentaries, they occur, in brief, in these four places only:

"in the sense of the object of a verb meaning 'to go'," "in the sense of the object of a verb meaning 'to lead'," "in the transformation of a case ending," and "in the sense of that [word] itself"; and in detail, [they occur]...

However, they are seen in seven places. But as for their not being mentioned here to show this distinction—that they are not seen in any instance of the domain of giving (*sampadāna*) when there is a division such as giving (*dāna*), announcing (*rocana*), maintaining (*dhāraṇa*), delighting (*namana*), or joining (*yoga*)—one might object:

"In the context of the act of giving, since we see the form of the dative singular ending in *-ā* (with the substitution of *ā* for *e*) in the example 'A beautiful maiden should be given' (*abhirūpāya kaññā deyyā*), [should they not be included here too?]"
In the *Saddanīti* treatise, forms such as “purisāya” and “bhūtāya” ought to be stated;
this being so, why is it said that “in the various instances of giving, announcing, holding, and the like, they are not seen in any case within the domain of the recipient”?

Because they do not follow the method of the Pāḷi. For the rule “a beautiful maiden should be given” is a principle derived from grammatical science (*saddasattha*), not from the Buddha’s word (*buddhavacana*). Indeed, the Buddha’s word...

Having understood that the word-form "abhirūpassa kaññā deyyā" will occur [in this sense]. But surely, sir, even in cases such as *namo-yoga* and others, the substitution of *ā* for the dative singular is observed?
For even those within the Dispensation who are skillful and wise, having uttered such phrases as "namo buddhāya," pay homage to the Triple Gem. However, some—
Homage to the Buddha, to the Awakened One;
homage to the Dhamma, to the one who possesses the Dhamma;
homage to the Saṅgha, to the Community.
“By the act of homage, may there be safety for me,” and:
“Upon your face, a blossoming lotus; upon your eyes, blue-lotus ponds;
by this worship of your lotus feet, may I constantly give to the Buddha.”
"Do men ask a man for some object, or is a messenger sent by a man to another man?"—do they even compose verses such as this?
True; those who follow the Dispensation, being skillful and wise, pay homage to the Triple Gem by saying "Homage to the Buddha" and so forth, and they also compose verses.
Nevertheless, it is by virtue of their proficiency in the science of grammar that they do so.
Having grasped the method from the science of grammar (*saddasattha*), they compose verses and even fragments of prose in that same manner;

by uttering "Homage to the Buddha" (*namo buddhāya*) and so forth, they pay homage to the Triple Gem. Furthermore, even those who have not cultivated familiarity with the science of grammar, down to young children, upon hearing the words of others, [utter] "Homage to the Buddha" and so forth by virtue of having acquired familiarity through that influence.
Having spoken thus, they pay homage to the Triple Gem; however, those who say "Namo Buddhassa" are fewer still.
For in certain regions, teachers teaching children the alphabet have them learn the beginning of the letters as "Namo Buddhāya," and not "Namo Buddhassa.
Nevertheless, according to the method of the Pāḷi and the method of the ancient commentaries—
Furthermore, when examining [the grammatical forms], with the exception of the four bases beginning with *gatyattha* (verbs meaning "to go") and *kamma* (object),

no forms of the singular dative case accompanied by the substitution of *ā* for *e* are seen anywhere among the seven or eight bases— whether distinguished by the categories of giving (*dāna*), announcing (*rocanā*), holding (*dhāraṇa*), or sharing (*namayoga*)—
within the domain of the recipient (*sampadāna*). Therefore, those [forms] such as "namo buddhāya" and "buddhāya" have been artificially constructed by some.

It should be understood that while the phrases "giving a gift" (*dānaṃ dentī*) remain as they are in the canonical text (*pāḷi*), the phrases "homage to the Buddha" (*namo buddhassa*) and "giving a gift to the Buddha" (*buddhassa dānaṃ dentī*) take on different forms.
This, however, is a construction of the application of the *āy* substitution in accordance with both the method of the canon and the method of the commentary—

such as "he goes for refuge to the Buddha" (*buddhāya saraṇaṃ gacchati*) or "he goes to the Buddha for refuge" (*buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchati*), or "they lead the city to the Buddha" (*buddhāya nagaraṃ nenti*).
Or [saying], "They are leading him to the city of the Buddha"; or, "The Dhamma is honored by the Buddha, the Dhamma is honored by the Buddha";
or, "He renounces his life for the sake of the Buddha, he renounces his life for the sake of the Buddha";

or, "The followers of other sects depart from the Buddha, the followers of other sects depart from the Buddha"; or, "The nature of things belonging to the Buddha, the nature of things belonging to the Buddha..."

Or as in "dhammatā," or "pasanno buddhāya" (faithful to the Buddha), or "pasanno buddhe" (faithful in the Buddha)—apart from these seven instances, the substitution of *ā* for *a* is not seen elsewhere.
For instance, in the *Pāṭha*: "In the *Mahānāma-kkāra*, known as Sādhunandana..."
In the case of the dative case (*sampadāna*) and the *nama*-construction (*namo-yoga*), the substitution of *ā* (*āy-ādeso*) is not observed.
Here, the reading of the *Mahānāma-kāra* is the text: “*Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassā*.
Even here, the substitution of *ā* is not observed. In the *Vammika-sutta* as well, it says: “*Namo karohi nāgassā*,” where likewise the substitution of *ā* is not seen.
It is not seen [there]. In the Ambaṭṭha Sutta as well, in the phrase “May there be safety for the King, O Venerable Sir; may there be safety for the country,” the substitution with *ā* is not seen.
Even in the commentary on the meaning of the reading “Suppabuddhaṃ,” and in the case of the dative case or the use of *nama*, the substitution with *ā* is not seen.
For it is said:
"Well awakened indeed they awaken, the disciples of Gotama at all times,
whose mindfulness is constantly directed toward the Buddha by day and by night."

In the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) on this passage, a specific linguistic refinement is seen that avoids the elision of *ā* (āyādesavajjita), stating: "The son of one possessed of right view, while throwing sugar, recollects the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*) and throws the sugar after saying, 'Homage to the Buddha' (*namo buddhassā*).
Furthermore, in the commentary on the Dhanañjānī-sutta within the Sagāthāvagga-vaṇṇanā, it says: "Whether you are standing or sitting..."

Even in cases such as "having spat" (*khipitvā*) and "having coughed" (*kāsetvā*), a specific excellence of phonetic composition is observed that avoids the fault of *āyādesa* (the substitution of *e* for *aya*), namely:
"Homage to the Buddha! (*namo buddhassā*)—thus you pay homage to that shaven-headed little ascetic. Likewise, in various places there is seen:
"He gives alms to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha"; "Food does not please that man"; "It pleases the ascetic."

In such expressions as *saccaṃ, buddhassa chattaṃ dhāreti* (“He holds the Buddha’s umbrella for the sake of truth”) and *buddhassa silāghate* (“He praises the Buddha”), a specific phonetic arrangement is seen that is devoid of the substitution of *ā*.
Thus, in many instances of the dative case involving objects of giving, praise, and so forth, a form of the singular dative accompanied by the substitution of *ā* is not observed.
However, it is observed in four places: the object of verbs meaning "to go" (*gatyattha*), and so on. For instance: “*Mūlāya paṭikasseyya*” (“One should send back to the root”). Appo...

And here, in the phrase "he goes to heaven" (*saggāya gacchati*), it is seen as having the sense of motion (*gaty-attha*). For in this context, the meaning is: "He should draw back the root; few go to heaven.

And here, in the word "should draw back" (*paṭikasseyya*), because the verbal root *kasa* (meaning "to move") is qualified by the prefix *pati*, the meaning becomes "he should pull back" (*ākaḍḍheyya*). "This man desires my welfare..."
In the phrase, "He who, having taken me, leads me to the water," the sense of the action of leading (*nayanatthakamma*) is seen.
For here, "the water leads me" means it causes me to reach its own pool where it dwells.
In the phrase, "Venerable sirs, desist from my word," the change of case ending (*vibhattivipariṇāma*) is seen; for "desist from my word" is expressed by way of the ablative case (*nissakkavacana*).
The meaning is as follows. In the phrase “I am the food for a great flock,” there too a change of case ending is observed.
For the meaning, according to the genitive construction, is: “I am the food for my great flock of swans. And here the intended sense is: “I am the [food] of my swan-king.
In the phrase “And we were not honored by Dhanañjaya,” there too a change of case ending is observed; [the sense is]: “We [were not honored] by King Dhanañjaya.”
The genitive case is used here in the sense of the agent (*kattutthe*), as in the phrase "we were not honored by His Majesty.

For instance, although one should have said "by Dhanañcaya" (*dhanañcayassa*) or "with Dhanañcaya" (*dhanañcayena*), instead of saying that, the dative case "to Dhanañcaya" (*dhanañcayāya*) is employed;

this is appropriate only through a change of case-ending (*vibhattivipariṇāma*), because there is no recipient (*sampadāna*) for an action such as giving. Therefore, we were not honored by King Dhanañcaya.
The meaning "existence" (bhava) should be understood here. Other instances of the modification of case endings should also be sought.
Furthermore, many thousands of verbal forms containing the substitution of *ā*—such as “for the sake of dispassion, for the sake of peace, for the sake of cessation”—occur in that sense.
Indeed, when the masters of the commentaries explain the meaning of the words *dhamma* and *vinaya*, they say: “Of phenomena... [and so forth].

"For the sake of discipline. Since this discipline (*vinaya*) has the purpose of a faultless state (*anavajjadhammattha*), and not the purpose of existence, enjoyment, and so forth, they employed the verbal form *āyādesa* (the substitution of *ā*) precisely for that purpose.
Thus, the forms of the fourth singular ending accompanied by the substitution of *ā* occur only in these four instances:
in the sense of motion (*gatyattha*), in the sense of leading (*nayanattha*), in the alteration of case endings (*vibhattivipariṇāma*), and in that specific meaning (*tadattha*).
[These] are seen in specific instances, but not in every instance of the recipient (sampadāna) category, such as in the case of "giving" (dāna) or "confessing" (rocana).
For instance, in the *Niruttipiṭaka*, the phonetic form accompanied by the substitution of *ā*—namely, "atthāya"—is stated as the word for the recipient;
however, such forms are not stated [there] by way of words like *purisa* (man), etc., because such phonetic forms [do not occur] where...
Because it does not occur in certain instances. For even in the *Kaccāyana-ppakaraṇa*, in the commentary on the rule "āya for the singular dative case" (*āya catutthekavacanassa tū*), it is stated:
"for the sake of, for the welfare of, for the happiness of gods and humans" (*atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānam*);
however, it is not stated as "purisāyā," "samaṇāyā," or "brāhmaṇāyā."

Here it might be asked: "But surely, sir, in that very *Vutti*, because it was stated—'For what purpose [is] the fourth case? As in: *purisassa mukhaṃ* (the face of the man). For what purpose [is] the singular number?
As in: *purisānaṃ dadāti* (he gives to the men). For what purpose [is] the particle *vā*? As in:

*dātā hoti samaṇassa vā brāhmaṇassa vā* (he becomes a giver to a recluse or to a brahmin)'—therefore, word-forms such as *purisāya*, *samaṇāya*, *brāhmaṇāya*, and so forth, have been shown by way of method (*naya*); they are merely..."

But [one might ask]: "Do not forms such as *purisāya* fail to be established because of their connection with the word *mukha*, because they are plural in number, and because of the optional rule (*vikappana*), whereas they would necessarily be established in places where there is no connection with the word *mukha* and so forth? To this it is said:

"When one asks, 'What is the purpose of the fourth case [ending]?'—as in 'the mouth of the man' (*purisassa mukham*)—if the substitution of *ā* (*āyādeso*) were to occur, it would occur only for the fourth case."
Showing that [the substitution] does not occur in the sixth case, he presented the word "mukhaṃ.

He does not, however, show by this that "the substitution of *ā* occurs when the word *mukha* stands in a locative sense, such as in the case of a verb where it is the object of the recipient (sampadāna)," as in "he gives in the place of the mouth.

Furthermore, even one who asks, "What is the purpose of the singular number [in the rule]? Why does he say 'to men' (*purisānaṃ*)? shows that "the substitution of *ā* occurs only for the singular, not for the plural."

The word “dātī” was stated in order to indicate that the word “purisānaṃ” functions as a recipient (sampadāna), but it does not intend to convey the meaning that “the substitution of *ā* for the singular dative ending occurs only when there is a verbal form such as ‘deti’ [gives] that constitutes a domain of the recipient.
Furthermore, [the question] “Why is ‘vā’ used? [Is it] ‘he gives to a recluse or to a brahmin’? is asked.

Even when speaking thus, he makes it known that the substitution of *ā* occurs only by way of a formal designation (*vikappa*), and does not indicate that the prescription for the substitution of *ā* depends upon actions such as giving.

However, if the prescription for the substitution of *ā* were dependent upon actions such as giving, then the author of the *Vutti* [would have stated so] in his commentary on the grammatical rule (*lakkhaṇa*).

In the very same root examples, just as there are applications for that purpose such as "for the sake of" (*atthāya*) and "for the benefit of" (*hitāya*), one might have expected expressions such as "it is given to a man" (*purisāya dīyate*) and so forth to be stated;
yet they were not. Why? Because such usage is absent in the Buddha’s word (*buddhavacana*) and in the ancient commentaries (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*).
For in the *Niruttipiṭaka*, the Venerable Mahākaccāna, who had attained the analytical knowledges (*pabhinnapaṭisambhidā*), [said]: "To a man... [and so on].
By stating "it is given," the Elder shows only those forms devoid of the *āy* substitution;

and even though he says, "‘Atthāya’ is a word in the dative case," the Elder points out only the form of the dative singular that includes the *āy* substitution, without regard for the action of giving and so forth.
Therefore, it is understood that this usage is a usage in that specific sense. Thus, by these reasons, it should be known that [the term refers to] the action of giving and so forth.

"...the rule for the substitution of *ā* [for *e*] has not been made. If that were so, would only "for the sake of" (*atthāya*), "for the benefit of" (*hitāya*), and so forth—those very applications of that meaning—be the domain of the grammatical rule "but for the dative singular ending, *ā* [is substituted]," and no others? That is not so; other instances are also indeed its domain.
Which ones? "He should restore to the root," "few go to heaven," "he leads for the sake of water" (*dakāya*), etc.

“Cease, venerable sirs, from my word; [cease] for the sake of the community and the meal,” and so forth. However, phrases such as “by going to heaven” and so on are not within the scope [of this discussion], because they fall under the heading of "alternatives" (vā).
But surely, sir, if that is the case, why did the author of the commentary (*vutti*) include in the original examples [the phrase]: “for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans”?
Having said this, the phrases beginning with "one should be sent back to the beginning" (*mūlāya paṭikasseyya*) and so forth should also be stated.
But why, in the example, is it asked: "Or what is the purpose of going to heaven? (*vāti kimatthaṃ saggassa gamanena vā*)? True; there is a reason for not stating them, so listen to it:
for in the passage, "One should be sent back to the beginning; few go to heaven," the words "to the beginning" (*mūlāya*) and "to heaven" (*saggāya*) [are implied].

Words expressing the pure recipient (*suddhasampadāna*) do not occur when [a verb] functions with respect to the object of a motion (*gatyatthakamma*), and therefore they were not mentioned in the primary examples.
Likewise, in the phrase "he leads water" (*dakāya neti*), the word "water" (*dakāya*) is not stated [as a pure recipient] because it functions as the object of the action of leading.
In the phrase "Venerable sirs, abstain from my words" (*viramathāyasmanto mama vacanāyā*), here...
However, because the word *vacanāya* is used in the sense of the ablative (*nissakka*), because the word *gaṇāya* in the phrase *gaṇāya bhattā* is used in the sense of the genitive (*sāmī*),

and because the word *dhanañcayāya* in the phrase *asakkatā casma dhanañcayāya* is used in the sense of the genitive with respect to the agent (*kattā*), it is not stated that these are pure dative cases (*sampadāna*).
Even in the example, because the word "of heaven" (*saggassa*) functions as the object of a verb meaning "going" due to its proximity to the word "going," it is not a pure dative;
therefore, it was not stated, "Or [the particle] *vā*—for what purpose? Is it 'by going to heaven'?
For in this way, having reached both the Buddha's word and the method of the ancient commentaries according to the stated principle, the fourth singular ending...

It should be understood that forms accompanied by the *ā* elision are seen only in the four instances beginning with the sense of motion (*gati*) and action (*kamma*), and not in any instance whatsoever regarding the domain of the recipient (*sampadāna*), such as in the varieties of giving (*dāna*) or announcing (*rocana*).
But is it not the case, sir, that in the usage of giving, as in: "He gave sandalwood essence to the eldest sister, and a golden garland to the youngest"?
Since the form associated with the substitution of *ā* for the fourth singular case ending is demonstrated [in the examples], there ought to be such applications as:

"The ornament is given to the princess (*rājakaññāya*), the ornament is pleasing to the princess (*rājakaññāya*), she holds the parasol for the princess (*rājakaññāya*), pay homage to the princess (*rājakaññāya*), may it be well for the princess (*rājakaññāya*), he praises the princess (*rājakaññāya*)," and so forth;
yet, why then [is it not found] in the Buddha’s word (*buddhavacana*)?
