The meaning of our statement is as follows: all feminine gender forms are exactly equal in the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh case singulars when used in the singular number;

only a few are unequal. Therefore, setting those aside, regarding masculine and neuter gender forms such as *purisa* and *citta*, which stand with *a*-stems as their base, [the following] are provided along with the substitution of *ā* for the fourth case singular:
The forms [ending in -ā] are not seen in any instance within the domain of giving (sampadāna) in the Buddha’s word and other texts—

such as in the various cases of *dānāya*, *rocanāya*, and so forth. For this very reason, while there are hundreds of such triple-gendered words where the suffix *-ā* occurs in the sense of the three [kārakas],

namely the object of motion (*gati*), the object of action (*kamma*), and so on— as in *mūlāya*, *saggāya*, *dakāya*, *vacanāya*, *gaṇāya*— and others such as *abhiññāya*, *sambodhāya*, *nibbānāya*, these belong exclusively to that same sense [of the object].
These [suffixes] are seen in these four instances. However, they are not seen in cases such as *deti*, *roceti*, and *dhāreti*, where the scope is purely that of the dative case.
Herein, there are these verses:
The fourth singular ending, joined with the substitution of *ā*;
One should explain that *rūpa* (form) is established in four places among those [bases] that do not possess the feminine gender:
in the object (*kamma*) of a verb meaning "to go," in the object (*kamma*) of a verb meaning "to lead," in the case endings (*vibhatti*), and in the sense of the suffix *tad*.
“One should be sent back to the beginning; few go to heaven”—thus have we seen in the Teaching regarding an action whose purpose is going (*gatyarthakarma*).
Likewise, in the case of an action whose purpose is leading (*nayanārthakarma*), as in the expression “he leads to water.”
“Vacanāya” is used in the ablative sense, because of the application of abstention.
“Gaṇāya” is used in the genitive sense, because of its connection with the word “bhattā.
The word “Dhanañcayāya” indicates the genitive sense in the meaning of the agent.
One should explain the word “asakkatā” (unhonored) by way of its phonetic connection (*yogato*);
furthermore, a different permutation (*vipallāsa*) should be sought by the discerning one.
However, as for these [phrases]: “for direct knowledge,” “for full awakening,” and “for Nibbāna.”
One should explain its meaning by means of the three genders.
Thus has the origin of the letter *ā* been told in accordance with the sequence of the recitation;
however, this subtle point must be contemplated again and again.
This garland of words of the Great Sage, adorned with various methods and consisting solely of vowels, has been proclaimed for the sake of the Dispensation.
If they should listen to this exceedingly sweet [work] with respect, [they will attain the goal].
The virtuous, by means of the excellent method of grammar—
which is variegated with diverse systems— should thoroughly cut away their doubt regarding the word-meanings of these words of the Best of Conquerors, just as the moon cuts through the night-lotus.
Thus ends the section on the base forms of masculine nouns ending in vowels,

with their respective grammatical analyses, in the *Saddanīti* treatise composed for the benefit of the wise in understanding the modes of expression within the Three Pitakas together with the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
The Fifth Chapter, titled "The Classification of the Series of Nominal Words," is concluded.
This concludes the section on masculine nouns ending in *a*, *i*, *u*, *o*, and *ū*.

6. The Nominal Paradigm for Masculine Nouns Ending in -ā Now, having placed the opinion of the ancient masters at the forefront, we shall explain the nominal paradigm for the base form *abhibhavitum* (to overcome) among the masculine nouns ending in -ā.
Nomative: *satthā*, *satthā*, *satthāro*. Accusative: *satthāraṃ*.
Teachers. By the teachers, by the teachers, by the teachers. Of the teacher, of the teacher, of the teacher; of the teachers, of the teachers.
By the teacher, by the teachers, by the teachers. Of the teacher, of the teacher, of the teacher;
of the teachers, of the teachers. In the teacher, in the teachers. O teacher, O teacher, sirs, teachers.
This is the method according to the *Cūḷanirutti* composed by the Great Thera Yamaka.

Furthermore, in this context, even though the word "satthunā" does not appear in the *Niruttipiṭaka* or in *Kaccāyana*, it must certainly be accepted, as seen in the expression "dhammarājena satthunā.
The sequence—namely, "satthārā, satthunā, satthārehi, satthārebhi"—should also be understood. Herein...

Furthermore, the demonstration of another word (*saddantara*)—whether based on a distinction in the phrasing despite there being no difference in meaning, or based on a difference in meaning despite there being no distinction in the phrasing—is called *niruttikkama*.
Thus, it should be understood that the word "Teacher" (*satthā*) is stated twice, once in the singular and once in the plural.
However, in the *Niruttipiṭaka* and other such texts, the nominative plural form "satthāro" does not appear.

Even though [the word] has not been encountered [elsewhere], nevertheless, because the form "avitakkitā" is seen as a nominative plural in the Pāḷi passage, "The unreflecting ones set out toward death," the word "satthā" must necessarily be accepted as a nominative plural.
Likewise, this applies to "vattā," "dhātā," "gantā," and so forth, as they belong to the same grammatical category. Similarly, there is also the accusative plural "satthāre" in the *Niruttipiṭaka*.
The forms *satthussa* and *satthānaṃ* appear as the singular and plural of the fourth (dative-locative) and sixth (genitive) cases respectively, yet they do not appear in the *Cūḷanirutti*.

Therein, because of the examples "he supports his mother and father" (*mātāpitaro poseti*) and "he surpasses his brothers" (*bhātaro atikkamati*), the form *satthāre* appears as if it were an inappropriate form for the plural accusative.
In the works of Kaccāyana and others, however, we find: "O Teacher! (*bho sattha*, *bho satthā*).
Thus, two forms of the singular vocative were stated by way of the short and long vowels.
In the *Niruttipiṭaka*, after stating the singular vocative in the short vowel as “*bho sattha*,” the plural vocative with the *ārādesa* [substitution] is stated as “*bhavanto satthāro*.
In the *Cūḷanirutti*, after stating the singular vocative in the short vowel as “*bho sattha*,” [the form] “*bho satthā*” is stated...
The plural form of address was spoken by way of lengthening [the vowel]. All of this should be understood in such a way that it does not contradict the Āgama after having investigated it therein.
Now, we shall show whatever other forms of the word *satthu* have been seen by us—for instance: "imesaṃ..."
In the Pāḷi text, the word "satthūnaṃ" is seen in the passage: "Mahānāma, is there one final goal for the three teachers, or are there various final goals?
Therefore, this case-form sequence should also be understood as follows: *satthu*, *satthussa*, *satthuno*, *satthānaṃ*, *satthārānaṃ*, *satthūnaṃ*.
[The nominative forms are: *abhibhavitā*, *abhibhavitā*, *abhibhavitāro*. [The accusative forms are: *abhibhavitāraṃ*...
Abhibhavitāro. Abhibhavitārā, abhibhavitunā, abhibhavitārehi, abhibhavitārebhi.
Abhibhavitu, abhibhavitussa, abhibhavituno, abhibhavitānaṃ, abhibhavitārānaṃ, abhibhavitūnaṃ.
Abhibhavitārā, abhibhavitārehi, abhibhavitārebhi. Abhibhavitu, abhibhavitussa, abhibhavituno.
*Abhibhavitānaṃ*, *abhibhavitārānaṃ*. *Abhibhavitari*, *abhibhavitāresu*. "O *abhibhavita*," "O *abhibhavitā*," "you, sirs, *abhibhavitāro*.

Just as here the nominal paradigm of the base form *abhibhavitu* has been constructed according to the method of the Teacher (*satthunaya*), so too [should it be understood] for *paribhavitu* and others that are similar to it.

The series of nominal forms should be applied according to the method of the Teacher. Herein, other similar names are the base forms (*pakatirūpa*) of words such as "speaker" (*vattā*) and "bearer" (*dhātā*), namely *vatti*, *dhāti*, and so forth.
Speaker, bearer, goer, leader.
A giver, a doer, a buyer, a father;
a cutter, a breaker, a slayer, a mother;
a conqueror, an awakener, a knower, a hearer.
Thundered, rained, ate, fainted, was restrained;
spoke, asked, endured, arose, ascended, stretched;
requested, counter-requested, declared, conformed to, and enjoyed.
Words such as *netā* (leader) and *vinetā* (guide) occur in the sense of the pure agent (*suddhakattari*).
Furthermore, words such as *uppādetā* (producer), *viññāpetā* (informer), *sandassetā* (demonstrator),
*pabrūhetā* (expounder), and *bodhetā* (awakener), as well as other similar terms, are to be understood in the sense of the cause (*hetu*).
The maker, the asker, the leader, the supporter, the father, and the brother—these, however, do not undergo any change [in case] within the sutta;
I shall explain that distinction. In examples such as "the Teacher" (*satthā*), some [grammarians] hold that [the word is declined] with the accusative (*upayoga*) and the genitive (*sāmī*).
These very [suffixes] always occur, yet some do not occur at all.
Among them, words such as *katta* differ slightly from the word *satthu* by virtue of their different forms. For instance, in the passage: “Arise, O *katta*, in haste;
having gone, speak to Vessantara,” the word *katte* here is a form of the singular vocative case.
For thus, "O maker" (*bho kattā*) is one form distinct from another form.
In the phrase "Therefore, O minister (*khatte*), go to where the brahmin householders of Campā are," the word "minister" (*khatte*) here is a singular form used for addressing.
Likewise, "O ministers" (*bho khattā*) is one form distinct from another form. In the phrase "When the leaders have gone straight," the word "leaders" (*nette*) here—
The singular form of the locative case is *sattamiyā ekavacanarūpaṃ*; this too is a different form from the form *nettarī*.
In the phrase “*ārādhayati rājānaṃ, pūjaṃ labhati bhattūsū*,” the word *bhattūsū* is the plural form of the locative case.
It is a different form from the form *bhattāresū*, as seen here by the occurrence of *bhattūsū*. In the phrase “*mātāpitūsu paṇḍitā*,” the word *pitūsu*...
And from the perspective of the [grammatical] seeing (dassana), the method should also be understood in such a manner as:
"in those who go, in those who lead, in those who give, in those who act," and so forth. This method appears to us as something that should be desired even for the word *satthu* (teacher).
Father: *pitā*, *pitā*, *pitaro*. Accusative: *pitaraṃ*, *pitaro*. Instrumental: *pitarā*, *pitunā*, *pettyā*, *pitarehi*, *pitarebhi*.
From the father: *pitūhi*, *pitūbhi*. Of the father: *pitu*, *pitussa*, *pituno*, *pitānaṃ*, *pitarānaṃ*, *pitūnaṃ*. By the father:
*pitarā*, *pettyā*, *pitarehi*, *pitarebhi*, *pitūhi*, *pitūbhi*. In the father: *pitu*, *pitussa*, *pituno*, *pitānaṃ*, *pitarānaṃ*, *pitūnaṃ*.
In the father: *pitari*; in the fathers: *pitaresu*, *pitūsu*. O Father! O Father! O you sirs, Fathers! Now, in this regard:
Excluding these two forms, *petiyā* and *pitūnaṃ*, the paradigm of the word *bhātu* (brother) should be applied.

In this regard, because we see such instances as “What was done by the mother and by the father is very good; you are permitted by your mother and father, after the passing of your mother and father,” there is a variation in the forms of the word *pitu* (father), namely:
*petiyā*, *pitūhi*, *pitūbhi*, and *pitūnaṃ*; and [the form] *pitaro*.
In these and similar cases, there is both shortening [of the vowel] and a distinction from the word *satthu*.
Furthermore, in this context, the form *petyā* should be understood as an inconceivable masculine form, similar to such words as *jantuyo*, *hetuyo*, *hetuyā*, and *adhipatiyā*.
Here, the objection and its resolution are as follows: words such as *satthā* and *pitā* are considered to end in the vowel *-ā* by virtue of their being derived forms (*nipphannattam*).
Furthermore, you say that words ending in *u* should be placed first, taking the base form (*pakatirūpa*) as the standard—as in the examples:
“The cause is seeing the Teacher,” “One not raised by a mother and father,” and “A designation of the agent. But how do you explain words such as *satthāraṃ* (the Teacher) in these instances?
We reply: we also say that these, too, end in *u*, taking the base form as the standard.

"But surely, sir, these [words] end in *a*? "No, they end in *u*. "But surely, sir, those words ending in *ya*, *am*, *na*, etc., which follow [the preceding word], are not seen, by means of which there could be a substitution of *ār* for the final of words ending in *u*; therefore, they must end in *a*?
"No, because in such a case there is no opportunity for the words ending in *ya*, *am*, *na*, etc., which follow [the preceding word]. Likewise...
For this [usage] falls within the domain of compounds (*samāsa*). Indeed, in the domain of compounds, even inconceivable forms are observed.

Nevertheless, O Venerable Sir, because we see the canonical commentary (*niddesa-pāḷi*) stating "he goes from the Teacher to the Teacher" (*satthārato satthāraṃ gacchati*)—which is not a compound, just like the usage "he departs from the village" (*gāmato nikkhamati*)—it follows that in expressions such as "the cause is the sight of the Teacher" (*hetu satthāradassanaṃ*), the word *satthāra* and others end in the vowel *-a*.
"Should they be considered? No, they should not be considered. In the case of "satthārato satthāraṃ gacchati," it is because of the presence of the vowel *u*.
For here, even when there is no compound (*asamāsatta*), the vowel *u* of the word *satthu* receives the substitution (*ārādesa*) by virtue of the suffix *to*.
As for those reasons you desire for the substitution of *ā* for *u*—namely, the words beginning with *yo*, *aṃ*, and *na*—they [do not apply] in such a situation.
They are not authoritative for the wise. If one asks, "What then is authoritative?"—in such a context, only these are invariably authoritative:

the suffix *-to* in cases where there is no compound, the subsequent members [of a compound] in cases where there is a compound, and the case-endings (*syādi-vibhatti*) in the absence of a subsequent member.
For instance, in the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*, it says: "Insofar as knowledge arises in a fool, it leads only to his harm."
In the commentary on the meaning of this passage, regarding the phrase "there is no punishment for one who has struck [someone] here who is 'nimmātāpitā'":

because *nimmātāpitā* is a compound (*samāsa*), when the locative singular suffix *sim* follows, the vowel *u* undergoes the substitution (*ārādesa*) of *ā*. Subsequently, the suffix *si* undergoes the substitution of *o*.
Thus, by virtue of its original form (*pakatirūpa*), this word ends in the vowel *u*. This is stated with reference to its completed state (*nipphannatta*).
Like the words *puriso* and *urago*, it also ends in the vowel *o*. Here, however, the analysis of the compound (*samāsaviggaha*) is as follows:
"Mother and father" is *mātāpitaro*; "one who has no mother and father" is *nimmātāpitaro*.
For when the base form stands as *nimmātāpitu* and the nominative plural suffix (*si*) follows, the substitution of *ār* occurs for the letter *u*. However, in some instances...
In the manuscript of the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*, the reading “*ayaṃ nimmātāpitiko*” is seen;
however, we consider this to have been inserted by those who thought the phrase “*ayaṃ nimmātāpitaro*” was incorrect. That is not an incorrect reading of the commentary.
For it accords with the use of the *simhi* replacement for the *ārādesa* [of the genitive] in the expression “*ekapitaro*” in the *Ummagga-jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*. Thus: [text follows].
“Just as a kinsman, a brother,
a uterine sibling born of the same mother,
so is Pañcālacanda to you.”

By the venerable teachers who are experts in the method of the scriptures, while commenting on the meaning of this passage—"He should be cherished, O bull among charioteers"—the formulation of the *ārādesa* (substitution) for the locative case was made as follows:

"One's own (*niyaka*) means internal (*ajjhattika*), born of the same father and the same mother. And not only was the masculine usage employed in the *ārādesa* of the locative case by us; [so too is the feminine].
It has indeed been seen; moreover, the application of the feminine gender is also seen within the Teaching (Sāsana).

For instance, in the Cūḷavagga of the Vinaya Piṭaka, the phrase “she becomes one who is not a *samaṇī*, not a daughter of the Sakyas” (*assamaṇī hoti asakyadhītarā*) is found. Here, however, the analysis of the compound is as follows:
“Because she was born in the Sakyan clan, she is a daughter of the Blessed One, the Sakyan; not a daughter of the Sakyas is a ‘non-Sakyan-daughter’ (*asakyadhītarā*).”

Here too, because the feminine gender is intended, the substitution of *ār* for the vowel *u* in *simhi* has been made, the suffix *āp* is applied, and the elision of the final syllable (*silopa*) should also be understood.

Thus, when these are compound words such as *satthu*, *pitu*, and *kattu*, certain specific forms are observed that differ from the forms stated in the declensional paradigm (*nāmikapadamālā*). Other specific forms should also be sought by one who knows the method.

Regarding the Suttantas: for who indeed is capable of extracting and displaying, in their entirety, the various jewel-like words scattered throughout the ocean of the Buddha’s word—which cause wonder in the hearts of the wise?
Therefore, we have presented only a small portion.
One who is naturally free from violence, wise by nature, and constant here in this world—
if such a person practices the yoga of the Teacher, they will have no doubt regarding the Pāḷi.
Furthermore, as for those words we have explained here, such as "Teacher," "Conqueror," "Speaker," and "Doer," some of them—
The forms "pucchitā" (asked) and "okkamitā" (fallen asleep), among others, always occur together with the instrumental case. Indeed, many such usages are seen, such as:
"Do you remember, Great King, having asked this question of other ascetics and brahmins? Having fallen asleep...
Similarly, certain forms always occur together with the genitive case, such as "abhibhavitā" (conqueror) and "vattā" (speaker).
For indeed, many such usages are seen, such as: "He is a conqueror of enemies; there will be those who speak of him; he is a giver of the Deathless; he is a withstander of perils;
he is the arouser of the unarisen Path, the supreme among men.
However, some do not even use [the word] with the accusative case, because it functions according to a fixed technical designation (*paññatti*). That...
How so? For example: "teacher," "father," "brother," "nephew," and so forth.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the statement beginning with "they always occur together with the accusative case" was made with reference to meanings that function as objects (*kamma*).
Thus, those who desire proficiency in words and their meanings should understand the occurrence of these *ākāra*-ending words belonging to the *ukāra*-ending class.

Furthermore, by way of the gender endings, one should determine the meaning of the triplet—“satthā, sattho, sattha”—as well as the nominal declension of the base form, and the similarities and differences between the words.
For therein, “satthā” is a masculine noun that first stands with the vowel *u* as its base and subsequently becomes one ending in *ā*; “sattho,” however, [is formed from the same base].
This [term] is a masculine noun that first exists with the nature of ending in the vowel *a* and subsequently becomes one ending in *o*;
however, this term “sattha” is a neuter noun that first exists with the nature of ending in the vowel *a* and subsequently becomes one ending in the nasal *m*.
In that context, “satthā” means one who instructs (*sāsati*) and guides (*anusāsati*) the world together with its devas; who is he? The Blessed One. “Sattha” means...
*Sattha* means "caravan" (*saha atthena*); it refers to a multitude of people who have taken merchandise and traveled to another region for trade. *Sattha* also means "treatise" (*sattham*);
it is that by which one instructs (*sāsati*) or explains (*ācikkhati*) the meaning, such as the grammatical treatises (*byākaraṇa-ādi-gantha*). Alternatively, it is "weapon" (*sattham*);
it is that by which one injures (*sasati*) or harms (*hiṃsati*) living beings, such as a sword and so forth. [The declension is: *satthā, satthā, satthāro; satthāram, satthāro*.
Like a pure series of words (*padamālā*). The series of words according to the masculine method is: “*sattho*, *satthā*; *satthaṃ*, *satthe*.

The series of words according to the neuter method, occurring in the neuter gender, should be joined according to the mental method (*cittanaya*) as follows: “*satthaṃ*, *satthāni*, *satthā*; *satthaṃ*, *satthāni*, *satthe*.
In this way, within the nominal series of words divided into three ways, the similarity and dissimilarity of the words must be determined.
"The Teacher stands, the Omniscient One; the Teacher goes, those seeking wealth;
the Teacher departs, O men; sirs, give the Teacher alms.
In this way, there is similarity by virtue of the commonality of the word "Teacher" (satthā).
Having made the knife permissible with that which was sharp, he gave the fruit to the Teacher; the Teacher consumed it.
Thus there is dissimilarity by way of commonality of non-hearing, and likewise by way of gender and ending: "cetā" and "ceto."
Having formed the pair “tātā tāto,” one must determine the meaning of the words, the nominal declension of the base form,
and the similarity or dissimilarity between the words.
For therein, “cetā” first stands as a base ending in the vowel *u*, and subsequently becomes a masculine noun ending in the vowel *ā*.
Likewise, there is the word *tātā*. However, *ceto* is a masculine noun that first exists in an *a*-stem form and subsequently becomes an *o*-stem;
the same applies to the word *tāto*. In that context, *cetā* means one who piles up or makes a heap;
it refers to a person who builds a wall, specifically a mason (*iṭṭhakavaḍḍhakī*). *Ceto* means mind (*citta*); it is [the name] of such a person.
Or "luddo. And here, *citta* is called *ceto* in the sense of "it intends" (*cetayati*) or "it thinks" (*cinteti*), whereas *luddo* is [so called] by way of designation (*paṇṇatti*).
*Tātā* means "he protects" (*tāyati*), hence *tātā*. An example of this usage is: "The protector (*tātā*) from suffering and the provider of welfare.
In the word *tāto* as well, it is "he protects," hence *tāto*; [this term is used] among fathers toward their sons, among sons toward their fathers, and among other dear persons toward one another.
This is a conventional expression that should be stated. Its usage is to be understood in such instances as: “Surely that father of mine is wretched; he has long been fond of the hermitage.
Having acquired wealth with great difficulty, my father is now wasting it away. Come, father! and so forth. According to the method of the Teacher, the paradigm of forms is:
“cetā, cetā, cetāro; cetāraṃ, cetāro”; and “ceto, cetā; cetaṃ, cete; cetasā, cetena.”
It should be understood by way of mental enumeration (*manogaṇanā*). This is the nominal paradigm (*nāmikapadamālā*) of the word *cetas* when it denotes "mind" (*citta*):

“*Ceto*, *cetā*; *Cetaṃ*, *cete*; *Cetenā*”; it should be understood by way of the masculine paradigm (*purisanaya*). This is the nominal paradigm of the word *cetas* when it denotes a "designation" (*paṇṇatti*):
“*Tātā*, *tātā*, *tātāro*; *Tātāraṃ*”; it should be understood by way of the teacher’s paradigm (*satthunaya*). “*Tāto*, *tātā*, *tātan*” [should be understood] by way of the masculine paradigm.
Thus, even in these nominal chains (*nāmikapadamālā*), the similarity and dissimilarity of the words must be determined. Likewise, by way of gender and case-ending,
having formed the tetrad "ñātā, ñāto, ñātaṃ, ñātā," the meaning of the words, the nominal chain of the base form,
and the similarity and dissimilarity of the words must be determined.
For in that context, "ñātā" is first established as having an *ukāranta* (ending in *-u*) base, and subsequently becomes a masculine noun with an *ākāra* ending.

"Ñāto" and "ñātaṃ," however, stand respectively first as having an *akārantā* (ending in *-a*) base, and subsequently become nouns with *ukāranta* and *niggahītanta* endings among the declinable genders—namely, the masculine and neuter genders.
Thus it is said: "The known meaning brings happiness; this is known by the deer."
Their usage is seen [in the texts]. As for the word “ñātā,” this first stands as a feminine form ending in the vowel -ā;
subsequently, among the declinable genders, it is a feminine gender that has become an -ā-stem. For instance, there is the usage: “esā itthimayā ñātā” (this woman is known).
In that regard, in the case of the masculine gender, the meaning should be understood according to the agentive kāraka in the present tense: “he knows, thus he is ‘ñātā’.”

In the case of the feminine gender (*itthiliṅga*) and others, the meaning should be understood according to the object-case (*kamma-kāraka*), the past tense (*atītakāla*), and [the suffix] *-ta*, as in: “she is known (*ñātā*), she is known (*ñātā*), she is known (*ñātā*); the known (*ñāta*), the known (*ñāta*), the known (*ñāta*)”.

This same method should be observed elsewhere as well, according to what is applicable. “Known (*ñātā*), known (*ñātā*), knowers (*ñātāro*); knowers (*ñātāro*)”—this is to be understood according to the Teacher’s (Buddha’s) system.
“Known (*ñāto*), known (*ñātā*); the known (*ñāta*)”—this is to be understood according to the masculine system. “The known (*ñātaṃ*), the known (*ñātāni*), the known (*ñātā*)”.
They are to be understood according to the method of nouns to be explained as "ñātaṃ," "ñātāni," and "ñāte.

They are to be understood according to the method of feminine nouns to be explained as "ñātā," "ñātā," "ñātāyo," "ñātaṃ," "ñātā," and "ñātāyo. Thus, in these noun declensions as well, the similarity and dissimilarity of the words must be determined.
In other instances too, similarity and dissimilarity should be examined according to this same method as appropriate.

The etymologies for "speaker" (*vattā*), "bearer" (*dhātā*), "goer" (*gantā*), and so forth, should be understood according to their respective possibilities as: "one who speaks is a speaker," "one who bears is a bearer," "one who goes is a goer," and so on.
Furthermore, regarding the miscellaneous remarks we have made here, it should not be said that "this was spoken out of place."

Since this work called the *Saddanīti* was undertaken for the purpose of elucidating the correct and incorrect applications of words and their meanings, it shines only when it explains the entire Magadha usage in its various aspects; otherwise, it does not.
Therefore, because there exists the possibility of wishing to speak in various classifications, one should not say, "This was stated in an inappropriate place."
Furthermore, because this work was undertaken for the purpose of making it known to the wise through various means, the fault of tautology should not be considered here;
rather, this *Saddanīti* should be diligently mastered by sons of good family endowed with faith for the benefit of the Three Pitakas.
Thus have been shown words such as *vattā*, *dhātā*, and *gantā*, which resemble the word *abhibhavitā*. Now we shall show those that do not resemble it, as follows:
Possessed of virtue and possessed of the community, likewise powerful and renowned;
possessed of wealth, possessed of learning, wise, possessed of the ascetic practices, and also one who has performed his duty.
Possessed of welfare, the Blessed One, and likewise possessed of steadfastness and strength.
The words *yatavā*, *cāgavā*, *himavā*, and so forth—
generally ending in the masculine and neuter genders with the vowel *a*—
are followed by the suffix *-vant*; those [words] ending in that [suffix] are adjectives (*guṇavāda*).
One should explain that this [suffix] occurs in certain instances for feminine gender and so forth,
due to the imitation of the phonetic form (ākāra) and the phoneme *u* (vaṇṇa),
as seen in examples such as *saññāvā*, *rasmivā*, *massuvā*, and *yasassivā*.
Possessed of mindfulness, possessed of understanding, possessed of insight into the goal, and likewise possessed of fortitude;
possessed of wisdom, possessed of intelligence, and likewise possessed of radiance, as well as possessed of moral shame.
Possessed of praise, possessed of delight, and likewise possessed of restraint, as well as possessed of strength.
Kasimā, Sucimā, Dhīmā, Rucimā, and Cakkhumā;
Bandhumā, Hetumā, Āyasmā, Ketumā, and likewise Rāhumā;
Khāṇumā, Bhāṇumā, Gomā, Vijjumā, Vasumā, and others.
The words *pāpimā*, *puttimā*, as well as *candimā* and so forth,
should be understood by the discerning as examples of sounds that resemble [the suffix] *-taṃ*.
When followed by the vowels *i*, *u*, or *o*, the word *mantu* occurs.
One should discern those ending in *ā*, *ī*, and *im*.
Guṇavā, guṇavā, guṇavanto. Guṇavantaṃ, guṇavante. Guṇavatā, guṇavantena, guṇavantehi, guṇavantebhi.
Guṇavato, guṇavantassa, guṇavataṃ, guṇavantānaṃ. Guṇavatā, guṇavantā.
From the virtuous one: *guṇavantasmā*, *guṇavantamhā*; from the virtuous ones: *guṇavantehi*, *guṇavantebhi*.

Of the virtuous one: *guṇavato*, *guṇavantassa*; of the virtuous ones: *guṇavataṃ*, *guṇavantānaṃ*. In the virtuous one: *guṇavati*, *guṇavante*; in the virtuous ones: *guṇavantasmiṃ*, *guṇavantamhi*, *guṇavantesu*. O virtuous one! (*bho guṇavā*); O virtuous ones! (*bhavanto guṇavā*, *bhonto guṇavanto*).
In this context, however, it is said: "Come, friends, you who possess virtue," and:
"The strong become weak, even the steadfast fall away;
those with sight become blind when they have fallen under the power of women."
In the Pāḷi, because the first plural form “sīlavā, cakkhumā” is seen, the plural is used in place of the singular address “guṇavā.
The same principle applies in cases such as “guṇavā satimā.
For in the *Cūḷanirutti* as well, the plural forms of the singular address “guṇavā” are found, whereas in the *Niruttipiṭaka*, it appears only in the singular form.
In the *Cūḷanirutti* and in the *Niruttipiṭaka*, however, the singular form of address "bho guṇava" appears with a short vowel.
We, on the other hand, [prefer the long vowel], because we observe that in hundreds of readings such as "Taggha bhagavā bojjhaṅgā.
Kathan nu bhagavā tuyhaṃ sāvako sāsane rato," the singular form of address "bhagavā" possesses a long vowel.
In the place of the *vantu* suffix, we consider it more appropriate to use the plural form with a long vowel, such as “bho guṇavā”;
however, in the place of the *mantu* suffix and the place of the *imantu* suffix—as seen in Pāli passages such as “sabbaverabhayātīta, pāde vandāmi cakkhuma.
Evaṃ jānāhi pāpima”—the singular vocative address “cakkhuma” and so forth [is used].
Because it demonstrates the short vowel quality, we consider such expressions as “bho satima, bho gatima,” etc.,
to be more appropriate in their short form; alternatively, because the commentary on the *Mahāparinibbāna-sutta* shows the use of the singular vocative in its long form—
as in “āyasmā tissa”— we take the mere words “bhagavā, āyasmā” to be stated in their long form.

Setting aside the method for the *vantu* suffix, the method for the *mantu* suffix should also be applied; and setting aside the method for the *mantu* suffix, the method for the *vantu* suffix should also be applied.

For instance, in the *Kaccāyana* and other grammars, three forms of the singular vocative are stated according to the nasalized (*niggahīta*), short, and long [vowel endings]: "bho guṇavaṃ," "bho guṇava," and "bho guṇavā.
By this same principle, there is also the sequence: "bho satimaṃ," "bho satima," and "bho satimā," and so forth.
The singular form has been shown. In the place of the first plural number, however, three words are stated: "guṇavanto," "guṇavantā," and "guṇavantī.
By this, the method beginning with "satimanto," "satimantā," and "satimantī" is also demonstrated.
Among those, these words—"bho guṇavaṃ," "bho satimaṃ," "guṇavantā," and "guṇavantī"—follow this same grammatical pattern, as do others.
Regarding words that are not well-known in the Pāḷi— such as the word "āyasmantā," which is well-established—
whatever has been stated in the *Cūḷanirutti*, in the *Niruttipiṭaka*, and in works such as the *Kaccāyana*,
all of that is consistent with neither contradicting the Pāḷi nor its commentaries; rather, it flows together entirely like the waters of the Yamunā merging with the waters of the Gaṅgā.
It should be understood accordingly.

Furthermore, this distinction should also be noted here. How so? Because in the Pāḷi text, in the phrase “Your daughter, O Great Hero, is wise and radiant,” the word “paññavantā” is seen as a singular vocative.
[And it is said: “All these [verses] are thus concluded.”
Though fame may overwhelm him who is wise,
and though he has attained former, exalted renown,
he should not abandon his former strength of virtue.
Since the singular form of address “paññavanta” is seen in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) on this Jātaka text,
the singular forms of address “bho guṇavanta,” “bho guṇavantā,” “bho satimanta,” and “bho satimantā” must also necessarily be accepted.
For instance, in that same text, there is the form of address “yasassi paññavanta.”

The commentators of the *Aṭṭhakathā* maintain this. For the word *naṃ* is merely a particle used for metrical completion (*padapūraṇa*). The term *paññavantaṃ*, however, is stated by adding the suffix *-āgama* for the purpose of preserving the meter.

Thus, the occurrence of vocative forms in the sacred texts (the *Pāvacana*)—such as those containing suffixes like *-vantu*—should be understood according to the method demonstrated by examples such as: "Bhagavā," "Āyasmā," "Paññavanta," "Cakkhuma," and "Pāpima."
And here, because it is seen in such passages as “The river named Gaṅgā-Bhāgīrathī was brought forth from the Himālayas” and “From where have you come, venerable sir?
From the Himālayas, Great King,” the fifth case singular form “guṇavantā” has been stated.
Just as the nominal paradigm for the word *guṇavant* has been applied, so too [should it be understood] for *dhanavant*, *balavant*, *satimant*, and others.
The nominal declension series for *gatimant* and so forth should also be applied.
Now, in order to remove the confusion of listeners regarding the fact that words such as *vidvat* share the same grammatical behavior (*samānagatika*) as adjectives denoting qualities (*guṇavāpada*),
the nominal declension series for the paradigmatic forms such as *vidvantu* and so on is stated here, along with partial etymologies and other details.
One who possesses that which is called knowledge (*ñāṇa*) is a *vidvā*, a wise person. Here, the existence of the word *vidvā* is illustrated by the direct textual reading (*āhaccapāṭha*):
“Thus knowing, one should live equanimously,” and so forth. Herein is the paradigm of forms: *vidvā*, *vidvā*, *vidvanto*;
*vidvantaṃ*, *vidvante*; *vidvatā*, *vidvantena*. All the rest is to be understood accordingly. [The form] *vedanāvā*...
*Vedanāvā*, *vedanāvanto*. *Vedanāvantaṃ*, *vedanāvante*. *Vedanāvatā*, *vedanāvantena*. The rest is all to be understood accordingly.
The same applies to such cases as “*saññāvā*, *cetānavā*, *saddhāvā*, *paññavā*, *sabbāvā*,” and so forth.

And here, phrases such as “the self possessing feeling (*vedanāvantaṃ attānaṃ*)” or “the world possessing everything (*sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ*)” are illustrative examples. In that context, *sabbāvantaṃ* means...
“Possessing all beings” means being joined with all beings; for this word has its long vowel in the middle.
However, words such as “paññavā paññavanto” (wise, wise ones) generally have short vowels in the middle.

One who has people as his retinue is “yasassivā”; alternatively, one who is both “yasassī” and “yasassivā” is “yasassivā. This is an example of *ekadesasarūpekasesa* (retaining one part while omitting the rest).
Regarding the existence of the word "yasassivā" (renowned), [it is found in the verse]:
"A kshatriya, perfected by birth, noble-born and renowned;
a Dhamma-king of the Videhas, a son shall be born to you."
This is an illustration. “Yasassivā, yasassivā, yasassivanto; yasassivantaṃ,” and so forth, should be understood accordingly.
One who has the habit of seeing the goal (attha) is an “atthadassi”; what is that? It is knowledge (ñāṇa). One who possesses such an atthadassi is an “atthadassimā. And in this context:
“Having gone there, he is one possessed of progress, possessed of steadfastness, possessed of wisdom, and possessed of insight into the goal;”
“Having analyzed all phenomena, Vidhura spoke thus”—this is the statement that establishes the meaning of this [term].
“Atthadassimā, atthadassimā, atthadassimanto; atthadassimantaṃ,” and so forth, should be understood accordingly.
One who has evil (*pāpa*) is a *pāpimā*, one who is possessed of a heap of unwholesome states.
*Māra*. One who has sons is *puttimā*, meaning one with many sons. For in the phrase “one with sons grieves because of his sons,” it is the father of many sons who is called *puttimā*.

One who has the moon is *candimā*. Here, “moon” (*canda*) refers to the lunar mansion (*candavimāna*), while the son of a deity dwelling in that lunar mansion is called *candimā*. Thus, [it is said]: “The moon has risen; the moon by measure...”

In such passages as, “It is forty-nine yojanas in length, breadth, and height, and three yojanas less than one hundred and fifty yojanas in circumference,” the moon-palace is referred to as “the moon.
However, in such passages as, “The moon-deva went for refuge to the Tathāgata, the Arahant,” it is the moon-deity who is called “Candimā.
Another method: he possesses the moon, thus he is “Candimā. “Canda” means...
And here, the son of the deva Canda is intended; however, the moon-palace (*candavimāna*), which is his dwelling place, is called “Candimā.
For thus, in such passages as “Rāhu, release the moon! The moon dwells in a palace made of jewels,” the son of the deva Canda is referred to as “Canda. [As it is said:
“Whosoever, being a young bhikkhu, applies himself to the Buddha’s teaching...”
In such passages as, "He illuminates the world of Soma, like the moon freed from clouds," the term "Candimā" refers to the lunar mansion (*candavimāna*) which serves as his dwelling place.
Thus, it should be understood that both "Cando" and "Candimā" are names for both the son of the gods (the deity) Canda and the lunar mansion Canda. In this context, "Pāpimā..."

The forms *puttimā* and *candimā* should be understood as having attained their established form by means of the suffix *-iman-tu*, which occurs in the sense of "he has that" (*tad-assa atthi*) following words such as *pāpa*.
But is it not the case, sir, that these must be derived solely by means of the suffix *-mantu*? No; for the suffix *-mantu* does not occur after any word ending in *-a*.

“Non-existence. [The opponent asks: “But, sir, even if this is so, O Evil Son, is it not possible to establish [the form] by first adding the augment *ik* after *canda*, and then applying the suffix *mantu*?
[The teacher replies: “It is possible, because the mere formal shape (*rūpamatta*) is achieved; however, the method (*naya*) is not elegant.
For if one were to apply the augment *ik* after *pāpa-puttādi* ending in *akāra*, and then apply the suffix *mantu*...”
There would be the undesirable consequence (pasaṅga) that the suffix *mantu* must be applied after other words ending in *a*, such as *guṇa* and *yasas*, by adding the vowel *i*.

For nowhere among the hundreds of thousands of scriptural passages (*pāḷi*) is the suffix *mantu* seen following a word ending in *a*—such as *guṇa* or *yasas*—along with the addition of the vowel *i*;
rather, because it is impossible, [the suffix is not added] after words like *pāpa* or *putta*, even though they end in *a*.
[The opponent argues: "Even without the *iman* suffix, once the *mantu* suffix is applied, forms such as ‘pāpimā’ (possessing evil) and ‘puttimā’ (possessing a son) are established.
Even if that were so, sir, why is only the *mantu* suffix mentioned in the *Kaccāyana-ppakaraṇa*, and not the *iman* suffix? [The answer is: Both have indeed been stated.
If you ask how this is known, it is because in that [work] it says: "After *tapa*, etc., *sī*; after *daṇḍa*, etc., *ika*..."
Having stated these four rules— "ī," "madhvādito ro," "guṇādito vantū"— by virtue of the proximity of the words *to* and *anta*,
and having then stated a different rule in the middle, namely "satyādīhi mantū," the rule "saddhādito ṇā" was subsequently stated by virtue of the proximity of *to* and *anta*;
therefore, in that context, the rule "satyādīhi mantū" was treated as an exception.
By virtue of the sutta being stated, it is understood that this suffix *iman* is also stated.
For it is the nature of teachers to make their intention known by whatever means possible. And here, the second meaning should be taken according to the euphonic combination (*sarasandhi*);
for its first meaning is "the suffix *mantu* after *satya*, etc.," while the second is "the suffix *iman* after *satya*, etc."
Meaning: Thus, as in the usage “seto dhāvati” (the white one runs), in the sutta “satyādīhi mantū,” there occurs the realization of two meanings by way of the coalescence of distinct powers;

therefore, because this sutta possesses a meaning that is supremely subtle and profound, the suffix *mantu* is intended in some instances after words such as *sati*, *gati*, *setu*, and *go*, while in other instances it is intended after words such as *sati*, *pāpa*, and *putta*.
It should be understood that the suffix *imantu* is intended [here].

However, because the word *sati* shares the same grammatical category (*samānagatika*) with words such as *gati*, *dhī*, *sethu*, and *ithu* by way of the suffix *-mantu*, and with words such as *pāpaputta* by way of the suffix *-imantu*, it is therefore taken as being of the nature of a qualifier (*pakāra*).
Thus, the meaning of the sutta is as follows: "By means of *sati* and so forth..."

"The suffix *mantu* and the suffix *ima* occur after words ending in *sati*, according to their respective requirements, in the sense of ‘one who possesses that’ (*tadassatthi*). This is the intended meaning here:

just as in the word "satimā," the suffix *mantu* occurs after the word "sati" which ends in the vowel *i*, so too in cases such as "gatimā," "dhīmā," "setumā," and "gomā," [the suffixes occur] after words ending in *i*, *ī*, *u*, and *ū*.

The *mantu* suffix occurs. Just as in the case of "satimā," where the *mantu* suffix follows the word "satī" ending in the vowel *i*, likewise in cases such as "gatimā," "pāpimā," and "puttimā," the *mantu* suffix follows words ending in *i* or *a*.
Thus, the *mantu* and *iman* suffixes occur after sounds of the type "sati" according to their grammatical possibility.
If it were the case that, like the rule "ika ī from daṇḍa, etc. (which prescribes two conditions), one should have stated "imantu mantu from satya, etc.," why was it not so stated?
There is a reason for not stating it thus. For if the rule "imantu mantu from satya, etc.
had been stated just as the rule "ika ī from daṇḍa, etc. is, then at a single moment...

By this statement regarding the word *mantu*, one might expect two distinct forms—such as the two forms *daṇḍika* and *daṇḍī* which arise from the sound *daṇḍa*—to occur even from *sati*, *gati*, and so forth;
yet that is not the case. Therefore, it was not stated that "from *sati* and so forth, this is *mantu*.
Furthermore, if it were stated in that way, there would be a heaviness of the text due to the abundance of syllables. And because [the rule] is established by the Sutta...
A name ought to be concise, unambiguous, substantial, possessing a hidden meaning, comprehensive, and blameless. In the *Kaccāyana*, for the most part,
such suttas are seen whose meanings are profound and which fall within the scope of very clear knowledge— such as "In the case of the word *upājha*,
the suffix *dhika* is elided" and "Vowels [coalesce] with vowels"— and this [sutta] is also one of them.

Therefore, it was not stated as "from *satya*, etc., [the suffix] *iman*. Thus, even though the instruction regarding the suffix *u* (*sut*) has not been given, it should be understood that for the purpose of including the suffix *iman* as well, the expression "by *satya*, etc., [the suffix] *man*" is stated by way of the coalescence of distinct grammatical powers (*bhinnasatti-samaveta*).
Another method: in expressions such as "from *tapa*, etc., [the suffix] *si*," the fact that the word ending in *to* (*todanta*) is in the plural number is not clearly evident.
Because the suffix -ima occurs in the sense of both unity and plurality, the plural sense of the word *hi* in the phrase “*mantū satyādīhi hi*” is extremely evident;
therefore, it should also be understood that this suffix -ima is present by virtue of that plural inclusion.
But surely, sir, even without this suffix -ima, one who has evil (*pāpa*) is a “possessor of evil” (*pāpī*), and one who is simply a possessor of evil is a “wicked one” (*pāpimā*).

Is it not the case that once the suffix *mā* has been applied in the sense of possession (*sakatthe*), forms such as *pāpimā* and *puttimā* are established, just like the word *chaṭṭhamo* in the phrase *chaṭṭhamo so parābhavo*, where the word *chaṭṭhamo* is formed by the suffix *ma*? For instance, in cases such as "the sixth itself is the sixth," the application of the term should be understood according to the masculine method (*purisana*), as in "a sutta itself is a *suttanta*.

Being thus questioned, he will certainly remain silent, seeing no way to answer further.

There they were not seen, like arrows shot in the night.
At that time, I was a Naga king of great psychic power,
named Atula by name, possessed of merit and radiance.
“He is a sage possessed of wisdom, mindfulness, and fortitude;
the Elder Ānanda, the upholder of the True Dhamma, a mine of jewels.

Having thus understood the distinctions between words such as *himavanta*, *sati*, and *manta*, one should further determine—by way of gender—the meaning of words belonging to two genders, the nominal paradigm (*nāmikapadamālā*) of the base form, and the similarity or dissimilarity of words.
In that context, the word *sirimā* is divided into two types because it functions in both genders by virtue of its commonality as a nominal stem (*sutisāmañña*).

Both of these belong to the class of stems ending in *-ū*. Alternatively, however, the latter belongs to the class of stems ending in *-ā*.
"He who has glory (siri) is 'sirīmā'"—this is the derivation according to the masculine gender.

"She who has glory is 'sirīmā'"—this is the derivation according to the feminine gender. Although these two are identical in meaning both by way of their verbal root (*suti*) and their etymological sense (*nibbacanattha*), nevertheless, they should be understood as having distinct meanings because they denote a male referent and a female referent respectively.
This method should be applied to other similar instances as well. *Sirimā*, *sirimā*, *sirimanto*. *Sirimantaṃ*, *sirimante*. *Sirimatā*, *sirimantena*.
The declension of nouns follows the same pattern as the word *guṇavantu*. *Sirimā*, *sirimā*, *sirimāyo*. *Sirimaṃ*, *sirimā*, *sirimāyo*. *Sirimāya*.
These should be understood according to the method for feminine nouns that will be explained later. Thus.

The similarity and dissimilarity of words within the nominal paradigms (*nāmikapadamālā*) of sounds that are divided into two types—those with identical etymologies and those with different etymologies—must be determined.

For even in the case of the word *sirimā*, which has a different etymology despite having a similar meaning, not a single word from its nominal paradigm shares any identity with these [other] words. Regarding this, it is said:
The word *sirīmā* occurs in two ways, as it applies to both males and females;
one should understand that it is divided [into two genders], and here the masculine gender is intended.

Thus, by means of the word *abhibhavitā*, words such as *guṇavā*, *satimā*, and so forth—which are dissimilar [to the base]—have been shown along with their series of nominal inflections (*nāmikapadamālā*). However, in the grammatical treatises of Kaccāyana-rūpasiddhi, the forms "rājena, rājehi, rājebhi, rājesu" are stated. In the Cūḷanirutti and the Niruttipiṭaka, those...

for example: “āvutthaṃ dhammarājenā,” “sivirājena pesito,” and “pajāpatissa.”

In the canonical method, when examining such passages as "of the king of the gods, the tip of the banner" and "when the Great King was departing, the increaser of the kingdom of the Sivi people," we see that terms such as "by the king" and so forth are used in the singular;
not only in the canonical method, but also when examining the ancient commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) method, we see them used in the singular and not otherwise. Even though this is so...

And herein, the nominal declensions of the word *rāja* occurring at the end of a compound are stated in two ways, according to whether it ends in a vowel or a consonant.
In that regard, those ending in *o* include such forms as “mahārājo,” “yuvarājo,” “sivirājo,” and “dhammarājo.
Those ending in *ā*, however, include such forms as “mahārājā,” “yuvarājā,” “sivirājā,” and “dhammarājā.

Although these forms like “mahārājo” do not appear in the Pāḷi or in the ancient commentaries (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*), nevertheless, [the forms ending in *ā* are justified] by such passages as: “sabbamitto sabbasakho, sabbabhūtānukampako.”
Since the form "sabbasakho" is seen in the Pāli, forms such as "mahārājo" and so forth must necessarily be accepted.
For indeed, in compound words (samāsa), forms such as "dhammarājena" and "dhammarājassa" are seen.
These are exclusively forms ending in the vowel -o, not forms ending in the vowel -ā. [The declension is as follows: mahārājo, mahārājā; mahārājaṃ, mahārāje; mahārājena, mahārājehi.
[Instrumental] *mahārājebhi*. [Genitive] *mahārājassa*, *mahārājānaṃ*. [Ablative] *mahārājā*, *mahārājasma*, *mahārājamhā*, *mahārājehi*, *mahārājebhi*.
[Genitive] *mahārājassa*, *mahārājānaṃ*. [Locative] *mahārāje*, *mahārājasmiṃ*, *mahārājamhi*, *mahārājesu*. [Vocative] *bho mahārāja*, *bhavanto mahārājā*.
However, according to the methods of the *Kaccāyana-cūḷanirutti*, it is "bho mahārājā."

The singular and plural forms should also be observed. Just as [the paradigm] for the word ending in *-o* was given by way of "mahārājo," so too should the nominal paradigm of the base form be constructed by way of other words ending in *-o*, such as "sivirājo," "dhammarājo," and "devarājo.

However, this is the nominal paradigm by way of those ending in *-ā*: Singular: Nominative: mahārājā Accusative: mahārājaṃ Instrumental: mahārājena Dative: mahārājassa Ablative: mahārājato Genitive: mahārājassa Locative: mahārāje Vocative: mahārāja Plural: Nominative: mahārājā Accusative: mahārāje Instrumental: mahārājehi Dative: mahārājānaṃ Ablative: mahārājehi Genitive: mahārājānaṃ Locative: mahārājesu Vocative:
mahārājā [The same pattern applies to] "sivirājā," "dhammarājā," "devarājā," and so forth.
Mahārājā, mahārājā, mahārājāno. Mahārājānaṃ, mahārājaṃ, mahārājāno.
Mahāraññā, mahārājinā, mahārājūhi, mahārājūbhi. Mahārañño, mahārājino, mahāraññaṃ, mahārājūnaṃ.
Mahāraññā, mahārājūhi, mahārājūbhi. Mahārañño, mahārājino, mahāraññaṃ, mahārājūnaṃ. Mahāraññe.
*Mahārājini*, *mahārājūsu*. "O Great King," "you Great Kings.
Here too, according to the method of the two grammatical treatises (*pakaraṇa*), both the singular and plural forms—such as "O Great King" (*bho mahārājā*)—are to be understood.
And just as by way of the word ending in the vowel *ā* (*mahārājā*), so too [should it be understood] for *sivirājā*, *dhammarājā*, *devarājā*, and so forth.
The nominal paradigm of the base form should be constructed by way of words ending in the vowel *ā*.
Here, for the sake of further clarifying the meaning, the mixed nominal paradigm of words ending in *ā* and *o* is stated in conjunction with verbs:
Mahārājā, mahārājo tiṭṭhati, mahārājāno, mahārājā tiṭṭhanti. Mahārājānaṃ, mahārājaṃ.
He sees, O Great Kings; he sees the Great Kings. Done by the Great King, by the Great Kings, by the Great King: *mahāraññā*, *mahārājīnaṃ*, *mahārājassa*;

done by the Great Kings, by the Great Kings, by the Great Kings: *mahāraññā*, *mahārājānaṃ*, *mahārājehi*, *mahārājebhi*. Given to the Great King, to the Great Kings, to the Great King: *mahārañño*, *mahārājīnaṃ*, *mahārājassa*;

issued from the Great King, from the Great Kings, from the Great King: *mahāraññā*, *mahārājānaṃ*, *mahārājasmiṃ*, *mahārājamhā*; [issued] by the Great Kings, by the Great Kings: *mahāraññā*, *mahārājānaṃ*, *mahārājūhi*, *mahārājūbhi*.

[It is] escaped from the great kings, from the great kings (*mahārājehi*, *mahārājebhi*). It is the possession of the great king, of the great queen, or of the great king (*mahārañño*, *mahārājino*, *mahārājassa*);

it is the possession of the great queens, of the great king (*mahāraññaṃ*, *mahārājūnaṃ*, *mahārājānaṃ*). It is established in the great queen, in the great queen (*mahāraññe*, *mahārājini*), in the great king, in the great king (*mahārāje*, *mahārājasmiṃ*, *mahārājamhi*);
it is established in the great queens, in the great kings (*mahārājūsu*, *mahārājesu*). O great king, you stand!
"Venerable great kings, you great kings, please remain. The same applies to expressions such as "crown prince, crown prince," and so forth.
Here, some might ask: "Why has the author of this treatise exerted such great effort and such great diligence on this point?

Wise people should say this to them:

"The author of this work has here exerted great effort and great diligence for the sake of benefiting the Dispensation by generating thorough proficiency in both words and meanings among listeners regarding the Teacher’s ninefold dispensation along with its commentaries; and as for those words shown by him, in these..."
"Some [passages] exist in the Buddha’s word, while others do not. Here, those that exist in the Buddha’s word are included by virtue of their existence;
those that do not exist there are included by virtue of their existence in the ancient commentaries and so forth, and by virtue of the method of the Canon.
Herein, this is the explanation of the intended meaning in brief:
“Having said this, the great king Kaṃsa, the ruler of Bārāṇasī, laid aside his bow and quiver and entered upon self-restraint.
This is an illustration of the word *mahārāja* ending in the vowel *ā*. For the Pāḷi reading “Sabbasakho” is found [in the text].

Thus, once the status of the word "mahārāja" as ending in *o* is established, [the forms] "mahārājā," "mahārājasmā," and "mahārājamhā" [are derived] for the fifth case.

The singular forms “mahārāje,” “mahārājasmiṃ,” and “mahārājamhi”—that is, the singular forms of the locative case—are indeed established, because even those not found in the canonical texts (pāḷi) must be accepted by way of logical extension (nayavasena). However, forms such as “rājena” and “rājassa” are not to be accepted by way of logical extension.
Why is that? Because [the grammatical rules apply] to cases such as “rājā,” “brahmā,” “sakhā,” and “attā.”
They are not entirely identical to one another like [the terms] "puriso" (man) and "urago" (snake), for instance;
for indeed, they possess dissimilar forms such as "raññā," "brahmunā," "sakhinā," "attanā," "attena," "sānā," "pumunā," and so forth.

Therefore, it is not possible to know them by means of grammatical rules (*naya*). Because they are thus difficult to understand, [the details] are found in the Pāḷi and the ancient commentaries (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*).

And the words must be understood exactly according to their literal form. However, since the status of words such as *mahārāja* as ending in the vowel *o* is already established, we see the application of the rule stating, "These words follow the method of masculine nouns" (*purisanaya*);
therefore, we have stated [the forms] *mahārājā*, *mahārājasmā*, and so forth, by way of that method. For example:
“Indeed, this is difficult for you to understand, that you lie here like one who is dead, while the staff does not leave your hand as you drag it along. Here, the word “hand” (*hatthā*) is used;
however, in the phrase “Fear has arisen from the staff” (*attadaṇḍā bhayaṃ jātaṃ*), the word “staff” (*daṇḍā*) ends in the vowel *ā*.

Since the singular ablative case is seen in [the forms] *pañcamī*, *ekavacanassa*, etc., forms such as *uragā*, *paṭaṅgā*, *vihagā* must also be understood as singular ablative endings ending in the vowel *o*.
And just as in the phrase, "O fanged ones, do not despise me; the jackal is my provider of food," there is the verb form *maññavho*;
and in the phrase, "Pure ones, dwell together with the pure, being mindful," there is the verb form *kappayavho*.
By way of illustration, forms such as "gacchavho," "bhuñjavho," and "sayavho" should also be included.

Those who are highly skilled in the Teaching (Sāsana) do indeed accept such word-forms; therefore, we too have stated "mahārājā," "mahārājasmā," and so forth by way of grasping the underlying method (nayaggāha).
However, if there is no grasping of the method, how can there be a nominal paradigm (nāmikapadamālā)?
They will become complete; indeed, they are complete in that very [grammar].

For in the word of the Buddha, there are many hundreds of thousands of nominal words and verbs, each distinct, categorized by the seven or eight nominal case-endings—both singular and plural—and by the ninety-six verbal terminations.

These [forms] do not exist as distinct grammatical applications; however, they certainly exist by way of method (*naya*). Thus, it is by way of method that we have established such forms as “mahārājā” and “mahārājasmā.
Furthermore, the forms “mahārājā tiṭṭhanti” and “mahārājā tumhe tiṭṭhatha” are based on the passage:
“Then the four Great Kings, together with a great army of *yakkhas* and a great army of *kumbhaṇḍas*... (Dīgha Nikāya 31).
“They four great kings, from all four directions,
stood gazing intently upon the Kāpilavatthava forest”—
these were spoken because they were seen. Furthermore, the words beginning with “O Great King” were also spoken only after having observed both the Pāḷi and the method of the Pāḷi.
In non-compounds, we do not see forms such as "rājaṃ" or "rājenā"; therefore, this point must be thoroughly investigated.
For this is a subtle matter, difficult to perceive, and to be understood by those of heroic nature.
However, if you, venerable sirs, should find "rājaṃ," "rājenā," and so forth in the Buddha’s word or in the ancient commentaries in non-compounds, then you should attend to it well.

Make [an effort]. For who indeed, other than those great ones whose taints are destroyed and who possess the analytical knowledges (patisambhidā), would be capable of knowing the distinctions in terminology within the Buddha’s word in every respect?
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Free from craving, without grasping, skilled in the analysis of words;
one who knows the combination of syllables as well as those that precede and follow.
Brahmā, brahmā, brahmāno. Brahmaṇaṃ, brahmaṃ, brahmāno. Brahmunā, brahmehi, brahmebhi.
Nominative: brahmā, brahmāṇo, brahmāṇo (brahmūhi, brahmūbhi). Genitive: brahmaṇo, brahmaṇo, brahmaṇam, brahmaṇam (brahmassa, brahmuno, brahmānam, brahmūnam). Instrumental:

brahmaṇā, brahmaṇā, brahmaṇehi, brahmaṇebhi, brahmaṇūhi, brahmaṇūbhi (brahunā, brahmehi, brahmebhi, brahmūhi, brahmūbhi). Dative: brahmaṇo, brahmaṇo, brahmaṇam, brahmaṇam (brahmassa, brahmuno, brahmānam, brahmūnam).
Locative: brahmaṇi, brahmaṇesu (brahmani, brahmesu). Vocative: bho brahma, bho brahme, bhavanto brahmāno.
According to the preference of the Great Thera Yamaka, there may be the plural form “bho brahmā. However, here,

because we see the commentary’s statement, “by wise men, by devas, by Brahmās,” and because we see the commentarial statements, “there is the sound of speech from the Brahmās,” and “among the Brahmās,
sensual-taint (kāmāsava) as desire and lust for palaces and so forth does not exist,” [the text reads] “perceiving injury...”

“I have not spoken what is unskillful; I have proclaimed the sublime Dhamma among men, O Brahmā”—because these words were spoken directly, the forms *brahmūhi*, *brahmūbhi*, *brahmūnaṃ*, and *brahme* are stated;
these do not appear in the *Cūḷanirutti*, the *Niruttipiṭaka*, or the *Kaccāyana*. *Sakha*, *sakha*, *sakhino*, *sakhāno*, *sakhāyo*. *Sakhaṃ*, *sakhāraṃ*, *sakhānaṃ*, *sakhino*, *sakhāno*.
Sakhāyo (Nominative plural). Sakhinā, sakhārehi, sakhārebhi, sakhehi, sakhebhi (Instrumental singular and plurals).
Sakhissa, sakhino, sakhīnaṃ, sakhārānaṃ, sakhānaṃ (Genitive singular and plurals). Sakhārasmā, sakhinā, sakhārehi, sakhārebhi, sakhehi, sakhebhi (Ablative singular and plurals).
Sakhissa, sakhino, sakhīnaṃ, sakhārānaṃ, sakhānaṃ (Genitive singular and plurals). Sakhe, sakhesu, sakhāresu (Locative singular and plurals). Bho (Vocative singular).
*Sakha*, *bho sakhā*, *bho sakhi*, *bho sakhī*, *bho sakhe*, *bhavanto sakhino*, *sakhāno*, *sakhāyo*.
According to the opinion of the Great Elder Yamaka, "bho sakhā" may also be used as a plural form.

However, in the Pāli Canon, in the *Suvaṇṇakakkaṭajātakā*, the word *sakhā*—as in the phrase "O friend (*hare sakhā*), why indeed have you abandoned me?"—is stated in the long vowel form and serves as a singular vocative.
If it is argued that, therefore, the method of the Great Thera Yamaka is not tenable, we say: no, it is not untenable.
Because in the *Manoja-jātaka*, the word *sakha* (friend) occurs both in the singular and the plural—as in: “There are no such friends; a friend is hard for me to find while I live.
For in that verse, the plural form appears in the first quarter and the singular form in the second quarter; therefore, [the method] of the Great Thera Yamaka...
The word *sakha* is used in the sense of the singular, the vocative, and the plural.

Here, following the reading "sabbamitto sabbasakho, sabbabhūtānukampako," the nominal paradigm (*nāmikapadamālā*) for the word *sakha* as it occurs within the compound is formed according to the pattern of masculine nouns (*purisanaya*), beginning with:
"sabbasakho, sabbasakhā, sabbasakhaṃ, sabbasakhe," and so forth. In this regard:

And they are seen. Furthermore, it is stated thus in the *Niruttipiṭaka*:
“Sā tiṭṭhati, sāno tiṭṭhanti. Sānaṃ passati, sāne passati. Sānā kataṃ, sānehi kataṃ, sānebhi kataṃ. Sāssa dīyate, sānaṃ dīyate.

Regarding this, it should be said: just as in cases such as “not satisfied with one’s own wife (*sehi dārehi asantuṭṭho*)”, where the word “one’s own (*sako*)” occurs in the masculine gender...

Forms (*rūpāni*) exist. Or, as in such passages as: “For they harm themselves, like a fruit whose core is its bark;

*saṃ*, *sāni*, *sā*; *saṃ*, *sāni*, *se*; *sena*, *sehi*, *sebhi*.
The forms *sassa*, *sānaṃ*; *sā*, *sasmiṃ*, *samhi*, *sehi*, *sebhi*; *sassa*, *sānaṃ*;

This being so, why did those teachers state "saṃ, se, senā" in the place of the second and third [cases], and why?
And why is it stated as *sā*, *sasmā*, *samhā* in the fifth case, and as *se*, *sasmiṃ*, *samhī* in the seventh case?
All of this is without foundation; it is grasped merely through speculative assumption and lacks justification.
For the word *sā* denoting a dog has the vowel *ā* as its defining characteristic (*pakatika*), whereas words such as *purisa* and *citta* have the vowel *a* as their defining characteristic.

That nature by which such forms as these might exist does not exist. Nor is this [the word *go*] like [words such as] "king," "Brahmā," "friend," or "self," which first remain in a state ending in the vowel *a* and subsequently acquire the state of ending in the vowel *ā*;
rather, it is like the word *go*, whose nature is eternally to end in the vowel *ā*. For that which has a nature eternally ending in the vowel *ā*...

Furthermore, such forms do not exist; therefore, they were not mentioned by the Venerable Mahākaccāyana, who possessed the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) regarding the Piṭaka of Language (Niruttipiṭaka).
Even if they should think, "Because one sees 'self' (attaṃ) as 'by the self' (attenā), these two—'saṃ' and 'senā'—should be included," they should not be included.
[The examples are: "king" (rājā), "Brahmā," "friend" (sakhā), "self" (attā), "she" (sā).

Furthermore, something else should be said here: Just as when it is said, “*sāhi nārīhi te yantī*,” [the word *sā*] means “her own women,” so too, regarding the feminine-gendered pronoun *sā*—which is similar to the word *kaññā* in its meaning—the forms are:

The forms *sāya*, *sāyam*, and *sāsū* occur according to the paradigm of feminine nouns (*kaññānaya*), but the forms of this word *sā* denoting "dog" do not occur in that same way.

This too is not a valid reason, because the word *sā*, which denotes a dog, belongs to the class of words ending in *ā*.
And for the word *sā*, which belongs to the class of words ending in *ā*, just as for a word belonging to the class of words ending in *a*—
The form *purisassa*—the singular dative-genitive case of the word *purisa*—occurs because of the absence of such a form [as *purisāya*].

For this very reason, when venerable Kaccāyana was demonstrating the form of the word *sā*, which denotes a dog, in the *Niruttipiṭaka*, he stated the form *sāssa* by lengthening the preceding vowel in the place of the singular dative-genitive case. Why?
Furthermore, do those teachers desire the form "sāya" in the place of the fourth case singular? This too is without reason;

for, setting aside the substitution of *āy* for the following *nām*-suffixes after the vowel *ā* when it is designated as *gha* in the feminine gender ending in *ā*, and the substitution of *āy* for the following fourth case singular after the neuter gender ending in *a*, [this would apply] only in the masculine gender ending in *ā* where it is not designated as *gha*.
Nowhere is the substitution of *āy* for the dative singular of a word ending in *-ākāra* seen.

Furthermore, such a form is not mentioned in the *Niruttipiṭaka*; its non-mention is more appropriate, as it does not appear in the Buddha’s word (*buddhavacana*) nor in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) and so forth.
As for our [use of it], based on the *Niruttipiṭaka* and the Buddha’s word, [we have used it] for the sake of expressing the word "dog."
The nominal paradigm for *sā-sadda* has been stated; it alone should be understood according to its essential meaning.

Here too, regarding the three words *sā*, *so*, and *saṃ*—which function in various senses and are included within the three genders—one should observe the similarity and dissimilarity of the case-forms among the words in the nominal paradigms of their respective base forms.

Here it might be asked: "How do people know that the word *taṃ*—which you maintain refers to the meaning of *taṃ*, to a dog, and to the sense of 'one's own action' (*sakam-icc-attha*)—is the designator of this particular meaning when it is uttered as *sā*? They do not know it by themselves;

However, because the word *daḷhadhammā* appears in this textual passage (*pāḷi*) in the plural form, it is not well-established whether the term *daḷhadhamma* ends in the vowel *-ā* (ākāra) or *-o* (okāra), since the forms are identical when used as plurals ending in those [vowels].
Nevertheless, we have constructed the paradigm (*padamālā*) according to the *-ā* ending alone; for in such instances, the word *daḷhadhamma* may indeed be taken as ending in *-ā*.
It is indeed appropriate to say that it ends in the vowel *o*, because its form is not clearly manifest.

However, in another passage of the Pāḷi, the word *daḷhadhamma*—which is extremely clear and ends in the vowel *o*—is seen in two ways, according to whether it expresses a quality (*guṇa*) or a conventional designation (*paṇṇatti*).
In this regard, in the phrase: "He is skilled in sovereignty and is known as *daḷhadhamma*," the word *daḷhadhamma* ends in the vowel *o*.
The word *guṇa* is a quality-denoting term. However, in the passage, “In Bārāṇasī, a king named Daḷhadhamma reigned,” it is a term denoting a conventional designation (*paṇṇatti*).
Thus, the word *daḷhadhamma*, ending in the vowel *o*, is seen in two ways.

Its nominal paradigm should be understood according to the pattern of masculine nouns as follows: *daḷhadhammo*, *daḷhadhammā*; *daḷhadhammaṃ*, *daḷhadhamme*. This applies to all words ending in *ā* and *o*.
