Addhunā, addhānehi, addhānebhi. Addhuno, addhānaṃ. Addhani, addhāne, addhānesu.
Bho addha, bhavanto addhā, addhāno.

In this regard, we shall show some applications: *tayo addhā* (three periods), *addhānaṃ vītivatto* (having passed through a period), *iminā dīghena addhunā* (by means of this long period), *dīghassa addhuno accayena* (at the passing of a long period), *pathaddhuno pannaraseva cando* (like the moon on the fifteenth day of the path-period), *ahū atītamaddhāne* (there was [a person] in the past period), *samaṇo khantidīpano* (the ascetic who illuminates forbearance), *addhāne gacchante paññāyissati* (as the period passes, he will become known)—these and others are to be understood. This, moreover, is the rule here.
It should be understood that the form *addhānaṃ* is stated here as a dual ending, as well as in the plural forms of the fourth (dative) and sixth (genitive) cases.
It is similar, by way of commonality of sound, to the neuter term *addhāna* used to denote a long journey, as in such passages as "he has set out on the journey-path" (*addhānamaggapaṭippanno hoti*).
Now, the nominal declension of the word *muddha* is stated:
Nominative: *muddhā*, *muddhā*, *muddhāno*. Accusative: *muddhaṃ*, *muddhe*, *muddhāne*. Instrumental: *muddhānā*, *muddhehi*, *muddhebhi*.
Genitive: *muddhassa*, *muddhānaṃ*. Ablative: *muddhānā*, *muddhehi*, *muddhebhi*. Locative: *muddhassa*, *muddhānaṃ*, *muddhani*.
*muddhanesu*. O fool (*muddha*), sirs, you fools (*bhavanto muddhā*), fools (*muddhāno*).

Thus, through the word *abhibhavitā*, dissimilar forms arise. In this way, by means of various methods, words ending in the vowel *ā*—such as *vatta* and others which are similar to the word *abhibhavitā*, and *guṇavādī*, *rāja*, *sādicca*, and others which are dissimilar—have been demonstrated.
Together with the series of nominal forms.
If a person of wise nature applies himself here,
his supreme knowledge will expand regarding the various divisions of linguistic usage.
Thus ends the section on the base forms of masculine nouns ending in long vowels (*ākāra*),

with detailed analysis, from the *Saddanīti* treatise composed for the benefit of the wise in understanding the modes of expression within the Three Baskets (*Piṭaka*) together with their commentaries (*Sāṭṭhakatha*).
The sixth chapter, titled "The Classification of the Series of Nouns," concerning words ending in *u* and those having the nature of ending in *avaṇṇa*.
The section on masculine nouns ending in *ā* is completed.
7. The paradigm of masculine nouns ending in *niggahīta*.
Now, having placed the opinion of the ancient masters at the forefront, we shall explain the paradigm of masculine nouns ending in *niggahīta*, such as the base forms *bhavanta* and *karonta*.
Going, walking, standing, giving, eating, hearing, cooking;
winning, aging, falling away, dying; remembering, doing, muttering, avoiding.
*Gacchaṃ*: going, *gacchanto*, *gacchantā*. *Gacchantaṃ*, *gacchante*. *Gacchatā*, *gacchantehi*, *gacchanteti*.
Of one going, of the one going, of those going, of the ones going. By one going, by those going, by the ones going.
From one going, from the one going, from those going, from the ones going. In one going, in those going, in the ones going. O you who are going, O you who are going, O you gentlemen who are going.
"Forms such as *gaccha* and others that are similar to these should be understood in this same way; this is the opinion of the Great Elder Yamaka.

Although these words—*gacchantena*, *gacchantā*, *gacchantasmā*, *gacchantamhā*, *gacchantasmiṃ*, *gacchantamhī*—do not appear here in the third-person singular case-positions and so forth, nevertheless they should be accepted because they are seen in various applications elsewhere."

In that regard, the Elder Yamaka stated the plural form for words such as "gacchanto," "mahanto," and "caranto" in the place of the vocative case, and the singular form in the place of the nominative case.
However, some have stated both the singular and plural forms in the place of the nominative case, and only the plural form in the place of the vocative case. "Gacchaṃ..."
However, in the case of *mahaṃ*, *caraṃ*, and so forth, there is the singular form used in the sense of address.

Yet, we do not see in the Buddha’s word (*buddhavacana*) across numerous commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) instances where plural usages such as *gacchanto* and *mahanto* are replaced by singular usages of address with the suffix *-ānusāra*, such as *gacchaṃ* and *mahaṃ*.
Therefore: "Bhāradvāja was going; he, going... [is the correct reading]. *Sa gacchaṃ na*... [is incorrect].
However, because we see only such singular-number usages as “nivattati” (it returns) and “mahanto lokasannivāso” (the great world-dwelling),
we consider such forms to be, as it were, incapable of being reflected upon [in the plural]. In the *Niruttipiṭaka*, under the section on the vocative case (*paccatālapana*),
only the plural form is stated for examples such as “mahanto, bhavanto, caranto,” and not the singular form.
For instance, in that context, after stating the verse, "May your honor walk;

may you stand," there are expressions such as "your honor stands" (*mahāṃ tiṭṭhati*), "the great ones stand" (*mahanto tiṭṭhantī*), "O great one" (*bho mahā*), "you, sirs" (*bhavanto mahanto*), "your honor stands" (*bhavaṃ tiṭṭhati*), and "you, sirs, stand" (*bhavanto tiṭṭhantī*).
However, in this case, the words *bhavaṃ* and *bhavanto* do not express an action-meaning (*kriyāttha*) such as "being" (*honto*, *hontā*).
In this context, singular and plural forms occur because they fall into another meaning, as in such examples as “Venerable Kaccāna; do not speak thus, sirs.

Therefore, just as the word “santo” (the good) occurs in the phrase “santo sappurisā loke,” and just as the word “arahanto” occurs in the phrase “arahanto sammāsambuddhā,” so too does the word “bhavanto” [occur].
The plural form of the word *pada* is acceptable upon reflection; however, the plural forms of words such as *mahanto*, *caranto*, and *tiṭṭhanto* do not appear to us to be so acceptable.
For nowhere else do we find hundreds of various words—such as *gacchanto*, *mahanto*, and *caranto*—excluding [the specific] words *santo*, *arahanto*, and *bhavanto*.
We observe the application of the plural ending.

For instance: while forms such as "jāna" (know) and so forth are seen in some instances to express plurality, forms such as "gacchanto" (going) and so forth are not seen in that way when expressing plurality.
In some places, even forms such as *santo* (being) and so forth appear in the plural;
however, forms such as *gacchanto* (going) do not appear thus in the plural.
The form *arahanto* (worthy ones) appears exclusively in the plural.
In the majority of instances, [terms] such as "going" (gacchanto) and so forth are not seen [to apply to a single entity];
rather, they are found in hundreds of readings in cases such as "dwelling" (viharanto),
where even for a single [subject], a plurality of occurrences is observed.
According to the principle of the plural number, if the word "gacchanto" (going) were taken [in the plural], many faults would truly be seen.
Just as when one house is burned, the neighboring houses are considered burned.
Likewise, regarding the word "gacchanto" (going) when it expresses plurality,
there may be a plural expression for words such as "viharanto" (dwelling) and so forth.
The method of grammatical forms (*rūpanaya*) is not fixed and should be understood in various ways.
Even though this is so, since it is well known in the world that "the *Niruttipiṭaka* was composed by Mahākaccāyana,
who had attained the analytical knowledges (*patisambhidā*) and whose taints were destroyed," this point must be investigated again and again.

Although this has been stated here out of respect for the Elder, nevertheless, honoring the method of the Canon (*pāḷinaya*), [one should proceed] according to the method of singular number seen [therein].
The method of plural forms not seen [in the examples] should be discarded. This being so, the method is elegant in the case of those words ending in a *niggahīta*.
However, this is our own preference:
"Bhavaṃ, karaṃ, arahaṃ, saṃ, mahaṃ" are the word-forms.
Dissimilar things arise; one should observe them as being distinct from one another.
For [terms] such as "going," "moving," "giving," "standing," "thinking," "cultivating," "speaking," "knowing," and "seeing" are indeed similar.
In that context, one should discern how terms such as “*jānan*” and others undergo transformation in certain instances by way of case, gender, and number.

First, the nominal paradigm of the word *bhavant* is stated: for the word *bhavant* expresses the meanings “increasing” (*vaḍḍhanto*) and “being” (*honto*). Based on these meanings, this is the nominal paradigm.
Bhavaṃ, bhavanto, bhavantā. Bhavantaṃ, bhavante. Bhavantena, bhavantehi, bhavantebhi. Bhavantassa, bhavantānaṃ.
Bhavantā, bhavantasmā, bhavantamhā, bhavantehi, bhavantebhi. Bhavantassa, bhavantānaṃ. Bhavante, bhavantasmiṃ, bhavantamhi, bhavantesu. He bhavanta, he bhavantā.
In this context, the meaning of such terms as *bhavaṃ* and *bhavanto* should be understood as "increasing" (*vaḍḍhanto*) and so forth.
For instance: "He is easy to recognize (*suvijāno bhavaṃ hoti*); he is one who desires the Dhamma (*dhammakāmo bhavaṃ hoti*); 'Your Majesty' (*bhavanto*), the king, rejoices in various prosperities;
the Kūḷīra lake is connected to the Ganges; when the Ganges is full, it is filled with Ganges water; when the water subsides..."

There are such applications as, "Sirs, water flows from the burning [place] into the Ganges. Therefore, this series of nominal forms (*nāmikapadamālā*) should be understood according to its essential meaning.

Here, omitting the mere word *bhavaṃ*, just as in the case of the words *gacchamāna* and *carimāna*, the masculine pattern—namely *bhavanto* and *bhavantā*—is also applicable to the word *bhavant* when it is intended to express the neuter gender.

The mental application (*cittanaya*) of "bhavantaṃ" and "bhavantāni" is also obtainable. Thus, the nominal paradigm (*nāmikapadamālā*) of the word *bhavanta*, which expresses the sense of "becoming" in the sense of increasing, should be understood.
And this is the distinction: the word *bhavanto* is exclusively plural when it functions in a sense other than that of "becoming" in the sense of increasing.
It occurs as in “Sirs, you are coming. When used in the senses of growth or becoming, it remains in the singular number only.
Here are examples of its usage: “Gradually, sir, one attains full consciousness”;
“A recluse indeed ought to be unoccupied with such matters; for in this way, sir, a recluse would be a true recluse. Thus is the word *bhavaṃ*.
However, in both cases, the singular number alone is used; therefore, now,
by way of showing such usages as “Venerable Ānanda,” “The venerables are coming,” “May the venerables be quiet,” and “Do not make a noise, venerables,” another series of noun forms is stated,
based on a different meaning that occurs in specific modes of expression:
Bhavaṃ, bhavanto, bhonto. Bhavantaṃ, bhavante. Bhavatā, bhotā, bhavantena, bhavantehi, bhavantebhi.
Bhavato, bhoto, bhavantassa, bhavantānaṃ, bhavataṃ. Bhavatā, bhotā, bhavantehi, bhavantebhi. Bhavato, bhoto, bhavantassa, bhavantānaṃ, bhavataṃ. Bhavati.
*bhavante*, *bhavantasmiṃ*, *bhavantamhi*, *bhavantesu*. *Bho*, *bhavanto*, *bhonto*.

Now, since these three words beginning with *bho* function as forms of address used in specific modes of discourse, they do not take the prefixes *āvuso* or *bhante*—unlike other words—as in the case of *bho purisa*.

For in expressions such as "bhavanto brāhmaṇā" (O venerable brahmins), "bhonto samaṇā" (O venerable recluses), and "bho rāja" (O King), it is the words *purisa* and so forth that possess the honorific particles *bho*, *bhavanto*, and *bhonto*.
And here, in the phrase "bhavaṃ Ānando" (Venerable Ānanda), the words "bho," "bhavanto," and "bhonto" are used as synonyms for the word "bhavaṃ";
however, this is not the case in the expression "dhammakāmo bhavaṃ hoti" (the Venerable one is a lover of the Dhamma).

These have the same meaning as the word *bhavaṃ*. For, according to the first method, in the sense of "increasing" (*vaḍḍhana*), the words *bho*, *bhavanta*, *bhavanto*, *bhavantā*, and *bhonto* serve as adjuncts (*upapada*) for vocative expressions such as "O sir," whereas this is not the case in the second method.
However, by way of repetition (*āmeḍita*), [the forms] are used as "bho bho," "bhavanto bhavanto," and "bhonto bhonto."
There are words such as "Venerable sir, venerable sir.
Herein, this is a brief presentation of the Pāli text by way of the earth element (bhūdhātu): "Why does your reverence dwell in the forest of knowledge?
But how, sir, shall I know that venerable Gotama? Thus spoke the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha.
Having assented to the brahmin Pokkharasāti, [he said]: "Sirs, do not speak thus. Listen to this, sirs:
'O man, know this: they are of evil nature and unrestrained,' and so forth. Herein, it should be understood that words such as "bhavaṃ" (sir) are noun-words derived from the verbal root *bhū*.
Furthermore, it should be determined that among those [words], *bho*, *bhavanto*, and *bhonto* are also indeclinable particles (*nipātapada*).
Regarding [expressions] such as *bho purisā*, no dispute should be made as to whether they are particles or not.
For in the *Kaccāyana*, it is stated: *“bho ge tū”* [Kacc 195]. Elsewhere, however, it is stated: *“an indeclinable in the sense of addressing,”* and so forth. Likewise, in the *Niruttimañjūsā*:
It is said: "The word *bho* is a particle used in the sense of addressing. It is not only a singular form, but it can also be a plural form;
thus, the plural usage *bho purisā* is also included. However, since the word *bhavanto* is exclusively a plural form, the word *purisā* is stated again.
For in both the canonical texts (*pāḷi*) and the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), [this word] functions as a particle.
The word *bho* is seen in two ways, by way of both the singular and the plural; the others, however, are seen only by way of the plural.

Since these are indeclinable words (*nipāta*), they have no function in the formation of grammatical forms. Among them, because the word *bho* is an indeclinable, when used in direct address—that is, in lifeless speech directed toward a female—there is the feminine-gender application:
"O large stone, emerge! O [stone], float about! (*ummujja bho puthusile, pariplava bho*).
The usage "puthusile" is also seen. Here are these verses illustrating the occurrence of the word *bho*:
"Bho, go from here to a happy destination, to the company of humans";
in such instances as these, the word *bho* is considered to be in the singular number.
In such expressions as “Behold this son of good family,
sirs,” one should understand that the word *bho* is used in the plural number.
It is employed both in addressing individuals and in addressing the Dhamma.
Regarding the address to one who is lifeless: the word *bho* is seen in three contexts.
Among these, in addressing a phenomenon (*dhamma*), only the singular form is obtained;
in the other two cases, it may be either singular or plural.
The state of possessing qualities is certainly to be ascertained when speaking of the Dhamma;
"How wonderful indeed!"—this is the illustration for this.
However, the state of possessing qualities is to be desired when speaking of a person.
“‘Know thus, O man!’—this is the illustration here.
However, even when a word of quality is absent, one may bring it forward and express the meaning in addressing a person, as in ‘Come, sir! and so forth.”
Addressing objects such as a jar would be speaking to the inanimate;
yet sometimes in the world, worldly people address things as if they were living beings.
Speaking to the inanimate is of little value, though it may serve to convey a meaning.
"‘O, dive down upon the broad stone,’ this is the Pāḷi illustration.
Regarding this, some wise ones accept a reversal of gender;
according to their opinion, one should change the gender to ‘bhotī’ (feminine)."
Alternatively, the word *bho* is a particle, like *sopadaṃ*;
therefore, it possesses no contradiction regarding the three genders or the two numbers.
Even so, the word *bho* occurs mostly only in the two genders.
Since it is seen by the wise that [the form] is used only for those with two genders,
when the feminine gender is reached, one should employ the word "bho.
Indeed, the wise have declared such usage to be excellent usage.
If you say that what has been shown by you is thus a misuse,
because of the abrupt phrase, "O, lift up this large stone," it is not a misuse,
since it was spoken by one skilled in conventional expression.
In the Dhamma spoken by the Victor, no improper applications are found.
Regarding the application of the word *bho* to the feminine gender,
I have thus declared that it is pleasing to poets.

Thus, the nominal paradigm of the word *bhavant* has been analyzed in two ways according to the method of the Pāḷi: by way of the sense of "increasing" (*vaḍḍhana*) and the sense of "being other than that" (*tadaññattha*).
As for the word *karonta*: Nominative: *karaṃ*, *karonto*, *karontā*. Accusative: *karontaṃ*, *karonte*. Instrumental: *karotā*, *karontena*, *karontehi*, *karontebhi*.
The forms are: *karoto*, *karontassa*, *karontānaṃ*, *karotaṃ*; *karontā*, *karontā*, *karontasmā*, *karontamhā*, *karontehi*, *karontebhi*;
*karoto*, *karontassa*, *karontānaṃ*, *karotaṃ*; *karonte*, *karontasmiṃ*, *karontamhi*, *karontesu*;
and *bho karonta*, *bhavanto karontā*. These are the forms that occur.
“*Karoto na kariyati pāpan*” (For one who acts, no evil is done)—this is the indication of the existence of the word *karoto* here.

When it is intended to be expressed in the feminine gender, forms such as “*karontī*, *karontiyo*” and so forth should be applied; when it is intended to be expressed in the neuter gender, forms such as “*karontaṃ*, *karontānī*” and so forth should be applied.
Of the word *arahanta*: Nominative: *Arahaṃ*, *arahanto*. Accusative: *Arahatam*, *arahante*. Instrumental: *Arahatā*, *arahantena*, *arahantehi*, *arahantebhi*.
Genitive: *Arahato*, *arahantassa*, *arahantānaṃ*, *arahataṃ*. Ablative: *Arahatā*, *arahantā*, *arahantasmā*, *arahantamhā*.
*arahantehi*, *arahantebhi*. *Arahato*, *arahantassa*, *arahantānaṃ*, *arahataṃ*. *Arahante*, *arahantasmiṃ*, *arahantamhi*, *arahantesu*.
*Bho arahanta*, *bhavanto arahanto*—such are the forms that occur.
This is the nominal declension of the word *arahanta*, which denotes a quality. [The nominative singular and plural are] *arahā*, *arahanto*, *arahantā*.
Indeed, this form is seen in the *Samantapāsādikā* in the context of the human community (*manussaviggaha*).
However, in the *Uttarimanussadhamma-pāḷi*, the phrase "we are not arahants" (*mayañcamhā anarahanto*) is seen. [The forms] *arahantaṃ*, *arahante*;

[the instrumental] *arahatā*; the remainder is to be expanded in detail. This is the nominal declension (*nāmikapadamālā*) of the word *arahant* when it expresses a conventional designation (*paṇṇatti*).

For instance, in such passages as “The Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One; the Worthy One, the Sugata in the world; the Worthy Ones, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones,” the word *arahant* and others denote qualities.
[In contrast, it is used in other senses: “He was a Worthy One”; “For I am a Worthy One in the world”; “There was one Worthy One, sixty-one Worthy Ones were in the world.”
In such passages as, “Whether in the village or in the forest, whether in the lowlands or on the highlands, wherever the Arahants dwell, that ground is delightful;
and we are not Arahants,” the word *arahā* and others should be understood as denoting conventional designations (*paṇṇatti*). Here, [the term] is used according to the feminine and neuter genders.
The method of speaking separately [of the genders] is not well-established. If this is so, how should a woman who has attained the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*) be spoken of?
And how should a mind that has attained the destruction of the taints be spoken of? First, a woman should be called "Arahant" by way of her qualities, based on the statement:
"If a woman were an Arahant, she would be a Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddho*"); however, by way of designation (*paṇṇatti*), she is called "woman."
One should say, "He has become an arahant. Furthermore, by way of its qualities, the mind itself should be called "the arahant mind.
Regarding the word *santa*:
Nominative: saṃ, santo, santo, santā. Accusative: saṃ, santaṃ, sante. Instrumental: satā, santena, santehi, santebhi, sabbhi.
Sato, santassa, santānaṃ, sataṃ, satānaṃ. Satā, santā, santasmā, santamhā, santehi, santebhi, sabbhi.
Sato, santassa, santānaṃ, sataṃ, satānaṃ. Sati, sante, santasmiṃ, santamhi, santesu.
Bho santa, bhavanto santa—such are the forms that occur.
In this context, however, the term "of the wise" (*satānaṃ*) is used because it is seen in the *Jayaddisa Jātaka* commentary: "Truly, dear father, this is the Dhamma of the wise.

For there, the analysis of the phrase "satanesa" is "satānaṃ esa" (this is of the wise), and the formation of the word should be understood through the elision of the short vowel, the *niggahīta*, and the *sa*-suffix.
Thus, in its commentary, it says: "Truly, with certainty, dear father, this is of the wise..."

The meaning stated is: "the nature of the wise is the Dhamma. This is the nominal declension (*nāmikapadamālā*) of the word *santa*, which denotes those in the world who are called "true persons" (*sappurisā*), "noble ones" (*ariyā*), and "wise ones" (*paṇḍitā*).
However, for its negation, there are *asaṃ*, *asanto*, and in some instances *asantā*. For it is said: "Indeed, the base ones, O dear one, [regard] me as non-existent (*asantā*)."
The Pāḷi is seen as “tātāti bhāsare. It should be construed with such forms as “asaṃ, asantaṃ, asante, asatā,” and so forth.
In this sense, the words “santo” and “asanto” are exclusively plural; they are never used in the singular. Why? Because they express a conventional designation (paṇṇatti).
However, in other instances, such as “santo, danto,” and so on, they are used exclusively in the singular.
Why [is there] the word *santa*, which denotes something existing? It should be understood that this is because it does not denote a formal rule (*apaṇṇatti*).
Now, we shall explain some usages of those words that do denote formal rules (*paṇṇatti*):

"One sits together with the non-existent" (*asatā asanti sameti*). For whatever one associates with, O King—whether it be the virtuous (*santa*) or the non-virtuous (*asa*)—that is not an assembly (*sabhā*) where...
"The virtuous do not exist; the non-virtuous go to hell, while the virtuous are destined for heaven.
A wise person should not associate with the non-virtuous, but should serve the virtuous. One should dwell only with the good. Such are the verses beginning with "The Dhamma of the good.
Furthermore, as for the word "sabbhī" (with the good) which we have applied in our *padamālā* (verse sequence) according to the third and fifth case plural endings:
And this [term] "santo" is according to the declension ending in *-a*; elsewhere, however, it should be construed according to the declension ending in *-i*, namely as "sabbhī.
For thus, "sabbhī" refers to a good person (*sappurisa*) and to Nibbāna; or rather, "sabbhī" is a synonym for "beautiful" (*sundara*).
And all this meaning is [explained] in the commentary on this passage: "Bahumpetaṃ asabbhi jātavedā," by way of the word "santo."
And this should be illustrated by the verse: “...have proclaimed [it] with the virtuous.
A wise person should apply the word *sabbhi* (with the virtuous) in the vocative and the nominative cases, as well as in the instrumental and ablative cases, and within compounds.
Here is the application [of the words]: "O virtuous ones, stay!"—he stays with the virtuous, he goes with the virtuous, he departs with the virtuous;

such a person is one who conforms to the virtuous. Because this [work] is in accordance with the Teaching (sāsana), we shall here demonstrate its conformity to that Teaching by showing its usage according to the Sāsana, for the sake of listeners regarding the diverse methods of the Sugata’s scriptures which are beyond the reach of mere logic (atakkāvacara).
"For the sake of attaining confident intelligence. How so? O Jātaveda, it is much that we honor you with our tails;
one should cultivate intimacy with the virtuous. That evil deed which Senaka committed in the Sāla grove was unseemly for a virtuous man.
This affliction is unseemly; he was unfriendly, stubborn, and unseemly. Therein, in the words of address, it is seen...
Even if the nominative case does not appear explicitly in its own form in the text, it is nonetheless seen [implied]. Likewise, when the instrumental case is seen, the ablative case is also seen.

When the phonetic form is seen in a compound, the phonetic form in its analytical (byāsa) state is also seen as far as possible, with the exception of cases such as “*hetusatthāradassanaṃ*” and so forth. And therein, if it is a term denoting Nibbāna, ...

The word *sabbhi* is feminine, like the words *santi*, *visuddhi*, and *nibbuti*. Furthermore, according to the system of the Great Elder Yamaka, it should be applied according to the rule for the night (*ratti-naya*).

For that rule is common to all feminine nouns ending in the vowel *-ī*. If it expresses the sense of "beautiful," it should be applied according to the rules for fire (*aggi*), night (*ratti*), or bone (*aṭṭhi*), because its gender depends on the word it qualifies (*vācca-lingatta*). [As in the phrase: “Nirvana is the state of being all phenomena.”
For here the meaning is that Nibbāna is the "good Dhamma" (*sundara-dhamma*).

Thus, having understood the occurrence of the word *sabbhi* in the five instances beginning with "addressing" according to the method of the Pāḷi, its occurrence should further be understood according to the method of the Aṭṭhakathā. How so?
Because in the commentary on the Sagāthāvagga it says: "The good man (*santo*) [speaks] the Dhamma of the good (*sataṃ dhammo*) together with the good (*sabbhīhi saddhiṃ*)."
In this passage, the teachers of the commentaries have shown a specific arrangement of sounds by means of the plural form "sabbhīhi" in the phrase "na jaraṃ upetīti pavedayantīti.
Therefore, the word *sabbhi* should be applied to all case endings as well. Regarding this, we say:
The venerable teachers explained the meaning of the text as "together with the good" (*sabbhīhi saddhiṃ*).
Therefore, a wise person should apply the word *sabbhi* everywhere.
Since it is heard in the context of compounds that there is also the form *asabbhirūpa*,
for that reason the learned should apply the word *sabbhi* in all instances.

Regarding the phrase, “One should advise and instruct, and restrain one from what is unwholesome,” it should be understood that the word *asabbhā* (from what is unwholesome) is derived through the addition of the *ṇya*-suffix among the various types of secondary (*taddhita*) suffixes. How so?

For the most part, that which exists among the unwholesome is "unwholesome" (*asabbha*). What is that? It is the unwholesome; therefore, one should restrain [the person] from those unwholesome states (*akusaladhammā*).
And the meaning is: "one should establish [them] in wholesome states. Regarding the phrase, "They will revile us with foul words and strike us with sharp weapons," the derivation is as follows:
they are *asabbhā* because they belong to those who are not noble (*asabbha*); alternatively, they are *asabbhā* because they do not belong to those who are noble (*sabbha*).
The formation of the word should be understood through the addition of the suffix *-ya*. And furthermore, that which here belongs to us—
Regarding the word *santa*, the paradigm is shown as “*saṃ*, *santo*; *saṃ*, *santaṃ*, *sante*,” and so forth.

In that context, when the word “*asa*” is seen in the Pāḷi passage—“*sameti asatā asa*”—the word “*sa*” is already seen even though it has not been explicitly included in the Pāḷi, because it exists as a member of a pair.
Thus, one should understand that by what is seen, the unseen is apprehended.

Alternatively, in the word *asa*, because it is to be understood through the analysis of the compound (*samāsaviggaha*) as "they do not exist" (*na saṃ asanti*), the form *sa* is indeed seen [as the underlying element].
This same method applies elsewhere as well. In that context, *santi* refers to a true person (*sappurisa*); *asanti* refers to a false person (*asappurisa*).
When expressing the feminine gender, the forms are *asatī* and *asā*. [The declension is: *asatī, asatī, asatiyo, asā; asatiṃ, asatī, asatiyo.*

The nominal declension should be applied according to the feminine pattern that will be explained as: *asāya*, *asatiyā*, *asatīhi*, *asatībhi*, *asatiyā*, *asatīnaṃ*. Here, however, such passages as “*Asā lokitthiyo nāma, velā tāsaṃ na vijjati;
mā ca vasaṃ asatīnaṃ nigacche*” (Fickle indeed are worldly women; no fixed time for them exists; do not fall under the power of fickle women) should be cited.
Furthermore, *asā* and *asatī* here have the same meaning; for their sense is “of a non-existent nature.”

However, because the commentators on the *Jātakaṭṭhakathā* have explained the meaning thus: "Asā means 'non-pleasurable' (*asatiyo*), that is, base; or alternatively, 'sāta' is said to mean happiness, and since that is not present in them, they are 'asā';

the meaning is that they give only what is non-pleasurable to those whose minds are bound to them, being painful and the basis for suffering," therefore, in the sense that "there is no pleasure (*sāta*) in this," the word "asā" [is used].

Just as the nominal declension series for the word *rittassa*—which has its final vowel elided—is to be constructed according to the mental method (*cittanaya*) as "rittassaṃ, rittassāni, rittassa," because there is no gratification here, so too [the declension] for *asa* is to be constructed according to the *kaññānaya* method as "asā, asā, asāyo; asaṃ, asā, asāyo; asāyā."
And here, the word "santo" (the peaceful ones) which has been shown by us, in some instances expresses the meaning of a word existing in both the singular and plural numbers.
According to that [word], this is the paradigm of noun forms: Santo, santo, santā. Santaṃ, sante.
Satā, santena, santehi, santebhi. Sato, santassa, sataṃ, santānaṃ. Satā, santā, santasmā, santamhā, santehi, santebhi. Sato, santassa.
The forms are: *sataṃ*, *santānaṃ*. *Sati*, *sante*, *santasmiṃ*, *santamhi*, *santesu*. *Bho santa*, *bhavanto santo*, *bhavanto santā*. Here, however:
“Monks, this is the eighth noble thoroughbred horse found existing in the world.
Monks, these four persons are found existing in the world. By means of what is non-existent, empty, false, and unreal...”
They misrepresent [the teaching]. There are such applications as, "When there is becoming, birth comes to be.

However, in such passages as, "When there are volitional formations, consciousness comes to be," it should be understood that the word *sati* stands by way of a grammatical inversion (*vacanavipallāsa*).
Among the two ways the word *santi* is established—namely, by way of the singular and the plural—one should take the plural form *santi*.
Excluding those [specific cases], the remaining [grammarians] also state that it has the meaning of "equal" (*samāna*); therefore, the meaning should be explained as:
"being present is *samāna*, being present (plural) is *samānā*," and so forth. Furthermore, the meaning of this word *samāna* is "being able" (*honta*), as in such passages as:
"Being able (*pahu samāno*), you who contemplate vast aims, for what reason do you not remove my suffering? The applications (*payoga*) are as follows:
“He who, though being able, does not support his mother or father when they are aged and past their youth— that is the first cause of downfall.
Even while remaining right here, having become a god...”
“O noble sirs, know this: my life has been regained.
Such sayings as these occur.
Furthermore, since the word *santosa* expresses the meanings of “weary,” “calmed,” and “ceased,” [it is used here].

Therefore, by way of those [grammatical forms], the nominal declension of the word *santa* should be understood according to the pattern for masculine nouns as follows: "santo, santā; santaṃ, sante; santena," and so forth.

In this context, there are such applications as: "santo tasito" (the peaceful one is tormented), "dīghaṃ santassa yojanaṃ" (a long league for the peaceful one), "santo danto niyato brahmacārī" (the peaceful, tamed, self-controlled, holy life-walker), and "santo niruddho atthaṅgato abbhatthaṅgato" (the peaceful one who has ceased, passed away, and utterly vanished).
When it is to be expressed in the neuter gender, the nominal series (*nāmikapadamālā*) follows the method of *citta*, namely: "santaṃ, santāni.
This should be understood as possessing words that illustrate the meaning, such as "saṃvijjamānaṃ, samānaṃ, kilantaṃ, upasantaṃ, niruddhaṃ.

Alternatively, since the word *santa* is seen used in the neuter in passages such as "When there is clinging (*upādāna*), there is becoming (*bhava*)," it denotes the meaning of the word *saṃvijjamāna* (that which is existing).
In the places of the third, fifth, fourth, sixth, and seventh [cases], the additional words “satā, sato, sataṃ, satī” should be stated;
the remaining [forms] are to be understood according to the method for *citta*. However, when the feminine gender (*itthiliṅga*) is to be expressed, [the forms] are “santā, santā, santāyo;
santaṃ, santā, santāyo; santāya,” following the method for *kaññā*; and also “santi, santi, santiyo; santiṃ.”
The nominal declension should be applied according to the feminine gender as follows: *santi*, *santiyo*, *santiyā*.
Among these, the first [form] possesses words that illustrate the meaning as "existing, wearying, calmed, ceased," and the applications here are indeed easy to understand.
The second, however, possesses words that illustrate the meaning as "being existing. For instance: "An existing offense (*santī āpatti*) should be confessed."
That which is found here is said to "exist.
"By means of which a man supported by his mother surveys this world;"
"Even one who grants life and peace, the angry worldling destroys.
Here, however, *santi* is used as a feminine noun (*samānā*). Another series of words (*padamālā*) should also be understood when the feminine gender is intended.

For when the word *santī* expresses an existing referent (*saṃvijjamāna-saddattha*), since feminine gender usage is seen in such passages as “When there is birth, there is aging and death,” the forms for the locative case should be stated as:
*sati*, *satiyā*, *satiyaṃ*, *santiyā*, *santiyaṃ*, *santisu*.
The remaining [forms] are to be understood according to the feminine paradigm. This is the third [case]; and here, regarding *asatiyā*...
The canonical text, “one should remain silent regarding an offense,” is an illustration of the existence of the words beginning with “santiyā.

According to another method: because of the appearance in the canon of the word *satī* used in the sense of “being equal” (*samānā*)—as in “O you who are so young, being [equal] to one who is old,” and “those who gave her to one who is old, being [equal] to one so young”—it means “being equal.”
The forms *satī*, *satiyo*; *satiṃ*, *satī*, *satiyo*; and *satiyā*—these and other such forms should also be applied, either by way of sandhi or through the elision of the letter *n*.
Now, we shall explain the determination of usage for the two words *santo* and *santā*, so that listeners may not be confused regarding their application.
For instance, when one wishes to express the meaning in the plural, such as "good persons" (*sappurisā*) or "wise ones" (*paṇḍitā*), [one uses] "those who are good" (*santo*).
Just as the singular form “danto” (tamed) has been stated, the plural form “santo” (peaceful ones) should be spoken.
When one wishes to express the meaning by means of the singular form “saṃvijjamāno” (existing), the singular form “santo” should be spoken.

When one wishes to express the meaning by means of the plural form “saṃvijjamānā,” it should be spoken as “santo sappurisā” (peaceful, good persons), or as “santo saṃvijjamānā” (the peaceful ones who exist).
In the same way as the plural form used above, one may use the plural forms "santo" or "santā.

Alternatively, when wishing to express the meaning through the singular—such as "kilanto," "samāno," "upasanto," or "niruddho"—one should use the singular form "santo," similar to the plural form "santo sappurisā" used previously. These refer to the same meanings.
However, for one wishing to speak by way of the plural number, the plural form "santā" (being) should be used, as in the verse: "Being with feet that are sound, who will seize them by the hand?
This principle should be carefully kept in mind. For this is a point of confusion for those of dull intellect.
Furthermore, the following summary should be understood here:
“The word *sati* is seen in the sense of gender (*tiliṅga*), in the sense of oneness (*ekattha*), and also in the sense of plurality (*bahvattha*);
it ends in the locative case (*sattamī*), and it is used in the sense of inversion (*vipallāsa*) and in the plural.
Now, the nominal paradigm (*nāmikapadamālā*) of the word *mahanta* is stated:
Mahaṃ, mahā, mahanto, mahantā. Mahantaṃ, mahante. Mahatā, mahantena, mahantehi, mahantebhi.
Mahato, mahantassa, mahantānaṃ, mahataṃ. Mahatā, mahantā, mahantasmā, mahantamhā, mahantehi, mahantebhi.
Mahato, mahantassa, mahantānaṃ, mahataṃ. Mahati, mahante.
*Mahanto*, *mahantamhi*, *mahantesu*. *Bho maha*, *bho mahā*, *bhavanto mahanto*—this is our preference.
Here, the masculine paradigm (*purisanaya*) is also applicable: *mahanto*, *mahantā*; *mahantaṃ*, *mahante*; *mahatena*.
Therefore, the vocative forms *bho mahanta* and *bhavanto mahantā* should be employed. When speaking in the neuter gender:
The method for the neuter gender is also applicable, as in: “mahantaṃ, mahantāni. When the feminine gender is to be expressed, the feminine method is also applicable, as in:
“mahatī, mahatī, mahatiyo; mahatiṃ, mahatī, mahatiyo; mahatiyā, mahatīhi, mahatībhī.
Examples of such phrases here include “mahatiyā ca yakkhasenāya,” and so forth. Furthermore, “mahantā... [is also used].
*mahantā*, *mahantāyo*. The form “*mahantā*” is also found as a feminine noun (*kaññānaya*), as seen in examples such as “*mahantā nidhikumbhiyo*” (great jars of treasure).

However, in the *Kaccāyana* grammar, the form “*mahantī*” is observed; since that is not well-established in the canonical texts (*pāḷiyaṃ*)—much like forms such as “*guṇavantī*” or “*kulavantī*” —it should be investigated.

[Objection: "But surely, sir, since such words as ‘gacchantī,’ ‘carantī,’ and so forth, as well as the word ‘iddhimantī,’ are found even in the Dispensation (sāsana), it must follow that there should also be forms such as ‘mahantī’ and ‘guṇavantī.
[Reply: It need not be so, because such a form should not be accepted on the basis of that particular grammatical method;
for we observe only the method of ‘mahatī,’ ‘guṇavatī,’ and so forth. Indeed, in the Pāḷi:
In the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), examples such as these are seen: “Just as if there were a great plowshare; there might be a woman who is beautiful, and she might be virtuous (*sīlavatī*).
She might be mindful (*satimatī*), possessed of vision (*cakkhumatī*), possessed of psychic power (*iddhimatī*), or possessed of attainment (*pattimatī*)”;
and “Having seen a great army, [Mandavya] said, ‘The army of Mahosadha is small; this army that is seen is exceedingly great’,” and so forth. But forms such as *mahantī* or *rūpavantī* are not seen.
However, some say: "The word *mahā* is not found in a compound; it is found only in a compound, as in the case of *mahāpuriso*.
This should not be accepted. For instance: "Great, O lay follower, is your renunciation!
Great indeed, venerable sir, is this earthquake! And the sound is vast and great! The sovereignty of Bārāṇasī is called great! The army appears great!"

Because it shows the usage. Thus it should be understood that [the forms] are also obtainable in the distributive sense (*byāse*); therefore: in the masculine gender, *mahaṃ*, *mahā*, *mahanto*, *mahantā*;
*bho mahanta*, *bhavanto mahantā*; in the neuter gender, *mahantaṃ*, *mahā*, *mahantāni*;
*bho mahanta*, *bhavanto mahantāni*; in the feminine gender, *mahantā*, *mahā*, *mahantā*, *mahantāyo*.
"Bhoti mahante, bhotiyo mahantā, mahantāyo"—in this way, everything should be applied in full for the feminine gender.

However, in compounds (*samāsa*), forms such as "mahāsatto" (Great Being), "mahāupāsako" (great lay follower), "mahāupāsikā" (great female lay follower), "mahabbalo" (of great strength), "mahāvanaṃ" (great forest), "mahaggataṃ" (lofty), "mahapphalaṃ" (of great fruit), and "mahabbhayaṃ" (of great fear) occur;
and in secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), [forms such as] "mahattano," "mahattaṃ," "mahantattaṃ," and "mahantatā" occur.

These are the forms for *rūpa*. Having stated the forms for the word *gacchant* as "gacchanto" and "gacchantā," the remaining forms should be understood by expanding them according to the method explained for the word *mahant*, including the series of nominal cases (*nāmikapadamālā*).

Likewise, the masculine paradigm for a person is "gacchanto, gacchantā," and the neuter paradigm for a mind (*citta*) is "gacchantaṃ, gacchantāni. Furthermore, [the feminine forms are] "gacchantī, gacchantī..."

The feminine forms, such as *gacchantiyo*, should also be understood. Thus, by way of the three genders, the nominal series for thousands of phrases—such as *caraṃ caranto carantaṃ carantī*, *dadaṃ dadanto dadantaṃ dadantī*, and so forth—should be expanded.
However, those teachers who [hold that] *gacchanto* and so on are the nominative and vocative plural, and [that] *gacchaṃ* and so on are...

They also maintain that there is a single form for the vocative case; however, since we have not observed such usage in the Teaching (Sāsana) and it should not be accepted on the basis of mere logic, we do not mention those points here. This distinction, however, is observed:
namely, that words such as "gacchaṃ vidhama" and so forth [are used] in the Sage’s Teaching.
In some instances they are verbal, while in others they are nominal:
“I shall go into his presence;
he will be my teacher.”
"O King, your son Vessantara is destroying your kingdom;
if you do not dig him out in the forest, the charioteer will practice unrighteousness."
Such applications as these should be understood by the wise here.
Regarding the words "I shall go" and "I shall dispel," and so forth,
the learned should explain their meaning according to various times and persons within the teaching of the Victor.

Regarding the nominative case, however, those who know the meaning should state the sense of words such as "gacchanto" (going) and "vidhamanto" (dispelling), as well as "gaccha" (go) and so forth. Now,
even though they share the same grammatical function (*samagatika*), there is a distinction between words such as "jānaṃ" (knowing) and "passaṃ" (seeing) according to their gender, case, and number.
That which is seen, we shall explain. For instance, in such passages as “knowing she said ‘I do not know’;

seeing she said ‘I do not see,’” it should be understood that there is a transformation of the words *jānaṃ* (knowing) and *passaṃ* (seeing) into *jānantī* (knowing [she]) and *passantī* (seeing [she]) by means of a change in gender.
By this same principle, the word *gacchaṃ* (going) may also, according to usage, become *gacchantī* (going [she]) when referring to a woman.
The meaning of the expression [“going”] is applicable to them because they share the same grammatical status (*samānagatika*);
however, the meaning of the expression “going” as applied to a woman—namely, “she who goes”—is not applicable to them because they do not share that same grammatical status.
This is the reason demonstrated in the passage: “Do you, venerable sirs, dwell knowing and seeing the world of absolute happiness? where [the terms] “knowing” and “seeing” [are used].
It should be understood that a transformation occurs by means of another grammatical form (*vacanantara*). By this, however, the reason is shown:

the plural sense of "those going" (*gacchantā*) is obtained for the word "going" (*gacchaṃ*) as well, according to its application, because it shares the same grammatical status (*samānagatika*) with them;
whereas the plural sense of "those going" (*gacchantā*) is not obtained for the word "going" (*gacchante*), because it does not share that same grammatical status with them.

It exists. This same method applies further on as well. In the phrase, "Parents support [their children], recollecting what was done in the past," there is a transformation of the word *anussaraṃ* by means of an alternative reading, *anussarantā*. In the phrase, "The true Dhamma is to be honored;
remember the teaching of the Buddhas," there is a transformation of the word *saraṃ* by means of an alternative case ending, *sarantaṃ*.
It occurs thus: “As one touching the stability of beings with the mind,” here there is also a transformation of the word *phusaṃ* by means of a change in case ending to *phusantassa*.
Likewise, in the phrase “one who does not give what is asked for becomes unloved,” there is also a transformation of the word *yācaṃ* by means of a change in case ending to *yācantassa*. They ask.
Or wealth may be requested; in this manner, the various types of transformation are to be understood.

Thus, there is the series of dissimilar words such as "bhavaṃkaraṃ" (making existence), etc., and the series of similar words such as "gacchaṃ" (going), "caraṃ" (wandering), etc., and in some cases, there is transformation according to gender, case, and number, such as "jānaṃ" (knowing), "passaṃ" (seeing), etc.; these three modes constitute the elucidation of the meaning of verbal roots.
This has been explained together with the excellent Word (Pāvacana) for the sake of listeners attaining a confident intellect regarding words and their meanings.
Indeed, with reference to all this, these verses were spoken:
"Bhavaṃ, karaṃ, arahaṃ, saṃ, mahaṃ"—these are the words.
Poisonous things arise, and one observes them as being distinct from one another.
For [terms such as] "going," "moving," "giving," "standing," "thinking," "cultivating," "speaking," "knowing," and "seeing" become identical [in their application].
In that regard, variations of "jānan" and so forth are seen through changes in gender, case, and number. Furthermore,
this is the base form (*pakati*) for all neuter nouns ending in a nasal stop (*niggahīta*), namely, in both genders and in the six [cases].
The shifting [of words] occurs by way of any one of the thirteen case-endings (vibhatti), genders (liṅga), or numbers (vacana).
Furthermore, this rule should be understood here:
"Gacchaṃ," "caraṃ," and so forth, may be incomplete utterances.
The phrases beginning with “gacchamāno caramāno,” as well as “mahaṃ bhave” and these [others],
may be either incomplete speech or complete speech, according to the sense.
“Arahant,” “he” (sa), and these [other terms]— when entirely liberated from [gender]—
the wise man should apply these three modes to the mind.
This is the definitive analysis of the nominal declension for the base forms of neuter nouns ending in a nasal consonant (*niggahīta*).
The section on the masculine gender ending in the vowel *ā* and having a final nasal (*niggahīta*) is completed.
Now, setting aside the views of former teachers as secondary, I shall explain the analysis of the nominal declension for the base form *dhanabhūti* and other similar nouns.
Masculine Nominative: *aggi*, *aggī*, *aggayo*. Masculine Accusative: *aggiṃ*, *aggī*, *aggayo*. Masculine Instrumental: *agginā*, *aggīhi*, *aggībhi*. Masculine Dative: *aggissa*, *aggino*.
*Aggīnaṃ*. *Agginā*, *aggīhi*, *aggībhi*. *Aggissa*, *aggino*, *aggīnaṃ*. *Aggismiṃ*, *aggimhi*, *aggīsu*.
"O *aggi*," "O *aggī*," "Venerable *aggayo*. This is the opinion of the Great Elder Yamaka.

Here, although the forms "from *aggi*" (*aggismā*) and "from *aggi*" (*aggimhā*) do not appear in the place of the ablative case, nevertheless they should be understood because similar usages are seen here and there. Furthermore, the sequence "by *aggi*" (*agginā*), "from *aggi*" (*aggismā*), and "from *aggi*" (*aggimhā*) should be known.
Dhanabhūti, dhanabhūtī, dhanabhūtayo. Dhanabhūtiṃ, dhanabhūtī, dhanabhūtayo. Dhanabhūtinā, dhanabhūtīhi, dhanabhūtībhi. Dhanabhūtissa, dhanabhūtino, dhanabhūtīnaṃ.
Dhanabhūtinā, dhanabhūtismā, dhanabhūtimhā, dhanabhūtīhi, dhanabhūtībhi. Dhanabhūtissa, dhanabhūtino.
[The forms] of Dhanabhūti: *dhanabhūtismiṃ*, *dhanabhūtimhi*, *dhanabhūtīsu*. "O Dhanabhūti," "O Dhanabhūtī," "O you, Dhanabhūtayas.
Siribhūti, Sotthibhūti, Suvatthibhūti, Aggini;
Fire, light, curd, water, sage, joint, sage, jewel;
disease, knot, sun, fist, poet, mountain, monkey, treasure;
belly, bladder, method, rice, heap of grain, snake, ink.
Sāti, kesi, kimi, bondi, bodhi, dīpi, pati, hari;
Ari, dhani, timi, kali, sārathi, udadhi, añjali;
Adhipati, narapati, asi, ñāti, nirūpadhi.
The compound *samādhi-jaladhiccādi* is considered to be like *dhanabhūti*.

Alternatively, since the Pāli text shows the word *adhipati* used in the locative case in the phrase "beings [who are] by way of dominance" (*adhipatiyā sattā*), the seventh-case form *adhipatiyā* should also be accepted here.
Furthermore, in the Pāli passage "those who perceive the essential in the unessential" (*asāre sāramatino*), it is derived from a compound word ending in the vowel *i*.

Because we observe the non-substitution of the *yova* suffix in certain instances, nominative and accusative case forms such as *adhipatino* and so forth must be accepted for compound words ending in *ikāra*, such as *adhipati*.
This is just as the nominative, accusative, dative, and genitive forms *daṇḍino* and so forth are accepted for words ending in *īkāra*, such as *daṇḍī*.
However, for compound words such as *gahapati*, *jani*, and *pati*, such nominative and accusative forms [ending in *-o*] do not occur.
The forms *gahapatayo* and *jānipatayo* should not be adopted [as vocatives], because they must be understood according to the specific wording of the text as they appear there.
However, in the case of the words *isi* and *muni* when used in an address, alternative forms such as *ise* and *muse* should also be accepted, as seen in the instances:
"A son has been born to you, O *ise*; accept him, O Great *Mune*."

Regarding the terms *aggi* and *gini* used by us here, some say: "The term *aggini* is found only in the nominative singular, and not in the nominative plural, nor in the accusative and other cases. Others, however, say:
"The word *aggini* does not exist in the Canon; there is only the word *gini*. Still others say: "The word *gini* does not exist; there is only the word *aggini*."

They say this. All of this is untenable because the words *aggi* and *gini* are found [together], and because it is shown that they must be applied to both numbers in all case-endings. For instance, in the *Kokālika-sutta* of the *Sutta-nipāta*:
"Indeed, those who speak do not speak what is charming..."
They do not find protection nor do they reach refuge;
they lie upon glowing embers,
entering a blazing fire.
In this passage, the accusative case "agginiṃ" is seen. Therefore, the commentator said:
"‘Agniṃ sampajjalitaṃ’ means a fire that is ablaze all around, burning intensely in every direction. And in that very place, in the *Kokālika-sutta* of the *Sutta-nipāta*:
"Then [he saw] an iron cauldron..."
They enter into what is ablaze with fire;
for they are roasted within them for a long time,
as they float upon those things that are like fire.
In this passage, because it falls within the scope of a compound (*samāsa*), the meaning "blazing with fires" (*aggini-sañjalita*) is obtained as "blazing by means of fires" (*agginīhi sañjalita*);
