From the point of view of the Pāli [grammar]: however, for words such as *amma*, one should speak according to the paradigm of *kaññā* (e.g., *ammā, ammā, ammāyo*), and at the end [of the declension], it should be applied as follows:
*bhoti amma, bhoti ammā, bhotiyo ammā, ammāyo*.
[The forms are: *mātā, mātā, mātaro*; *mātaraṃ, mātaro*; *mātarā, mātuyā, matyā, mātūhi, mātūbhi*; *mātu*.
Genitive: *mātuyā*, *matyā*, *mātarānaṃ*, *mātānaṃ*, *mātūnaṃ*. Instrumental: *mātārā*, *mātuyā*, *matyā*, *mātūhi*, *mātūbhi*. Ablative:
*mātu*, *mātuyā*, *matyā*, *mātarānaṃ*, *mātānaṃ*, *mātūnaṃ*. Locative: *mātari*, *mātuyā*, *matyā*, *mātuyaṃ*, *matyaṃ*, *mātūsu*.
Vocative: *bho mātā*, *bhotiyo mātā*, *mātaro*.

In this context, however, because in the canonical text (pāḷi) feminine forms ending in *sakāra*—such as *ehi*, *ebhi*, *esuka*, and so forth—as well as those ending in *enanta* and so on, are not seen, therefore even though they have been mentioned by some, such forms as "mātussa mātarehi" and so forth have not been stated;
this same principle applies to the others as well. "Whatever merit has been performed by you, by me, and by my mother, [with that] permitted..."

However, from the perspective of the canonical text (*pāḷi*) stating "by me" (*mayā*), the forms "of the mother" (*mātuyā*) and "by me" (*matyā*) are used in place of the instrumental, ablative, genitive, and locative cases because those words share the same grammatical behavior (*samānagatika*) in the feminine gender.
For instance, in the *Ummādanti-jātaka*, the word "by me" (*matyā*) occurs as both the fifth (ablative) and third (instrumental) case singular; whereas the word "khattiyā" [occurs similarly].
By way of the elision of the medial *s*, it becomes “khatyā”; likewise, the forms “mātuyā” and “mātuyā” become “matyā” and “matya. This rule does not apply to words such as “dhītā.
Nominative: dhītā, dhītā, dhītaro. Accusative: dhītaṃ, dhītaraṃ, dhītaro. Instrumental: dhītu, dhītūhi, dhītūbhi. Ablative: dhītu...
Dhītuyā, dhītarānaṃ, dhītānaṃ, dhītūnaṃ. Dhītarā, dhītuyā, dhītūhi, dhītūbhi.
Dhītu, dhītuyā, dhītarānaṃ, dhītānaṃ, dhītūnaṃ. Dhītari, dhītuyā, dhītuyaṃ, dhītūsu.
Bhoti dhītu, bhoti dhītā, bhotiyo dhītā, dhītaro. Herein, however:
“Even while giving away Jāli, my daughter clad in black antelope skin, and Queen Maddi, my devoted wife, I did not worry, solely for the sake of enlightenment.
Because the word “daughter” (*dhītā*) appears in the Pāli text in the accusative case, it is stated here as “*dhītaṃ*” in the place of the accusative; therefore, this is the essential meaning.

It should be accepted; likewise, because the compound word "assamaṇī hoti asakyadhītarā" is seen in the Pāḷi, a compound word such as "seṭṭhidhītarā," which resembles the third-person singular form, must also be accepted even though it is in the nominative singular.
Furthermore, in the *Niruttipiṭaka*, the two words "mātā" and "dhītā" are included within the section on etymological derivation (*saddhānaya*).
Just as we do not see the forms "mātāyā" and so forth in the Pāḷi texts and elsewhere when analyzed—as we do with the word "saddhāyā"—it was therefore taken separately;
for we see such a grammatical form only in the compound state, as in "rājamātāya," "rājadhītāya," and "seṭṭhidhītāya.
Thus, the rule for feminine nouns (*kaññānaya*) is also applicable in part; likewise [we find]: "Acchariyaṃ nandamāte, abbhutaṃ nandamāte."
Since the word "nandamāte" is seen in the Pāli, forms such as "bhoti rājamāte" (O Queen Mother) and "bhoti rājadhīte" (O Princess) are also obtainable;
therein, "nandamātā" means the mother of Nanda, and "bhoti nandamāte" is its vocative form.
Such a grammatical derivation occurs precisely when there is a compound (samāsa). Therefore, when it is a compound word, [the suffixes apply] to these original forms: *mātu*, *dhītu*, and *duhitu*.
Two portions are to be grasped: first, the portion of matter already shown, and second, the portion of matter according to the method of the maiden (*kaññānaya*).
Words such as *nattā* (granddaughter) and so forth are not exclusively masculine; rather, they are also feminine. For instance:
“Visākhā’s granddaughter has died”; “Four mice have made a burrow, but have not lived there,” and so on.
The grammatical applications are seen in the Teaching as follows:
Nominative: *nattā*, *nattā*, *nattāro* Accusative: *nattaṃ*, *nattāraṃ*, *nattāro* Instrumental:
*nattārā*, *nattuyā*, *nattūhi*, *nattūbhi* Genitive: *nattu*, *nattuyā*, *nattārānaṃ*, *nattānaṃ*, *nattūnaṃ* Ablative: *nattārā*, *nattuyā*, *nattūhi*, *nattūbhi*
Nattu, nattuyā, nattārānaṃ, nattānaṃ, nattūnaṃ. Nattari, nattuyā, nattuyaṃ, nattūsu.
Bhoti natta, bhoti nattā, bhotiyo nattā, nattāro.

Likewise, in cases such as "kattā" (doer), "vasitā" (dweller), and "bhāsitā" (speaker), when they function as members of a compound, forms such as "rājanattāya" and "rājanatte" arise, just like "rājamātāya" and "nandamāte."
This is the section on nouns ending in long *ā* and *ū*, concerning feminine gender, which analyzes the nominal declension of their basic forms.
The section on feminine gender ending in long *ā* and *ū*,
based on those basic forms, is completed.
Now, having placed the tradition of the ancient teachers at the forefront, we shall explain the nominal declension of words such as *bhūmi* (earth), beginning with *ratti* (night):
Nominative: *ratti*, *rattī*, *rattiyo*. Accusative: *rattiṃ*, *rattī*, *rattiyo*. Instrumental: *rattiyā*, *rattīhi*, *rattībhi*.
Genitive: *rattiyā*, *rattīnaṃ*. Dative: *rattiyā*, *rattīhi*, *rattībhi*. Ablative: *rattiyā*, *rattīnaṃ*. Locative: *rattiyā*, *rattiyaṃ*, *rattīsu*.
*Bhoti*, *bhotiyo*, *rattiyo*. This is the opinion of the Great Elder Yamaka.
“*Bhūmi*, *bhūmī*, *bhūmiyo*; *bhūmiṃ*, *bhūmī*, *bhūmiyo*”—all [forms] should be understood in this way.
Likewise, *bhūti*, *satti*, *patti*, *vutti*, *mutti*, *kitti*, *khanti*, *titti*, *siddhi*, *iddhi*, *vuddhi*, *suddhi*, *buddhi*, *bodhi*, *pīti* [are to be declined similarly].
The series of nominal forms (*nāmikapadamālā*) for *nandi*, *mati*, *asani*, *vasani*, *sati*, *gati*, *vuḍḍhi*, *yuvati*, *aṅguli*, *bondi*, *diṭṭhi*, *tuṭṭhi*, and *nābhi* should also be applied.
Furthermore: "The nights pass not in vain; they who take the offering by day and by night.
Not four fingers' breadth from the ground does he lie, nor does he groan upon the ground. Upon the ground he [sees] what has fallen... [and so forth].
"A girdle he fastens around his neck; these navels, adorned with a hundred spokes, shine like lightning, radiant and beautiful.
From the observation of such applications as these, this particular series of nominal forms for the words *nābhi* (navel) and *ratti* (night) should be understood.
How so? *Ratti*, *rattī*, *rattiyo*, *ratyo*. *Rattiṃ*, *rattī*, *rattiyo*, *ratyo*. *Rattiyā*, *ratyā*, *rattīhi*.
*Rattīhi*, *rattībhi*. *Rattiyā*, *ratyā*, *rattīnaṃ*. *Rattiyā*, *ratyā*, *rattīhi*, *rattībhi*. *Rattiyā*, *ratyā*, *rattīnaṃ*.
*Rattiyā*, *ratyā*, *rattiyaṃ*, *ratyaṃ*, *ratto*, *rattīsu*. *Bhoti ratti*, *bhotiyo rattī*, *rattiyo*, *ratyo*.
Here, excluding the form *ratto*, everything else—such as *bhūmi*, *bhūmī*, *bhūmiyo*, *bhūmyo*—should be understood accordingly.
Nābhi, nābhī, nābhiyo, nabhyo. Nābhiṃ, nābhī, nābhiyo, nabhyo. Nābhiyā, nabhyā, nābhīhi, nābhībhi. Nābhiyā, nabhyā, nābhīnaṃ. Nābhiyā, nabhyā, nābhīhi, nābhībhi.
Nābhiyā, nabhyā, nābhīnaṃ. Nābhiyā, nabhyā, nābhiyaṃ, nabhyaṃ, nābhīsu. Bhoti nābhi, bhotiyo.
nābhī, nābhiyo, nabhyo.
Bodhi, bodhī, bodhiyo, bojjho. Bodhiṃ, bodhiyaṃ, bojjhaṃ, bodhī, bodhiyo, bojjho.
Bodhiyā, bojjhā, bodhīhi, bodhībhi. Bodhiyā, bojjhā, bodhīnaṃ. Bodhiyā, bojjhā, bodhīhi.
Bodhibhi. Bodhiyā, bojjhā, bodhīnaṃ. Bodhiyā, bojjhā, bodhiyaṃ, bojjhaṃ, bodhīsu.
Bhoti bodhi, bhotiyo bodhī, bodhiyo, bojjho.

Here, however, because various forms of the scriptural tradition (pāḷi) are seen—such as “bujjhassu jina bodhiyaṃ” and “aññatra bojjhā tapasā”—this declensional paradigm (nāmikapadamālā) is stated according to various methods (vicitranaya). This entire method should also be applied appropriately elsewhere.
This is the section on the declensional paradigm of nouns ending in the vowel *i* that are feminine by nature.
The section on feminine nouns whose natural form ends in the vowel *i* is completed.
Now, having placed the tradition of the ancient teachers at the forefront, we shall explain the nominal declension of the word *bhūrī* and others:
Itthī, itthī, itthiyo. Itthiṃ, itthī, itthiyo. Itthiyā, itthīhi, itthībhi. Itthiyā, itthīnaṃ.
Itthiyā, itthīhi, itthībhi. Itthiyā, itthīnaṃ. Itthiyā, itthiyaṃ, itthīsu.
*Bhoti*, *itthi*; *bhotiyo*, *itthiyo*. This is the opinion of the Great Elder Yamaka:
“*Bhūrī*, *bhūrī*, *bhūriyo*; *bhūriṃ*, *bhūrī*, *bhūriyo*”—this is the same as for the feminine.
In this manner, the nominal paradigm (*nāmikapadamālā*) should be applied to other words ending in long *ī*, such as *bhūtī*, *bhotī*, and *vibhāvinī*, which are derived from the verbal root *bhū*.
Here are other words ending in long *ī*:
“Mātulānī and bhaginī, bhikkhunī, sāmugī, ajī;
vāpī, pokkharaṇī, devī, nāgī, yakkhinī, rājinī.”
Indeed, there are applications such as "the maidservant," "the Brahmin woman," "one of confused mindfulness," "one who walks quickly," and "the Sakyan woman.
In that regard, the application of terms such as "lotus pond," "maidservant," and "Brahmin woman" follows the same pattern.
In other instances, it may be otherwise in the *Gāthācuṇṇiya* according to the requirements—as is especially the case with verses such as "Kusāvatī.
In those verses, the forms appear differently; one should speak of them in the singular.
One should state "Kāsī, Avantī," and so forth, using the plural number;
"Candavatī," and so forth, according to the requirements of the application.
For it is said: "Well-laid-out lotus ponds. And seven hundred wives, and seven hundred female slaves. [And] children..."
And I shall go, O Brahmin, to the attendants of the Brāhmaṇī. Rivers flow. On the bank of the river Nerañjarā, there is the dwelling place of Lakṣī.
In Bārāṇasī, O Great King, dwells the king of crows, surrounded by eighty thousand well-winged followers.

Based on the observation of such canonical passages as “Rājā yathā Vessavaṇo Naḷinjan,” the nominal declensions for words such as *pokkharaṇī* (lotus pond) should be applied with their specific distinctions. How so?
Having stated them as follows: “*Pokkharaṇī*, *pokkharaṇī*, *pokkharaṇiyo*, *pokkharañño*, *pokkharaṇin*” and so forth.
In the place of the instrumental case (karaṇa), the dative-locative (nissakka), and the genitive (sāmivacana), the singular forms “pokkharaṇiyā” and “pokkharaññā” should be used.
In the place of the locative case (bhummavacana), however, the singular forms “pokkharaṇiyā,” “pokkharaññā,” “pokkharaṇiyaṃ,” and “pokkharaññaṃ” should be used.
In all instances, the words must be made complete. Likewise, “dāsī,”...
Having stated "dāsī, dāsiyo, dāsyō; dāsiṃ, dāsiyaṃ, dāsī, dāsiyo, dāsyō," one should state the singular forms as "dāsiyā, dāsyā" in the places of the instrumental case and so forth.
However, in the place of the locative case, the singular forms "dāsiyā, dāsyā, dāsiyaṃ, dāsyaṃ" should be stated. In all instances, the word-forms must be made complete.
In this context, however, because we see such usages as “*yaṭṭhiyā paṭikoṭeti, ghare jātaṃva dāsiyaṃ.
Phusissāmi vimuttiyan*,” the word *aṃ* is stated as *dāsiyaṃ* by way of its substitution with *yam*.
And among those, in the phrase “*ghare jātaṃva dāsiyaṃ*,” another grammatical method (*saddanaya*) is also obtainable through the substitution of *yam* for the word *aṃ*. How so?
Just as one who is young is called "dahariyā," so too a female slave is called "dāsiyā.
In this context, however, the canonical texts provide the illustrations: "I see you, a young girl, beautiful to behold" and "those who gave her to the old man while she was still so very young";
here, the form "dāsiyaṃ" is used because of the requirement for the accusative case.
In this intended sense, however, the nominal paradigm follows the pattern of *kaññā* exactly, as in the case of the word *kumāriyā*: "dāsiyā, dāsiyā, dāsiyāyo; dāsiyaṃ, dāsiyā, dāsiyāyo; dāsiyāyā.
Likewise, the Pāli text is seen as "kumāriye upaseniye. Similarly: "pupphavatiyā, pupphavatiyaṃ, pupphavatiyāya, pupphavatiyāyaṃ," and so forth.
The nominal paradigm occurs according to the singular number based on the word *kaññā* (maiden) as in the phrase *bhoti pupphavatiyā*.
Here, the canonical text and the reading of the commentary serve as illustrations: “In the past, this Bārāṇasī was named Pupphavatī;
there was a king of cruel deeds, a sole monarch in Pupphavatī”; and “Depart from the east of Pupphavatī.”
Another method: In cases such as *dāsiyā*, *dahariyā*, and *kumāriyā*, the substitution of *ya* for the letter *ka* should also be observed.

Regarding the word *brāhmaṇī*, however, after stating the forms *brāhmaṇī*, *brāhmaṇī*, *brāhmaṇiyo*, *brāhmaṇyo*, and *brāhmaṇim*, etc., the singular instrumental forms *brāhmaṇiyā* and *brāhmaṇyā* should be employed in places where the instrumental case is required, and so on throughout all instances.

And the case-forms (padāni) must be made complete. Having stated the word *nadī* as “nadī, nadī, nadiyo, najjo, nadi,” and so forth, one must also state “nadiyā, najjā” and “nadiyaṃ, najjaṃ,” and in all instances the case-forms must be made complete.
For in the feminine gender, once the plural nominative has been seen, the plural accusative follows.
Even when [a case ending] has not yet arrived, it is indeed seen; likewise, when the plural of the instrumental is seen, the plural of the nominative is also seen even if it has not yet arrived.
Similarly, among the plural endings of the instrumental, dative, ablative, genitive, and locative, when one is seen, the others are also seen.
For instance, in the phrase: "dāsā ca dāsyo anujīvino cā" (slaves, slave-girls, and dependents).
When the plural form "dāsyo" (female slaves) is seen as the nominative case, another instance of "dāsyo" is also seen as the accusative plural because of its similarity to it.
"If Sakka were to grant me a boon, and that boon were granted to me:
for one night or two nights, may I become a ferryman."
Regarding the phrase, "Having sported with Ummādantī, Sivirāja might then [be]," here,
when the instrumental case (*karaṇavacana*) "with Ummādantī" is seen, the corresponding cases— the dative, ablative, genitive, and locative— are likewise seen.
In the phrase "among the attendants of the Brahmin woman," when the genitive case (*sāmivacana*) "of the Brahmin woman" is seen...
Expressions similar to those [of the locative]— namely, the instrumental, the abstract noun (*sampadāna*), the ablative (*nissakka*), and the genitive (*bhummavacana*)— are indeed seen as well.
In the cases of “*seti bhūmyā anutthunam*” and “*pathabyā cārupubbaṅgī*,” where the singular locative forms *bhūmyā* and *pathabyā* are seen,
expressions similar to them— the instrumental, the abstract noun, the ablative, and the genitive— are likewise seen.

[They] exist. Regarding the phrase "In Bārāṇasī, O Great King," since the locative form "Bārāṇasyām" is seen here, other similar locative forms such as "brāhmaṇyam," "ekādaśyām," and "pañcamyām" are likewise seen.
And ancient masters also employ such forms by way of composing verses. Furthermore, in the Dispensation (Sāsana), such forms appear for the most part in the verses.
Kusāvatī. Kusāvatiṃ. Kusāvatyā, kusāvatyā. Kusāvatiyaṃ, kusāvatyaṃ.
O Kusāvatī! Bārāṇasī. Bārāṇasiṃ. Bārāṇasiyā, bārāṇasyā. Bārāṇasiyaṃ, bārāṇasyaṃ, and also bārāṇassaṃ.
O Bārāṇasī! Naḷinī. Naḷiniṃ. Naḷiniyā, naḷiññā. Naḷiniyaṃ, naḷiññaṃ. O Naḷinī! Other [feminine stems] should also be applied accordingly.
But when reaching the scope of verses (*gāthā*), even forms such as "in Kusāvatī," "in Bārāṇasī," and "in Naḷinī" should be employed.
For indeed, in the Canon (*pāḷi*), forms ending in *-mhi* such as "Kusāvatimhi" and so forth appear only in verses, not in prose compositions (*cuṇṇiyapadaracanā*).
However, in metrical syllables (*akkharasamaya*), such forms are not prohibited, as in "nadimhā."

This is because of the observation [of the text] beginning with “and so forth. However, as for the feminine forms such as “in right view” (*sammādiṭṭhimhi*) that appear in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) and in the *cuṇṇiyapadaracanā*, they should be understood as stated by way of a transposition of syllables (*akkharavipallāsa*).

This is because, in the place of the *cuṇṇiyapada*, one sees [the masculine forms] such as “in right view,” “in rebirth-linking,” “in a happy destination,” and “in an unhappy destination. Now, here [is the summary]:
In the rule regarding the *sugata-sāsana* (the teaching of the Well-Gone One), specifically in the section on the analysis of words (*cuṇṇiya-padaṭṭhāna*),
it is stated that in the case of feminine nouns ending in the five suffixes— namely *kaññā*, *ratti*, *itthī*, *yāgu*, and *vadhū*— the forms *nā*, *smā*, *smiṃ*, *mhā*,
and *mhi* do not undergo substitution with those [feminine] stems. However, the form *mhi* does undergo such substitution with feminine stems ending in the vowel *i*.
It goes. Regarding this, it is said:

"In this verse, both in the *cuṇṇī* commentary and in the original text itself, the feminine suffix *-ī* does not follow immediately after a word ending in the vowel *ā*, nor after one ending in a consonant."
Furthermore, regarding the word *mhi* in this verse,
when combined with feminine bases ending in *i* or *u*, its subsequent position [before the suffix] occurs in actual usage.
Just as, for example, a male is never found within the womb of a crane.
“In the city of Kusāvatī, there was a king, a lord of the earth.
Thus, words such as *kusāvatī* and others vary; however, because they are names of cities, they take the singular number, and unlike names of provinces (*janapada*), they do not take the plural.
For example: *kāsī*, *kāsiyo*; *kāsīhi*, *kāsībhi*; *kāsīnaṃ*; *kāsīsu*; *bhotiyo kāsiyo*.
In this way, a series of nominal forms should also be constructed for "Avantī," "Avantīyo," and so forth. Other words should also be taken [as examples].
Likewise, because they are names of countries, terms such as "Kāsī" and others are used only in the plural by conventional usage (*rūḷhi*), even though the referent is singular.
For example: *Candavatī*, *candavatiṃ*, *candavatiyā*, *candavatiyaṃ*, "O Candavatī"—thus it is according to the singular number.

Or, *candavatīyo*, *candavatiyo*, *candavatīhi*, *candavatībhi*, *candavatīnaṃ*, *candavatīsu*, *bhotiyo candavatiyo*—thus the nominal paradigm should be understood according to the plural number; other words should also be applied accordingly.
For terms such as *candavatī* and so forth constitute the designation for one or many women.
They should be applied according to the usage, either in the singular number or in the plural number. This same method applies elsewhere as well.
This concludes the analysis of the noun declension series for the base form of feminine nouns ending in the vowel *ī*.
The section on feminine nouns whose base form ends in *ī* is finished.

Now, because words ending in *u* with the feminine gender derived from the earth element (*bhūdhātu*) are not well-known, we shall complete the paradigm of noun forms using another word ending in *u* with the feminine gender:
*yāgu*. Nominative: *yāgu*, *yāgū*, *yāguyo*. Accusative: *yāguṃ*, *yāgū*, *yāguyo*. Instrumental:

*yāguyā*, *yāgūhi*, *yāgūbhi*. Dative: *yāguyā*, *yāgūnaṃ*. Ablative: *yāguyā*, *yāgūhi*, *yāgūbhi*. Genitive: *yāguyā*, *yāgūnaṃ*. Locative: *yāguyā*, *yāguyaṃ*, *yāgūsu*. Vocative: *bho yāgu*, *bhotiyo yāgū*, *yāguyo*.

In this way, there are forms such as *dhātu*, *dhenu*, *kāsu*, *daddu*, *kaṇḍu*, *kacchu*, and *rajjū*. Among these, the word *dhātu*—when signifying the bodily constituents known as chyle, blood, flesh, fat, sinews, bones, marrow, and semen—is masculine;
however, when signifying intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), the physical relics of the Sugatas and so forth, the world-system (*lokadhātu*), or the eye and other sense faculties, it is feminine.
Furthermore, when signifying the roots *bhū*, *hū*, *karapac*, and so on, it is both feminine and masculine. Here, however, the feminine form is intended.
This is the section on nouns ending in the vowel *u* among feminine gender terms;
the analysis of the noun paradigm for feminine stems ending in *u* is completed.
Now, having placed the doctrine of the ancient masters at the forefront, we shall explain the noun paradigm for words beginning with *bhū*.
Jambū, jambū, jambuyo. Jambuṃ, jambū, jambuyo. Jambuyā, jambūhi, jambūbhi. Jambuyā, jambūnaṃ.
Jambuyā, jambūhi, jambūbhi. Jambuyā, jambūnaṃ. Jambuyā, jambuyaṃ, jambūsu.
Bhoti jambu, bhotiyo jambū, jambuyo. This is the opinion of the Great Elder Yamaka.
In this context, the feminine gender of the word *jambū* is well-established through such examples as “the mango trees, the sal trees, and the *jambū*s.
However, in the phrase “these are those *jambuka* trees,” it should be understood that the masculine designation “*jambukā*” is employed in view of the word “trees” (*rukkha*).
For indeed, they are called “*jambuka*” because they are to be spoken of as *jambū*. The verbal root is *ke-re-ge-sadda*.
Alternatively, by way of the feminine gender, *jambū* itself is *jambukā*; and since they are both *jambukā* and trees (*rukkhā*), they are called *jambukārukkhā*.

This is like the case of Laṅkādīpa. Or, in the masculine gender, although one should say "jambukarukkhā" according to the rules of compound formation, it is stated as "jambukārukkhā" with a long vowel for the sake of preserving the meter because it falls within the scope of a verse, just as in the expression "kañci saraṇāgamane."

*Bhū*, *bhū*, *bhuyo*. *Bhuṃ*, *bhū*, *bhuyo*. *Bhuyā*, *bhūhi*, *bhūbhi*. *Bhuyā*, *bhūnaṃ*. *Bhuyā*, *bhūhi*, *bhūbhi*. *Bhuyā*, *bhūnaṃ*. *Bhuyā*, *bhuyaṃ*, *bhūsu*. *Bhoti* becomes *bhu*, *bhotiyo* becomes *bhū*, *bhuyo*.

In the same way, they should be applied starting with “*Abhū*, *abhū*, *abhuyo*; *abhuṃ*, *abhū*, *abhuyo*; *abhuyā*” and so forth. Here, the illustrative verse is: “*Abhuṃ me kathaṃ nu bhaṇasi, pāpakaṃ vata bhāsasī*” (Why do you speak thus to me?
You speak indeed an evil word). Also: “*Vadhū ca sarabhū ceva, sarabū sutanū camū*.”
“Vāmūrū, nāganāsūrū,” and so forth, are equal to *jambū*.
However, this subtle point must be carefully attended to: “vadaññū, vadaññū, vadaññuyo; vadaññuṃ, vadaññū, vadaññuyo;
vadaññuyā”—this should be applied in the same way as *jambū*. Likewise in cases such as “maggaññū, dhammaññū, kataññū,” and so on.
But surely, sir— it was said:
"Having gone from here, having obtained a human birth,
being generous and endowed with virtue, I shall perform much wholesome merit."
The masculine gender of words such as *vadaññū* is established by the observation of their usage in such forms;

this being so, why is the feminine declension shown here? Because words like *vadaññū* lack an absolute masculine gender and possess both genders, they take the gender of the word they refer to (*vācyaliṅga*). For instance:
“Having gone to the human state, being generous and free from stinginess,
I shall give gifts to the Saṅgha, heedful again and again”—
and also “The wrathful and the ungrateful”— many such passages employing the feminine gender are seen in the Canon; therefore, this principle has been established by us.
This is the section on noun declensions for the base form of feminine nouns ending in *ū*.
The section on feminine nouns ending in *ū*, according to their basic forms, is completed.
Nouns derived from the root *bhū* that end in *o* and belong to the feminine gender are not well-known; however, other feminine nouns ending in *o* are well-established.
One should understand that the word *go* is a feminine noun ending in the vowel *o*.
Some, however, say that its form is the same as that of the masculine word *go*;
for instance, some have stated the forms of the masculine word *go* according to the following method: "go, gāvo, gavo, gāvu," and so forth.

Just as they accept the forms of the word *go* (cow) as feminine gender, according to their view, because there is no distinction of form—just as there is no distinction of color among pieces of gold broken in the middle—the presentation of the word *go* as having a feminine gender is not capable of withstanding scrutiny. Why is that?
Because in the case of the word *mātugāma* (woman), [the forms] appear according to the method: "mātugāmo, mātugāmā, mātugāman" and so forth.
This statement appears to us as if it were saying, "Having made two word-sequences— one a word-sequence of the masculine gender and one a word-sequence of the feminine gender"—

and therefore it is not capable of withstanding critical examination. Furthermore, although the forms of the feminine word *go* are identical to the forms of the masculine word *go*, [the author] says:
How could the word *go* (cow) possess the feminine gender? Because of the absence of a specific formal characteristic (*rūpamālāvisesa*).

For instance, although the words *ratti* (night), *aggi* (fire), and *aṭṭhi* (bone) are identical in having the vowel *i*, a specific formal characteristic is observed that serves as the defining mark for the feminine, masculine, and neuter genders respectively.
However, this is not the case with the two words *dhātu* (element), which, though included within both the masculine and feminine genders, [lack such a distinguishing feature].

A distinction in the formal structure (rūpamālāviseso) is observed [in the case of the word *go* used as a noun], whereas such a distinction in the formal structure is not observed for the word *go* when used as a term denoting the feminine gender (*itthiliṅga*),

even though that was the intention of those teachers. However, just as there is a distinction in the formal structure between two words for "element" (*dhātu*) belonging to the masculine and feminine genders respectively,
or between two words for "cow" (*go*) belonging to the masculine and feminine genders respectively, by means of that distinction in the formal structure—
Just as a distinction in the sequence of forms (*rūpamālāviseso*) is observed between the two words *āyu* when they are included in the masculine and neuter genders,
so too there ought to be a distinction in the sequence of forms between the two words *go* when they are included in the masculine and feminine genders. If there were no such distinction,
how could their classification into masculine and feminine genders be established, and how could there be a usage characterized by clear or unclear forms?
It may be so. This matter is exceedingly subtle and refined, supremely profound, and a great thicket;

it is not possible for anyone who does not correctly understand the method of the natural language of Magadha—spoken by the Omniscient Jina and serving as the root language of all beings—to plunge into it or unravel it, unless they have accumulated the requisite knowledge. However, in our opinion, for two...

It should be understood that among words for "cow" (go), a specific variety of forms is seen, as well as the distinction between masculine and feminine genders, the usage of clear and unclear forms, and the usage of forms that are distinct from both [masculine and feminine] for the neuter gender.
Now, in order to clarify this meaning, we shall establish this rule in this place. For when it is thus:
Those who have entered the practice in the teaching of the scriptures (pariyatti-sāsana) will not grow weary because they are free from doubt.
Here, first of all, for the sake of generating skill in the comprehension of meaning among the wise, we shall explain three sets of noun declensions (nāmika-padamālā): namely, as follows?
Cow, cow, cows. Cow, cow, cows. Of the cow, by the cows, by the cows. Of the cow, of the cows.
Gāviyā, gāvīhi, gāvībhi. Gāviyā, gāvīnaṃ. Gāviyā, gāviyaṃ, gāvīsu. Bhoti gāvi, bhotiyo gāvī, gāviyo.

This is the nominal declension of the feminine noun *gāvī*, ending in long *ī* (ī-kāranta-itthiliṅga), which expresses the feminine gender and is derived from the word *go* by means of the suffix *ī*.
Go, gāvo, gavo. Gāvuṃ, gāvaṃ, gavaṃ, gāvo, gavo. Gāvena, gavena, gohi, gobhi. Gāvassa, ...
Genitive: *gavassa*, *gavaṃ*, *gunnaṃ*, *gonaṃ*. Ablative: *gāvā*, *gāvasmā*, *gāvamhā*, *gavā*, *gavasmā*, *gavamhā*, *gohi*, *gobhi*.
Genitive: *gāvassa*, *gavassa*, *gavaṃ*, *gunnaṃ*, *gonaṃ*. Locative: *gāve*, *gāvasmiṃ*, *gāvamhi*, *gave*, *gavasmiṃ*, *gavamhi*, *gāvesu*, *gavesu*, *gosu*.
Vocative: *bho go*, *bhavanto gāvo*, *gavo*.
This is the nominal paradigm (*nāmikapadamālā*) of the word *go*, which is masculine, ends in the vowel *o*, and denotes a male being.
Nominative: *go*, *gāvī*, *gāvo*, *gāvī*, *gavo*. Accusative: *gāvaṃ*, *gavaṃ*, *gāviṃ*, *gāvo*, *gāvī*, *gavo*. Instrumental: *gohi*, *gobhi*. Genitive:
*gavaṃ*, *gunnaṃ*, *gonaṃ*. Ablative: *gohi*, *gobhi*. Locative: *gavaṃ*, *gunnaṃ*, *gonaṃ*. Vocative: *gosu*. Vocative (plural): *bho ti go*, *bhotiyo gāvo*, *gāvī*.
*Gavo*. This is the nominal paradigm for the word *go*, which is a noun ending in long *o* (*okāranta*) expressing both the masculine and feminine genders.
Here, however, it should be understood that the form *gāvu* is not stated because it expresses exclusively the masculine gender;
its status as an exclusive masculine expression is known from the canonical text itself: "In this case, monks, a woman invited a monk who had entered the rains retreat, saying, 'Come..."
"Venerable sir, I will give you silver, or I will give you gold, or I will give you a field, or I will give you a site, or I will give you a bull, or I will give you a cow.
Or I will give you a male slave, or I will give you a female slave, or I will give you my daughter for the sake of a wife;
or I myself will become your wife, or another woman shall be your wife."
"Bring [her]," thus it is known from the direct recitation (āhacca-pāḷi).
For here, by the word "gāvu," the masculine is expressed; by the word "gāvi," the feminine.
As for the word "gāvī" which is stated four times in this paradigm of words ending in long vowels (okāra) in the feminine gender, that is the same as the word "kaññā."
It is capable of making known the state of being designated by an indistinct form for the feminine gender.
Indeed, among the other genders, there is not even a single word that occurs four times with identical phonetic form;
furthermore, we shall explain later how the words *gāvī* and *gāvi* function in certain places as common designations for both the feminine and the masculine. As for...

By means of the *panamha* [section], the paradigm (*padamālā*) for the feminine noun ending in long *o* has been constructed according to the method beginning with: "go, gāvī, gāvo, gāvī, gavo; gāvaṃ, gavaṃ, gāvi.
In that context, after the word *go*, the vowel *ī* is substituted for the nominative case endings (*si*, *yo*, *naṃ*), and the vowel *iṃ* is substituted for the accusative case ending (*aṃ*).
Thus, the forms "gāvī, gāvī, gāvi" are shown for the feminine noun ending in long *o*. For it is thus:

In the *Mukhamattadīpanī*, the teacher Vajirabuddhācariya, an expert in the science of grammar (*saddasattha*), has stated that according to the method of etymology (*niruttinaya*), the substitution of the vowel *ī* occurs for the *o* in the word *go*.

Just as the substitution of *ī* for *o* occurs in the word *go*, so too does the substitution of *ī* for *e* occur, as well as the substitution of *iṃ* for the syllable *aṃ*. To illustrate this method of grasping the underlying principle, here are these verses:
Even though [the forms] are established by virtue of the *īp* suffix in cases such as "gāvī,
gāvī" and so forth, where the feminine gender of the word *go* is expressed by the vowel *ī* at the end of the nominative singular and other case endings in the Jina’s dispensation;
It is not our view that the method has been given for the purpose of explaining *avisadatta*.
Furthermore, in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*),
after saying "cows" (*gāvo*), the word "cow" (*gāvim*) is used to indicate the feminine gender.
It is not our view that the method [of counting] has been given for the purpose of explaining the *Avisadatta* [Sutta];
for in the commentaries such as the *Samantapāsādikā*, it is said:

"A clever cowherd, having taken pebbles in his lap and holding a rope and staff in his hands, goes to the cattle-pen early in the morning, strikes the cows on their backs, and [stands] at the top of the crossbar."
In this passage, by stating "cows" (*gāvo*) and then using the word "cow" (*gāviṃ*)— referring to one sitting and counting each cow that arrives at the door by throwing pebbles and saying "one,
two"— the fact that the word *go*, which denotes both female and male, is a feminine noun ending in a long vowel (*okārantitthiliṅga*),
is shown to be used here in an indistinct form of expression. For by the word "cows" (*gāvo*), [both] females and males are referred to in a general sense.
The bull is included; likewise, by the word "gāvī," both the female and the male bull are included.

Thus, the words "gāvo" and "gāvī" have been grouped together by the masters of the Aṭṭhakathā, who are experts in the method of etymology (nirutti), within a single treatise and even within a single sentence, on the basis of their having the same grammatical gender (liṅga). For if [the word] were in the feminine gender...
In the paradigm of the word *go*, which is currently used to denote a female or male and ends in a long vowel as a feminine noun, the forms "gāvī" and "gāvi" would not be obtainable;

in the Aṭṭhakathā, having stated "gāvo," one should have said "gāvaṃ" instead, and "gāviṃ" should not have been stated. And just as by the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā [the form] "gāvo" [is established]...

Having stated a term that includes all cattle by way of both female and male, they again constructed the verbal expression "the cow (gāvi) has reached the gate, the cow has reached the gate" with reference to those very same cattle; therefore, this word "gāvi" also should be understood as a term inclusive of all.
If it is argued that this is not an inclusive term because only the female is to be understood by the word "gāvi"?
No, because a different meaning is understood through the context of the treatise (*pakaraṇa*).
For it is not possible to say of all excluded places that "only women live there, not men," or "only men live there, not women. Furthermore, the following canonical text (*pāḷi*) is seen:
"Even upon seeing a cow, they flee, thinking, 'It is a monk. Here too, by the mention of the word "cow" (*gāvī*), [the meaning is established].
It should be understood that the word *go* (cow) includes both the female and the male. Otherwise, one would fall into the position that "only the female cow is to be considered the *go-bhikkhu*.

Thus, according to the method of the Pāḷi, it is understood that when the feminine gender is present, the vowel *aṃ* of the suffix is replaced by *iṃ* after the word *go*, which denotes both female and male.
Vajirabuddhācariya, moreover, did not apply the suffix *īp* to the word *go*, but instead performed the substitution of the vowel *ī* for the final *o*.

His intention may have been this: if the suffix *īp* were applied to the word *go*, the resulting form "gāvī" would—by virtue of that suffix—denote only the feminine gender in whatever context it appeared, just like words such as "migī," "morī," and "kukkuṭī," and would never [denote the masculine].
It denotes both female and male; therefore, by way of an application conforming to the Teaching (sāsana), the substitution of *ī* for *yo* should be made.
Thus, according to the opinion of the teacher Vajirabuddha, it is understood that from the word *go*, there is the substitution of *ī* for *yo*.
Furthermore—because the teachers of the Commentaries [use] the method beginning with "having struck the cows on the back," and so forth...
In this composition of words ending with the statement, “Having thrown a pebble for each cow, he counts ‘one,
two’,” the method of connecting the meaning must be stated as “one cow, two cows,” and the accusative case-form “gāvim” is indeed seen.
Thus, according to the opinion of the Aṭṭhakathā masters, from the word *go*, there is the substitution of *si* for *o* and the substitution of *im* for the vowel *a* in the accusative case-ending.
It is known as "hoti. Therefore, the paradigmatic series of forms for the feminine noun *go*, which ends in a vowel (okāra) and follows the *apakatika* pattern—
established by us in the manner of "go, gāvī, gāvo, gāvī, gavo, gāvaṃ, gāvi," and so forth— is consistent with the method of the Pāḷi, consistent with the method of the Aṭṭhakathā,
and in accordance with the opinion of the teacher Kaccāyana, as well as that of the venerable [author] who produces the derivation of the words.

It conforms to our own view; furthermore, because the word *gāvī* occurs four times, it establishes that the word *go*, being a feminine noun ending in a vowel (*okāra*), is used here as an imprecise form (*avisadākāra*).
Thus, when the Pāli method and other criteria are correctly examined with wisdom, this [explanation] is highly appropriate;
there is not even the slightest fault herein. Now, regarding the cases of the direct object (*paccatta*), the accusative (*upayoga*), and the vocative (*ālapanā*)...
In the place of the plural, the word *gāviyo*; in the place of the singular for the instrumental, dative, ablative, and genitive, the word *gāviyā*;
in the place of the plural for the instrumental and ablative, the words *gāvīhi* and *gāvībhī*;
in the place of the plural for the dative and genitive, the word *gāvīnaṃ*; and in the place of the locative, the word *gāviyā*.

The words *gāviyaṃ* and *gāvīsū*—these sixteen words in detail—should be understood as not being explicitly mentioned because they are established exclusively by means of the suffix *-īp* and because they denote exclusively females.
However, this definitive conclusion is stated here for the sake of the listeners' freedom from doubt: for among the words denoting the feminine gender, "gāvī... [and so forth].
The forms *gāvī* and *gāvi* are established either by means of the suffix *īp* or by means of the substitution of the vowels *ī* and *i*.
Among these, the latter method is intended here, while the former method applies elsewhere.

Likewise, because *gāvī* and *gāvi* are established both by means of the suffix *īp* and by means of the substitution of the vowels *ī* and *i*, they predominantly denote the feminine. In some instances, [the two forms] exist at one and the same moment.
By way of encompassing all [forms], these are terms denoting both female and male. Among these, however, only the latter method is intended here;

the former method applies elsewhere. But as for the forms “gāviyo,” “gāviyā,” “gāvīhi,” “gāvībhi,” “gāvīnaṃ,” and “gāviyaṃ,” “gāvīsū,” since they are established solely by means of the suffix *ī*, they denote females exclusively in every respect.
Because they occur specifically by way of worldly convention (*lokasaṅketa*) only with respect to things that possess the female form (*itthibhūta*),
words such as "deer," "peahen," and "hen" occur exclusively with reference to the female form, just like those terms. Furthermore,

although feminine gender forms such as "river" (*nadī*) and "earth" (*mahī*) are established by means of the suffix *īp*, nevertheless, because their referents lack consciousness, they [do not apply] to the female form.
It is not appropriate to say that they "occur," for those meanings are devoid of the states of feminine, masculine, and neuter.
However, because the suffixes *en* and *esukāra* are not found following the word *go* when it bears a feminine gender, the forms *gāvena*, *gavena*, *gāvesu*, and *gavesū* have not been stated.

Furthermore, because the case endings *sasmiṃ* and *smiṃ* do not [apply] to the word *go* when it is in the feminine gender by virtue of its own form (*sarūpato*), [the forms *gosmā* and *gosmiṃ* are not used].
They do not undergo the substitution for the *paratta* (the following vowel), therefore the forms "gāvassa, gavassa, gāvasmā, gavasmā, gāvasmiṃ, gavasmiṃ" are not stated.

And because there, neither the substitution *ākāra* nor the substitution *mhākāra* for the *smā*-case ending is obtained, therefore the forms "gāvā, gavā, gāvamhā, gavamhā" are not stated. And because [there is no substitution] for the *smiṃ*-case ending...
The forms *ekāro* and *mhikāro* are not found; therefore, the word-forms *gāve*, *gave*, *gāvamhi*, and *gavamhi* have not been stated.

Furthermore, because they would be unsuitable to be joined with coreferential words such as *yāya* and *tāya*, the forms *gāvena*, *gavena*, and so forth, have not been stated in the place of the feminine gender.
For instance, [words like] *gāvena* and *gavena* cannot be used together with *yāya*, *tāya*, and so on.
They should not be applied here because they are exclusively masculine in form.

However, some might say here: "The paradigmatic series of words for the feminine noun *go* ending in *-o*, which was established by you in the manner of 'go, gāvī, gāvo, gāvī, gavo' and so forth, [is applicable] to the word *mātugāma* as 'itthī mātugāmā'..."

Is it not the case that [the word *itthi*] is similar to what was stated regarding "women"? No, that is not so. For the words *mātugāma* and *itthī* possess different genders by virtue of being masculine and feminine respectively, and they consist of different roots by virtue of the roots *gam* and *is*.
However, in this instance, the words *go* and *gāvī* possess the same gender by virtue of being feminine, and they consist of the same root by virtue of the root *gam*.
If this is so, then [the form] of the word *goṇa* [arises] by way of the substitution of the word *go*.

Is it because it is stated by Kaccāyana that, due to its being a substitute for that [word] and its having a single verbal root, the series of forms (*padamālā*) should be stated by mixing it with that [other word]?
No; because the word *goṇa* is exclusively masculine and belongs to the category of words ending in the vowel *a*.
For it is taught separately in the section on the masculine gender. This, however, is the series of forms beginning with "go, gāvī, gāvo, gāvī, gavo," and so forth.
One should not perceive these as words ending in *o* and *i* formed by mixing [the two]; rather,

they should be understood in their true essence as a paradigm of feminine nouns ending in *o*, because they possess word-forms stated through the substitution of *ī* and *īṃ* for the case endings *si* and *am* following the word *go* by way of alternative forms (*vikappa*).
Now we shall explain the scriptural passages and worldly applications that establish the feminine gender of the word *go* (cow):
"Just as, monks, in the last month of the rains, at the time of autumn when the fields are thick with grain, a cowherd might guard his cows;
he would drive those cows here and there, striking them with a staff."
“Those cows give food, they give strength, they give beauty, and they give happiness;
knowing this fact, they would not have killed those cows.
“He collects all the cows together. ‘The cows will go, venerable sir, longing for their calves,’ these are the words of the Sutta.”

Expressions such as “he went while the cows were being milked” are worldly applications. Thus, the feminine gender of the word *go* should be understood as having substantial reality (*sārato*), just like its masculine gender.
In that regard, although forms such as *go*, *gāvī*, *gāvo*, *gāvī*, and *gavo* are stated with a feminine gender, nevertheless—

Just as the words "people" (*pajā*) and "deities" (*devatā*) are used according to their application to denote both female and male, so too, when one says "that cow" (*sā go*) or "those cows" (*tā gāvo*) using the feminine gender, it should be understood that all cattle, whether female or male, are included.
For in such instances, the gender is not absolutely the primary factor; rather, the meaning alone is primary. As in the expression: "The bulls are milking the cows. (*vajegāvo duhantīti*)

When this is said, although the word "gāvo" can also apply to males, nevertheless, because the act of milking is impossible in the case of males, they are understood to be females by virtue of the meaning.

But when it is said, "The cows are being milked," what wise person would fall into doubt, since it is expressed according to both gender and meaning? When it is said, "Those cows are grazing," [it is so] by virtue of the feminine gender.
From the wording alone, someone might occasionally have a doubt, thinking, "Are these not women?

However, when it is stated with the masculine gender as in "those cows are grazing" (*te gāvo caranti*), there is no doubt; both females and males are understood because the masculine plural is used in some instances to include both female and male.
This is similar to expressions such as "Then here are lions and tigers," where one says "a cow is grazing" (*gāvī carati*).
And when it is said, "he sees a cow" (*gāvim passati*), a female is understood because the word *gāvī* is intended to denote a female.
For in both worldly usage and in technical (Sāsana) usage, the word *gāvī* is taken to mean a female.
However, with reference to certain technical usages, we stated that "*gāvī*" and "*gāvim*" are terms common to both male and female. Thus, for example: [the passage continues].
The Pāli text is seen as follows: “Bhikkhus, suppose a skilled butcher or a butcher’s apprentice, having slaughtered a cow and divided it into portions, were sitting at a crossroads.

And in the commentaries, having used the word “gāvo” (cows) as a gender-neutral expression for both female and male, they then refer back to that same [gender] for both female and male by saying, “each portion, each portion, is a ‘gāvī’ (cow).”
A well-composed arrangement is seen here.
For in this context, both a female and a male belonging to the bovine species are designated as "gāvī. Specifically, however, "gāvī" is a term for a female.
Thus, in various passages of the Pāḷi and elsewhere, [it is said]: "Not long after he had departed..."

Because of the usage seen in such expressions as: "A cow with a young calf fell upon the Blessed One Bāhiya Dārucīriya and took his life," and "I give you either a bull (*gāvuṃ*) or a cow (*gāviṃ*)," and "The grass-lion is like a dove-colored cow," it must be said that the word *itthī* (woman) is used here [to denote the female animal].
Furthermore, by means of the word *go* (cow), we have examples such as: *goduhanaṃ* (milking the cow), *gadduhanaṃ* (milking a she-goat), *gokhīraṃ* (cow’s milk), and *godhano* (a herd of cows).
Since it is seen that "those having the form of cows" refers to both females and males, it should be stated that [the word] applies to both.

Now, for the sake of generating proficiency in the wise, the method of meaning based on the Pāli system and other principles is stated regarding the paradigm (*padamālā*) of the feminine noun *go* ending in *-o*:

*Sā go gacchati*, *sā gāvī gacchati* (She, the cow, goes; she, the cow, goes). *Tā gāvo*, *gāvī*, *gavo gacchanti* (Those cows go; those cows go; those cows go). *Tam gāvam*, *gāvim* (That cow; that cow).
He sees cows: *tā gāvo* (those cows), *gāvī* (cows), *gavo passati* (he sees cows).

By those cows: *tāhi gohi*, *gobhi kataṃ* (done by them). To them, the cows: *tāsaṃ gavaṃ*, *gunnaṃ*, *gonaṃ deti* (he gives). From those cows: *tāhi gohi*, *gobhi apeti* (he goes away). Of them, the cows: *tāsaṃ gavaṃ*, *gunnaṃ*, *gonaṃ siṅgāni* (the horns).
In those cows: *tāsu gosu patiṭṭhitaṃ* (established). "O lady, you cow, stand! (*bhoti go tvaṃ tiṭṭha*). "O ladies, you cows" (*bhotiyo gāvo*). "By you, O cows, stand! (*gavā tumhe tiṭṭhatha*).
Another example is stated:
"That cow (*sā gā*) goes crossing the river; that cow (*sā gāvī*) goes crossing the river; those cows (*tā gāvo*), that cow (*gāvī*), those cows (*gavo*) go crossing the river.
He sees that cow (*taṃ gāvaṃ*), that cow (*gāviṃ*), that cow (*gavaṃ*) crossing the river; those cows (*tā gāvo*)."
She sees cows (*gāvī*) or bulls (*gavo*) crossing the river. [The action] was done by those cows (*tāhi gohi*, *gobhi*), while they were crossing the river.
She gives to them—the cows (*tāsaṃ gavaṃ*, *gunaṃ*, *gonaṃ*)—while they are crossing the river. She departs with them—the cows (*tāhi gohi*, *gobhi*)—while they are crossing the river.

for in the places of the nominative, accusative, and vocative cases, there are four forms of *gāvī* [in the feminine], just as there are four forms of the word *kaññā*.

Because it has been so stated. For indeed, a distinction between two words for "element" is seen by way of their masculine and feminine genders. How is that?

For indeed, discourse in a distinct form is the masculine gender; discourse in an indistinct form is the feminine gender; discourse in a form that transcends both is the neuter gender.
Now, having made this very point more evident, we shall explain it briefly:

Men stand; men have escaped; "O sirs, men, you go. Women stand; women see;

The usage of a distinct form is seen; the usage of an indistinct form for the feminine gender is seen. However, for the neuter gender, in the three cases of the nominative, accusative, and vocative—namely, *rūpaṃ*, *rūpāni*, *rūpā*;

It is seen that in the three instances of the masculine and feminine genders, forms accompanied by honorifics do not exist at all times;

And if gender were something existing in the ultimate sense, how could those [words] which are mutually contradictory [in gender] apply to a single referent?

There is a convergence [of these meanings]. Therefore, it should be understood that for any given meaning, a designation in an indistinct mode is the feminine gender (*itthiliṅga*), a designation in a distinct mode is the masculine gender (*pulliṅga*), and a designation in a mode free from both is the neuter gender (*napuṃsakaliṅga*).

In this context, however, the state of being designated in an indistinct mode and so forth should be understood solely by way of the literary compositions known as noun-inflection series (*nāmikapadamālā*).

Not by way of each individual word. For instance, in such cases as "a girl, a man, a mind" (*kaññā puriso cittaṃ*) or "girls, men, minds" (*kaññāyo purisā cittāni*), the state of being expressed with an indistinct form and so forth is not seen in each individual word.

However, since the state of being expressed with a distinct form and so forth is established by way of the continuous connection (*pabandha*), the state of being expressed with an indistinct form and so forth for each individual word is necessarily established as well, because [the individual words] are the components (*avayava*) of the whole (*samudāya*).

However, some, without adhering to the composition known as the *nāmikapadamālā* (the series of nominal forms), desire that even by means of individual words alone there be such designations as "indistinct form" (*avisadākāra*) and so forth.

They should be asked: "If the state of having 'indistinct form' and so on belonged to each individual word alone, then in the case of words such as ‘kaññā’ (maiden), ‘purisā’ (men), ‘satthā’ (teacher), ‘guṇavā’ (virtuous), and ‘rājā’ (king), [would they not appear] according to their respective forms and numbers—as in ‘puriso’ (man) and ‘satthāro’ (teachers)?"

"But since [in words] such as *kaññāyo* there is the occurrence of identical sounds (*samānasuti*) due to the hearing of the vowel *o*, and in [words] such as *cittaṃ purisaṃ kaññaṃ* there is the occurrence of identical sounds due to the hearing of the nasal *anusvāra*, how could they be designated as having an indistinct form?
Even if they were to say, "It may be so, but their difference is difficult to discern," they should be told: "Do not speak thus."
“Even Nibbāna, though extremely difficult to know, is known by relying on a person capable of explaining it; therefore, speak only after having investigated thoroughly.
Having said this, he should further question them regarding the following point:
“Of what grammatical gender are the words *bodhi* and *āyu*? Those who know will say: “The word *bodhi* is both feminine and masculine.”
Furthermore, the word *āyu* is both neuter and masculine; thus, these words possess two genders. They should be asked:

“If the word *bodhi* and the word *āyu* are words possessing two genders, then, this being the case, how can there be a designation of non-clarity (*avisadākāra*) regarding two instances of the word *bodhi* that are established as a single term and are absolutely identical in sound?”
"And how could there be a usage of both forms when two words for 'life-span' (*āyu*)—
which are established as a single compound and are identical in their phonetic form— are used in a manner that excludes one another, such that there is both a usage of both forms and a clear,
distinct usage? When addressed thus, those experts in grammar, seeing no further way out, will surely become speechless.
However, taking the method from the science of grammar (saddasattha), they say:
“That which is this,” “this is that,” and so forth— those meanings in which the world is established [are conventional].
“‘Feminine, masculine, and neuter’—these are the names that are so called.
It is said that their intention is as follows: “This is a man; this is a woman; this is a king; this is a female; this is a creeper.”

"This is neuter, this is mind"—in this way, regarding those meanings such as "male" and so forth for which the world has the established usage of "this (eso)," "this (esā)," or "this (etaṃ)," those names are called "masculine, feminine, and neuter genders. By means of that [principle], other [names] are also [to be understood].
Thus, by those who speak in this manner, names are [designated] in the form: "this (eso), this (esā), this (etaṃ)."
The distinction that "others receive names such as masculine and so forth" has not been shown here;
however, it has been shown by the etymologists (Neruttika) who know the method of the True Dhamma, in such passages as:

"The designation for any object whatsoever that expresses an indistinct form is the feminine gender," and so on. Yet some say: "The designation that expresses objects of indistinct forms is the feminine gender," and so forth. That [is incorrect].

It should not be accepted. For if conventional expression (*vohāra*) that denotes meanings of non-distinct forms were the feminine gender, then in that case, conventional expressions such as "woman," "wife," "thorn," and "bush" would also be feminine genders, because the meanings they denote are of non-distinct forms.
But if conventional expression that denotes meanings of distinct forms were the masculine gender, then in that case, [expressions such as] "deity" and "faith" [would be masculine].
Terms such as “ñāṇa” (knowledge) and so forth may also be masculine because their referents possess a clear form. Alternatively,
if a term denoting referents with an unclear form is feminine, whereas a term denoting referents with a clear form is masculine,
then this being the case, it would be impossible for a single referent to be expressed by two genders simultaneously.
“You are one who desires my welfare, O yakkha; you are a deity who desires my benefit.
I shall carry out those words of yours, for you are my teacher.
And if the grammatical expression denoting things that are free from both genders is the neuter gender, then, such being the case, regarding things free from both genders—
In the case of grass, trees, and so forth, because there is no fixed determination such as "this is [of this specific gender]," the gender and number might be contradictory.

Furthermore, by using neuter gender and number—as in "the jewel of wisdom" (*paññāratanaṃ*) or "the pair of disciples, Sāriputta and Moggallāna" (*sāvakayugan*)—it may be stated that even the referents of those terms possess a form that transcends both [genders].
Moreover, even a single bank is expressed as "taṭaṃ, taṭī, taṭo."

It should not be expressed by means of the three genders. Furthermore, even a single instance of knowledge—such as "wisdom (paññāṇaṃ), wisdom (paññā), understanding (pajānanā), non-delusion (amoho)," and so forth—should not be expressed by means of the three genders;
therefore, one should not adopt that method, but rather adopt the method exactly as stated.
For in the world, the lower body of women is sharp-witted (visada), while the upper body is not sharp-witted; the flesh of the chest is not sharp-witted.
Walking and so forth are also indistinct. For when women walk, they walk indistinctly;

when they stand, lie down, sit, eat, or consume food, they do so indistinctly. Indeed, even seeing a man indistinctly, people say, "She walks, stands, lies down, sits, eats, or consumes food like a woman. Thus, just as...

Women, for the most part, have an indistinct appearance; likewise, whatever designations there are for any object—whether animate or inanimate—that are for the most part indistinct in appearance, these alone are called feminine gender-terms (*itthiliṅga*).

For example: "young woman" (*kaññā*), "deity" (*devatā*), "girl" (*dhītalikā*), "dūbā grass," "faith" (*saddhā*), "night" (*ratti*), "woman" (*itthī*), "rice-gruel" (*yāgu*), "bride" (*vadhū*)—and so forth.
In men, however, the lower body is coarse, while the upper body is refined;
the flesh of the chest is refined, and even their movements such as walking are refined. For when men walk, they walk with refinement;
when standing, lying down, sitting, eating, or consuming food, they do so with refinement. In women, too, these movements such as walking are refined.
Seeing him performing [an action], they say, "He goes like a man," and so forth.

Thus, just as men are for the most part of clear form, so too, whatever conventional designations (vohārā) are for the most part of clear form regarding any object—whether conscious or unconscious—those alone are called masculine genders (pulliṅga). For example: "A man, a woman."
“Or else, water, a tree, delusion, a weapon”—such are these and others like them.

Furthermore, just as neuter nouns have forms that are free from both [masculine and feminine] genders, so too, whatever designations for any object—whether conscious or unconscious—are free from both genders, those alone are called neuter genders. For example: “consciousness, form, the women’s quarters, wife.”

"nāṭakaṃ," "ratanaṃ," "ñāṇaṃ," "aṭṭhi," "āyu"—these and others such as these. Thus, for all conventional designations (vohāra) that possess names, the characteristic of gender (liṅga-lakkhaṇa) is to be known from the series beginning with *syādi* (the declensional endings):
the forms are clear or unclear, and the form is free from both [masculine and feminine].
This point—this dense, great forest thicket that is difficult to penetrate—is shown by having been made free of thickets and free of tangles;

it should be attended to with great care. Thus, because the state of being feminine gender and so forth arises from the fact that all nominal words, by virtue of depending on their formal arrangement, possess a mode of expression that is non-distinctive and so on, [this applies] to both instances of the word *go* (cow) by virtue of their dependence on formal arrangement and their possession of a mode of expression that is non-distinctive and so on.
The specific feminine gender and so forth of each term should be understood accordingly.
This concludes the detailed analysis of the nominal paradigm for nouns ending in long *ī* that possess a feminine gender, including the determination of their meanings.
The section on feminine nouns ending in long *ī*, which constitutes the primary category of nouns ending in long *ī*, is finished.
Thus, in every respect, the six types of feminine nouns—ending in *ākāra*, *ivaṇṇa*, *uvaṇṇa*, and *okāra*—are included without exception.

Now, however, that distinction which is observed in some of these *ākāra*-ending and *īkāra*-ending nouns, arising from the substitution of *ekāra* for the singular locative case ending, will be stated. For instance:
“O Rādha, you do not understand that the night has not yet reached its midpoint;
you lament for what is imperishable, O Kosiya’s son who has turned away from passion.

In this Rādha Jātaka, although it should have been stated as *virattā* with a long vowel (*ākāra*) by way of the nominative case, it is expressed as *viratte* through the substitution of the diphthong *e* for the nominative ending.

It is said, “viratte. Likewise, although it should have been stated as “Kosiyāyanī” with the long vowel *ī*, it is stated as “Kosiyāyane” by means of the substitution of the long vowel *e* for the nominative singular ending. By this, the commentator of the Aṭṭhakathā explained the meaning as follows: “Viratte Kosiyāyane:
our mother, the Brahmin woman Kosiyāyanī, has become detached; she has become devoid of love toward our father.”
But surely, sir, since we see the nominative singular forms "viratte" and "kosiyāyane" in the Pāḷi, one ought to say that there exists a feminine gender ending in *e*?
It should not be so said, because those forms are specific instances included within the categories of words ending in *ā* and *ī*.
For, since they are established by way of substitution (*ādesa*), there is no such thing as a separate feminine gender ending in *e*; therefore—
The sixfold nature of feminine gender signs should be understood exactly as previously stated.
Thus, this *Padamālā* (Garland of Words), endowed with various methods,
has been analyzed by me for the sake of the Teaching of the Self-Existent One.
This *Saddanīti-sūriya* (Sun of Grammar),
a mass of rays consisting of numerous fine analyses,
dispels the darkness of doubt.
In whom does the lotus of the intellect not blossom?
Thus ends the *Saddanīti* treatise, composed for the sake of the proficiency of the wise in the modes of expression within the three Piṭakas together with their commentaries— these ninefold branches.
The eighth chapter: The analysis of the nominal paradigm for feminine gender.
9. The nominal paradigm for neuter gender.

Now, having placed the opinion of the ancient teachers at the forefront, we shall explain the paradigmatic declensional series (*nāmikapadamālā*) for neuter nouns with a final nasalized vowel (*niggahīta*), such as *bhūtaṃ* and others:
Cittaṃ, cittāni. Cittaṃ, cittāni. Cittena, cittehi, cittebhi.
Cittassa, cittānaṃ. Cittā, cittasmā, cittamhā, cittehi, cittebhi. Cittassa, cittānaṃ. Citte, cittasmiṃ.
In *cittamhi* and *cittesu*. [The forms] *bho citta*, *bho cittā*, and *bhavanto cittāni* are according to the opinion of the Great Elder Yamaka.

Here, although the nominative plural *cittā* and the accusative plural *citte* have not yet appeared, nevertheless, because such forms with a final nasalized neuter gender are seen in various places elsewhere, [they are accepted].
Furthermore, it must be accepted because it is shown in the *Vibhaṅga-pāḷi* in such passages as “six consciousnesses are indeterminate.
Therefore, the sequence should be understood as: “cittaṃ, cittāni, cittā; cittaṃ, cittāni, citte.

For in some instances, the nominative and accusative plural endings of neuter nouns ending in a nasal consonant (*niggahīta*) occur just like those of masculine nouns ending in *-o*. And these [plural forms] follow the masculine paradigm.

In the teaching, these terms circulate either in conjunction with their respective characteristics (*liṅga*) or without their characteristics, whether in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) or as isolated words.
For example: “The four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*). The four right efforts (*sammappadhāna*).
‘All garlands approach this one. ‘He who possesses these riches. The four great elements (*mahābhūta*). The three faculties (*indriya*). The two faculties. The ten faculties. The two...”
"Dependent on the great elements, there are two great elements; the five consciousnesses; having resolved upon four factors, I dwell at the top of an anthill:
forms, sounds, tastes, and odors. In forms and sounds, and likewise in tastes..."—such hundreds of scriptural passages as these are to be seen.
Furthermore, in this context, words such as “satipaṭṭhānā” should not be understood as being stated by way of a change of gender,
because one does not see the words beginning with “satipaṭṭhāna” existing in the nominative singular as having the form of a masculine noun ending in the vowel -o.
Rather, it should be understood that only words such as “cattāro” (four) are stated by way of a change of gender.

This is because it demonstrates their state of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with neuter nouns ending in a nasalized vowel (*niggahīta*), such as the word *satipaṭṭhāna* and others.

Here, some might object: "Is it not the case that from the observation of usages such as ‘the phenomenon of the foundation of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna’), ‘the phenomenon of consciousness (*citta’), and ‘phenomena that are consciousness (*cittā dhammā*)’, the status of the words *satipaṭṭhāna* and others as masculine nouns ending in the vowel *-o* is obtained? This being so, why do you [claim] that the words *satipaṭṭhāna* and others..."
It has been stated: "Because in the first singular case, the state of existing as a vowel-ending masculine noun is not seen.

But why is it that the neuter gender ending in a *niggahīta* (anusvāra) is accepted exclusively for words such as *satipaṭṭhāna*, given that we see forms such as "the phenomenon is *satipaṭṭhāna*" (*satipaṭṭhāno dhammo*), "the phenomenon is *citto*" (*citto dhammo*), and "the phenomena are *cittā*" (*cittā dhammā*)? Would it not also be so in cases such as "the four foundations of mindfulness" (*cattāro satipaṭṭhānā*)?
Should it be said that "the words *satipaṭṭhāna*, *sadda*, and so forth, are spoken by way of a change of gender"? It should not be so said.

Why? Because even in such cases as "*satipaṭṭhāno dhammo* (the state of mindfulness-establishment), *citto dhammo* (the state of consciousness), *cittā dhammā* (states of consciousness)," the words *satipaṭṭhāna*, *citta*, and so forth, are not intended to be used by way of a change of gender.
For in those instances, the Lord of Dhamma (*dhammissaro*) joined them with the word *dhamma* in the masculine gender.
The Blessed One, having regard for the grammatical gender of the word *dhamma*, spoke thus: "Satipaṭṭhāna, Citta, *citta*.

For indeed, there are no instances anywhere where the words *satipaṭṭhāna* and *citta* are applied as masculine nouns ending in the vowel *-o*; rather, they are applied as neuter nouns ending in the nasal *niggahīta*.
Thus, even in the phrase "Citta the householder" (*citto gahapatī*), [the word *citta*] refers to consciousness (*viññāṇa*) by depending on the masculine noun *gahapati*.
The word "Citta" is spoken by superimposing the designation "mind" upon a person and making it a term denoting that person.
However, if what was intended were the mind known as consciousness (*viññāṇa*), it would simply be called "citta.
Therefore, in instances such as "the householder Citta" or "the woman Citta," one should not accept a change of gender, because words such as "citta" are dependent [on a referent].

And just as it is here, so too in such expressions as “the state of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāno dhammo*), the mind-state (*citto dhammo*), the mental states (*cittā dhammā*)”, a change of gender is not intended.

However, in cases such as “the four foundations of mindfulness (*cattāro satipaṭṭhānā*)”, there are no words to be expected following the term *satipaṭṭhāna* and the rest by which they would become masculine; therefore, one should simply transpose the words “four” and so forth.
Having taken them as neuter gender by saying, "All these four," they are to be joined with such terms as "foundations of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhānā*) and "right efforts" (*sammappadhānā*).
In such instances, some commentators maintain that the negative particle *na* is elided, as in the passage:
"The signs which were seen before by the Bodhisattvas when they sat upon the excellent throne. For [the meaning] is not seeing...
There is an elision; therefore, the construction should be made as: “the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, all the *mālā* [garlands],” and so forth.

However, some, imagining the word *mālā* to be feminine in gender in the phrase “all the *mālā* come to me,” transpose the masculine word *sabbe* into the feminine gender and explain the meaning as “all the *mālā*. Although that is so...
Although this appears more appropriate, it should nevertheless not be accepted. For the Blessed One did not fail to recognize gender;
nor was he unable to speak the two phrases, "All the garlands come to me," by making them feminine gender.
He uttered such words of differing genders precisely because he knew them and was fully capable of speaking them.
And because he uttered the words with dissimilar grammatical genders, namely, “all garlands come to me,” therefore, having changed the word *sabbe*— which is masculine—

to the neuter gender as *sabbāni*, and having joined it with the word *mālā* in the neuter gender by means of elision (as in the case of the term “three faculties” in the Vibhaṅga text), [the phrase becomes] “all garlands.”
The meaning must be understood in some cases as “one for whom these are riches,” as in the example given. For here, the meaning is “one for whom these riches exist.
This point also should be noted: the word *mālā* is of two genders, namely feminine and neuter.
Let its feminine gender stand aside because it is easily understood; however, in the neuter, there are three *mālāni*. [Use] “*mālehi*... [etc.]
Furthermore, many neuter applications are seen, such as: “...and with perfumes they worship the body of the Blessed One.
Now, if the word *mālā* is indeed of two genders—feminine and neuter—then what fault is there in assuming the feminine gender for the word *mālā* in the passage:
“All garlands come to me”? There is indeed [a fault] in [assuming] a word that is feminine in gender [to be neuter].

This is because a neuter gender [noun] lacks the state of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇabhāva*) with a masculine gender pronoun, whereas a neuter gender [noun] is observed to possess the state of grammatical coreferentiality with a masculine gender pronoun.
For this very reason, many such usages as "ete dhanā" (these riches) are seen frequently in the scriptures (*pāvacana*). Here, however, they might say:
“The words *dhana* and so forth are exclusively masculine because they are joined with coreferential terms such as *ete* [in the masculine],” it is said.

This is not so; these are indeed neuter. For if *dhana* and so forth were masculine, then in certain instances where the singular case ending occurs, one would expect words like *dhana* ending in *-o* to be joined with coreferential terms ending in *-o*, such as *eso*. Such forms [do not occur].
However, due to their neuter nature, words such as *dhanā*, *indriyā*, and *viññāṇā* are exclusively neuter.

This rule applies only in the case of the nominative plural. For neuter nouns, appearing in distinct forms like masculine ones, sometimes occur alongside masculine words—just as eunuchs who wear men's attire move about together with men.
The conclusion should be understood as follows.
Furthermore, if they were to turn back the words spoken previously and say: "In such cases as 'Citta the householder' and 'Cittā the woman,' he has mind (citta), thus he is Citta;
she has mind, thus she is Cittā—just as [one is called] 'Saddha'..."
In the phrase "saddhā" (faith), because it must be understood according to its meaning as "one who is confident," a change of gender is to be recognized.

However, in cases such as "the state of establishing mindfulness is a phenomenon (dhamma), consciousness is a phenomenon, [or] mental states are phenomena," since such a meaning is not intended, one should say "the state of establishing mindfulness is a phenomenon, consciousness is a phenomenon, [or] mental states are phenomena"; thus, in what ought to be stated, there is a change of gender.

Is it to be accepted that there is a change of gender (liṅgavipallāsa) because [the text] says, “The state of establishing mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) is a phenomenon (dhamma); the mind (citta) is a phenomenon; mental states (cittā dhammā) are phenomena,” and so forth?

No, for in cases such as “the householder Citto” and in cases such as “the state of establishing mindfulness is a phenomenon,” the words *citta*, *satipaṭṭhāna*, and so on, are always intended to have the masculine gender by virtue of their dependence upon the referents—the householder, the phenomena, and so forth.

For instance, although the word *puñña* is exclusively neuter in gender, it becomes masculine in the form "meritorious volitional formation" (*puñño abhisaṅkhāro*) by virtue of its dependence on the concept of volitional formation (*abhisaṅkhāra*).
Similarly, words such as *paduma* (lotus) and *maṅgala* (auspiciousness), though exclusively neuter, become masculine and feminine respectively when depending on another referent:
"the Blessed One is a lotus" (*padumo bhagavā*), "the queen is a lotus" (*padumā devī*), "the Blessed One is auspicious" (*maṅgalo bhagavā*), and "the woman is auspicious" (*maṅgalā itthī*).

They are born [with specific genders]. Even words denoting particular types of elephants, such as *kālāvaka* and *gaṅgeyya*, which are exclusively masculine, become neuter by virtue of depending on a collective group (*kulāpekkhanavasena*), as in the expression “the *kālāvaka* and the *gaṅgeyya*.

Indeed, it is by virtue of depending on that [collective] that the masculine designation “the *kālāvaka* and the *gaṅgeyya*” is seen in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). Thus, it is by virtue of depending on their respective referents...
The grammatical description is seen after one has caused the respective original gender to disappear and established another gender;

yet, not all of those genders have become different genders by means of secondary derivation (*taddhita*), but rather they have become different genders precisely by virtue of their dependence on the state of being a householder (*gahapati*) and so forth.
Therefore: "O lady, these are your sons, whom you are devouring..."

In such passages as, “Pure, they call them the sons of Śiva; having heard these teachings thus, the wise become serene,” a change of gender (liṅgavipallāsa) is to be accepted because the words *dhamma* and so forth mentioned therein do not depend on anything else.

However, this is not the case for the word *citta* and others in such instances as “the householder Citta, the woman Cittā, the teaching of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), the teaching Citta, the teachings Cittā.”
"O householder, perversion must be expected because of the partiality toward phenomena and so forth; this is how the conclusion here should be understood.
And this is a point of confusion for some; therefore, for the endurance of the true Dhamma, this principle should be carefully attended to by sons of good family who are endowed with faith."
However, Ācariya Dhammapāla, a resident of the Badaratittha Monastery, stated:
"In the passage of the Pāḷi, 'aparimāṇā padā aparimāṇā akkharā aparimāṇā byañjanā,' it should be understood that a change of gender has been made, such that 'padā, akkharā, byañjanā' [are used].
Regarding this as well, we maintain that the word "padā" here is indeed in the neuter gender, just like [the usage] in "indriyā rūpā" and so forth.
We say this because, by virtue of ending in the vowel *o*, the status of being a nominative singular form is absent;

however, the other two [cases] should be understood as both neuter and masculine, since the status of being a nominative singular form is found in them by virtue of having the nasal *ṃ* (*niggahīta*) followed by the vowel *o*.
For instance, only in cases such as "puttāni," "latāni," "pabbatāni," and "dhammāni" should a reversal of gender be admitted.
This is because, by way of the *niggahīta*, the state of having a nominative singular ending is not perceived;

whereas for those [words] ending in *-o* and *-a*, the state of having a nominative singular ending is seen. Furthermore, "May what is subject to aging not age" (*jarādhammaṃ mā jīrī*) should be understood as being neuter by virtue of its reference to another substantive (*aññapadattha*).
Bhūtaṃ, bhūtāni, bhūtā. Bhūtaṃ, bhūtāni, bhūte. Bhūtena, bhūtehi, bhūtebhi. Bhūtassa, bhūtānaṃ.
Bhūtā, bhūtasmā, bhūtamhā, bhūtehi, bhūtebhi. Bhūtassa, bhūtānaṃ. Bhūte, bhūtasmiṃ, bhūtamhi, bhūtesu.
Bho bhūta, bhavanto bhūtāni, bhavanto bhūtā. In this manner, according to the method for *citta*.
This is the series of nominal forms (*nāmikapadamālā*).

By this method, the series of nominal forms for words ending in a *niggahīta* (anusvāra) derived from the verbal root *bhū*, such as “*mahābhūtaṃ*,” “*bhavittaṃ*,” “*bhūnaṃ*,” and “*bhavanaṃ*,” as well as for other words ending in a *niggahīta* such as “*vattaṃ*,” should be understood.
*Vattaṃ* (duty), *rūpaṃ* (form), *sotaṃ* (ear), *ghānaṃ* (nose), *dukkhaṃ* (suffering), *pupphaṃ* (flower), *jhānaṃ* (meditation), *ñāṇaṃ* (knowledge).
Generosity, virtue, merit, evil, fault, truth, vehicle, umbrella;
cart, gold, tagara, city, crossing, foot, earth, death;
eye, face, doing, cutting, dwelling, forest, abode, sky.
Amata, puḷina, māla, āsana, savana, mukha;
paduma, uppala, vassa, locana, sādhana, sukha.
Tāṇa, mūla, dhana, kūla, maṅgala, naḷina, phala.
Gold, a lotus, grain, a net, a phallus, a footprint, water;
a limb, a leaf, a cemetery, the syllable *saṃ*; a weapon, a heart, a forest;
a staircase, a robe, a living being, a firebrand, a faculty, and a clan.
One should extract [the following terms]: *lohaṃ*, *kaṇaṃ*, *balaṃ*, *pīṭhaṃ*, *aṇḍaṃ*, *ārammaṇaṃ*, *puraṃ*, *araññaṃ*, *tīraṃ*, *assatthaṃ*, and so forth.
These are in every respect similar to the word *citta*; however, these others are dissimilar. Namely:
Expressions such as “skin is a house” are divided in only one way;
however, expressions such as “action is strength, action is virtue” are divided in many ways. How so?
Camme, cammasmiṃ, cammamhi, cammani; vesme, vesmasmiṃ, vesmamhi, vesmani; ghamme, ghammasmiṃ, ghammamhi, ghammani. In this same way, other [forms] should also be applied.
Kammaṃ, kammāni, kammā. Kammaṃ, kammāni, kamme.
Kammena, kammunā, kammanā, kammehi, kammebhi. Kammassa, kammuno, kammānaṃ. Kammasmā, kammamhā, kammunā, kammehi, kammebhi.
*Kamma*, *kammuno*, *kammānaṃ*. *Kamme*, *kammasmiṃ*, *kammamhi*, *kammani*, *kammesu*.
*Bho kamma*, *bhavanto kammāni*, *bhavanto kammā*.

However, for the word *thāma*, in the place of the third case singular and so forth, one should apply the forms: *thāmena*, *thāmunā*, *thāmassa*, *thāmuno*; and *thāmā*, *thāmasmā*, *thāmamhā*, *thāmunā*.

Furthermore, for words ending in a nasal consonant (*niggahīta*) that possess the *imantupaccaya* suffix, such as in the usage examples "guṇavaṃ cittaṃ" (a virtuous mind), "rucimaṃ pupphaṃ" (a beautiful flower), and "pāpimaṃ kulaṃ" (an evil family), the forms are as follows:
Nominative: guṇavaṃ, guṇavantāni, guṇavantā, guṇavanti. Accusative: guṇavantaṃ, guṇavantāni, guṇavante guṇavanti.
