Instrumental: guṇavatā, guṇavantena, guṇavantehi, guṇavantebhi. Ablative: guṇavato, guṇavantassa, guṇavataṃ.
Of those possessing qualities (*guṇavantānaṃ*). [The forms are: *guṇavatā*, *guṇavantā*, *guṇavantasmā*, *guṇavantamhā*, *guṇavantehi*, *guṇavantebhi*.
[The genitive forms are: *guṇavato*, *guṇavantassa*, *guṇavataṃ*, *guṇavantānaṃ*. [The locative forms are: *guṇavati*, *guṇavante*, *guṇavantasmiṃ*, *guṇavantamhi*, *guṇavantesu*.
[The vocative forms are: *bho guṇava*, *bhavanto guṇavantāni*, *guṇavanti*.
In this way, it should be applied by means of such forms as “*rucimaṃ*, *rucimantāni*, *ruciman*,” and so forth, and also by such forms as “*pāpimaṃ*,
*pāpimantāni*, *pāpiman*,” and so forth. Furthermore, in this context, applications such as “*guṇavaṃ*, *balavaṃ*, *yasavaṃ*, *satimaṃ*,
*gatimaṃ*,” and so forth, should be expanded upon.
Based on the usage of the word *karonta* (doing) in such phrases as "the mind doing" (*karontaṃ cittaṃ*) and "a family doing" (*karontaṃ kulaṃ*), [the forms are]:
Nominative: *karontaṃ*, *karontāni*, *karontā*, *karonti*. Accusative: *karontaṃ*, *karontāni*, *karonte*, *karonti*.
Instrumental: *karotā*, *karontena*, *karontehi*, *karontebhi*. Genitive: *karoto*, *karato*, *karontassa*, *karontānaṃ*, *karotaṃ*.
Karotā, karontā, karontasmā, karontamhā, karontehi, karontebhi. Karoto, karato, karontassa, karontānaṃ, karotaṃ.
Karoti, karonte, karontasmiṃ, karontamhi, karontesu. Bho karonta, bhavanto, karontāni, karontā, karontīti should be applied accordingly.
However, for the word *gacchanto* (going), according to usage such as "the going mind" (*gacchantaṃ cittaṃ*) or "the going family" (*gacchantaṃ kulaṃ*), [the forms are]:
Nominative: *gacchantaṃ*, *gacchantāni*, *gacchantā*. Accusative: *gacchantaṃ*, *gacchantāni*, *gacchante*.
Instrumental: *gacchatā*, *gacchantena*, *gacchantehi*, *gacchantebhi*. Genitive: *gacchato*, *gacchantassa*, *gacchantānaṃ*, *gacchataṃ*.
Gacchatā, gacchantā, gacchantasmā, gacchantamhā, gacchantehi, gacchantebhi.
Gacchato, gacchantassa, gacchantānaṃ, gacchataṃ. Gacchati, gacchante, gacchantasmiṃ, gacchantamhi, gacchantesu.
O gacchaṃ, o gacchantā, bhavanto gacchantāni, gacchantāti should be construed.
In the same way, the series of nominal forms should be applied to such examples as “moving,” “giving,” “standing,” and “thinking.

However, there is a certain distinction regarding the word *mahanta*; for instance, because we see the neuter usage “*mahā*” in the expression “the sovereignty of Bārāṇasī is called *mahā*,” [the forms are]:
*mahantaṃ*, *mahā*, *mahantāni*, *mahantā*. [And likewise: *mahantaṃ*, *mahantāni*, etc.
*Mahante*. It should be understood that the sequence [ends with] *mahatā*. All of these differ from those ending in the word *citta*.
This is the analysis of the nominal paradigm for the base form of neuter nouns ending in a *niggahīta* (anusvāra), including a determination of their meanings.
Nouns ending in a *niggahīta* have as their inherent nature the endings *-ava*, *-aṇ*, *-u*, and *-anta*.
The neuter gender is completed.

Now, having placed the doctrine of the ancient masters (pubbācariya) foremost, we shall explain the declensional paradigm (*nāmikapadamālā*) of the word *aṭṭhi*—meaning "bone"—which expresses that sense of moral conduct (*sīlattha*).
Nominative: *aṭṭhi*, *aṭṭhī*, *aṭṭhīni*. Accusative: *aṭṭhiṃ*, *aṭṭhī*, *aṭṭhīni*. Instrumental: *aṭṭhinā*, *aṭṭhīhi*, *aṭṭhībhi*. Genitive: *aṭṭhissa*.
*Atthi*, *atthinam*. *Atthinā*, *atthīhi*, *atthībhi*. *Atthissa*, *atthino*, *atthīnam*. *Atthismiṃ*, *atthimhi*, *atthīsu*.
"O bone! (*bho atthi*), "Sirs, bones! (*bhavanto atthī*), "Sirs, bones! (*bhavanto atthīni*).
This is the opinion of the Great Elder Yamaka. Although the forms *atthismā* and *atthimhā* have not been included here for the ablative case, nevertheless...
In each respective case, the forms should be understood by observing their corresponding applications.
Just as with the word *aṭṭhi*, so too are the forms of *satthi*, *dadhi*, *vāri*, *akkhi*, *acchi*, and so forth.
*Atthavibhāvi*, *atthavibhāvī*, *atthavibhāvīni*. *Atthavibhāviṃ*, *atthavibhāvī*, *atthavibhāvīni*.
Atthavibhāvinā, atthavibhāvīhi, atthavibhāvībhi. Atthavibhāvissa, atthavibhāvino, atthavibhāvīnaṃ.
Atthavibhāvinā, atthavibhāvismā, atthavibhāvimhā, atthavibhāvīhi, atthavibhāvībhi. Atthavibhāvissa, atthavibhāvino, atthavibhāvīnaṃ. Atthavibhāvismiṃ.
In the case of *atthavibhāvimhi* and *atthavibhāvīsu*: "O *atthavibhāvi*," "you two *atthavibhāvī*," "you [plural] *atthavibhāvīni*.

Likewise for *dhammavibhāvi*, *cittānuparivatti*, *sukhakāri*, and so forth. In that regard, words such as *aṭṭhi* (bone) and *satthi* (thigh) are primary gender markers because they do not depend on anything else;
whereas *atthavibhāvi*, *dhammavibhāvi*, and so forth, are secondary gender markers because they depend on something else.
This is the section on noun declensions for the base forms of neuter nouns ending in the vowel *i*.
The treatment of neuter nouns ending in the vowels *i* and *u* is thus completed.
Now, having placed the opinion of the ancient masters at the forefront, we shall explain the noun declension of the word *gotrabhū*.
Āyu, āyū, āyūni. Āyuṃ, āyū, āyūni. Āyunā, āyūhi, āyūbhi. Āyussa, āyuno, āyūnaṃ. Āyunā, āyūhi, āyūbhi. Āyussa, āyuno, āyūnaṃ.
Āyusmiṃ, āyumhi, āyūsu. Bho āyu, bhavanto āyū, bhavanto āyūni.
This is the opinion of the Great Elder Yamaka.

Although the words *āyusmā* and *āyumhā* do not appear here in the sense of the ablative case (*nissakkavacana*), nevertheless they should be understood because similar usages are seen in various places. Furthermore, the word *āyu* should be regarded as being of both masculine and neuter gender;
for its dual-gendered nature is observed in both the Pāli Canon and the Commentaries. "And [the word] *punarāyu*..."
In such passages as “He has been obtained by me; know this thus, dear sir; his life-span (āyu) has come to an end,” the word *āyu* is masculine.
Accordingly, the nominal paradigm should be constructed according to the rules of the Bhikkhu-naya as appropriate, beginning with “āyu, āyū, āyavo,” and so forth.
However, in such passages as “The foremost [qualities] are life-span (āyu) and beauty (vaṇṇa); but how much is his life-span (āyu)?”, it is neuter. Accordingly...
“Āyu, āyū, āyūni” is thus conjugated.
*Gotrabhu*, *gotrabhū*, *gotrabhūni*. *Gotrabhuṃ*, *gotrabhū*, *gotrabhūni*. *Gotrabhunā*, *gotrabhūhi*, *gotrabhūbhi*.
*Gotrabhussa*, *gotrabhuno*, *gotrabhūnaṃ*. *Gotrabhunā*, *gotrabhusmā*, *gotrabhumhā*.
Gotrabhūhi, gotrabhūbhi. Gotrabhussa, gotrabhuno, gotrabhūnaṃ. Gotrabhusmiṃ, gotrabhumhi, gotrabhūsu.
Bho gotrabhu, bhavanto gotrabhū, bhavanto gotrabhūni. Bho gotrabhū, bho gotrabhūni; thus the plural may be formed.
This is our opinion, and it applies likewise to "cittasahabhu" and so forth.
The nominal declension series (*nāmikapadamālā*) should be applied to words ending in *ū* that are derived from the *bhū* root, as well as to other similar words.
However, the word *gotrabhū*, which denotes a person and ends in *ū*, is included in the system of the Omniscient One (*Sabbaññu*) because it is comprised within the masculine gender.
In this regard, other such words include: *cakkhu*, *vasu*, *dhanu*, *dāru*, *tipu*, *madhu*, *siṅgu*, *hiṅgu*, *cittagu*, and so forth.
This is the section on noun declensions for the basic forms of neuter nouns ending in *u*.
The section on neuter nouns ending in *u* and *o*,
which constitute their basic forms, is completed.
Thus, neuter nouns ending in the *niggahīta* (anusvāra), in *i*, and in *u* have been taken in their entirety in three ways.
Among these, a distinction is seen in some *niggahīta*-ending nouns due to the substitution of *e* for both the singular and plural forms of the locative case.
For example: "In happiness, in suffering" (*sukhe dukkhe*); "forty-nine hundred Ājīvaka followers" (*ekūnapaññāsa ājīvakasate*).
“...among the four hundred and ninety-nine wanderers,” and so forth. One might ask: “Since such forms are seen in the Canon, should it not be said that there exists a neuter gender ending in -e?

It should not be so stated, because those forms are specific instances included within the category of the nasalized (niggahīta) ending. For since they are established by way of substitution (ādesa), there is no separate neuter gender ending in -e.
Therefore, for neuter nouns, only the threefold classification as previously stated should be accepted.
Thus, this *Padamālā*, rich in methodological principles regarding genders,
has been analyzed by me for the sake of the Dispensation of the Great Sage.
He for whom this grammatical science of words is mastered and well-cultivated is a refuge and a final resort for noble sons within the Dispensation.
Thus [ends the section] concerning the modes of expression in the Three Baskets, together with their commentaries, for the wise.
In the Saddanīti treatise composed for the sake of proficiency,
the ninth chapter: the analysis of the nominal paradigm of the neuter gender in its base form.
10. The Series of Nouns with Mixed Gender-Triads From this point forward,
beginning with words that have more than one syllable,
I shall present an orderly series of nouns by mixing the three genders together.
I shall explain, according to my ability, the meaning of the profound course of wisdom regarding various subtle conventions used by the wise in their respective fields:
*itthī* and *thī*, *pabhā* and *bhā*, *girā* and *rā*, and *pavanaṃ* and *vanaṃ*.
*Udaka*, *daka*, and *kañca*; *vitakko* and so forth;
*bhū*, *bhūmi*, and *araññaṃ*; *araññāni* and so forth;
*paññā*, *paññāṇaṃ*, and *ñāṇaṃ*—these and others may occur in three ways.
*Ko*, *vi*, *sā*, *ceva*, *bhā*, *rā*, *ca*, *thī*, *dhī*, *ku*, *bhū*, *tathēva*, *kaṃ*;
*khaṃ*, *go*, *mo*, *mā*, *ca*, *saṃ*, *yaṃ*, *taṃ*, *kimiccādī*—these are each single [words].
This is the enumeration of noun-forms (nāmikapadamālā) mixed with the three genders. Therein: *itthī*, *itthī*, *itthiyo*. *Itthiṃ*...pe... *bhotiyo itthiyo*.
Thī, thī, thiyo. Thiṃ, thī, thiyo. Thiyā, thīhi, thībhi. Thiyā, thīnaṃ. Thiyā, thīhi, thībhi. Thiyā, thīnaṃ. Thiyā, thiyaṃ, thīsu. Bhoti thi, bhotiyo thī, bhotiyo thiyo. Herein:
“Cocks, jewels, and staffs, and women with auspicious marks, Arise for a person who has done merit and is free from evil.”
"One should not disclose a secret to a woman;
the nature of women is difficult to understand"—these and others are illustrative phrases. Pabhā, pabhā, pabhāyo. Pabhaṃ... pe... bhotiyo pabhāyo.
Bhā, bhā, bhāyo. Bhaṃ, bhā, bhāyo. Bhāya, bhāhi, bhābhi. Bhāya, bhānaṃ. Bhāya, bhāhi, bhābhi. Bhāya, bhānaṃ.
Bhāya, bhāyaṃ, bhāsu. Bhoti, bhe, bhotiyo; bhā, bhotiyo bhāyo. And here, "the sun is the maker of light" (bhākaro bhānu) and so forth are the illustrative examples.

*Girā*, *girā*, *girāyo*. *Giraṃ*... [and so on] ... *bhotiyo girāyo*. “*Vācā girā byappatho. Ye vohaṃ kittayissāmi, girāhi anupubbaso*” — these are the illustrative examples for the feminine gender of the word *girā*.
The word *rā* signifying "gold" is masculine; however, here the word *rā* signifying "sound" is feminine.
*rā*, *rā*, *rāyo*. *raṃ*, *rā*, *rāyo*. *rāya*, *rāhi*, *rābhi*. *rāya*, *rānaṃ*. *rāya*, *rāhi*, *rābhi*. *rāya*, *rānaṃ*. *rāya*, *rāyaṃ*, *rāsu*. *bhoti re*, *bhotiyo rā*, *bhotiyo rāyo*.
*Rā* means sound. For it is stated in the *Aggaññasutta-ṭīkā*: "It is called *ratti* because beings are quieted (*tiyati*) or cut off (*chijjati*) therein;
it is the time for the subsiding of the sounds of living beings. Therefore, since the word *rā* denotes sound, the word "*ratti*" serves as an illustration.
*pavanaṃ*, *pavanāni*, *pavanā*; *pavanaṃ*, *pavanāni*, *pavane*.
*Vanaṃ*, *vanāni*, *vanā*. *Vanaṃ*, *vanāni*, *vane*. The rest is to be understood in the same way.
The words *pavana* and *vana* are sometimes synonymous and sometimes have different meanings. For they are synonymous when expressing the sense of "forest," as in:
"Fulfilling those qualities, I then entered the *pavana*; with my son, I entered the *vana*," and so forth. [The forms] follow their respective sequences.
However, in the sense of expressing a forest of wind-thirst (*vāyutaṇhāvana*), they have different meanings in such passages as:
“O monks, having cut down the forest and the thicket, become free from the forest (*nibbāna*).
[The forms for *udaka* are: *udakaṃ*, *udakāni*, *udakā*; *udakaṃ*, *udakāni*, *udake*.
Dakaṃ, dakāni, dakā. Dakaṃ, dakāni, dake. The remainder is all to be understood accordingly.
Examples here include such phrases as “cool water from ripe mangoes,” “land-born and water-born flowers,” and so forth.

However, in certain passages of the Pāḷi, such as “blue water from the middle of the forest,” “the great ocean,” and “by the falling of a drop of water, even a water-jar is filled,” [the term *udaka* is used].

The meaning of "water" is expressed by the word *uda* alone because it occurs at the end of a compound, just as the meaning of "taste for what is empty" (*rittassāda*) is expressed by the word "of the empty" (*rittassa*) in place of what ought to be "taste for the empty" (*rittassāda*).
For the word *uda* by itself has never been seen before in the Pāli;
if it does exist, it should be carefully noted.
Kaṃ, kāni, kā. Kaṃ, kāni, ke. Kena, kehi, kebhi. Kassa, kānaṃ. Kā, kasmā, kamhā, kehi, kebhi.
Kassa, kānaṃ. Ke, kasmiṃ, kamhi, kesu. Bho ka, bhavanto kā, bhavanto kāni.
Or the plural should be joined with the word *bho*: "bho kāni, bho kā."
In this context, *kaṃ* refers to water and happiness. Here, one should understand such usages as “*kantāro*, *kandaro*, *kevaṭṭā*, *kesā*, *karuṇā*, *nāko*,” and so forth.
Among these, *kantāra*: *kaṃ* means water; that which is to be crossed over or traversed by means of that [water] is a *kantāra*, a waterless region.
However, in expressions such as “*corakantāra*” (a wilderness of thieves), it refers to a place difficult to traverse by way of conventional usage (*rūḷhi*).

It should be understood that the word *kantāra* occurs here. Regarding *kandara*: here too, *kaṃ* refers to water; it is called *kandara* because it is split (*dārita*) or pierced (*bhinnā*) by that [water].
In the case of *kevaṭṭa* and so forth: they are called *kevaṭṭa* because they move (*vattanato*) for the purpose of catching (*gahaṇa*) in the water (*ke*).
They are called *kesā* because they grow or arise on the head (*sīse*). It is called *karuṇā* because it obstructs (*rundhati*) happiness (*kaṃ*). *Nāka* is heaven (*sagga*).
*Kaṃ* means happiness (*sukha*); *akaṃ* means suffering (*dukkha*). Since that [suffering] does not exist here, the meaning to be understood is *nāka*.
Just as the nominal declension series for words such as *itthī* has been applied here, so too should it be applied to [words] such as *vitakko*, *vicāro*, *ābhā*, and *padīpo*.
*Bhū*, *bhū*, *bhuyo*. *Bhuṃ*, *bhū*, *bhuyo*. *Bhuyā*, *bhūhi*, *bhūbhi*. *Bhuyā*, *bhūnaṃ*. *Bhuyā*, *bhūhi*, [bhūbhi].
Bhūbhi. Bhuyā, bhūnaṃ. Bhuyā, bhuyaṃ, bhūsu. Bhoti bhu, bhotiyo bhū, bhotiyo bhuyo.
And here, “bhūruho, bhūpālo, bhūbhujo, bhūtalaṃ” are the illustrative words.
Bhūmi, bhūmī, bhūmiyo; the rest should be expanded accordingly.
*Araññaṃ*, *araññāni*, *araññā*; the rest should be expanded in detail. *Araññānī* is said to be "great forest";
it is a feminine-gendered word that should be derived by means of the suffix *-inī*, like the word *gahapatānī*. Indeed, the reading *araññānī* is also seen in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
[The forms are: *araññānī*, *araññānī*, *araññāniyo*. [The accusative forms are: *araññāniṃ*, *araññānī*, *araññāniyo*. [The instrumental forms are: *araññāniyā*, *araññānīhi*.
Araññāniyā, araññānīhi, araññānībhi. Araññāniyā, araññānīnaṃ. Araññāniyā, araññāniyaṃ, araññānīsu. Bhoti araññāni, bhotiyo araññānī, bhotiyo araññāniyo.
Just as they have been applied here according to the sequence of subsequent cases, so too should they be applied in such instances as “sabhā, sabhāya,” and so forth. [The form] sabhāyaṃ.

It is indeed *sabhā*; however, it is stated thus by way of the distinction of gender. The canonical text (*pāḷi*) "One should dwell in the assembly hall or at the foot of the door" is the illustration here.
[Feminine noun *paññā* (wisdom): singular nominative *paññā*, dual *paññā*, plural *paññāyo*; accusative singular *paññaṃ*, dual *paññā*, plural *paññāyo*; instrumental singular *paññāya*.
*Paññāṇaṃ*, *paññāṇāni*, *paññāṇā*. *Paññāṇaṃ*, *paññāṇāni*, *paññāṇe*. *Paññāṇena*. Examples here include:
“For thus, Bhante, is the Blessed One’s knowledge of virtue (*sīlapaññāṇaṃ*). A person possessing knowledge is good,” and so forth.

*Ñāṇaṃ*, *ñāṇāni*, *ñāṇā*. *Ñāṇaṃ*, *ñāṇāni*, *ñāṇe*. *Ñāṇena*. All the rest should be understood accordingly. Even in cases such as “*aggi*, *aggini*, *gini*,” the series of noun declensions should be applied according to the subsequent suffixes.

What is called "brahmā" when it consists of a single syllable, even among consonants? It refers to both "wind" (*vāta*) and "body" (*sarīra*). Since these words denote those meanings, there are the following applications.
For example: "I worship the lotus-feet of Him by whom the immeasurable welfare of the world was brought forth—the feet served by swarms of bees that are [the rays of] His crown."

“Kakudha tree,” “body born of karma,” and so forth. Regarding these, the wise maintain that *kamoḷialisevitaṃ* means “served by the bees that are the crests of hundreds of Brahmās who are bowing down.
As for the term *kakudharukkho*, here *ko* refers to the wind; that which wards off what is hostile to it—by means of removing wind-diseases—is therefore called a *kakudha* tree.
The teachers say: Regarding the term "body born of karma" (*karaja-kāya*), what is here called the "body"? It is the physical frame. The "dust" (*raja*) that occurs therein is "born of karma.

What is that? It is semen and blood. For, because it is the fruit of the passion-dust described in the passage, "Passion is dust, but it is not called 'reṇu'," it is designated by the word "karma-born" (*karaja*)—using the term *ka* as a synonym for the body—to express it figuratively as the result.
It is said thus: the teachers maintain that the body produced from the "karaja"—which is to say, from semen and blood—is called the *karajakāya*.

For it is stated [in the Suttas] that "the body is produced from mother and father"; however, in the commentary on the *Mahā-assapura-sutta*, it is explained: "It is 'kara' because it is cast (*kariyati*) or thrown into the womb;
it is 'sambhava' (origin). It is 'karaja' because it is born from the *kara* [semen]; it is 'produced from mother and father' (*mātāpettikasambhava*)."
[The word] *attha*. Others say it is "born from that which acts by way of establishing [the body] of the mother and so forth";

however, in either case, "kārakaja-kāya" refers to the material form of the fourfold continuity (*catusantatirūpa*). But this meaning is not intended here; rather, the former meaning alone is intended because of the governing rule concerning the suffix *-ka*.

[The declensions are as follows: Nom. sg. *ko*, pl. *kā* Acc. sg. *kaṃ*, pl. *ke* Instr. sg. *kena*, pl. *kehi*, *kebhi* Dat. sg. *kassa*, pl. *kānaṃ* Abl. sg. *kā*, *kasmā*, *kamhā*; pl. *kehi*, *kebhi* Gen. sg. *kassa*, pl. *kānaṃ* Loc. sg. *ke*, *kasmiṃ*, *kamhi*; pl. *kesu* Voc. sg. *bho ka*, pl. *bhavanto kā*

In this context, he is called a bird (*pakkhī*). For it is said that Vinda, the king of *supaṇṇas*, is the lord of birds. It was with reference to this very meaning that the ancient teacher also spoke this verse:
“O Lord of Munis, I place upon the heads of those who lack faith your supreme excellence, which is free from all blame;
that lotus-foot of yours is not surpassed by the assembly of the lords of gods, the lords of *nāgas*, and the lords of men.”
In this context, *vīnaṃ* means *inda*, that is, a king; the meaning is "king of the *supaṇṇas* born of the bird species.

[The following are the case endings: *viṃ*, *vī*, *vayo*; *viṃ*, *vī*, *vayo*; *vinā*, *vīhi*, *vībhi*; *vissa*, *vino*, *vīnaṃ*; *vinā*, *vismā*, *vimhā*, *vīhi*, *vībhi*; *vissa*, *vino*, *vīnaṃ*; *vismiṃ*, *vimhi*, *vīsu*. *Bho vi*, *bhavanto vayo*.
The word *sā* refers to a dog, as in such expressions as "I have a mother, she must be supported by me," where the word *sā* is included among the pronouns (*sabbanāmika*).

The word *tasaddena* should be understood as occurring in the sense of "behind one's back" (*parammukha*). The nominal declension series for the words *sā*, *bhā*, *rā*, *thī*, *bhū*, and *kasadda* has been explained below.

*Dhī* is said to mean "wisdom" (*paññā*). Here, too, there are illustrative examples such as: "O dear one, know [these] ministers, who are wise and skilled in matters of state," and "the wise man" (*dhīmā*), "the wise woman" (*dhīmatī*), "one of excellent wisdom" (*sudhī*), "one of excellent wisdom" (*sudhinī*), and "one endowed with wisdom" (*dhīyutta*).

Dhī, dhī, dhiyo. Dhiṃ, dhī, dhiyo. Dhiyā, dhīhi, dhībhi. Dhiyā, dhīnaṃ. Dhiyā, dhīhi, dhībhi. Dhiyā, dhīnaṃ. Dhiyā, dhiyaṃ, dhīsu. Bhoti dhi, bhotiyo dhī, bhotiyo dhiyo. *Ku* means earth (*pathavī*). Here, these are the illustrative examples:
"a pickaxe" (*kudāla*), "a white water lily" (*kumuda*), and "an elephant" (*kuñjara*).
In that context, it is called *kudāla* because one cleaves, breaks, or splits the earth (*kuṃ*) with it. It is called *kumuda* because it delights (*modati*) in the earth (*kuyaṃ*).

*Kumudaṃ*. That which wears out the earth (*kuṃ*) is an *elephant* (*kuñjaro*). For it is said in the *Vimānavatthu-aṭṭhakathā*: "It is an elephant because it wears out the earth (*kuṃ*) by its trampling.
[Declension of *ku* (earth): Nominative: *ku*, *kū*, *kuyo*.

Accusative: *kuṃ*, *kū*, *kuyo*. Instrumental: *kuyā*, *kūhi*, *kūbhi*. Dative: *kuyā*, *kūnaṃ*. Ablative: *kuyā*, *kūhi*, *kūbhi*. Genitive: *kuyā*, *kūnaṃ*. Locative: *kuyā*, *kuyaṃ*, *kūsu*. [Addressing forms: O [Earth]: *bho ti ku*. O [Earths]: *bho ti kū*. O [Earths]: *bho ti kuyo*.
The sense-faculty is explained as "space" (kha); space is declared to be the sky (ākāsa).
Heaven is also called "space," and emptiness is likewise considered "space.

In this context, the sense-faculty is called "space" because it serves as the locus and dwelling place for eye-consciousness and the other [sensory consciousnesses]; whereas the sky is so called in the sense of being secluded.
Heaven (sagga) is designated as “kha” because it is a place that must be reached exclusively by those who have performed wholesome deeds (*sucarita*). Examples for this are:
“Just as a bird (*khaga*) perching on the top of a tree shakes a branch,” and “The Self-Existent One (*sayambhū*) moved through the sky (*khe*), having manifested eight hundred [forms].
Such passages serve as illustrations here.
Khaṃ, khāni, khā. Khaṃ, khāni, khe. Khena, khehi, khebhi. Khassa, khānaṃ.
Khā, khasmā, khamhā, khehi, khebhi. Khassa, khānaṃ. Khe, khasmiṃ, khamhi, khesu. Bho kha, bhavanto khāni, bhavanto khā.
The analysis of the meaning of the word "go" is stated as follows:
The word *go* applies to a bull, a sense-faculty, the earth, speech, and intellect;
It also applies to the sun, a ray of light, and water.
Among those meanings, the word *go* is feminine when referring to a cow (*goṇa*), and masculine in other cases.
For instance, in such expressions as “He went while the cows were being milked” (*gosu duyhamānāsu gato*) and “With the cow as the fifth” (*gopañcamo*), the word *go* refers to a cow.
In the word *gocara*, it also refers to the sense-faculties (*indriya*); for *gocara* means that the senses—the eye and so forth—move (*caranti*) therein. Thus say the ancients.
They said: "It is called *gocara* because cattle graze there; like a pasture (*gocara*), it is a place to be frequented constantly.

Alternatively, 'cattle' refers to the sense faculties such as the eye; the place to be traversed by them is the *gocara*. However, in the ancient poetic formulation, "I bow to Gotama, the possessor of cattle (*gomatiṃ gotamaṃ*"), it refers to the earth.
[As it says: "I pay homage to the Perfectly Enlightened One, Gotama, of vast wisdom (*bhūripaññaṃ*)."
This is the meaning. Likewise, in the commentary on the Vāseṭṭha Sutta in the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated in the section of the sub-commentary:
“‘Cattle-tending’ means tending the fields; ‘plowing-tending’ is what is meant. For the earth is called ‘go,’ and its various divisions are the ‘field.
However, in the expression “Gotama by way of lineage,” the suffix *-tva* applies both to the word and to the intellect (*buddhi*). Therefore, the ancients said: “He protects the *gaṃ* (earth).”
*Gotta*. For the word *gotra*, as it occurs in the form *gotama*, protects (*tāti*) both speech and cognition by way of its definitive object;
thus it is a *gotta*. Just as cognition does not function without an object that serves as its referent, so too the designation does not function without that which is designated.
Therefore, that referent termed "lineage" (*gotta*) protects and preserves those two.

It is said: "Who, then, is he? He should be understood as the common generic form belonging to that clan, originating from its first progenitor, shared by that clan, and common to all members included within it.

For even those born into that lineage, such as the Great King Suddhodana and others, are called "Gotama" alone. By this [name], the Blessed One [referred to] his own father, the Great King Suddhodana.

“The Tathāgatas, Gotama, have indeed transcended all boons,” he said. The Great King Vessavaṇa also said to the Blessed One, “We pay homage to the Buddha, Gotama, who is perfected in true knowledge and conduct.
And the Venerable Vaṅgīsa said to the Venerable Ānanda, “Please speak of Nibbāna out of compassion for us, Gotama.
Thus, because it protects one’s lineage (gaṇa), it is called a clan (gotta).
Furthermore, that [lineage] is manifold, such as the Gotama-gotta, the Kassapa-gotta, and so forth.
Likewise, the word *go* (cow) is used for the sun. An example of this is the ancient poetic composition:
“I bow to Gotama of the *gogotta* lineage. The meaning is: “I pay homage to Gotama, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the Kinsman of the Sun. For even the sun was born in the Gotama lineage.
The Blessed One, too, is praised in various places by that same clan-name as “Kinsman of the Sun” (Ādiccabandhu) and so forth;

for instance: “I ask you, Kinsman of the Sun, about seclusion and the state of peace, O Great Seer,” and “I constantly revere Jetavana, the monastery of the Kinsman of the Sun,” and “the Sole Kinsman of the World, the Kinsman who is a companion to the Lotus-born.”
Furthermore, in the word *uṇhagu*, the term *go* refers to a ray. Thus, *uṇhagu* means "one whose rays (*gāvo*) are hot (*uṇhā*)," namely, the sun.
Indeed, the ancient teachers (*pubbācariyā*) have also explained this very meaning in their treatises on prosody (*chandovicitisattha*).
In the phrase *gosītacandana*, it refers to water; for by the word *go*, water is expressed. It is cool (*sīta*) like a cow (*go*).
Sandalwood; however, when that [sandalwood] is thrown into the boiling oil that has been removed from the hearth, at that very moment the oil becomes perfectly cool.
Regarding this, some say: "Why, sir, is the word 'cow' (*gosadda*), while denoting the footprint of a cow, both feminine and masculine?"
If you say this, then why do you say that [the word *go*] is masculine when it occurs in the senses of "faculty," "earth," "intellect," "sun," and "water"?

Let it be masculine when occurring in the sense of "sun"; but surely, when occurring in the senses of "faculty," "water," "earth," "intellect," and "ray," should it not be neuter by virtue of the word *go*?
And when occurring in the senses of "earth," "intellect," and "ray" [should it not be feminine]?

"Is it because we see that words such as *indriya* and *pathavī*, which function with reference to the meanings of 'faculties' and 'earth' respectively, are presented according to the neuter and feminine genders? No, for there is no such rule.
For even a word that functions with reference to a feminine object is seen to be presented in the masculine gender, as in the case of "orodho" (a harem).
Furthermore, even for certain words that refer to a male person (*purisapadattha*), a designation by way of the feminine gender (*itthiliṅga*) is observed, as in:
"O *yakkha*, you are desirous of my welfare; O deity, you are desirous of my benefit.

Moreover, there are certain words that do not refer to either a female or a male person, yet when they refer to a single meaning such as knowledge (*ñāṇa*), etc., they appear according to the feminine, masculine, and neuter genders.
An explanation is seen such as "wisdom is non-delusion, knowledge," and "taṭaṃtaṭītaṭo.

For instance, even though it is not female, a tree receives the name "Mātulā" by way of the feminine gender, and by that [name], the city [is also called Mātulā]. Therefore, it was said in the commentary on the Cakkavatti Sutta:
"Mātulā is a certain tree that has received its name by way of the feminine gender; because of that [tree], in the nearby location..."
Because it was measured out, the city itself became known as "Mātulā. Therefore it is said: "In the city named Mātulā.
The nominal declension of the word *go* has been explained above.
*Mo* refers to the moon; however, in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), the reading with a long vowel is seen: "*Mā* refers to the moon."

It must be read with a vowel ending (*okārantapāṭhena*), having adopted the method from the *Ekakkharakośa* of the Sanskrit language, because it ought to be stated as a vowel-ending according to the rule: “*mo* [is] *siva* and *candimā*.
And here, since the word *ma*, spoken as a vowel-ending, denotes the moon, the illustrative examples are “*puṇṇamī*” and “*puṇṇamā*. In that context, *mo* is full.
"Ettha" means "on the full moon day" (*puṇṇamī*); thus, *puṇṇamā* is a feminine noun in view of the night. Here, however, the example is:
"On the night of the Visākha full moon, during the first watch, he recollected his former existences. It might be asked here:
if this word *puṇṇamā* is a feminine noun in view of the night, [how is it so]?
“Just as the moon on the full-moon night shines forth perfectly pure, even so do you,
O one of fulfilled mind, shine throughout the ten thousandfold world-system.
On the fifteenth day of every half-month, on the full-moon Uposatha day...”

In such passages as, "Without having mounted a vehicle, he came to give a gift," how is the word *puṇṇamāye* grammatically established? It is by means of the substitution of the vowel *e* for the consonant *y*.
For when the Blessed One, the Master of Dhamma, should have said *puṇṇamāyā*, he said *puṇṇamāye*; thus, the vowel *e* was pronounced in place of the consonant *y*.
Just as in the case of the feminine gender, there is the substitution of *tte* for *ttā*, and likewise the substitution of *ne* for *nī*.
For instance, in this Rādhā-jātaka passage, "abyayataṃ vilapasi viratte kosiyāyane," where one should have said "virattā," the word "viratte" is used;
thus, the substitution of *tte* for *ttā* is established. And [likewise] "kosiyāyanī."
When one says "Kosiyāyane," while it should have been said as "Kosiya-āyane," the letter *e* has been read in place of the letter *i*.
Likewise, when it should have been said as "Puṇṇamāyā," by saying "Puṇṇamāye," the letter *e* has been read in place of the letter *ya*.
And just as in this passage from the Mahāsamaya Sutta, "dakkhitāye aparājitasaṅghan," where it should have been said as "dakkhitāyā," [the letter *e* is read].
Just as the vowel *e* was taught by the teacher in place of the consonant *y*, so it is here as well.

However, whereas in the phrase "in the assembly hall (*sabhāye*) or at the gate" (*dvāramūle*), the word "assembly hall" (*sabhā*) is expressed through a change of gender (*liṅgabyattaya*), it is not so here with "on the full moon day" (*puṇṇamāya*).
Here, it is not the "full moon" (*puṇṇamā*) that is expressed through a change of gender; rather, it is expressed by way of the feminine noun ending in *-ā* (*ākārantitthiliṅga*).
For thus, the word *puṇṇamāyo* should be understood as a locative case form produced by the pronunciation of *yekāra* in place of *yakāra*.
*Mā* means glory (*sirī*). For instance, while explaining the meaning of the word *mālinī* in the *Vidvamukhamaṇḍana-ṭīkā*, it is stated:
"*Mā* means *lakkhī* (fortune/luck), and *alinī* means a female bee. Furthermore, the word *lakkhī* is synonymous with the word *sirī*.

Therefore, the meaning “one who is not called ‘Sirī’” is approved by us; likewise, the ancient masters have also explained the meaning as “Mandhātā because he bears (dhāreti) and bestows (vidadhāti) upon me (maṃ) glory (siriṃ).
Consequently, “Mālinī” and “Mandhātā” are the illustrative examples here. Regarding that, first, this is the nominal paradigm for the masculine form of the word *ma*:
Masculine *ma*: Nominative: mā Accusative: maṃ Instrumental: mēna Dative: mēssa Ablative: mēto Genitive: mēsa Locative: mēsmim Vocative: mā [The paradigm continues accordingly.]
*Ma*, *mā*. *Maṃ*, *me*. *Mena*, *mehi*, *mebhi*. *Massa*, *mānaṃ*. *Mā*, *masmā*, *mamhā*, *mehi*, *mebhi*. *Massa*, *mānaṃ*. *Me*, *masmiṃ*, *mamhi*, *mesu*. *Bho ma*, *bhavanto mā*.
Now, however, this is the nominal paradigm for the feminine noun *mā*:
*Mā*, *mā*, *māyo*. *Maṃ*, *mā*, *māyo*. *Māya*, *māhi*, *mābhi*. *Māya*, *mānaṃ*. *Māya*, *māhi*, *mābhi*. *Māya*, *mānaṃ*. *Māya*, *māyaṃ*, *māsu*. *Bhoti me*, *bhotiyo māyo*.

In this context, however, the word *mā* signifying "glory" (*sirī*) and the word *rā* signifying "sound" (*sadda*) belong to the same grammatical category because they consist of a single syllable, are always base-forms ending in the vowel *ā*, and are feminine in gender.

Therein, *saṃ* refers to a person whose mind is peaceful. This is a designation for one whom people in the world call a "true person" (*sappurisa*), a "noble one" (*ariya*), and a "wise man" (*paṇḍita*);
that is to say, it is "saṃ. Thus, [the term] which denotes a true person, a noble one, and a wise man...
Regarding the existence [of the word] by way of the nominative case of the *saṃ* sound, the example of its usage is: “*sameti asatā asaṃ*.

For here, in the analysis of the compound (*samāsa*) as “not together with the non-existent” (*na saṃ asaṃ*), it is understood that the referents of the terms “good person” (*sappurisa*) and “non-good person” (*asappurisa*) are expressed by the words *saṃ* and *asaṃ*.
Therefore, [it is concluded that] “the referent of the term ‘good person’ is not expressed by the word *saṃ* in the nominative case.”
Such a statement should not be made. The words of those who say "it does not exist" are not to be accepted.
Its declensional paradigm, however, has been explained below as "saṃ, santaṃ, sante," and so forth.

Because it is neuter gender, *saṃ* denotes wealth, as in: "manussassaṃ (the wealth of a person), parassaṃ (another's wealth), sabbassaṃ (all wealth), sabbassaharaṇaṃ (the seizing of all wealth), parassaharaṇaṃ (the seizing of another's wealth)," and so on.
These are the illustrative words. In this context, *saṃ* means "of a person" (*manussassa*), thus *parassaṃ* means "of another," and *sabbassaṃ* means "of all.
The compound *parassaharaṇaṃ* (the taking away of another's) and *sabbassaharaṇaṃ* (the taking away of all) is formed in this way.
Likewise, *saṃ* is said to mean both happiness (*sukha*) and peace (*santi*). For its denotative nature has been stated in an ancient poetic composition:
“He is the God of Gods, free from doubt; he is inferior to none, yet superior to the gods.
Having destroyed the cycle of rebirth and transmigration, may that Essence grant security to embodied beings.
Therefore, this is the verse here: regarding the phrase “Saṅkara Dīpaṅkara,” the word “Saṅkara” is an indication [of his name].
“Saṃ, sāni, sā; saṃ, sāni, se; sena,” and so forth, should be understood according to the method previously explained.

And here, for the sake of generating proficiency among listeners in this most excellent teaching of the Sugata, we shall provide a complete declensional paradigm of the word *saṃ* occurring at the end of a compound, and explain it as follows:
Manussassaṃ, manussassāni, manussassā. Manussassaṃ, manussassāni, manussasse. Manussassena, manussassehi, manussassebhi. Manussassassa, manussassānaṃ.
Manussassā, manussassasmā, manussassamhā, manussassehi, manussassebhi. Manussassassa, manussassānaṃ. Manussasse.
*Manussassamhi*, *manussassamhi*, *manussassesu*. *Bho manussassa*, *bhonto manussassāni*, *manussassā*.
This same method applies to “*parassaṃ sabbassa*” and so forth; all these words should be understood as taking the gender of the object they denote.
That which belongs to the interrogative pronouns (*kiṃ*-words) is the list of names consisting of seventy-two.
In the section on all nouns (*sabbanāma-pariccheda*), I shall explain [them] according to their three genders.

Thus, the nominal paradigm for *ko*, *vi*, *sā*, and so forth, which were enumerated above, has been analyzed together with illustrative phrases for various meanings. Herein is the determination of their genders:
*Ko*, *vi*, and *sā* are in the masculine; *bhā*, *rā*, *thī*, *dhī*, *ku*, *bhū*, and *thiyaṃ* are in the feminine.
*Kaṃ* and *khaṃ* are neuter, while *go* is masculine; *ce* is feminine.
*Mo* is masculine, *mā* is feminine, and *saṃ* is both masculine and neuter;
*yaṃ*, *taṃ*, and *kiṃ* function as pronouns across all genders. Thus they proceed according to their respective genders.
From this, other single-syllable [words] should also be examined and grasped.
Thus, for the sake of attaining a supremely pure and vast intelligence regarding the domain of word-formation by the wise who understand the methods,
and for the sake of non-confusion regarding applications involving extremely subtle and delicate meanings, [this work is like] the lion’s yawn upon a golden surface by the maned lion.
Just as there is a stretching out in the Buddha’s word consisting of the Three Piṭakas through the stretching out of knowledge, so too, for the purpose of such a stretching out,
the series of nominal cases is analyzed by mixing the three genders according to the predominance of one or another vowel.
They are skilled in the sound, but not in the meaning.
Wholesome states arise because of meaning, but not at all because of sound.
Skillfulness alone is supreme in both respects;
therefore, the wise should constantly apply themselves to it—so they say.
Thus ends the section on the analysis of nominal word-strings mixed with the three genders,
composed in the *Saddanīti* treatise for the sake of proficiency among the wise in the modes of expression within the Three Piṭakas together with their commentaries.
The Tenth Chapter.
11. The Nominative Paradigm Series: An Exposition of Gender and Other Attributes According to the Designated and the Denoted.
Hereafter follows [the exposition] by way of gender and other attributes of the designated and the denoted.
I shall explain the series of grammatical genders (padamālā) in accordance with what has been stated.
In this context, "genders of the expressed" (vāccaliṅga) refers to those genders that are subordinate, or rather, those genders designated as adjectives (guṇanāma).

"Genders of the denoted" (abhidheyyaliṅga) refers to those genders that are primary, or rather, those genders designated as substantive nouns (guṇīpada). Furthermore, among these, those called "genders of the expressed" are...

[These suffixes] follow the gender of the thing denoted (*abhidheyya*). Therefore, all [words] consisting of the element *bhū* (earth), as well as those whose gender is expressed by the case-ending (*vācya-liṅga*), should be applied according to the gender of the thing denoted.

As for their case-endings (*nāmika-padamālā*) consisting of the element *bhū*, although they have not been formally applied here in their own form, they have been applied in various places according to the underlying method;
therefore, we shall not demonstrate them now. This also applies to those not consisting of the element *bhū*.

Although these have already been applied according to the grammatical rules (*naya*), we shall nevertheless explain them for the sake of generating skill in the practical applications (*payoga*) for listeners;
and while stating some of their applications, we shall also present a series of nouns (*nāmikapadamālā*).
Long, short, blue, yellow.
White and black, good and evil;
faithful and pure, high and low,
"done" and "past," and so forth.
Long is the night for one who is awake; long is the league for one who is weary;
long is saṃsāra for fools who do not understand the True Dhamma.
Dīgho, dīghā. Dīghaṃ, dīghe. Dīghena, dīghehi, dīghebhi. Dīghassa, dīghānaṃ. Dīghā.
Dīghasmā, dīghamhā, dīghehi, dīghebhi. Dīghassa, dīghānaṃ. Dīghe, dīghasmiṃ, dīghamhi, dīghesu.
Bho dīgha, bhavanto dīghā. “‘Dīgha,’ thus you should address me”—this is the illustration here.
Dīghā, dīghā, dīghāyo. Dīghaṃ, dīghā, dīghāyo. Dīghāya. The remainder is to be understood according to the paradigm of *kaññā*.
*Dīgham*, *dīghāni*, *dīghā*. *Dīgham*, *dīghāni*, *dīghē*. *Dīghēna*. The remainder should be understood according to the method for *citta*.
The forms beginning with *rassa* (short) should be expanded in exactly the same way. This is the nominal paradigm for adjectives whose gender is expressed by their declension;
it is appropriate to call it "the nominal paradigm for qualitative adjectives" (*guṇanāmānaṃ nāmikapadamālā*).
Regarding the genders of the meanings [of words], those which indeed possess specific distinctions—
I shall now explain their sequence of terms according to the text.
What are those terms that possess specific distinctions?
"Becoming and non-becoming," "The island of Laṅkā," and so forth;
as well as "Awakening" (bodhi), "conjunction" (sandhi), and so on—these indeed possess specific distinctions.
For among these:
The term *bhavābhava* may be used in the singular or, in some cases, in the plural;
its occurrence is accepted both in compounds and in non-compounds.
Having stated the analysis and the meaning of this word for me, [the following is said]:
Listen attentively as it is being spoken, to this garland of verses.
"Becoming and non-becoming" (*bhavābhava*); or alternatively, "becoming and non-becoming" refers to the plural "becomings and non-becomings"—this is the grammatical analysis (*viggaha*).
In that context, "becoming" (*bhava*) is minor becoming; "non-becoming" (*abhava*) is great becoming. Here, the vowel *a-* has the sense of "growth."
And here, smallness and greatness should be understood by way of happy and miserable destinies, and by way of inferior and superior [states].
Alternatively, "becoming" (*bhava*) means growth; "non-becoming" (*abhava*) means non-growth. This is the meaning of the words.
Now, the series of nominal forms is as follows: *bhavābhavaṃ*, *bhavābhavaṃ*, *bhavābhavena*, *bhavābhavassa*, *bhavābhavā*, *bhavābhavasmā*.
*bhavābhavasmā*, *bhavābhavassa*, *bhavābhave*, *bhavābhavasmiṃ*, *bhavābhavamhi*, *bho bhavābhava*.
Thus, the word *bhavābhava* takes the singular number. Its singular nature is seen both in the Pāḷi and in the Aṭṭhakathā:
"Having set aside [the deeds] performed in past aeons, in each successive existence (*bhavābhave*)."
“In this kappa, I shall declare his conduct; listen to me.
Or: “In this way, manifold suffering and manifold prosperity [have occurred].”
"Having experienced existence after existence, he attained supreme enlightenment"—
thus the singular number of the term *bhavābhava* is seen in the Pāḷi.
And in the Commentary as well:
“Unawakened to that which is practiced by the Buddhas,
the world of living beings goes from existence to existence;
homage to the net of defilements beginning with ignorance— ”
“Of that excellent Dhamma which destroys [defilements]”—
thus its singular number is seen.
*Bhavābhavāni*, *bhavābhavā*, *bhavābhavāni*, *bhavābhave*, *bhavābhavehi*, *bhavābhavebhi*.
*bhavābhavānaṃ*, *bhavābhavehi*, *bhavābhavabhi*, *bhavābhavānaṃ*, *bhavābhavesu*, *bhavanto bhavābhavāni*.
Thus, the word *bhavābhava* occurs even in the plural. Its plural usage is seen in the Pāḷi: “For the one who has shaken off [defilements], there is nothing anywhere in the world;
for the speculative, there is view regarding states of existence (*bhavābhavesu*)” (Sn 859). Both [the singular and plural] are used.
Having assigned the gender, the series of nominal forms (*nāmikapadamālā*) should be joined. How so? It should be joined according to this method of application (*cittanaya*):
“Bhavābhavaṃ, bhavābhavāni. Bhavābhavaṃ, bhavābhavāni. Bhavābhavena, bhavābhavehi, bhavābhavebhi,” and so forth.
These are the singular and plural forms in the neuter gender.
One should explain how the *Padamālā* was composed.
A wise person should discern that words are of two kinds: compound words and non-compound words;
likewise, words are twofold as those pertaining to existence and non-existence.
The neuter is used for a compound, while the masculine is used for the other [members];
however, one should generally state the neuter in the singular.
"Both existence and non-existence"—thus should the wise man state the meaning of the compound.
The word *bhava* signifies the meaning of existence (*bhava*) when it is not part of a compound;
it should be understood as being in the masculine gender, derived from the ablative or locative case.
Thus, the wise should know the term *bhavābhava* specifically in this way.
Just as the series of nominal forms for the term *bhavābhava* has been applied here, so too should the series of nominal forms for such terms as *kammākamma*, *phalāphala*, and others be applied.
Their meaning should also be explained as appropriate; generally, these are used in the singular.
Thus, first of all, the specific nature of terms such as *bhavābhava* is to be understood.
Laṅkādīpo, laṅkādīpaṃ, laṅkādīpena, laṅkādīpassa, laṅkādīpā, laṅkādīpasmā, laṅkādīpamhā, laṅkādīpassa, laṅkādīpe, laṅkādīpasmiṃ, laṅkādīpamhi, O Laṅkādīpa!
This is the paradigm of noun cases for the term *laṅkādīpa* when used in composition.
It should also be applied when not in composition.
Laṅkādīpo, laṅkaṃ dīpaṃ, laṅkāya dīpena, laṅkāya dīpassa, laṅkāya dīpā, laṅkāya dīpasmā, laṅkāya dīpamhā, laṅkāya dīpassa, laṅkāya dīpe, laṅkāya dīpasmiṃ, laṅkāya dīpamhi; "O Laṅkādīpa!
This is the nominal paradigm for the expanded form. This same method applies here to the term "Jambudīpo."
The word *jambu* alone does not denote Jambudīpa, because it is not used exclusively for that purpose—just as the word *laṅkā* alone denotes Laṅkādīpa.
However, this method of expanded word-formation (*padamālā*) is particularly beneficial for poets in the composition of poetry and also for the Dispensation (*sāsana*).
Indeed, ancient poetic compositions are seen to employ this method of expansion.
“I pay homage to the mountain Samantakūṭa,
which shines like the crest of the island of Laṅkā,
the dwelling place of the flower-named deity.”
"...that path for the Buddha’s foot-walking.
In the *Sāsana* as well, according to the method of Vyāsa, such scriptural passages (*pāḷi*) are seen as "A divine chariot appeared for the illustrious Videha," and so forth.
However, just as this method is not applicable here in the case of "Jambudīpa," it is likewise [inapplicable] in cases such as "Nāgadīpa" when used alone.
Just as Jambudīpa is not expressed by the word *jambu* alone, so too Nāgadīpa and the others are not expressed by the word *nāga* alone.

But is it not the case, sir, that in the ancient poetic composition, "We, the people of Jambu, bow to that tooth of the Buddha who shines like the Jambu river," the word *jambu* denotes Jambudīpa because the meaning "people of Jambudīpa" is possible? True; [the phrase] "people of Jambudīpa" [is used].
The meaning arises; however, the word *jambu* alone does not express the sense of Jambudīpa.

Rather, where one ought to say "the people of Jambudīpa" (*jambudīpanarā*), because it falls within the scope of a verse, the word *dīpa* was elided to avoid the fault of excessive syllables, and thus it was stated as "the Jambu-people" (*jambunarā*).
In this way, the word *jambu*, being spoken with the elision of the latter member of the compound, [conveys its meaning] by the power of the compound in dependence upon the word *nara*.
“Jambudīpanara” means one who is capable of elucidating the meaning, not merely at the time of recitation.
For instance, when “jambu” is mentioned, Jambudīpa is not understood; rather, only the jambu tree is understood.
But, sir, is this grammatical rule applicable in cases such as “kāko dāso,” “kākaṃ dāsaṃ,” or “kākena dāsenā”? It is not applicable.
It is possible; by means of the word "crow," there occurs the mention of a slave named Crow.
If that is so, might one not also take the meaning of "Jambudīpa" here to be "the island named Jambu," and thus apply this same method: "Jambū-dīpo," "jambuṃ dīpaṃ," or "jambuyā dīpena"?
This is not possible, because the word "jambu" does not function with respect to the island in the sense of a conventional designation (paṇṇatti).
For the word *jambu* occurs by way of conventional designation (*paṇṇatti*) only for the tree, not for the island. However,
just as the term *citta* occurs for both the householder named Citta and for the mind— as in "Citta the householder" and "mind, thought, ideation"—
and just as the term *kusa* occurs for both the king named Kusa and for the *kusa* grass— so too [is the case here].
“Taking Pabhāvati and the Verocana jewel,
King Kusa of great power went to Kusāvatī.
Just as a blade of kusa grass, if grasped incorrectly, cuts the very hand that holds it.”
In these cases, the word *kāka* applies both to a crow and to a slave of that name, as in such expressions as "the crow caws" or "the slave named Kāka travels sixty leagues," and so forth.

However, the word *jambu*, like the words *citta*, *kusa*, and *kāka*, does not apply to the island by way of designation (*paṇṇatti*)—as it might to a householder, a tree, etc.; therefore, one should attend to the method exactly as it has been stated.
Just as the nominal declension of the word "Laṅkādīpa" (the island of Laṅkā) has been applied here both through compounds and through analytical expansions,
so too should the nominal declensions of such terms as "Pubbavidehadīpa" (the eastern continent), "Aparagoyānadīpa" (the western continent), "Uttarakurudīpa" (the northern continent),

"Assayujakkhattaṃ" (the constellation Assayuja), "Citramāso" (the month Citra), "Vessantararājā" (King Vessantara), "Setavatthaṃ" (the white cloth), and "Dibbaratho" (the divine chariot) be understood through their compounds.

And they should be analyzed according to their expansion (*byāsa*). It should also be understood that by means of terms such as "Pubbavideha," the islands of Pubbavideha and so forth are being described.
Furthermore, it should be understood that when there is a purpose for compound words such as "divine chariot" (*dibbaratha*), they may be separated individually through analysis;
for instance, by way of analysis, one may express them as two separate words in apposition, such as "a divine [chariot]" (*dibbo ratho*).

When there is the state of being joined with the *pacceka-vibhatti* (the singular case ending), there arises the merit of preserving the euphonic junction (*vutti*), maintaining the meter, and facilitating easy pronunciation within verses.

Furthermore, this method has been established as being in conformity with the Dispensation (*sāsana*). For indeed, many such scriptural passages (*pāḷi*) are seen in the Word of the Buddha (*pāvacana*), such as: “A divine chariot appeared for the illustrious Vedeha. In this way, words such as *Laṅkādīpa* (the island of Laṅkā) acquire their specific significance.
Now, the distinction between *bodhi*, *sandhi*, and so forth is stated:
*Bodhi*, *sandhi*, *vibhatta*, *āyu*, *dhātu*, and *pajāpati*;
*dāma*, *dāma*, likewise *saddhā*, *saddha*, *taṭa*, *taṭī*, and *taṭo*.
The letter is the letter, the meaning is the meaning; the syllable is the syllable, the meaning is the syllable;
uprightness is uprightness, and likewise gentleness and reverence.
"Speech" and "speech-act," and so forth—these are identical in form according to their similarity.
Two genders occur; they should be pointed out according to their occurrence.
For among these, first regarding the word *bodhi*: as in “*Bodhi* the prince,” and “the noble disciple is called ‘*bodhi*’;
a factor of that *bodhi* is a *bojjhaṅga* (enlightenment factor),” thus it is a term for a person: *bodhi*, *bodhī*, *bodhayo*.
*Bodhiṃ*, *bodhī*, *bodhayo*. With *bodhinā*—thus is the nominal paradigm in the masculine gender according to the pattern of *aggi*.

However, for the word denoting the tree, the path, Nibbāna, or omniscient knowledge, the nominal paradigm in the feminine gender according to the pattern of *ratti* is: *bodhi*, *bodhī*, *bodhiyo*; *bodhiṃ*, *bodhī*, *bodhiyo*; *bodhiyā*.
Some, however, say that the word *bodhi* denoting a tree is masculine; that appears to contradict the traditional authority (*āgama*).
This must be investigated by way of observation. For in the traditional texts (āgama), the masculine gender of the word *bodhi* when it denotes a tree is not observed;
however, its masculine gender is observed when it denotes a person.

And if the word *bodhi*, when denoting a tree, were to possess a masculine gender—just as in the case of "sāla, dhava, khadira," and so on—then words such as *jambū*, *simbalī*, and *pāṭalī* would also possess a masculine gender, because they denote trees.
It might be argued that even though these words denote a tree, their masculine gender is not observed. For if the word *bodhi*,
when denoting a tree, were masculine, then the word *bodhi*— when denoting Nibbāna and omniscient knowledge— would have to be neuter,
because it expresses meanings such as Nibbāna which are indicated in the neuter gender, as in the expression "Nibbānam" and so forth.
Those who say, "The word *bodhi* refers to a tree and is masculine," should keep in mind the meaning already stated: "Bodhi is said to be the knowledge in the four paths;
since the Blessed One has attained that here, even the tree is called 'Bodhi'.
Thus, by way of this derivation—"it is awakened to (*bujjhati*) here, therefore it is *bodhi*"—they ask: "Does the word *bodhi* refer to a tree?"
"They say this, thinking, 'It will not be masculine. It should not be viewed in that way; rather, it should be viewed thus:
'Enlightenment (bodhi) is said to be the knowledge in the four paths. Since the Blessed One has attained that here, even the tree is called "enlightenment" (bodhi),' so say the teachers.
[They hold] that the word for knowledge, which is feminine in gender, is 'bodhi'. Of that knowledge—

The word *bodhi* is spoken of as "the tree" by superimposing it upon a tree that serves as a locus for awakening, while one imagines a meaning through the conceptualization of a name and a designation;
therefore, in such instances, no strict adherence to the etymological derivation should be made.
For the act of deriving it as "that wherein one awakens is *bodhi*" does not establish the masculine gender of the word *bodhi* when it refers to a tree.

Because conventional usage is established by convention, one is able to do so; therefore, although the tree itself is not enlightenment, the members of the Dispensation (sāsanika) refer to it by the feminine designation "Bodhi" through a convention established by agreement, because it is the place where enlightenment was attained.
Or, because it is the cause of enlightenment, they refer to it by the designation of the fruit. It is with reference to this very point that it is said: "Enlightenment is called [the four...]"
It should be understood that this was said because the Blessed One has attained the knowledge of the paths;
thus, the name of the tree occurs as "bodhi" by way of the feminine gender.

Therefore, the Venerable Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, who turns the wheel in accordance with the Dhamma and is skilled in conventional usage, [spoke] by way of the feminine grammatical designation: "Of the Buddhas..."
“At the root of the Bodhi tree, together with the attainment of omniscient knowledge, the realization was designated for the Blessed Ones as ‘the Buddha.
Furthermore, in various places there, it is said: “a branch of the Bodhi,” and “in what sense is it the Great Bodhi, and to whom does it belong?”
“Just as soon as it was released from his hand, it rose eighty cubits into the sky and then emitted beautiful rays of six colors.
Such are the usages seen where the word *bodhi*, denoting a tree, appears in the feminine gender.
Alternatively, the word *bodhi*, denoting a tree, is of two genders according to its masculine and feminine forms.

For instance, in the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya, such a verbal construction is seen from the master Buddhaghosa, who was a great grammarian well-versed in the methods of the Pāli:
"My dear, will you be able to go to Pāṭaliputta and [bring back] the noble Therī Saṅghamittā together with the Mahābodhi?"

And regarding the phrases, “Let it be brought,” and “That ship, having embarked upon the Great Enlightenment (mahābodhi), plunged into the surface of the great ocean while the Great King was looking on”—by means of the etymological derivation of that tree-denoting word *bodhi* as “that wherein one awakens (*bujjhati*) is *bodhi*,” the series of nominal forms (*padamālā*) should be understood as follows:
*bodhi*, *bodhī*, *bodhayo*; *bodhim*, *bodhī*, *bodhayo*; *bodhinā*, and so forth.

Furthermore, for that word denoting a tree, the paradigm of forms should be understood as follows—by way of the neuter gender usage occurring in its knowledge [of the state], established by convention and indicating a conventional meaning:
"bodhi, bodhī, bodhiyo; bodhiṃ, bodhī, bodhiyo; bodhiyā," and so forth. Thus, in this manner—the word *bodhi* denoting a person would be masculine.
A word denoting knowledge and so forth shall always be feminine in gender.
A word denoting the Bodhi tree may be masculine or feminine;
nevertheless, this [word "Bodhi"] is indeed feminine in gender.
Since that which is more desirable has been stated by the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta), the nominal paradigm for words such as *saṇdhi* should also be constructed according to the same method.

For the word *saṇdhi* is masculine when denoting "conjunction" (*sarasandhi*) and so forth, as seen in forms such as *saṇdhino* and *saṇdhiyā*; however, it is feminine when denoting "rebirth-linking" (*paṭisandhi*) and so forth. As for the word *vibhatti*...

The word *vibhatti* is feminine when denoting case-division (*vibhajanavācaka*), and masculine as well as feminine when denoting the nominal suffixes (*syādivācaka*), as seen in such forms as *vibhattissa* and *vibhattiyā*.

The word *āyu*, however, is neuter only when denoting the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), as seen in such passages as “O worthy ones, know this: I have regained my life-span again” and “Your life-span is only this much; the time of your passing away will come.”

The word *dhātu* is feminine when denoting intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) and so forth; it is both masculine and feminine when denoting a hand, a foot, and so on, as seen in the examples: “of the eye-element (*cakkhudhātuyā*), of this element (*karotissa dhātussa*), [and] ‘the elements (*dhātuyo*), the element (*dhātuyā*)’.
The word *pajāpati* is masculine when denoting a particular deity, as seen in:

“you should look up at the crest of the banner of the king of gods, Pajāpati”; it is feminine when denoting a wife, a conqueror, or a paternal aunt, as seen in: “together with her own wife, Mahāpajāpatī,” and so forth.
The words *dāmā* and *dāma* are feminine and neuter genders respectively for a single object that is distinguished by various types such as *mālatī-dāma* (jasmine garland) and so forth.

For instance, worldling usage (*lokiyappayoga*) consistent with the Teaching (*sāsana*) is seen in the occurrence of both genders, as in: “The jasmine garland is playful like the sport of a bee’s antennae” (*mālatīdāmā lolāliṅgalīlā*); “a jasmine garland” (*mālatīdāma*); “a garland humming with bees” (*siṅghitaṃ dāma bhamarehi*);
and “jewel garlands” (*ratanadāmā*) and “a jewel garland” (*ratanadāma*). Thus, these usages are observed to conform to the grammatical tradition.
However, the word *saddha*—referring to faith as the basis for various things—is feminine and neuter in gender;
the word *saddhā*, signifying clarity (*pasāda*), is feminine; and the word *saddhaṃ*, signifying funeral offerings (*matakabhatta*), is neuter, as seen in such expressions as:
“Faith is believing. We, the Brahmins named Assubho Gotamo, give gifts and perform acts of faith (*saddhāni*).”
In this context, however, the terms "faithful man" (*saddho puriso*), "faithful woman" (*saddhā itthī*),

and "faithful family" (*saddhaṃ kulaṃ*) should be understood as not being included [in the grammatical gender classification] because they possess variable genders (*vācya-liṅga*). The words *taṭaṃ*, *taṭī*, and *taṭo*— all signifying a bank— are feminine, masculine, and neuter respectively, yet they refer to one and the same object, namely, the shore.
The word *byañjana* (condiment/sign) is neuter when it denotes a condiment, a sexual characteristic, a sentence, a unique quality, or a limb of the body;
it is both masculine and neuter when denoting a syllable (*akkhara*). Regarding its use as a condiment, the neuter designation is seen in the expression:

"either broth or *byañjana*. Likewise, regarding sexual characteristics, the neuter designation occurs in: "the female characteristic (*itthibyañjana*) and the male characteristic (*purisabyañjana*). Regarding a sentence, [it is used in]: "words and *byañjanas* (*padabyañjanāni*)."
"Having mastered it thoroughly"—this is a neuter gender designation. Regarding the unique [marks], there is the neuter designation "eighty minor marks" (*anubyañjanāni*).

Regarding the parts of the body, there is the neuter designation: "because they make manifest, part by part (*anu anu*), the manifestation of the defilements, they are called 'minor marks' (*anubyañjana*).
For here, what is called a "minor mark" consists of the various distinctions such as hands, feet, smiles, laughter, speech, and glances.

The term *ākāra* means "body part"; it is precisely this that is called a "limb of the body. Regarding the word *akkhara*, the term *byañjana* (consonant) is used as a masculine or neuter designation.

The word *attha* (meaning/purpose), when referring to *nibbāna*, is neuter; however, when it refers to the signified object, wealth, cause, purpose, protection, intention, and so forth, it is masculine.
For instance, in the commentary on the passage from the *Kathāvatthu*, "atthatthamhi," [it is explained as follows]:
The word *attha* is stated with a neuter gender designation in the passage, “*atthaṃ vuccati nibbānan*. Thus, the word *attha* is of two genders.

As for the word *akkhara*, it is seen from such instances as “the first syllable (*pubbo akkharo*)” and “syllables (*akkharāni*)”; furthermore, the word *akkhara*—when it denotes Nibbāna and when it denotes a name or a conventional designation—is always neuter, as in:
“the unshakable state, the syllable (*padamaccutamakkharaṃ*), which is honored by the great multitude.”
In such passages as, "Vāseṭṭha, the syllable ‘Mahāsammata’ was indeed the first to arise," [the term *akkhara*] is used.

Furthermore, in the rule, "He teaches by means of a syllable; for each syllable, there is an offense of *pācittiya*," it may be described as having either the masculine gender or the neuter gender, but it must not be described as having the feminine gender.
For this [term] is [used in the sense of]: "And you were not honored by Dhanañjaya. May the venerable ones refrain... [and so on].

In such phrases as "for my word" (*mamavacanāya*), the words are expressed with a shift in case-ending (*vibhattivipallāsa*), just as in the expressions "for Dhanañcaya" (*dhanañcayāya*) and "for the word" (*vacanāya*);
they are not used by way of a shift in gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*).

However, the words *ajjava*, *maddava*, and *gārava* possess both masculine and neuter genders, as seen in such instances as: "Rectitude and gentleness" (*ajjavo ca maddavo ca*), "Rectitude-and-gentleness" (*ajjavamaddavaṃ*); and "Veneration and humility" (*gāravo ca nivāto ca*), as well as: "When the stupa was brought to mind together [with these], then I felt veneration" (*saha āvajjite thūpe, gāravaṃ hoti me tadā*).
However, the words *vāc* and *vācī* possess masculine and feminine genders respectively, just like the words *ghaṭo* and *ghaṭī*.
In that regard, the nominal paradigm for the word *vāc* should be constructed as follows: "vācī, vācī, vāciyo; vāciṃ, vācī, vāciyo; vāciyā.

Some maintain that when followed by other words such as *duccarita-payoga-viññatti-sadda*, the final vowel of the word *vācas* becomes long *ī*; thus, forms such as "vācī-duccaritaṃ" and others are seen.

They say [this], but that should not be accepted, because we see the word *vaci* appearing separately from the word *vacī*. Here are illustrative passages from both the Canon (*pāḷi*) and the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*):
“Speech (*vacī*), the volitional formation of speech (*vacī-saṅkhāra*); the volitional formation of speech is speech (*vacī*).

Apart from both speech and the volitional formation of speech, the remainder is neither speech nor the volitional formation of speech. [It is] uttered by means of speech (*vacībhi*)."... [and so forth].
“Be mindful and rejoice”—these are the illustrative phrases from the *pāḷi*. “That which is called ‘co-presentation’ is speech itself as intimation, thus it is ‘vocal intimation’ (*vacīviññatti*);
the differentiation of speech is ‘vocal differentiation’ (*vacībhedo*)”—these are the illustrative phrases from the *aṭṭhakathā*.
In this manner, the dual or triple gender of other words—both those that are identical in form (*sarūpa*) and those that are not (*asarūpa*)—should be determined as appropriate. Thus...
Among the genders of the expressed meaning, the genders of the expressed meaning should be understood as having specific distinctions.

Now, the nominal paradigm for words such as *dhamma* is stated, according to which the gender of the expressed meaning and the gender of the word-form (the grammatical gender) may sometimes differ. For instance:
*Dhammā bho puggalā ceva, dhammapuggalatopi ca;* (O sirs, the phenomena and the persons, both from the perspective of phenomena and persons).
From both the absolute Dhamma and likewise from absolute individuals,
there may be chains of words (*padamālā*) according to the cases beginning with the nominative (*paccatta*);
one should know that these words may be even, uneven, or even in every respect.
How so? The nominal declension for these terms—*micchādiṭṭhi*, *micchāsaṅkappo*, *micchāvācā*, *micchāvāco*, *micchādiṭṭhiko*, and *micchāsaṅkappī*—should be understood as follows.
In terms of the phenomenon (*dhammato*), it is: *micchādiṭṭhi*, *micchādiṭṭhī*, *micchādiṭṭhiyo*; *micchādiṭṭhiṃ*, *micchādiṭṭhī*, *micchādiṭṭhiyo*;
*micchādiṭṭhiyā*. In terms of the person (*puggalato*), it is: *micchādiṭṭhi*, *micchādiṭṭhī*, *micchādiṭṭhino*; *micchādiṭṭhiṃ*.
"Wrong view, those with wrong view; by means of wrong view"—thus from the perspective of the person (*puggala*).
"Wrong intention, those with wrong intention; wrong intention"—thus from the perspective of both phenomena and persons (*dhamma-puggala*).
"Wrong speech, wrong speeches, wrong speeches; wrong speech, wrong speeches, wrong speeches; by means of wrong speech"—thus exclusively from the perspective of phenomena (*ekanta-dhamma*).
“Micchāvāco, micchāvācā; micchāvācaṃ, micchāvāce; micchāvācena”—thus it is a nominal series from the perspective of a single individual;
likewise, “micchādiṭṭhiko, micchādiṭṭhikā, micchādiṭṭhikaṃ”—this too is from the perspective of a single individual;
and likewise, “micchāsaṅkappī, micchāsaṅkappino, micchāsaṅkappi”—this too is a nominal series from the perspective of a single individual.
Furthermore, a word may be similar, dissimilar, or entirely identical according to the distinctions of person, usage, number, and so forth.
This same method applies to right view, right intention, and the rest.
Here are some examples of such applications as they have been spoken: "Monks, in one who is immersed in ignorance and lacks true knowledge, wrong view arises."
In one of wrong view, wrong intention arises. In one of wrong intention, wrong speech arises. In one of wrong speech, wrong action arises.
In one of wrong action, wrong livelihood arises. In one of wrong livelihood, wrong effort arises.
In one of wrong effort, wrong mindfulness arises. In one of wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration arises.
“Monks, for one who has reached true knowledge and is possessed of vision, right view arises. For one with right view, right intention arises,” and so on in detail.

Thus, in some instances, the series of nominal forms—consisting of words whose gender follows that of the suffix, those whose gender follows the meaning expressed, and those whose gender follows that of a secondary derivative (taddhita)—has been explained along with their grammatical applications.

Now, we shall explain certain distinctions among these: the word *bhavitabba* (which must take the gender of its referent), the words *sotthi* and *suvatthi* (which take the gender of their referents), the word *abbhuta* (which takes both the gender of its expressed object and the gender of its own referent), and the word *abhūta* (which takes the gender of its own referent);
and we shall also apply the sequence of nominal suffixes (*nāmikapadamālā*) as appropriate. For among these:
The word *bhavitabba* is a neuter gender term expressing absolute necessity (*ekantabhāva*), and it occurs only in the singular number.
It is to be construed with third-case endings as well as with words such as *evaṃ* and *na*. It does not admit of a nominal series (*nāmikapadamālā*);
here are some examples of its usage: "One must be one who values the true Dhamma, not one who values material things; this must be a thief."
"It must be these thieves; it must be this thievery; it must be these female thieves;
it must be with this mind; it must be with these minds; it must be thus; it must be otherwise. Regarding this, it is said:
The term "must be" (bhavitabba) is constant In the supreme teaching of the Omniscient One.
The first singular form is neuter and expresses a state of being.
A wise person should understand that it is connected with the third-person pronouns such as *evaṃ* (thus) and others; knowing this, one should discern [the grammatical application].
This is the specific application of the word *bhavitabba*.
*Sotthi bhaddante hotu rañño*, *sotthiṃ gacchati nhāpito*, *sotthināmhi samuṭṭhito*. *Suvatthi*, *suvatthiṃ*, *suvatthinā*: this is the specific application of words such as *dha-sātthi*.

However, this is the distinction between the two words *abbhuta* and *abhūta*. The substitution of *bbhū* for the word *bhū* occurs when followed by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), serving the purpose of prohibition.

When the particle *eti* follows as an upapada, it invariably undergoes shortening (*rassatta*). In what sense? In senses such as "that which was not previously become has become" (*abhūtapubbaṃ bhūtaṃ*).
In such cases, however, when followed by a non-conjunct consonant (*asañyoga*), it does not undergo shortening. In what sense? In senses such as "untruth" (*asacca*).
For instance, the word *abbhuta* has the meaning "that which was not previously become has become," and it also has the meaning "a marvelous deed" (*abbhutakaraṇa*).
The meaning is "existent. Furthermore, for the word *abhūta*, the meaning is also "untrue," and the meaning is also "unborn.
In that regard, expressions such as "It is wonderful indeed, sir! It is marvelous indeed, sir! A marvel indeed in the world, a wonder that makes the hair stand on end!
are instances where it is used in the sense of "having become what had not been before" (*abhūtapubbaṃ bhūtaṃ*).
“You cling to me as a serpent,
I to you as a female frog;
let there be something wonderful between us.”

“With five thousand,” and so forth—these are applications in the sense of performing a marvel. Thus, by way of short vowels, and by way of long vowels, in the absence of a conjunct consonant (nissaṃyoga), there are applications in the sense of non-truth, such as “unreal (abhūtaṃ), untrue (atacchaṃ), not-so (atathaṃ),” and so forth;
and [there are applications] in the sense of non-existence, such as “unbecome (abhūtaṃ), unborn (ajātaṃ), unarisen (asañjātaṃ).”
Such are the applications [of the term] in the sense of "not having been born. Regarding this, there are the following verses:
"That which has never before been, has now come to be"—in this sense, the word *abbhuta* is used;
it should be understood by the wise as established in its short vowel form.
In the sense of "producing the wonderful," the word *abbhuta* is likewise established with a short vowel; thus the wise should discern it.
However, when it is spoken with a long vowel as *abhūta*, it means "that which has not come to be."
The word *pada* denotes that which is to be attained and that which is not false or born. Regarding the term *abbhuta*:

- In the neuter gender (*cittanaya*), it is *abbhutaṃ* (singular) and *abbhutāni* (plural). - In the masculine gender (*purisanaya*), it is *abbhuto* (singular), *abbhutā* (dual), and *abbhutā* or *abbhutāyo* (plural).
- In the feminine gender (*kaññānaya*), it should be understood as *abbhutaṃ*. In this same manner, the nominal declension (*nāmikapadamālā*) of the word *bhūta* is also to be known.
It should be understood in three ways. Here, the word *abbhuta* takes both the gender of the grammatical subject (*vācya-liṅga*) and the gender of the referent (*abhidheyya-liṅga*).
However, the word *abhūta*—like the word *sacca*—may take either the gender of the grammatical subject or the gender of the referent in certain instances.
Thus, this noun series (*nāmika-padamālā*), together with its appropriate applications, has been explained accordingly.
Now, for the sake of generating proficiency among those who follow the traditional texts (āgamika), the nominal paradigm (nāmikapadamālā) is stated by way of the combination of words:

Following this method, in other instances as well, one should consider [the forms] according to the combination of words (*padasamodhāna*), and by way of gender, number, and case.

Herein, the phrase "humans are born there, without 'mine,' without possessions" is an illustration from the Teaching (*sāsana*).
However, the phrase "without 'mine,' without ego" (*amamo nirahaṅkāro*) is an illustration from the world (*loka*). When the feminine gender is to be expressed, [the forms are] *amamā*, *amamā*.
The series of words for the masculine is: *amamāyo*. When speaking in the neuter, the series of words is: *amamaṃ*, *amamāni*.
In that context, one who cries out, "This is mine, this is mine," is called a *mayhaka*; it is a particular kind of bird. For this is said in the Jātaka:
"A bird named Mayhaka, wandering in the mountain valleys..."
“Having climbed upon a ripe *pippali* tree, she cries out, ‘Mine!
Mine! When the feminine gender is to be expressed, the paradigm is: *mayhakī*, *mayhakī*, *mayhakiyo*. In that context, *āmā* means “yes”;
she acknowledges her status as a slave, saying, “Yes, I am your slave,” thus she is *āmā*. She is a domestic slave. For this has been stated in the *Jātakas*:
“Where a slave born of a mother [is], standing, he goes to the large [places]”; and “In the world, there are even slaves born of a mother.
Therefore, these alone are the illustrative phrases here.
Now, the distinction between the words *kati*, *katipaya*, and *katimi* will be stated, as well as their respective noun declension series (*nāmikapadamālā*), as appropriate. Therein:
The nominal paradigm (nāmikapadamālā) of the word *katimi* is not obtained, because it occurs merely as a question, such as: “Today, venerable sir, which [day] is it?

How many women? How many clans? How many flaws in the world where the mind does not abide?

By how many is one stained, and by how many is one purified? How many men? How many women?
A few minds. Now, these are the nominal declensions:
*kati*. [Instrumental] *katīhi*, *katibhi*. [Genitive] *katinaṃ*. [Locative] *katisu*. [Feminine nominative] *katipayā*.

All these should be understood according to the seven case endings; furthermore, in the rules for compound formation (*samāsa-vidhi*), the words *kati* and *katipaya* must be employed only in the plural.
As in: “The bhikkhu who has transcended the *kati-saṅga* is one who has crossed the flood.”

Now, the declensional series (*nāmika-padamālā*) of conventional terms (*rūḷhi-sadda*) is stated: here, conventional terms refer to words such as *yevāpanaka* (inclusionary) and others.
*Yevāpanako*, *yevāpanakā*; *yevāpanakaṃ*; *yevāpano*, *yevāpanā*; *yevāpanaṃ*; *yaṃvāpanakaṃ*, *yaṃvāpanakāni*.

There are mindless phenomena that have arisen dependently”—thus it is called *yevāpanaka* by means of the phrase *yevāpanā*; the same applies here to the term *yevāpano*.

This method should be applied accordingly to terms such as *yassakaṃ*, *yatthakaṃ*, and so forth.

Here it might be asked: "But surely, sir, the word *pana* is a particle (*nipāta*), and it is established that particles are indeclinables (*abyaya*) because they lack gender and number across the three genders and all case-endings and numbers;

however, it occurs in such expressions as “*ye vā pana tasmiṃ samaye*” (“or whatever [factors] at that time”) and “*yaṃ vā panaññampi*” (“or whatever else”).

In expressions such as “*vā*, ‘brāhmaṇā panā’ (*or*, ‘the brahmins indeed’”), it is a particle; however, in expressions such as “*yevāpanako*” (*and so forth*) or “*yevāpano*” (*and so forth*), it is not called a particle.
For this is merely an imitation; therefore, in such cases, constructions accompanied by the word *pana* should be understood as conventional terms (*rūḷhisadda*).
If this is so, why was the etymological analysis (*nibbacana*) cited? It is for the purpose of making the meaning clear.

In that context, “you claim to be a Fully Awakened One” (*sambuddho paṭijānāsi*) should be understood as meaning “you claim, ‘I am a Fully Awakened One’,” by way of the elision of the particle *iti*. This...
This method [of interpretation] also applies in cases such as, “You claim to be a farmer,” and so forth.

However, in the phrase, “Of you who claim to be a perfectly enlightened Buddha (*sammāsambuddha*),” there occurs a different arrangement of words by means of applying the elision of the particle *iti*—namely, “of you who claim, ‘I am a perfectly enlightened Buddha’”—and through that very [change], there arises a different penetration of the meaning.
This same principle applies in cases such as, “Of you who claim to be one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*),” and so forth.

The same method applies here. In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, regarding the phrase "claiming to be a Perfectly Enlightened One," the meaning stated as "of you who claim, 'I am a Perfectly Enlightened One;
