Having understood this kind of matter, a son of good family belonging to the class of the wise should not say, when we speak to him, "I am a Perfectly Enlightened One."
Regarding the meaning "you claim," this series of words should be defined using active verbal forms:

It is established in you who claim to be a Perfectly Enlightened One. Likewise, it should be expanded upon with such statements as, "You claim to be one whose taints are destroyed," and so forth.

Becoming many, and having become many, they become one and stand as monks.
Having been one, he sees a monk becoming many; having been many, he sees monks becoming one. Having been one, he sees [monks] becoming many;
having been many, he sees [monks] becoming one. Having been one, he becomes many; having become many... one.
The Dhamma was taught by a monk who, having been one, became many; it was also taught by monks who, having been many, became one.

The rest is to be expanded in detail. O, you who, having been one, become many, and having been many...
"Having become one, you, as a bhikkhu, teach the Dhamma; and may you, sirs, having been even one, become many, and having been many, become one again—teach the Dhamma.

"In this case, Kevaṭṭa, a bhikkhu experiences various kinds of psychic power (iddhividha). Being one, he becomes many..."

"Having become many, he becomes one; [he appears and disappears]... Then a certain person, faithful and confident, sees that bhikkhu experiencing various kinds of psychic power (iddhividha): being one, becoming many;
and having been many, becoming one again. This is the Kevaṭṭa Sutta.

For here, the term *ekoekāya* should be understood as a conventional expression (*rūḷhīpada*) similar to an indeclinable (*abyayapada*), and it should be recognized that it attains the status of a single word, just like the word *aññamañña*.
In this context—“a bhikkhu, being alone without a companion, together with a single woman”—the phrase *eko ekāya* (alone with one) should be understood as not being a conventional term (*rūḷhipada*).
Even so, the word *eko* is not in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the word *bhikkhu*.
If it were in apposition, expressions such as “sitting down” and so forth would be untenable.
It may be so. Furthermore, the word “ekāya” (by one) is not in grammatical apposition with the unstated word “itthiyā” (by a woman).
If it were in apposition, the term “mātugāmena” (by a woman) would not need to be stated, because there would be no distinction [between the two] and it would result in a tautology.
Moreover, since “mātugāmena” has already been stated, “ekenā” (by one) ought to have been said; however, absolutely—
The phrase “one with one” (*ekoekāya*) refers to the meaning designated as male and female, not to a term in grammatical apposition.
Therefore, it should be understood that this is a single compound word— just like the word “mutually” (*aññamañña*) in expressions such as “the husband and wife converse with each other”—
and that it functions as an adjective qualifying the monk who is sitting down.
Alternatively, when there is an act of sitting in which the monk is alone and the woman is also alone, that act is called "one with one" (*ekoekā*) by way of conventional usage (*rūḷhī*).
The meaning should be understood as: "by such an act of sitting, 'one with one,' together with a woman.
In this manner, the nominal declension series (*nāmikapadamālā*) for other conventional terms (*rūḷhīsaddā*) should also be applied according to the requirements of the context.

It should be applied according to the singular and plural numbers. Thus has the series of nominal declensions for the gender and other attributes of words and their meanings been explained in its various modes.

and neuter nouns composed of the earth element (*bhūdhātu*) has been shown in various ways, as appropriate, along with other genders, other words,

12. The Series of Nouns with Names Similar to All Pronouns:
Hereafter I shall explain the pronoun (sabbanāma) and its equivalents, as well as nouns specifically joined with various other nouns.
Those which possess the three genders and those which are concordant with them—
these words are distinguished by name among the three genders.
In terms of meaning, they are simply called "names" (nāma) because they are common to all [the genders].
All nouns are said to be twenty-seven in number.
Among them, some are joined with verbal roots (*rūpa*), while the rest are joined with other [elements].
Furthermore, some are joined with both; this is their defining characteristic.
A word that is free from this characteristic is not a pronoun (*sabbanāmika*);
therefore, words such as *atīta* (past) and so forth are called adjectives (*guṇanāma*).
Pronouns (*sabbanāma*) are as follows: *sabba*, *katara*, *katama*, *ubhaya*, *itara*, *añña*, *aññatara*, *aññatama*, *pubba*, *para*.
"Other," "south," "north," "below," "extent"—these are as follows: "this one," "such-and-such a person," "one," "both," "two," "four," "you," "we"—these are the twenty-seven [instances].

Among these, the word *sabba* has the sense of "all," and it should be understood according to its various applications such as *sabbasabba*. The words *katara* and *katama* have the sense of inquiry. The word *ubhaya* denotes a collection consisting of two parts.
The word *itara* denotes the counterpart of what has been mentioned. The word *añña* denotes something other than what has been attained.

The words *aññatara* and *aññatama* have the sense of indefiniteness. Words such as *pubba* (eastern) and so forth, ending with *uttara* (northern), are designations for the determination of directions, time, and so on.
For instance, when the words *pubba*, *para*, *apara*, *dakkhiṇa*, and *uttara* are in the masculine gender, they denote time, place, and so forth as appropriate;
when in the feminine gender, they denote direction and so forth; and when in the neuter gender, they denote location and so forth. The word *adhara* also expresses the sense of "lower."

It is precisely a term for delimitation (*vavatthā*), and it possesses three genders, as in: "the lower bowl" (*adharaḥ pattaḥ*), "the lower fire-drill" (*adharā araṇī*), and "the lower vessel" (*adharaṃ bhājanam*).
The word *yaṃ* has the sense of indefiniteness. The word *taṃ* refers to what is out of sight. The word *etaṃ* refers to what is near.
The word *imaṃ* refers to what is extremely near. The word *amuṃ* refers to what is distant. The word *kiṃ* has the sense of inquiry. The word *ekaṃ* refers to numbers and the like; for it is said:

"The conditions for these things are 'conditions-by-way-of-this' (*idappaccayā*); the state of being precisely those conditions-by-way-of-this is 'conditionality-by-way-of-this' (*idappaccayatā*); or, the collection of conditions-by-way-of-this is 'conditionality-by-way-of-this'.

And here, in the phrase "the state of being precisely those conditions-by-way-of-this is conditionality-by-way-of-this," the suffix *-tā* functions as a nominalizing particle (*tāsaddena*) upon the word.
There is no difference in meaning whatsoever, just as "devo" (the god) is the same as "devatā" (the deity).

The suffix *-tā* expresses the sense of a collection (*samūha*), as in "idappaccayatā" (conditionality by this), which is a collection of these specific conditions (*idappaccaya*), just as "janatā" (the populace) is a collection of people (*jana*).
In the *Cūḷanirutti* and in the *Niruttipiṭaka*, the word "idaṃ" itself is stated in its base form (*pakatibhāva*).
In a compound, when joined with a following word, the form of the word *idaṃ* becomes *idappaccayatā*;
furthermore, doubling [of the suffix] may occur in subsequent cases.
Now, the nominal paradigm of the word *amu* is stated:

The word *kiṃ* occurs in the sense of reproach, in the sense of indefiniteness, and in the sense of purposelessness; it also functions in the sense of acceptance and inquiry.

"He sleeps happily. What indeed is the reason? "For what reason, mother, do you wipe yourself?

"What sound is associated with which sounds has been seen in the teaching of the Sugata.

Now, since all nouns have been established, one might ask: what specific difference exists in the nominal paradigm (*nāmikapadamālā*) of other words for "bell" (*kaṃsa*) that share the same phonetic form as the aforementioned words?
This has already been explained below in the section on the mixture of the three genders.

However, because they are not universal nouns (*asabbanāmika*), they are analyzed according to the method used for masculine and neuter nouns. For instance, when the word *kosa* denotes the meaning of "Brahmā," "wind," or "body":
The word *kaṃ* signifies the head, hair, and happiness; at that time, those words are not pronouns (*asabbanāmika*). Why?
Because they consist of the sound *kaṃ*, because they are devoid of the unique forms designated as pronominal forms, and because they express a different meaning from the sense of inquiry.
Here, however, the word *ko* is stated as *kaṃ* for the purpose of making known the different meanings by way of their identical phonetic form (*samānasuti*).
However, it should be understood that when used as a pronoun (*sabbanāmika*), only the word *kiṃ* applies, whereas when used as a pure noun (*nāma*), only the word *ka* applies. Thus it is said:

The word *ka* occurs in three senses—referring to the body, the Brahmin, and the wind—and in three genders—masculine, feminine, and neuter. It also occurs in reference to the head, water, and happiness. Thus: In the body, the Brahmin, and the wind; In the head, water, and pleasures;
The word *ka* functions in these three [meanings], Masculine in three, and neuter in three.
In this way, the occurrence of all words that have become nouns (*sabbanāmabhūta*) containing the sound *kiṃ* should be understood.

which brings about the expansion of wisdom— is stated by way of a single portion.

one should [apply] the suffixes *ci*, *can*, and *canaṃ* respectively from the remaining forms as appropriate.
Having set aside [the others], such forms as these should be grasped.

*kismici*, *kesuci*. These should be understood according to the masculine and neuter genders. Here, *kismici* is stated with the elision of the *anusvāra*.

*kāyaci*, *kāhici*; *kāyaci*, *kassāci*, *kāsañci*; *kāyaci*, *kāhici*; *kāyaci*, *kassāci*, *kāsañci*; *kāyaci*, *kāsuci*. These are the forms.

In this regard, such usages as “*iti bhāsanti kecana, na naṃ hiṃsāmi kiñcanan*” (thus some say, I do not harm anything whatsoever) should be understood. Of some. From whomsoever, from anyone. Of whomsoever, of anyone. In whomsoever, in anyone.

Examples such as “there is some jewel in the abode of Dhatarattha,” “whatever wealth here or in the hereafter,” and “whatever forms there may be” should be understood. These are neuter gender forms:
*yā kāci itthī* (any woman), *yā kāci itthiyo* (any women); *yaṃ kiñci* (anything), *yā kāci* (any [feminine thing]); *yāya kāyaci*, *yāhi kāhici*; *yāya*... [and so forth].
*Kāyaci*, *yāsaṃ kāsañci*; *yāya kāyaci*, *yāhi kāhici*; *yāya kāyaci*, *yāsaṃ kāsañci*;
*yāya kāyaci*, *yāsu kāsuci*.
Here, applications such as “whatever feeling (*vedanā*)—past, future, or present”—should be understood. These are feminine gender forms.

Thus, it should be understood that expressions such as *yo koci*, *yā kāci*, and *yaṃ kiñci*, which are stated by way of the three genders, are words that exhaustively include everything without exception.
Furthermore, none of these are indeclinable particles (*nipāta*); they should be understood as verbal forms that resemble indeclinable particles.
If they were indeed indeclinable particles, they would remain uniform in form across the three genders and the seven case-endings; however, they do not.
And because they remain [as such], they are therefore not particles (*nipāta*); rather, they are merely sounds that resemble particles.

Furthermore, those words which are formed by applying the *ttaka* and *katika* suffixes according to gender to the pronouns *ya*, *ta*, *kiṃ*, *eta*, and *icca*, and which arise through the desire to express a specific meaning, are terms of delimitation (*pariccheda-vacana*) and are indeed non-pronominal (*asabbanāmika*). Of these...
The series of nominal words should be applied according to the method of "man," "mind," and "maiden. For example:
*yattako* (as many people), *yattakaṃ* (as much mind), *yattikā* (as many women); *tattako*, *tattakaṃ*, *tattikā*;
*kittako*, *kittakaṃ*, *kittikā*; *ettako*, *ettakaṃ*, *ettikā*. These words, although not all-encompassing pronouns (*asabbanāmika*), [function] by virtue of their grammatical suffixes.
These have been stated for the sake of the proficiency of the wise regarding the various meanings of the word *sambhūta*.
Now, the nominal paradigm (*nāmikapadamālā*) of the word *eka*, which signifies number and so forth, is being stated:

for the word *eka* is a term for number, a term for "unlike," a term for "without companion," a term for "a certain one," and a term for "mixed. When it signifies number, "unlike," or "without companion," it takes the singular number.

*Eko*, *ekaṃ*, *ekena*, *ekassa*, *ekasmā*, *ekamhā*, *ekassa*, *ekasmiṃ*, *ekamhīti*. Thus, the word *eka*, which denotes a number and so forth, is used in the singular. For indeed, in the domain of numbers, the word *eka* is used in the singular alone, as in “one, two, three.
Likewise, even when speaking of a peerless companion—as in “I am the Perfectly Enlightened One, alone” or “O King, I lie down alone”—the word *eka* is used in the singular.
This is the declensional series (*nāmikapadamālā*) for the singular pronoun.
However, when many things that are both "conditioned" (*saṅkhata*) and "without companion" (*asahāya*) are to be expressed, then by adding the letter *k* after the word *eka*, one forms:
*ekakā*, *ekake*, *ekakehi*, *ekakebhi*. This is the declensional series according to the masculine gender in the plural number.
[The term] should be joined [with the suffix -ka]. For indeed, even when used alone, there are many instances. Thus it is said: "There may be four *ekakas*.
There are also many instances where it is used without a companion. For instance, although one ought to say, "This householder also came alone;
this one also came alone," we find the usage "These householders came as *ekakas*. This principle does not apply to the side of all nominal stems (*sabbanāmika*).
It is used because it lacks a unique form [of its own], but it is stated for the purpose of indicating a different meaning.
When it has the sense of "some," then one should say: *eke*, *eke*, *ekehi*, *ebhi*, *ekesaṃ*, *ehi*, *ebhi*, *ekesaṃ*, *ekesu*.
This too is a declensional series (*padamālā*) of a pronominal adjective in the plural. Here, *eke* means "some. This same method applies.
The same applies to *sesa*. However, when it functions as a term denoting a collective (*missībhūta*), then it should be treated according to the masculine paradigm in the plural:
*ekā*, *eke*, *ekehi*, *ekebhi*, *ekānaṃ*. An example is found in the Pāli: “*Pañcālo ca Videho ca, ubho ekā bhavantu te*” (“May both Pañcāla and Videha become one”).
This method does not belong to the category of pronouns (*sabbanāmika*), because it lacks the common form [of pronouns]; rather, it is used for the purpose of indicating a different meaning.
However, it has been said: "Let them become one" (*ekā bhavantu*). Therein, the meaning of the words is: "let them become unified, let them become mixed;
let them indeed flow together and harmonize, like the waters of the Gaṅgā with the waters of the Yamunā.

But the teachers, without showing this distinction, take the word *eka* as being merely a pronoun (*sabbanāma*) and apply the series of nominal case-endings to it just as they do for the word *sabbā*. How so?
Eko, eke. Ekaṃ, eke. Ekena, ekehi, ekebhi. Ekassa, ekesaṃ, ekesānaṃ. Ekasmā, ekamhā, ekehi, ekebhi.
Ekassa, ekesaṃ, ekesānaṃ. Ekasmiṃ, ekamhi, ekesu. This should be understood as the paradigmatic series of forms for the pronoun *eka*.
Some say: "The word *eka* expresses number, equality, lack of companion, and 'other. When it expresses number, then in all cases it takes only the singular ending."

They state that the method of application for the three genders is as follows: "Elsewhere, even when plural, [the forms] *eko*, *ekā*, and *ekaṃ*—and so forth—are identical in all respects to the word *sabba*;
the distinction lies only in the case endings (*saṃsāsu*). However, those who speak thus do so without showing the specific divisions.
We, on the other hand, shall speak while showing the divisions, for the purpose of producing proficiency in practical applications among listeners.

Furthermore, this distinction here should also be noted: "In certain places in the Pāḷi, such as ‘eke ekaṭṭhe same samabhāge,’ even the singular ending of the word *eka* is seen in the form of a feminine noun.
Masculine forms: *ekaṃ*, *ekāni*. *Ekaṃ*, *ekāni*. The rest is the same as the masculine. Therein, *ekāni* means "some. This method applies to the remaining plural forms as well.
Feminine forms: *ekā*, *ekā*, *ekāyo*. *Ekaṃ*, *ekā*, *ekāyo*. *Ekāya*, *ekāhi*, *ekābhi*. *Ekāya*, *ekissā*, *ekāsaṃ*. *Ekāya*,...
*Ekāhi*, *ekābhi*. *Ekāya*, *ekissā*, *ekāsaṃ*. *Ekāya*, *ekāyaṃ*, *ekissaṃ*, *ekāsu*.
Here, in place of the plural, *ekā* means "some," *ekāhi* means "from some," *ekāsaṃ* means "of some," and *ekāsu* means "in some. These are feminine gender forms.
All these pronouns have been stated according to both the singular and the plural.
Furthermore, although one might expect a distributive sense (*vicchā*) to apply to the word *eka*, the forms for all three genders appear only in the singular number.
How so? The masculine gender forms are: *ekeko*, *ekekaṃ*, *ekekena*, *ekekassa*, *ekekasā*, *ekekamhā*, *ekekassa*, *ekekasmiṃ*, *ekekamhi*.

The neuter gender forms are: *ekekaṃ*, *ekekaṃ*. The remainder is the same as the masculine. The feminine gender forms are: *ekikā*, *ekekaṃ*, *ekikāya*, *ekikissā*, *ekikāya*, *ekikissā*, *ekikāyaṃ*, *ekikissaṃ*.
It is appropriate to say that all these are names used distributively (*vicchā*). However, plural forms do not exist here because there is no application [of such usage].
Thus, regarding these forms in the three genders expressed distributively, no consideration of compounds (*samāsa*) should be raised, because distributive words are indeclinable (*anibbacanīya*).
For instance: "Having become joint by joint, seam by seam, and rim by rim, upon the heated pot..."

In such passages as “the formations break up with a *taṭataṭā* sound like sesame seeds being thrown [into a pan],” the derivation of terms such as *pabbapabba* by means of forming a compound (*samāsa*) has not been shown by the ancient teachers. Furthermore,

since the reduplication occurring in distributive repetition (*vicchā*) is established solely by worldly usage and not by grammatical rule, no consideration of compounds should be raised in that context.
Now, the nominal paradigms for the words *ekacca*, *ekatiya*, and *ekacciya* are stated. First, in the masculine gender: *ekacco*, *ekacce*. *Ekaccaṃ*, *ekacce*.
The remainder is the same as the word *purisa*. Here, *ekacce* is only the nominative plural, identical in form to the pronominal forms because it is an uncommon form.
Examples are: "In this world, a certain clansman" (*idhekacco kulaputto*) and "In this world, certain foolish persons" (*idhekacce moghapurisā*).

*Ekatiyo*, *ekatiye*. *Ekatiyaṃ*, *ekatiye*. The remainder is the same as the word *purisa*. Here too, *ekatiye* is the nominative plural only, identical in form to a pronoun because it is an uncommon form. *Ekatiye manussā* (Some people).
“One should not place trust in some people alone, whether they be householders or those who have gone forth.”
“Having been good, they become bad; having been bad, they become good again”—these are the illustrative verses.
However, because of the existence of the word *ekacciya* (partiality/one-sidedness) here—
“Truly, as some men here say:
‘A log that has floated away is better than a single man;

even more so than a single man who eats alone’—these are the illustrative verses. *Ekacciyo*, *ekacciyā*; *ekacciyaṃ*, *ekacciyā*: in every respect, this follows the paradigm of the masculine noun. These are masculine forms.”
*Ekaccaṃ*, *ekaccāni*. *Ekaccaṃ*, *ekaccāni*. The remainder is like the masculine gender. *Ekatiyaṃ*, *ekatiyāni*. *Ekatiyaṃ*, *ekatiyāni*.
The remainder is like the masculine gender. *Ekacciyaṃ*, *ekacciyāni*. *Ekacciyaṃ*, *ekacciyāni*.
The remainder is like the masculine gender. These are the forms for the neuter gender.
“*Ekacca*, *ekacca*, *ekaccāyo*” according to the paradigm of *kaññā*; likewise, “*ekatiyā*, *ekatiyā*, *ekatiyāyo*.
*Ekatiyan*,” and “*ekacciyā*, *ekacciyā*, *ekacciyāyo*. *Ekacciya*,” should be applied according to the paradigm of *kaññā*. These are the feminine gender forms.
Now, the nominal declension series (*nāmikapadamālā*) is stated by way of the words *ekākī* and *ekākiya*:
*Ekākī*, *ekākī*, *ekākino*. *Ekākiṃ*, *ekākī*, *ekākino*. These are to be understood according to the paradigm of *daṇḍin*. *Ekākiyo*, *ekākiyā*. *Ekākiyaṃ*, *ekākiye*. *Ekākiyena*.

This is to be understood according to the paradigm of *purisa* (masculine). These are the masculine forms. *Ekāki kulaṃ*, *ekākī*, *ekākīni*. *Ekākiṃ*, *ekākī*, *ekākīni*. The remainder is similar to the masculine. *Ekākiyaṃ*, *ekākiyāni*. *Ekākiyaṃ*, *ekākiyāni*.
The remainder is similar to the masculine. These are the neuter forms. *Ekākinī*, *ekākinī*, *ekākiniyo*. *Ekākiniṃ*, *ekākinī*, *ekākiniyo*. *Ekākiniyā*—this is similar to the feminine paradigm.
*Ekākiyā*, *ekākiyā*, *ekākiyāyo*. *Ekākiyaṃ*, *ekākiyā*, *ekākiyāyo*. *Ekākiyāyā* is like [the form] *kaññā*; these are feminine gender forms.
All of these, however, should be understood as non-universal noun forms (*asabbanāmika-rūpa*) stated for the purpose of indicating a specific meaning.
Now, the nominal paradigm of the word *ubha*, which is a synonym for the word *dvi*, always ending in the plural number and being a universal noun (*sabbanāmika*), is stated:

“*Ubho*, *ubho*, *ubhohi*, *ubhobhi*, *ubhinnaṃ*, *ubhohi*, *ubhobhi*, *ubhinnaṃ*, *ubhosū*”—this is the series of forms stated according to the method of the Pāli tradition. Here are the applications (*payoga*): Both boys have been bought.
Both women stand; both minds stand; he gave both sons. He sees both girls. Both feet...
"Having broken through, I shall make you conscious. With both hands; with both arms;
with both minds; of both men, of both women, of both minds, among both men, among both women, on both sides—this is our preference.
However, the teachers also accept "ubhehi," "ubhebhi," and "ubhesu."
For in the *Kaccāyana* as well, it is stated: "Both [types of compounds] are *tappurisa*. All of these must indeed be taken into account.
A compound of the word *ubha* is not commonly established. These forms are common to all three genders.
Now, the nominal paradigms for the pronouns *dvi*, *catur*, and *sada*, which denote numbers and always take the plural, are being stated:
*Dve*, *dve*, *dvīhi*, *dvībhi*, *dvinnaṃ*, *duvinnaṃ*, *dvīhi*, *dvībhi*, *dvinnaṃ*, *duvinnaṃ*, *dvīsu*.
In the *Cūḷanirutti*, however, the paradigm for the word is given as “*dvinnanna*.

These [words], like the word *ahaṃ* (I) and others, are applicable in all three genders even when they are devoid of feminine gender and so forth, as in such examples as “*dve purisā* (two men), *dve itthiyo* (two women), *dve cittāni* (two minds),” and so on.
These are also forms common to the three genders:
“The form ‘dve’ belongs to the word ‘dvi’; that which occurs in a compound remains as the base ‘dvi’ alone, though it may appear through various phonetic substitutions.”
*Dvibhāva* and *dvebhāva*, *dvirattaṃ* and *duvassakaṃ*; *dohaḷinī* and *dupattaṃ*:
in the sense of secondary derivation (*taddhita*), these pairs [function].
*Tayo*, *tayo*, *tīhi*, *tībhi*, *tiṇṇaṃ*, *tiṇṇannaṃ*, *tīhi*, *tībhi*, *tiṇṇaṃ*, *tiṇṇannaṃ*, *tīsu*. These are the forms of the masculine gender.
*Tisso*, *tisso*, *tīhi*, *tībhi*, *tissannaṃ*, *tīhi*, *tībhi*, *tissannaṃ*, *tīsu*.

These are the forms of the feminine gender. In the *Cūḷanirutti*, the plural form for the fourth (dative) and sixth (genitive) cases appears as "tissannanna"; however, in the *Niruttipiṭaka*, it appears as "tiṇṇanna.
Having repeatedly examined these within the Buddha’s word (*buddhavacana*) consisting of the three baskets (*tepiṭaka*) along with the commentaries (*sāṭṭhakatha*).
If they are seen, they should be taken up.
*Tīṇi*, *tīṇi*, *tīhi*, *tībhi*, *tiṇṇaṃ*, *tiṇṇannaṃ*, *tīhi*, *tībhi*, *tiṇṇaṃ*, *tiṇṇannaṃ*, *tīsu*.
These are the forms for the neuter gender. However, in certain passages of the Pāḷi, there is also the elision of the suffix *-ṇika* in the word *tīṇi*.

“‘Two or three drops of water’—this is the demonstration of the existence of the word ‘three’ in the passage: ‘Monks, it is through the development and cultivation of three faculties that the monk Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja has declared final knowledge.
As for the forms mentioned as ‘three, three, three’;”
Regarding the subject of compounds, those [terms] would be *titippakatika* (having three bases).
This is because, in a compound, they are designated together with a subsequent word as "three feelings" (*tivedana*),
"three minds" (*ticitta*), and "three worlds" (*tiloka*).
In this case, the neuter gender alone is praised according to the common usage of the word;
however, some also desire the masculine gender here, as in the phrase, "the three worlds appear.
Cattāro, caturo, cattāro, caturo, catūhi, catūbhi, catubbhi, catunnaṃ, catūhi, catūbhi, catubbhi, catunnaṃ, catūsu. These are the forms of the masculine gender.
*Catasso*, *catasso*, *catūhi*, *catūbhi*, *catubbhi*, *catassannaṃ*, *catunnaṃ*, *catūhi*, *catūbhi*, *catubbhi*, *catassannaṃ*, *catunnaṃ*, *catūsu*. These are feminine gender forms.
Regarding the word *catunnaṃ* in the place of the feminine gender, it is seen in the Pāḷi of the *Niruttipiṭaka* (the Minor Grammar) and in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
It has been stated thus. For instance, in the *Cūḷanirutti*, the word "of four" (*catunnaṃ*) appears in the place of the feminine gender;

in the *Niruttipiṭaka*, it appears as "of four maidens" (*catunnaṃ kaññānaṃ*). However, in the Canon itself, in such discourses as the *Soṇadaṇḍasutta*, it appears as "the ascetic Gotama is dear and pleasing to the four assemblies" (*samaṇo gotamo catunnaṃ parisānaṃ piyo manāpo*). Furthermore, in the commentaries, in the commentary to the Suttantas, it says: "By the four... [and so forth].
It is stated [in the *Sattilaṅghajātaka-aṭṭhakathā*]: "He was endowed with wonderful and marvelous qualities and was dear and pleasing to the four assemblies.
And in the *Sattilaṅghajātaka-aṭṭhakathā*: "His teacher, moreover, knew the craft of leaping over four spears (*satti*).
Cattāri, cattāri, catūhi, catūbhi, catubbhi, catunnaṃ, catūhi, catūbhi, catubbhi, catunnaṃ, catūsu. These are the neuter gender forms.
The forms *cattāro*, *catasso*, and *cattārī* are pronounced; in the state of composition (*samāsa*), the word *rūpa* may take four types of declensional endings.
Here, one skilled in the sequence [of grammar] should apply the illustrative examples in their proper order.
“One should define ‘the fourfold four-hall’ as the Four Truths.

These two [words] and others like them are all plural nominative forms; they do not exist in the singular. However, in the *Cūḷanirutti*, it is stated that among the three genders there is the form “catassanna”; this appears to be something that cannot withstand critical examination.
Now, the nominal paradigm for the words *tumhe* (you) and *amhe* (we) is being stated. Among these, when one speaks to someone, those are the forms of address for *tumhe*.
Tvaṃ, tuvaṃ, tumhe. Taṃ, tuvaṃ, tvaṃ, tavaṃ, tumhe. Tayā, tvayā, tumhehi, tumhebhi. Tuyhaṃ, tava, tumhaṃ, tumhākaṃ. Tayā, tvayā, tumhehi, tumhebhi.
Tuyhaṃ, tava, tumhaṃ, tumhākaṃ. Tayi, tvayi, tumhesu. These [forms] are to be applied accordingly, such as:
“tvaṃ puriso” (you are a man), “tvaṃ itthī” (you are a woman), “tvaṃ cittaṃ” (you are the mind), and so forth.
In the first person (attayoge), there are the following forms: Nominative: ahaṃ, ahakaṃ, mayaṃ, amhe.
Accusative: maṃ, mamaṃ, amhe. Instrumental: mayā, amhehi, amhebhi. Genitive:
mayhaṃ, mama, amhaṃ, amhākaṃ, asmākaṃ. Dative: mayhaṃ, mama, amhaṃ, amhākaṃ, asmākaṃ. Ablative: mayā, amhehi, amhebhi. Genitive: mayhaṃ, mama, amhaṃ, amhākaṃ, asmākaṃ.
*Mayi*, *amhesu*, *asmesu*.

Here, however, because the Pāḷi text shows "kathaṃ amhe karomase" (how do we act?), it should be understood that, just like the personal pronoun *tumhe*, the personal pronoun *amhe* also exists; furthermore, another form, *ahakam*, should also be accepted.
Regarding its existence, the scriptural passage, “And I shall speak as one who follows the lead of his own mind,” serves as the illustration. For here, *ahakan* means simply “I.
In that context, it should be applied as “I am a man,” “I am a woman,” “I am the mind,” and so forth.
These forms are also common to all three genders.
In the *Kaccāyanacūḷanirutti* and the *Niruttipiṭaka*, however, the second-person plural form is stated as “tumhākaṃ” and “amhākaṃ.
In the *Kaccāyana*, the first and second person plural forms are stated as “tumhānaṃ” and “amhānaṃ”; the fourth and sixth person singular forms are stated as “tumhaṃ” and “amhaṃ”;
and the first and second person plural forms are also stated [as such] in the *Cūḷanirutti* and the *Niruttipiṭaka*.
However, the singular accusative forms *tumhaṃ* and *amhaṃ* have been stated, as well as the plural dative-genitive forms *tumhe* and *amhe*.
Having examined these, if they are seen in the Suttantas together with their commentaries (*sāṭṭhakatha*), they should be accepted.
Furthermore, regarding the words *tuma* and *amha*, when compounded with subsequent words, such usages as *maṃdīpā* and so forth [are found] from the mouths of the Tathāgata and others.
They arise [as follows]: from the mouth of the Tathāgata, it is said, “O village headman, these are my islands, my refuges, my resorts”;
from the mouth of those skilled in etymology (*nirukti*), it is said, “*tadyoga*, *mayyoga*”;
and from the mouths of poets, in the mirror of their verse, it is said, “Your face is like a lotus, equal to nothing else,” and “Your face is equal to the moon.”
In that context, "those for whom I am an island" are *mandīpā*; "those for whom I am a shelter" are *maṃleṇā*;
likewise, *maṃsaraṇā*. "Connection with you" is *tayyogo*; the meaning is simply "connection with the word *tuma*. "Connection with us" is *mayyogo*;
the meaning is simply "connection with the word *amha*. "Your mouth" is *tvam-mukhaṃ*. It may also be analyzed according to the plural number: "of you... (*tumhākaṃ*).

"Your face, your face. And here, because we see "my islands" (*maṃdīpā*) and so forth in the Pāḷi, and because we see "your face" (*tvaṃmukhaṃ*) in poetic works (*kābya*), one should understand *tvaṃvaṇṇo*, *tvaṃsaro*, *maṃmukhaṃ*, *maṃvaṇṇo*, *maṃsaro*, and so on.
In that context, *tvaṃdīpā* means "those for whom you are the island," or alternatively, "those who have you as their island."
*Tava vaṇṇo* (your color) and *tvaṃ vaṇṇo* (you are the color); *mama mukhaṃ* (my face), *maṃ mukhaṃ*, and *amhākaṃ vā mukhaṃ* (or our face)—these are the grammatical explanations (*nibbacana*).
This same method applies to other similar instances as well.
In a compound, the forms *tumha* and *amhākaṃ* become [the base] when followed by subsequent words.
“*Tvaṃmukhan*” and “*maṃdīpā, tayyogo mayyogo*. Here it is asked:

“Is this the only form for the words *tumha* and *amha*, or is there another as well? There is: “*te me*” and so forth. If that is so, why was the *padamālā* (declensional series) not stated separately? There is a reason for its omission. This is the reason here:
“The forms *te, me, vo, no* are [used] because they follow from the preceding words.”
Therefore, those [forms] have not been stated by me in the lists of nouns (*nāmikapantīsu*).
Here, we shall state the extraction of the meanings of the words *mayaṃ*, *me*, and *no*; however, the meaning of *tesaṃ* has already been stated.
This is because the commentators of the Aṭṭhakathā maintain that the word *mayā* occurs in the place of *mayaṃ*, and the word *mayaṃ* occurs in the place of *mayā*.
They say so; therefore, we also speak in that same way. The word *mayaṃ* occurs in the sense of the personal pronoun *asmad* (we) in such passages as:

“We are authorized and acknowledged, we are possessors of the threefold knowledge. In the passage: “Born from the blood of Hemā, we have come to be dull-witted,” it occurs in the sense of designation (*paññatti*).
In passages such as: “Mind-made, feeding on rapture, self-luminous,” it occurs in the sense of production (*nibbatti*). [In this case,] without any external condition, by mind alone...
*Nibbatta* means "mind-made" (*manomaya*). In such instances as "What if I were to make a hut entirely made of clay," it has the sense of a derivative or modification (*vikāratthe*).
In such instances as "consisting of giving" (*dānamaya*) or "consisting of virtue" (*sīlamaya*), it is used merely for the completion of the phrase (*padapūraṇamatte*).

In the case of "That sublime seat of yours is golden" (*sovaṇṇamaya*), it should be understood as having either the sense of a derivative or the sense of mere phrase-completion. For when the meaning is simply that gold itself is "golden" (*sovaṇṇa*), [it functions as mere phrase-completion].
In that case, when "made of gold" (*sovaṇṇamaya*) means "a modification of gold," the suffix *-maya* should be understood in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*).

It is also appropriate to say it has the sense of being produced (*nibbatti*). However, when the meaning is "produced by gold" (*suvaṇṇena nibbattaṃ sovaṇṇaṃ*), then *sovaṇṇamaya* means simply "gold itself";
in this case, the suffix *-maya* should be understood as serving merely to complete the word.

The particle *me* occurs in the sense of the instrumental case in such passages as “*Kicchena me adhigataṃ, alaṃ dāni pakāsituṃ*” (“It has been attained by me with difficulty; now it is enough to proclaim it”).

The meaning is “by me. In such passages as “*Tassa me bhante Bhagavā saṃkhittena dhammaṃ desetū*” (“May the Blessed One, venerable sir, teach me the Dhamma in brief”), they say the meaning is “to me,” [the particle occurring] in the sense of the dative.
[And in the passage: “*Pubbeva me bhikkhave sambodhā anabhisambuddhassa bodhisattasseva...*”.
In such instances as “sato,” they say that the sense is the genitive (possessive), meaning “of me. Regarding this, it is said:
The particle *me* should be understood by the wise who see the method as occurring in the sense of the instrumental, the dative, and the genitive.
Now, standing upon this, we shall explain the analysis of the meanings of those three words as formulated by the commentators (*aṭṭhakathācariya*),
in order to clarify their intended meaning (*adhippāya*) and thereby eradicate the doubts of listeners. For the commentators,
taking the sense of the dative case for those three words, have glossed their meaning as "for you" and "for me," and [also] in the sense of the genitive case...
But as for the restriction "of you" and "of me," shown by them without confusion— where could such a thing be found in the Buddha’s word consisting of the Tipiṭaka together with its commentaries?
For the words *tuyham* and *mayham*, which express the meanings of the term *te-me*, and the words *tava* and *mama*,
function without restriction in the senses of the recipient (*sampadāna*) and the possessor (*sāmī*).
In this regard, these were his methods: “I give this to you. I dedicate it to you.
O Brahmin, with your flesh, fat, and head, I shall offer a sacrifice. For he is your father, a lion among men. But where is your mother?
“An offering must be given to me alone, not to others; an offering must be given to my disciples alone, not to others.”
"She is not my wife; this hermitage is well-prepared for me. Omniscience is dear to me.
Father, my mother’s face is one way, yours is another. My husband will die now. It is you who is given [the credit], it is you who is praised, yet it is I who am praised.
Renunciation is what pleases me. He is your son. Both mother and father."
Thus, they occur without such fixed restriction as "mine.
For in the *Cūḷanirutti*, the Elder Mahāyama stated that the fourth and sixth cases are identical in form:
"The fourth and sixth cases are identical in all instances, as are the plural forms of the third and fifth cases. If this is so, [what of] the teachers of the commentaries?

In passages such as “Homage to you, O noble steed among men! Homage to you, O Buddha, the Hero! and so forth, [the case ending] is used in the sense of the recipient (*sampadāna*) by virtue of the word *tuyham*;
for the meaning is “to you. In passages such as “What indeed is your vow? What is your holy life? and so forth, it is used in the sense of the possessor (*sāmī*); for the meaning is “your.
Those who speak thus [assert that] they have either “commented upon an inappropriate commentary” or “failed to see what ought to be seen.”
Do they fall [into error]? They have indeed explained correctly; they have seen what ought to be seen.

For, out of compassion for others, thinking that "even a portion of the science of grammar (saddasattha) is in accordance with the Teaching," they adopted a method from the science of grammar and, by way of the sense of the dative case, explained the meaning of the words *te* and *me* as "for you" and "for me.
However, by way of the sense of the genitive case, [they explained them as] "your..."
"mine. For in the science of grammar (*saddasattha*), the forms of the dative and genitive cases are entirely dissimilar, whereas in the Teaching (*sāsana*), they are similar.

Therefore, having treated the dative and genitive forms occurring generally in the Teaching as being of the same grammatical category (*samānagatika*) as those occurring specifically in the science of grammar, [the Blessed One], out of compassion for others, used the form "to you" (*tuyhaṃ*) in the sense of the recipient (*sampadāna*).
The rule for the occurrence of the words *mayaṃ* and *amhākaṃ* has been shown, as well as the rule for the occurrence of the words *tvaṃ* and *mama* in the sense of the agent (*sāmī-atthe*).
Since this rule was established out of compassion for others, it is therefore the fault of compassion alone, and not of the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā.
For it was precisely because of that [compassion] that they composed the commentary in this manner.

However, some here might say: "But surely, O sir, by the commentators (Aṭṭhakathācariyas), relying on the method of phonology (saddanaya), when those words ending in *me* are used in the sense of the genitive (*sāmi*), the method of transposing the case-ending was shown through the statement of the meaning as 'your' and 'my'—as in such examples of the genitive domain as 'with your flesh and fat' and 'this wife is not mine,' and so forth. This is indeed possible.

Can it be said that, likewise, by relying on the *saddanaya* (method of phonology) alone, the method of transposing case endings (*vibhattivipallāsa*) is demonstrated even in instances such as "Bhattaṃ tava na ruccati, pabbajjā mama ruccati" (Food does not please you;

renunciation pleases me), where the words *tuyhaṃ* and *mayaṃ*—which function in the sense of the dative (*sampadānattha*)—are expressed by the meanings "for you" and "for me"? It cannot be said so, because in the verses...

For even in the case of the *cuṇṇiyapadaṭṭhāna* (prose word-commentary), the terms *tuyham*, *mayham*, *tava*, and *mama* function indifferently with respect to two meanings [the genitive and the dative].
Indeed, in such a context—whether in verse (*gāthā*) or in the *cuṇṇiyapadaṭṭhāna*—a change of grammatical case (*vibhattivipallāsa*) is not intended;
as in examples such as: “I am afraid of that kingdom,” or “Why indeed should I fear that happiness? and so forth.
...should be desired in certain instances.

If, by relying on the method of grammar (*saddanaya*), a transposition of case endings (*vibhattivipallāsa*) were to be desired in such cases as "with your flesh and fat," then [by that same logic], it would also have to be desired in such cases as "he gave the gift of his beloved son to the brahmin" or "the father of the brahmin gave. By the method of grammar...

Relying on the phrase "to the brahmin" (*brāhmaṇāya*) and so forth, the meaning of a case-reversal (*vibhattivipallāsa*) should be stated, because the forms of the fourth and sixth cases are mentioned separately in the grammatical treatises. If it is asked, "Even so, what is the fault?"—there is indeed a fault;

for in the Buddha-word consisting of the Three Pitakas along with the Commentaries, when used in connection with giving (*dānayoga*) or in connection with homage (*namoyoga*), the forms of the fourth and sixth cases are accompanied by the substitution of *ā* (*āyādesa*).
Since these [entities] are not apprehended, there is this fault in the statement "for the sake of a brahmin" and so forth,

which employs a change of case (vibhattivipallāsa) to express a meaning for something non-existent— namely, the grasping of what does not exist. Furthermore, because making a change of case in such instances is blameworthy,
a change of case is therefore not desired even in cases such as "with your flesh and fat."
For the forms of the fourth and sixth cases are seen to be identical, as in: "he gave to the man," "the wealth of the man," "he gave to the brahmins," and "belonging to the brahmins.

Thus, in the sacred word (Pāvacana), the particle *sa* occurs generally in the senses of the recipient (*sampadāna*) and the owner (*sāmī*), and its occurrence is to be illustrated by such applications as "the wise one is a giver of the foremost."
Regarding the phrase “The wise one is a giver of the best” (*aggassa dātā medhāvī*):

here, when the word “of the best” (*aggassa*) functions in the sense of the recipient (*sampadāna*) with reference to an action, it functions according to the meaning “a giver of the Three Jewels, which are the best.
However, when it functions in the sense of the possessor (*sāmī*)—that is, as the object (*kamma*)—with reference to the action, then [it means] “of the most excellent gift.”
The word “giver” (dātā) occurs by way of its meaning. Thus, in every respect, this perversion is no refuge for you.

Likewise, based on the method of phonology (saddanaya), because my word *mayhaṃ*—which you have firmly grasped as being in the dative case—is seen in its designation as having the sense of a genitive (possessive), this perversion of grammatical inflection is certainly no refuge for you either. For instance:
“A bird named *mayhaka*, wandering on mountain ridges and in valleys, having climbed a ripe *pipphali* tree, cries out, ‘It’s mine! It’s mine!
Here, *mayhaka* is the name of a certain species of bird. For, due to its greedy nature, it thinks, “This too is mine, this too is mine...”
It is called *mayhako* because it cries out "mine" (*mayhaṃ*); this is based on the root *ke* meaning "to cry out," with the word *mayhaṃ* as its prefix.

Herein is the analysis of the words: if the words *tuyhaṃ* and *mayhaṃ* were necessarily in the sense of the recipient (*sampadāna*), and the words *tava* and *mama* were in the sense of the possessor (*sāmī*), then [it would follow that] the Omniscient One, who is skilled in worldly convention, [would have addressed] that bird...
The designation “*mayhaka*” (mine) should not be used because it does not include the sense of inclusion (*anantogadha-sampadāna-atta*);

rather, because it includes the sense of identity (*antogadha-sāmya-atta*), the designation “*mamaka*” (my own) alone should be used. If it is argued that even here the term “*mayhaka*” is stated by way of a grammatical shift of case endings (*vibhatti-vipallāsa*), we say no;
for a transformation of case endings has no place and no occasion within the scope of a technical designation (*paññatti*).
Furthermore, here my word "my" (*mayaṃ*) stands as a base form ending in a case-suffix because it enters into a single compound with the word "crow" (*kasa*);

even so, this word "my-crow" (*mayhaka*), which denotes a specific kind of bird, remains in the nominative case while also slightly indicating the sense of the genitive, just like the words *sujampati* (Lord of the Sky) and *rājapurisa* (King’s man).
For this reason as well, there is a transposition of case-suffixes (*vibhattivipallāsa*).

"It is not your refuge. Thus, it is established that because the word *mayhaṃ*—which exists within the designation "belonging to me" (*mayhaka*)—is used as a component of a compound, no case-mutation (*vibhattivipallāsa*) is to be desired even in the words *tuyhaṃ*, *tava*, or *mama*, due to the non-perverted nature of its verbal expression.
Therefore, by the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā, [the suffix] is generally applied in the sense of the recipient (*sampadāna*) and the owner (*sāmi*).

It should be understood that even though the words *tuyham* and *mayham*, as well as *tava* and *mama*, are equally in common usage, this specific restriction was shown out of compassion for others by relying solely on the system of phonetics (*saddanaya*). Thus it is said:
"The teachers say that in the sounds *tuyham* and *mayham*, the dative case is expressed."
"Thine" and "mine" [are used] with respect to the owner, having taken this principle from the Teacher.
Even so, there is no fixed rule for these in the Canon;
nor has any distinction between them been observed by us—listen to that.
Where two things arise for the purpose of bestowing equality, the words "of you" and "of me" are used; such applications are not difficult to find.
The words "your" and "mine" are generally employed when referring to an owner.
The grammatical applications for the dative case (*sampadāna*) are indeed few.
In the Dispensation, the words *tava*, *mama*, *tuyhaṃ*,
and *mayhaṃ* alone occur throughout many thousands of readings to express the sense of the genitive (*sāmī*).
All these rules are extremely subtle and very difficult to perceive; they must be carefully attended to by one of heroic birth.

Furthermore, regarding the particle *vo*: the form *vosaddo* is seen in the functions of the direct object (*paccatta*), the accusative (*upayoga*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), the dative (*sampadāna*), the genitive (*sāmivacana*), and as a syntactic filler (*padapūraṇa*).
Indeed, in such passages as “Kacci vo anuruddhā samaggā sammodamānā,” it is seen in the sense of the direct object (*paccatta*). [And in: “Gacchatha bhikkhave... [it is seen in the accusative].
In such cases as “I dismiss you,” it is used in the sense of the accusative (*upayoga*). In such cases as “You must not dwell in my presence,” it is used in the sense of the instrumental (*karaṇa*).

In such cases as “Monks, I shall teach you the discourse on forest retreats,” it is used in the sense of the dative (*sampadāna*). In such cases as “Sāriputta, all that has been well-spoken by you,” it is used in the sense of the genitive (*sāmivacana*).
In such cases as “Those noble ones whose bodily actions are completely purified,” it is used merely for the sake of completing the meter (*padapūraṇamatta*). Regarding this, it is said:
“The particle *vosat* (i.e., *vā*) occurs in these six places: in the sense of individuality (*paccatta*), in the sense of usage (*upayoga*), in the instrumental case (*karaṇa*),
in the sense of what is to be attained (*sampadāniya*), in the expression of association (*sāmīsa-vacana*),
and likewise for the purpose of completing a metrical foot (*padapūraṇa*).”

The word *no* functions in the senses of the accusative, instrumental, ablative, dative, genitive, and the particle *avadhāraṇa* (restriction), as well as in the sense of negation and as a mere indeclinable (*nipātamatta*).
Indeed, it is seen in the sense of the accusative in the phrase: "May we go to the village" (*gāmaṃ no gaccheyyāma*). It is seen in the sense of the dative in such passages as:

"May the king’s cooks not cut [us] today in the kitchen" (*mā no ajja vikantiṃsu, rañño sūdā mahānase*). And in such passages as: "A marriage with the Nāgas was never before performed by us" (*na no vivāho nāgehi, katapubbo kudācanaṃ*).

In the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*): in such phrases as “Share with us the kingdom,” it is in the sense of the recipient (*sampadāne*). In such phrases as “The Blessed One, our Teacher, has arrived,” it is in the sense of the possessor (*sāmivacane*).
In the phrase “There is none equal to the Tathāgata,” it is in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇe*).
In such phrases as “Do you remember, Great King? it is in the sense of the particle *nu*; it is also appropriate to say that it expresses a question. “One should speak only what is well-spoken.”

In such passages as “no ca dubbhāsitaṃ bhaṇe” (and let him not speak ill), it is used in the sense of negation. In such passages as “na no sabhāyaṃ na karonti kiñci” (they do nothing for us in the assembly), it is used as a mere particle.
Herein, this is said: In the sense of identity (paccatta), in usage (upayoga), in the instrumental (karaṇa), and in the dative (sampadāniya);
The particle *no* occurs in the sense of equality, restriction, the meaning of the word *nu*,
prohibition, and likewise as a mere indeclinable (*nipāta*).
Now, the mixed paradigm of all pronouns (*sabbanāma*) is stated concisely according to their respective requirements:
*Yo so*, *ye te*; *yaṃ taṃ*, *ye te*; *yena tena*. The remainder should be expanded. *Yā sā*, *yā tā*; *yaṃ taṃ*, *yā tā*; *yāya tāya*.
The remainder should be expanded. *Yaṃ taṃ*, *yāni tāni*. The remainder should be expanded.
In this manner, the application for the three genders should be made.
“‘That is this; these are those. This is that; these are those. That is this; those are these’—in such ways, the sequence of words (*padamālā*) should be applied according to the requirements.
For instance, there are various applications such as: ‘He who is the Blessed One, the Self-Existent, the Teacherless...
These, O monks, are the two extremes which the Tathāgata, not approaching, has awakened to as the Middle Way... This is that charioteer who comes.’”
...are seen. Thus, the mixed paradigm of all noun stems should be applied.

This was composed by me for the sake of the proficiency of listeners everywhere in the teaching of the All-Seer, who has accomplished all goals, so that they may become well-versed in the entire dispensation.
All the nouns are listed here in order,
together with all the words that are not nouns but function as nouns.
For those who have applied themselves to these, there is the discernment of subtle meanings.
There will be no doubt regarding the difficult-to-penetrate [truth].
Thus ends the *Saddanīti* treatise, composed for the sake of the proficiency of the wise in the modes of expression within the Three Piṭakas together with the Eightfold Commentary (*Sāṭṭhakatha*).
The Twelfth Chapter, titled "The Analysis of the Nominal Paradigm for Words with Names Similar to All [Common] Nouns. 13.
The Non-Nominal Paradigm for Numerals with Determinative Names.
Henceforth, I shall explain the declensional series for numerals and pronouns;
how they are to be employed with the elements of the earth-constituent (bhūdhātu) and other forms.
For that declensional series of the numeral and pronoun stems—such as *eka*, *dvi*, *catur*, and so forth—which was previously given by us, [is now to be applied here].

Having set aside what has already been stated, the nominal paradigm for numbers such as five, six, seven, and so forth—which are not all [included] here—is now being explained for the purpose of joining them with forms derived from the root *bhū* (to be) and other forms:
*pañca*, *pañcahi*, *pañcabhi*, *pañcannaṃ*, *pañcasu*. This should be understood by way of the seven case-endings (*vibhatti*).
“Five elements, five masters, five types of men, five planes, five maidens, five beings, five minds”—in this way, [the suffixes] should be applied everywhere.
There are also *cha*, *chahi*, *chabhi*, *channaṃ*, *chasu*, and *chassu*. For the Pāḷi says: “The world has arisen through six; through six it forms intimacy.”
Satta, sattahi, sattabhi, sattannaṃ, sattasu. Aṭṭha, aṭṭhahi, aṭṭhabhi, aṭṭhannaṃ, aṭṭhasu.
Nava, navahi, navabhi, navannaṃ, navasu. Dasa, dasahi, dasabhi, dasannaṃ, dasasu.
In the same way, ekādasa. Dvādasa, bārasa. Terasa, tedasa, teḷasa. Catuddasa, cuddasa.
Pañcadasa, pannarasa. Soḷasa. Sattarasa. Aṭṭhārasa, aṭṭhārasahi, aṭṭhārasabhi, aṭṭhārasannaṃ, aṭṭhārasasu—all of this should be understood as being in the plural number. Also:
ekūnavīsati, ekūnavīsaṃ, and so forth. [Examples: ekūnavīsāya, ekūnavīsāyaṃ; "ekūnavīsa bhikkhū tiṭṭhanti" (nineteen monks stand).
One sees nineteen monks; in this same way, it should be applied to the phrases "maidens" and "minds," and so forth.
The Dhamma was taught by nineteen monks; it was done by nineteen maidens; it was done by nineteen minds;
one gives robes to nineteen monks; one gives wealth to nineteen maidens; it is pleasing to nineteen minds.
It departs by means of nineteen monks. Likewise with respect to girls and minds. [The property] belonging to nineteen monks;
likewise for girls and minds. Established among nineteen monks. Thus it should be applied as "among girls and among minds.
[The forms are: ekūnavīsati, ekūnavīsatiṃ, ekūnavīsatiyā, ekūnavīsatiyaṃ.
Vīsati, vīsatiṃ, vīsatiyā, vīsatiyaṃ; vīsa, vīsaṃ, vīsāya, vīsāyaṃ.
Likewise for ekavīsa, dvāvīsa, bāvīsa, tevīsa, catuvīsa, and so forth. Tiṃsa, tiṃsaṃ, tiṃsāya, tiṃsāyaṃ.
Cattālīsa, cattālīsaṃ, cattālīsāya, cattālīsāyaṃ; cattārīsa, and so forth. Paññāsa, paññāsaṃ, paññāsāya...
Fifty: *paññāsāyaṃ*, *paṇṇāsa*, *paṇṇāsaṃ*, *paṇṇāsāya*, *paṇṇāsāyaṃ*. Sixty: *saṭṭhi*, *saṭṭhiṃ*, *saṭṭhiyā*, *saṭṭhiyaṃ*.
Seventy: *sattati*, *sattatiṃ*, *sattatiyā*, *sattatiyaṃ*; also *sattari* and so forth. Eighty:
*asīti*, *asītiṃ*, *asītiyā*, *asītiyaṃ*. Ninety: *navuti*, *navutiṃ*, *navutiyā*, *navutiyaṃ*.
In this way, and otherwise as well, the forms of numerals are to be understood. [Examples: *ekūnavīsehi*, *ekūnavīsānaṃ*, *ekūnavīsesu*.

Furthermore, because the forms of numerals are seen in some instances with the word "channavutīnaṃ" and so forth, some experts in grammar employ the word *ūnavīsati* always in the singular number and exclusively in the feminine gender. Some [hold that] "twenty" (*vīsati*) and so forth...
They say that [the words] ending in *anavuti* are feminine singulars. However, some say:
“Words such as *vīsati* and so forth denote both the number to be counted and the counting itself in the sense of oneness;
but in the sense of the counted object, they express duality and plurality, and those [words] up to *anavuti* are feminine.”
In this context, the dual number should be discarded, as it does not exist in the Buddha’s word (*buddhavacana*).
Furthermore, among all those aforementioned expressions, some are appropriate when applied to certain passages of the Canon (*pāḷi*), while others are not;
for we see in the Canon the use of the plural even for words denoting numbers such as twenty, thirty, and so forth, and likewise in the *Kaccāyana*.

Because they show the state of possessing form produced by gender (yovacana). Therefore, according to what is possible and according to the gender of the word, their singular number should be understood when they refer to feminine gender, just like the words *atthi* and *natthi*.
For the words *atthi* and *natthi*, being particles (*nipāta*), function in both the singular and the plural: "There are sons; there is wealth."

In such passages as "There is no love equal to self-love" and "There are no [true] recluses or brahmins," although these [words] are not inherently feminine, their status as feminine forms is seen in certain instances.

For in the Abhidhamma, the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta), who turns the wheel of the Dhamma in accordance with the teaching, being skilled in conventional usage and a master of achieving skill in conventional usage, spoke of them using a singular feminine form:
"Nine for 'there is' (atthi); nine for 'there is not' (natthi)."

Since this has been demonstrated, it should be understood that even in cases such as *vīsati-vīsati-miccha* and so forth, there is a singular number (*ekavacanantatā*) when the feminine gender (*itthiliṅga-bhāva*) is applicable, according to the possibility and according to the scriptural statement.

In this regard, some consider that the phrases "in the sense of cause" (*hetuyā*) and "in the sense of predominance" (*adhipatiyā*) should be understood by way of a change of gender (*liṅga-vipallāsa*).

By way of its grammatical gender, the masculine state in the expression “*hetumhi adhipatimhī*” should be understood; the meaning is simply “in the cause-condition (*hetu-paccaya*) and the predominance-condition (*adhipati-paccaya*).

Alternatively, this pair—“*hetuyā adhipatiyā*”—should be taken as a masculine form that corresponds to feminine forms, just as there are masculine forms corresponding to feminine forms such as “*hetuyo jantuyo*.”
Because they exist, one should not take it that the phrase "in terms of 'is' and 'is not'" was stated by way of a change in grammatical gender;
for the words *atthi* (is) and *natthi* (is not) do not possess distinctions of gender. Indeed, the words *atthi* and *natthi* are not included within any of the three genders.
For among these, the word *atthi* is divided by way of verb (*ākhyāta*) and particle (*nipāta*), as in: "atthi, santi, saṃvijjati."
In such passages as “Atthikhīrā brāhmaṇī,” however, the word *natthi* is merely a particle (*nipāta*).

Thus, this explanation of the words *atthi* and *natthi*, as well as of particles, in terms of gender and number is appropriate, because they do not function according to feminine gender and so forth, nor according to singularity and so forth. And it has been said:
“That which remains unchanged across the three genders, all case endings, and all numbers—that is an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Here it might be asked:
But surely, sir, since it is stated that “*atthi*, *sakkā*, and *labbhā* belong to the nominative,” the word *atthi* [is not an indeclinable]?
If it is connected with the nominative case (*paṭhamā vibhatti*), why then was it stated that "it is the same in the three genders" and so forth?

It is true that the word *atthi* is connected with the nominative case; likewise, the word *natthi* is also [connected with the nominative] because it must be understood through the verbal form of *atthi* and because they form a pair of words.
However, this statement beginning with "it is the same in the three genders" refers to those [words] classified as prefixes (*upasagga*) and particles (*nipāta*).
This was stated with reference to the word *asaṅkhyā* as a class, not with reference to each individual instance of the word *asaṅkhyā*. For it is thus:
among the prefixes and particles that receive the designations "innumerable" (*asaṅkhyā*) and "indeclinables" (*abyaya*), all prefixes take all case-endings and numbers.
As for particles, some are joined with case-endings such as the nominative and so forth as appropriate, while others are not joined with case-endings.
In this context, those [words] which are connected with a particular case-ending at a certain point are, at that same point, of that number.
For it is not possible to identify a specific "number" for each individual preposition (upasagga) or particle (nipāta);
rather, by way of encompassing them all, the ancient masters stated, "It is the same in the three genders," and so forth. The teacher Kaccāyana also, with reference to this very point, [said]:
It is said: “And [the word] ‘friend’ (āvuso) [is used] with all [case endings], prepositions, particles, and so forth.

For it is not the case that all case endings are obtainable from the word *āvuso*; rather, because it expresses the sense of address (*ālapanattha*), only the nominative case endings—both singular and plural—are obtainable. This is our position.
However, some claim that there is elision of all case endings for all particles (*nipāta*); this should not be accepted.
This is because of such statements as: "The words *atthi*, *sakkā*, and *labbhā* belong to the nominative;

the words *divā*, *bhiyyo*, and *namo* belong to both the nominative and the accusative," and because particles such as *atha*, *khalu*, *vata*, and *vatha*—which are not connected with case endings—serve merely to fill out the meter.

Regarding the word *vacanato* (from the number of cases). Here too, one might ask: "But surely, sir, since particles (*nipāta*) that are not joined with case-endings (*avibhatti*) are possible, should there not have been a presentation of the words *atthi* and *natthi* without case-endings?
Why then was a presentation with case-endings made, stating 'nine for *atthi*, nine for *natthi*'?
[The answer is: Because it is impossible to present the meaning entirely without case-endings.

If it is the case that, according to the statement "‘Atthi’ and ‘sakkā’ and ‘labbhā’—these [are examples] of the nominative," the words *atthi* and *natthi* should be shown as belonging to the nominative case by virtue of having the nominative case-ending elided, why then are they shown as ending in the locative case in the form "of *atthi* and *natthi*" (*atthiyā natthiyā*), rather than doing so otherwise?
True; the words *atthi* and *natthi* are indeed connected with the nominative case-ending.

Although they should be demonstrated [in other cases], nevertheless, for the purpose of illustrating the meaning of "nine in the presence-condition (atthipaccaya) and nine in the absence-condition (natthipaccaya)," there is no occasion for the nominative case;
rather, it is only the locative case that applies. Therefore, it is stated as "nine in the sense of 'atthi' (being present) and nine in the sense of 'natthi' (not being present).
Thus, once it is established that the words *atthi* and *natthi* take the locative ending, their taking the instrumental, dative, ablative, and genitive endings is likewise established.

It is indeed established. Therefore, even in such cases as “the state of being existent (atthibhāva)” and “existence (atthitā),” one must necessarily accept a compound and derivative analysis such as:
the state of *atthi* is *atthibhāva*; the state of *natthi* is *natthibhāva*; the state of *atthi* is *atthitā*, and so forth.
What we have stated cannot be said to contradict the Canon, because it has been stated in accordance with the method of the Canon.

"Let it be so. But why, sir, is the feminine gender used in the expressions 'existence' (*atthiyā*) and 'non-existence' (*natthiyā*), when particles and prefixes are not subject to distinctions of gender?
True, but this matter is exceedingly subtle. Nevertheless, relying solely upon the authority of the ancient masters, we shall state the decision.
For instance, although numerals such as "twenty" (*vīsati*) and the like, by their very form, denote non-material things, [they are still treated as such].

Just as the status of being feminine is accepted by those learned in the science of grammar for words denoting non-living things—such as the words *latā* (creeper), *mati* (intellect), *ratti* (night), *itthī* (woman), *yāgu* (gruel), and *vadhū* (bride)—so too, even when not denoting non-living things, the status of being feminine for the words *atthi* (is) and *natthi* (is not) is accepted in certain instances by those learned in the True Dhamma.
Therefore, the Venerable Dhammasenāpati said: "There are nine [forms] of *atthi*, and nine of *natthi*. Alternatively, "of *atthi*..."
It should also be understood that these indeclinable words ending in the locative case—such as *natthiyā*—are free from gender and state (*liṅga-bhāva-vinimutta*).
One should not raise an objection here, such as: "There are no such indeclinable words spoken by the ancient teachers;
therefore, this statement must be discarded."
For in the Word (Pāvacana), numerous particles (nipātapada) are seen that were not specifically pointed out by the Teachers;

nor should a contradiction be raised on the grounds that "these are meaningless sounds" regarding such terms as "in the sense of cause" (hetuyā), "in the sense of predominance" (adhipatiyā), "in the sense of presence" (atthiyā), or "in the sense of absence" (natthiyā).

For, by means of unobstructed knowledge—produced through the merit of the perfections (pāramitāpuñña) and its inconceivable power—the entire circle of the knowable (sabbaṃ ñeyyamaṇḍala) [is encompassed].

When one sees [the truth] as directly evident before one's eyes, like an *āmalaka* fruit in the palm of the hand, the verbal confusion of others will inevitably be exposed within the words of the Buddha.

But is it not the case, sir, that this statement—"by way of cause (*hetu*), by way of predominance (*adhipati*), by way of presence (*atthi*), by way of absence (*natthi*)"—is the word of the Elder Sāriputta, since it was formulated by him?
For when the Tathāgata was teaching in the assembly of the Tāvatiṃsa gods...
"These words do not exist; if that is so, why do you call it 'the word of the Buddha'?
It is indeed the word of the Buddha. For the Venerable Sāriputta was given a method by the Tathāgata;

having received that method from the Teacher himself, he—who possessed the analytical knowledges and was like a second Teacher—was the foremost disciple, and he composed the phrasing with great skill.
For all noble ones who have attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) do not speak with faulty grammar, owing to their great skill in the distinctions of linguistic expression;
therefore, it should be understood that this mode of speech of the noble ones is beyond the scope of others.
Now, the nominal series for *sata* and the other terms is stated:
Sataṃ, satāni, satā. Sataṃ, satāni, sate. Satena, satehi, satebhi. Satassa, satānaṃ.
Satā, satasmā, satamhā, satehi, satebhi. Satassa, satānaṃ. Sate, satasmiṃ, satamhi, satesu.

In the same way, *sahassaṃ* (a thousand) and *sahassāni* (thousands) should be applied accordingly. [Likewise] *dasasahassaṃ* (ten thousand), *satasahassaṃ* (one hundred thousand), and *dasasatasahassaṃ* (one million).
The same method applies here as well. The application (payoga) in this case is as follows: "a hundred monks, a hundred women, a hundred minds;
a hundred monks, a hundred women, a hundred minds. The same method applies to thousands and so forth.
Thus do the forms of words occur, both in this way and otherwise: *koṭi*, *koṭī*, *koṭiyo*. It should be understood according to the principle of the night (*ratti-naya*).
The teachers say that as long as a number proceeds from one up to ten,
so long is that number "predominant in the object to be numbered" (saṅkhyeyyappadhāna).
However, as for the number from twenty up to a hundred, it is [predominant in the number itself].
They have described it as having number as its primary element and the numbered as its primary element.
Furthermore:
"Indeed, that [number] exists from twenty up to a koṭi."
One should explain [the compound] as having the number as the primary factor (*saṅkhyāppadhāna*) and having the thing numbered as the primary factor (*saṅkhyeyyappadhāna*).
For indeed, such Pāli passages are seen as: “Having abandoned eighty crores even of gold, he went forth,” and “A hundred crores, their taints destroyed and free from stain, have attained peace.
However, in this present context, for the sake of wise persons acquiring subtle knowledge by making all the forms of words for numbers clear, [it is explained as follows].
I shall present this by citing a portion of the *Udāna* text together with its commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), as well as other portions of the text and the words of the commentary:
“Visākhā, for those who have a hundred dear things, there are a hundred sufferings; for those who have ninety dear things, there are ninety sufferings.
For those who have eighty... [and so on] ...for those who have seventy. For those who have sixty. For those who have fifty... [and so forth].
“Forty, Visākhā; for those who have thirty, there are thirty sufferings. For those who have twenty dear things, there are twenty sufferings.
For those who have ten... nine... eight... seven... six... five... four... three... two... for those who have one dear thing, there is one suffering.”
In this context, *sataṃ piyāni* means "the objects of affection for the good. Some read it as *sataṃ piyaṃ*.
Furthermore, because from one up to ten the emphasis is on both the number and the numbered object, the text has come down as:
"For those who have ten dear things, for them there are ten sufferings," and so forth. However, some [read]: "For those who have ten dear things..."
They recite [the passage] beginning with, "Ten are their sufferings," and so forth; however, that is not correct.

Since, from twenty up to one hundred, the numbers are primarily concerned with the countable (saṅkhyeyya) as well as the number itself (saṅkhā), therefore, even in that context, taking only what is primarily concerned with the countable, the Pāḷi has come down as:
"For those, Visākhā, who have a hundred dear things, there are a hundred sufferings," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "sabbesampi ca yesaṃ ekaṃ piyaṃ, ekaṃ tesaṃ dukkhaṃ," the reading is "ekaṃ tesaṃ dukkhaṃ" (for all those who have one thing dear, for them there is one thing that is suffering), and not "dukkhassa.
For in a single progression of words, the Blessed One’s teaching possesses a single flavor. Therefore, the text should be understood according to the method already stated.
This, then, is the portion of the Udāna text together with its commentary.
Now, another passage from the Canon and a passage from the Commentary are cited:
“A hundred elephants, a hundred horses, a hundred chariots with mules;
a thousand maidens adorned with jeweled earrings.”
The Pāli text reads: “They are not worth a sixteenth part of a single stride.
Here, in the phrase “a hundred elephants,” etc., the words “hundred” and so forth are the qualificands (*visesita*), while “thousands” is the qualifier (*visesana*).
Therefore, the meaning should be understood by connecting the word “hundred” with the word “thousand,” and taking “elephants” and so forth as the accompanying terms (*upapada*). Elephants...
A hundred thousand elephants; a hundred thousand horses; a hundred thousand mule-carts;
a hundred thousand maidens adorned with jeweled earrings. This is the apprehension of the meaning by way of the predominance of the number.
However, by way of the predominance of the enumeration, this meaning should also be understood: "A hundred thousand elephants, a hundred thousand horses, [a hundred thousand] mule-carts..."
“A hundred thousand [maidens], adorned with jeweled earrings, and a hundred thousand young women. This method should be applied to other similar instances as well.
Regarding the phrase, “The Himavat mountain is five hundred yojanas high,” this is the reading found in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).

Here, by connecting the word “five” (*pañca*) with the word “hundred” (*sata*), it is understood that there are no more than a hundred artisans, as in the expression “there is no hundred of artisans.”
The meaning should be understood according to the predominance of the number, as in the phrase "like the Himavat mountain, five hundred yojanas high.

Furthermore, the term "five hundred" (*pañca satāni*) is used in the accusative case by way of absolute connection with the duration of time. This method should be applied to other similar instances as well.
The word *sataṃ* is singular in forms such as "I am a hundred" (*sataṃ homi*) or "I am a thousand" (*sahassaṃ homi*).
In such passages as “Then there were a hundred Khattiyas, illustrious followers,” the plural number is used. In this way, the singular and plural usage is also found for [numbers] such as a thousand.
For instance, in the phrase “He attends upon more than a hundred thousand yakkhas,” the term “satasahassaṃ” (a hundred thousand) is in the singular;
whereas in “He shall have more than a thousand sons,” it is in the plural.
In this context, "thousand" (sahassa) should be understood as a plural term.
[As it is said: "For one hundred thousand aeons and four incalculable aeons, there was a city named Amara, beautiful to behold and delightful."
Pāḷi: Here, in the phrase “kappe ca satasahasse caturo ca asaṅkhiye,” the accusative plural is used in the sense of the genitive (*sāmī-atthe*).
Therefore, the meaning should be understood as: “at the end of four incalculables and one hundred thousand great aeons (*mahākappa*);
and here the word “at the end” (*matthake*) is an ellipsis (*vacanasesa*). Thus, the meaning is simply: “at the conclusion of four incalculables plus one hundred thousand aeons.”
This method should be applied to other similar instances as well:
"Throughout one hundred thousand aeons and four incalculable aeons,
whatever conduct was practiced during that interval— all of it ripened into enlightenment."
Pāḷi. Here, in the phrase “in aeons” (*kappe*), it is the accusative plural used by way of continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*).
In the expression “in one hundred thousand aeons” (*satasahasse kappe*), this is a masculine designation and an accusative designation due to its connection with the word *kappa*.

For this [word] is in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the word *kappa*. In the phrase “and four incalculables” (*caturo ca asaṅkhiye*), these are accusative plurals used by way of continuous connection.
But for whom is it "incalculable"? Since nothing else has been mentioned and since the *kappa* (aeon) has been mentioned, this meaning—"of aeons"—is understood from the context itself.
For it is not appropriate to grasp something that has not been mentioned by excluding what has already been stated.
The word "and" (*ca*) serves the purpose of conjunction: "four incalculables and a hundred thousand great aeons (*mahākappa*) of great aeons."
This method should be applied to other similar instances as well.
The text reads: “Thousands of jars and many hundreds of pots. Here, *ghaṭā* means *ghaṭānaṃ*. This is a nominative plural used in the sense of the genitive.
Thus, the meaning is “thousands of jars. And “many hundreds of pots” (*kumbhīnañca satā bahū*).
And there were many hundreds of *kumbhīnas*. Here, the elision of the plural marker (*nikāra*) should be understood. This method should be applied to other similar instances as well:
“For ten or twenty thousand, there was the realization of the Dhamma;
for one or two, the realization was beyond counting.”
Pāḷi: Here, "ten thousand and twenty thousand" means ten thousand and twenty thousand.
"Realization of the Dhamma" (dhammābhisamaya) is the penetration of the Four Noble Truths. "One or two" is a statement made for the sake of illustration;
by this, the meaning is that they are "innumerable" according to the method beginning with "of one and two, and three, four... up to ten," and so forth. This same method applies to others as well.
In such instances, it should be cited:
“Four hundred thousand [monks], possessing the six higher knowledges and great psychic power,
always surround Dīpaṅkara, the Knower of the World.”

Pāḷi: Here, the phrase "four hundred thousand" functions as a grammatical coreferent (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with these two terms, "possessing the six direct knowledges" (*chaḷabhiññā*) and "of great psychic power" (*mahiddhikā*), by way of gender distinction.
For in such instances, even a word denoting an incalculable number (*asaṅkhyeyya*) takes the neuter gender;
therefore, "four hundred thousand," "possessing the six direct knowledges," and "of great psychic power" [are all neuter].

And these three words are in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Alternatively, in the phrase "those possessing the six super-knowledges, those of great psychic power" (*chaḷabhiññā mahiddhikā*), the word in the nominative case should be understood as expressing the sense of a genitive—that is, "of those possessing the six super-knowledges, of those of great psychic power.
In this sense, however, the term "four hundred thousand" (*cattāri satasahassāni*) functions as a numeral.
This is also the case in such expressions as "three hundred thousand well-adorned women" (*tīṇi satasahassāni, nāriyo samalaṅkatā*).

The method [of interpretation] should be applied. The text reads: “And those seven hundred wives, and seven hundred female slaves. Here, “seven hundred” (*satā*) should be understood in the neuter gender as “*satānī*,” and not in the feminine gender.
For the word *satā* is a neuter form, just like “five resultant consciousnesses” (*pañca cittā vipākā*) and so forth.
Indeed, there is no such word *sata* in the feminine gender, nor is there one in the masculine gender.

If the word *sata* were to possess both genders, then, this being the case, there would also have to be forms ending in long *-o* for the masculine and long *-ā* for the feminine, such as *puriso* and *kaññā*.
Yet neither of these two forms exists for the word *sata*; therefore, it is known that "the word *sata* is exclusively neuter.
But, sir, is it not seen here that the word *sata* occurs in the feminine gender in the passage: "Those deities, seven hundred noble ones"?
"It is neuter; it is indeed neuter. But is it not, sir, in grammatical apposition with the word *devatā* (deity)?
True, it is in apposition; nevertheless, it remains neuter. For in such cases concerning number, the state of being in apposition is not a determining factor.
Thus, for example: "Five hundred paccekabuddhas were long-time residents on this Isigili mountain."

The grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatā*) of a neuter gender term with a masculine gender term is observed; therefore, even in the phrase “those seven hundred noble deities,” it should be understood that the neuter state remains as “seven hundreds” (*sattasatāni*).
In expressions such as “having given seven hundred elephants,” the word *sata* is likewise exclusively neuter. This principle should be applied to other similar instances as well.
The Pāḷi reads: “By ninety thousand koṭis he surrounded the Great Sage.

Here, the meaning should be understood according to whether the number is subordinate to the thing numbered, as in “by ninety thousand koṭis of bhikkhus,” or whether the number itself is predominant, as in “of ninety thousand koṭis of bhikkhus.
This method should be applied to other similar instances as well.
“The lifespan of that Great Sage was one hundred thousand years,” is the Pāli text.

Here, “one hundred thousand years” is the accusative case by virtue of its absolute connection with time (*kālassa accantasaṃyogavasena*). The same applies to the Pāli passage: “For ten thousand years he lived in the midst of the household.
This method should be applied to other similar instances as well.
The textual passage reads, “In this hundred-thousandth aeon, the Leader appeared,” and also, “In the ninety-first aeon from here.
Here, regarding the phrase *satasahassamhi kappe*, the meaning is “at the end of a hundred thousand aeons.
