Regarding the phrase *ekanavute kappe*, the meaning of the locative case (*bhummavacana*) should be understood as a genitive-locative (*sāmibhummavacana*), meaning “at the end of ninety-one aeons.”

For instance, in the phrase “the holy life is lived under the Blessed One,” the locative case here is understood as having the sense of a genitive-locative, meaning “in the presence of the Blessed One. This same method should be applied to other similar instances as well.
“If there were thousands, hundreds, and tens of thousands there;”
“There is no fear for us from anyone in the forest, even among wild beasts,” so says the Pāḷi.
This is its meaning: therein, in that forest, even if there exist thousands, hundreds, and tens of millions (*nahuta*) of wild beasts;
or alternatively, “thousands and hundreds” means hundreds of thousands, and [there may be] hundreds of thousands and tens of millions of wild beasts.
And if [beings] exist, even though they exist in this way, the word *koci* (anyone) is used here with respect to some wild beast (*vāḷe*).
For the word *koci* functions in the sense of the suffix *kvaci*, just as the word *ko* functions in the phrase “What strength do you have, O Great King?”;

furthermore, this expression is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*). Therefore, it means: “There is no fear for us on account of any wild beast whatsoever—on account of even a single wild animal.”

The meaning should be grasped. Alternatively, "anything" (*koci*) means even something very slight. Here, however, in the phrase "among wild beasts" (*vāḷesu*), the locative case is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*). Thus, it means:
"On account of wild beasts, not even the slightest fear exists for us. This method of interpretation should be applied to other similar instances as well.
“One hundred thousand and thirty-six thousand,
ten thousand, and four hundred and fifty”— this is the reading in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. Herein,
because words that are identical in case, gender, and number [are joined] with words that are not identical in case, gender, and number...
Alternatively, when things are identical in meaning, there is a connection even for those situated far away, while for others, there is no connection even for those situated nearby;
therefore, this term "all" (*sabba*) must be connected with "perfectly round" (*parimaṇḍala*), and "thirty-six" (*chattiṃsa*) must be connected with "hundreds of thousands" (*satasahassāni*).
This method should be applied to other similar instances as well.
“Two hundred thousand and forty nahutas;
so much, by its thickness, is this earth reckoned to be”—this is the reading of the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).
Here, “two” (*duve*) is the qualifier, and “hundred-thousands” (*satasahassāni*) is the thing qualified. Likewise...

“Four” (*cattārī*) is the qualifier, and “ten million” (*nahutāni*) is the qualified. For instance, since these two terms—“one hundred thousand” (*satasahassāni*) and “ten million” (*nahutāni*)—are to be qualified by those two terms—“two” (*duve*) and “four” (*cattārī*)—they serve as explanations of the meaning as “two hundred thousand and four ten millions.
Even so, [the relationship] of the numeral words such as “two” with words such as “one hundred thousand” [is established].
The state of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatā*) with words denoting numbers was not taught by the ancient masters.

However, while coreferentiality is obtained in cases such as "two worldlings were mentioned" or "a hundred thousand monks," because the qualifying terms there denote substances (*dabba*), it is not so in cases such as "two hundred thousand [people]," because the qualifying terms there do not denote substances; therefore, in such instances...
Co-referentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatā*) is not to be accepted in these instances because of the absence of logical justification (*yutti*).

If this is so, would these [terms] be devoid of mutual connection, like the cases of "wholesome," "form," and "one possessing eyes"? No, because they are apprehended through the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*visesanavisesitabbabhāva*).
If that is so, would co-referentiality then be obtained? No, because there is no such restriction (*niyama*). Absolutely...

For the state of having a common substratum (samānādhikaraṇabhāva) belongs only to qualities and the possessor of qualities, or to the qualifier and the qualified, and not to others even when they stand in the relation of qualifier and qualified.
In this context, "ettakaṃ" is a term expressing measure. In "bahalattena," the instrumental case is used for the qualifier. By both [terms], he demonstrates this meaning:
"This earth, by its thickness, measures two hundred thousand and forty thousand yojanas."

"And it is reckoned as only this much. Regarding the word "ettakaṃ" (this much), its grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatā*) with either the phrase "two hundred thousand and forty nahutas" or with the word "vasundharā" (the earth) is not intended.

For "ettakaṃ" is a neuter abstract noun (*bhāvanapuṃsaka*); in the science of grammar (*saddasattha*), they say it is an adverbial modifier of action (*kriyāvisesana*). Its meaning is simply "by this much measure."

Furthermore, in the case of the words “two hundred thousand and four less,” one should not accept their grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatā*) with the word “Vasundharā,” because—as in the case of the word “hundred” in the phrase “of hundreds of bhikkhus”—it is merely a numerical expression.
For it has been stated [elsewhere] as “this much. However, for the words “reckoned” (*saṅkhātā*) and “this” (*ayaṃ*), [coreferentiality] with “Vasundharā” [is acceptable].
By this, grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatā*) is obtained. This method should be applied to other similar instances as well:
“In this [hand], there are ten white lines, beautiful and pleasing to behold;
six are tawny, fifteen are pale yellow, and fourteen are turmeric-colored.”
Pāḷi: Here, "six and fifteen piṅgalas" means that twenty-one *piṅgala* lines are to be understood.
Likewise:
"I have heard that he also had many sons who were 'of one name'."
“Eighty, ten, and one, the mighty ones named Indra”—thus says the Pāḷi.

Here, however, although one should have said “eighty-nine,” it is stated as “eighty, ten, and one. For the word of the Buddha (pāvacana) possesses a diverse arrangement of sounds. This method should be applied to other such instances as well:
“Thirty men and ninety, all individually fixed;”
The Pāli text reads: “I see no one equal to them, as they wander over this entire earth.
Here, it is said: “thirty thousand and nine hundred and thirty [and] ninety” (*tiṃsasahassāni navuti ca satāni tiṃsa nāvutyo*).
However, in this particular instance, there is an elision (*lopa*) of the word *sahassa* after the word *tiṃsa*, and of the word *sata* after the word *navuti*.
One should not accept the statement that it was said, “thirty and ninety. For if it were accepted in this way, such a construction of words could be made anywhere;
and when such a construction of words is made, the comprehension of the meaning would not occur for listeners without an instruction.
Therefore, it should not be understood in that manner. Rather, it should be understood thus: “thirty... [and so on].”

The phrase “a hundred thousand” is a term established by worldly convention; however, since the meaning of a conventionally established term is understood by those who have previously grasped that convention upon hearing it—
rather than through formal instruction— therefore, even at the time King Brahmadatta spoke it,
and even at the time the Teacher brought forth and spoke that discourse, all people [understood] the meaning of the words without any instruction.
"It is to be understood that they know.
"Thirty thousand and ninety hundred indeed;
thirty-nine thousand is what is called [the number] mentioned in the Umaṅga Jātaka."
Because in the sacred word there exist inconceivable methods and expressions whose meanings are well-refined, taught by one who has attained compassion;
therefore, the wise man [should apply himself] to the profound words of the Conqueror together with their commentaries.
One should always receive instruction and serve one’s teacher with proper respect.
For one who lacks a teacher’s instruction does not find the essence of the meaning;
and being deprived of the essence of the meaning, such a person falls away from the true Dhamma.
Having received the teacher’s instruction and being endowed with the essence of the meaning,
one who protects the True Dhamma does not fall away from the True Dhamma.
Therefore, for the sake of the True Dhamma, even this garland of numbers has been spoken by me.
Thus ends the *Saddanīti* treatise, composed for the benefit of the wise in understanding the modes of expression within the Three Pitakas together with their commentaries— the ninefold collection—
along with appropriate applications and the determination of meanings as they occur.
The Thirteenth Chapter, titled "The Determination of Verbs," which is the classification of the series of nominal words for the names of numbers.
14. The Analysis of the Eightfold Nature:
These two—the earth element and the matter derived from it—having made this our primary focus, all of this has been elaborated by us.
Now, by your permission, I shall explain the excellent triad of meanings:
here, the triad consists of the extraction of meanings (*atthuddhāra*) and those forms ending in *tum* and *tvā*, etc.
Therefore, first, the extraction of the meanings of the word *bhūta*, which proceeds from the verbal root *bhū*, is set forth:

The word *bhūta* occurs in reference to the aggregates (*khandha*), beings (*satta*), and human beings (*manussa*); it occurs in reference to that which exists (*vijjamāna*) and to the elements (*dhātu*); and it occurs in reference to trees and such things, as well as to those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).
Furthermore, the word *bhūta* should be understood by the discerning one as referring to arising (*uppāda*).
This prefix *vi-* is used in the senses of "extensive," "contempt," "dispersion," "defeat," "feeling," "name," and "manifestness.

For it has been said: "The word *bhūta* [is used] in reference to the five aggregates, human beings, elements, existing things, those whose taints are exhausted, sentient beings, trees, and so forth."
It is seen [in various senses]. For in such passages as, “Monks, regard this as ‘what has come to be’ (bhūta),” it refers to the five aggregates.
In the passage, “Whatever beings have gathered here,” it refers to non-human spirits. In the passage, “Monk, the four great elements (mahābhūta) are the causes,” it refers to the primary elements.

In such passages as, “There is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) regarding what has come to be,” it refers to that which exists. And in the passage, “He who is a being (bhūta) that devours time,” it refers to a living creature.

In the phrase "herein, those whose taints are exhausted," it refers to those with taints destroyed. In the phrase "all beings in the world shall lay down their aggregates," it refers to sentient beings.
In the phrase "for the destruction of the forest of beings," it refers to trees and so forth. This is the statement from the *Mūlapariyāya Sutta-ṭīkā*. In this *Ṭīkā*, by the word "etc.
(*ādi*), arising and so forth are included. For it has been said: "In such passages as 'born,' 'become,' and 'conditioned,' the word *bhūta* [refers] to arising."
It is seen [in various senses]. However, in such passages as “A noble person performs abundant merit,” it means *vipula* (abundant).
In such passages as “He was generally treated with contempt by the bhikkhus,” it means *hīḷana* (contempt). In such passages as “Sambhūta Sāṇavāsī,” it means *paññatti* (designation).

In such passages as “Māra has been overcome; the battle has been won,” it means *vidhamana* (dispelling). In such passages as “This naked Pāṭikaputta is indeed one who has come to ruin,” it means... [ruin].
In the sense of defeat, as in “suffering experienced” (*anubhūtaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ*) and so forth; in the sense of feeling, as in “made manifest by wisdom” (*vibhūtaṃ paññāya*) and so forth;
and in the sense of making something evident, it is seen [in such contexts]. All these [meanings] should be understood as being included by the phrase “in trees, etc.
Now, the forms ending in the suffix *-tuṃ* are stated:
To become, to arise, to arise together, to originate, to perish, to surpass, to come into being, to dissolve, to be,
to come into being together, to dissolve completely, to manifest, or to manifest clearly— to manifest clearly.
These are the infinitive forms (tumantapada) that take no object (akammaka).
*Paribhotum* means to despise, to treat with contempt; *abhibhotum* means to overcome, to conquer; *adhibhotum* means to prevail over;
*atibhotum* means to surpass; *anubhotum* means to experience; *samanubhotum* means to experience fully; *abhisambhotum* means to attain or achieve.
These are transitive infinitive forms (*tumantapada*), and all of them function solely as the agent (*suddhakattari*).

“*Bhāvetuṃ*, *pabhāvetuṃ*, *sambhāvetuṹṃ*, *vibhāvetuṃ*, *paribhāvetuṃ*”—these and similar forms ending in the infinitive suffix (*tumanta*) have the agent as the cause (the causal agent). Indeed, all infinitive forms having the agent as the cause are necessarily transitive.
This is the enumeration. In that regard, among words of identical meaning, one should provide the explanation by taking only the first word:
*bhavituṃ* means to be, to exist, to be found, to be discerned, or to obtain its own form. Following the method stated here, [the same applies] to the remaining infinitives as well.

The exposition should be expanded: all *tumantapada* forms function in the sense of the dative case, as in the example, “Having understood my mind, you have come to ask for the Eye. For the word *yācituṃ* means “for the purpose of asking.
Therefore, for words such as *bhavituṃ*, the meaning should be understood as “for the purpose of being,” or “being,” or “for the sake of being,” and so forth.

Furthermore, in the phrase “having seen renunciation as security” (*nekkhammaṃ daṭṭhu khemato*), because the word *daṭṭhu* shows the meaning of “having seen” (*disvā*), the forms ending in *tum* should be understood according to their respective meanings based on the sense of the word *tvā*. These [forms] are included among the indeclinables (*nipāta*).
For it is said in the section on indeclinables in the *Niruttipiṭaka*: “*tuṃ* is [a substitute] for the fourth case.”
In this context, the meaning is as follows: "The particle ending in *tum*, namely *tuṃ*, functions in the sense of the dative case.
The discussion on forms ending in *tum* is concluded.
Now, words ending in *tvā* and so forth are being stated:
*bhavitvā*, *bhavitvāna*, *bhavituna*, *bhaviya*, *bhaviyāna*. *ubbhavitvā*, *ubbhavitvāna*, *ubbhavituna*, *ubbhaviya*, *ubbhaviyāna*.
This same method applies here as well for the forms: *samubbhavitvā*, *parābhavitvā*, *sambhavitvā*, *vibhavitvā*, *pātubbhavitvā*.
These are intransitive verbal nouns (*yantapada*) ending in *-tvā* and so forth, which signify the sense of striving or exertion (*ussukkanattha*).
*Bhutvā*, *bhutvāna*, *paribhavitvā*, *paribhavitvāna*, *paribhavituna*, *paribhaviya*, *paribhaviyāna*, *paribhuyya*.
*Abhibhavitvā*, *abhibhavitvāna*, *abhibhavituna*, *abhibhaviya*, *abhibhaviyāna*, *abhibhuyya*.
This same method applies here as well for the forms *adhibhavitvā*, *atibhavitvā*, and *anubhavitvā*. And this is the point here:
An illustration: “Having experienced that, O King, you said to him: ‘Come quickly, I too shall perform an offering.
Having experienced, having experienced. Having overcome, having overcome.
‘For sixty thousand eons, he will delight in the world of the gods.’”
“Having overcome other deities, he will exercise lordship.
This is the citation from the Pāḷi here; these are the words *tvā* and *iyaṃta* used in the sense of exertion (*ussukkanattha*) with transitive verbs. These four [forms]—*bhāvetvā*, *bhāvetvāna*;
*pabhāvetvā*, *pabhāvetvāna*; *sambhāvetvā*, *sambhāvetvāna*; *vibhāvetvā*—occur only as pure agentive forms (*suddhakattari*).

Having analyzed (*vibhāvetvāna*), having cultivated (*paribhāvetvā*, *paribhāvetvāna*)—such words as these, which are transitive and denote the sense of exertion, occur only with the causal agent when followed by suffixes such as *-tvā* or *-ya*. This is the summary.
In that regard, among words of identical meaning, one should provide the exposition by taking only the first word: *bhavitvā* means "having become" (*hutvā*).

"Having appeared" means having obtained a physical form. Following the method thus stated, the exposition for the remaining participial forms ending in *-tvā* and so forth should be expanded in detail.
However, this is the distinction: in the case of *bhutvā*, the meaning should be understood as "having experienced prosperity," taking it as a transitive verb.
For those learned in the True Dhamma maintain that *bhutvā* and *anubhutvā* have the same meaning. On this point, it is said:
The words “having become, having become” (bhutvā bhutvāna) signify for him the sense of “having experienced” (anubhutvā);
however, they do not signify the sense of the word “having been” (hutvā).
Some, within the Teaching, desire that the word “bhūtvā” have a long vowel.
Both length and shortness are indeed seen here.
In the science of grammar (*saddasattha*), the word "having been" (*bhūtvā*) is associated with length;
it illustrates the meaning of the word "having become" (*bhavitvā*), but not according to the [Buddhist] Teaching (*sāsana*).
The word "having become" (*hutvā*) alone illuminates the teaching of the Conqueror;
the meaning of the word "having been" (*bhavitvā*) does not exist elsewhere.
Thus, this specific expression was uttered by the Seer of the Essence.
In the Dispensation and in the science of grammar, that which is to be examined by the wise is as follows:

even the words ending in *tvā* and the like, which occur in the sense of exertion (*ussukkanatthe*), have been explained; all of these should be understood as being without case-endings (*avibhattikāni*).
For in the section on particles (*nipātaparicchede*) of the *Niruttipiṭaka*, the words ending in *tvā* and the like are treated as being without case-endings.

[These forms] have been stated. However, according to the opinion of those learned in the meanings of words (*saddatthavidū*), they possess case endings by way of the first and subsequent case-inflections (*vibhatti*).
Furthermore, in this section concerning suffixes such as *tvā*, the following should be noted:

*bhutvā gacchati* (having eaten, he goes), *bhutvā gato* (having eaten, he went), *bhutvā gamissasi* (having eaten, you will go), *kasitvā vapati* (having ploughed, he sows). Also: *umaṅgā nikkhamitvāna, vedeho nāvamāruhi* (Having departed from Ummagga, Vedeha boarded the ship); *bhutvāna*.

In expressions such as "bhikkhu bhikkhassu" (O monk, beg for alms), the use of words like *tvā* occurs when there are verbal roots (*dhātu*) sharing the same agent (*samānakattuka*) at the prior time.

For instance, in the phrase "having eaten, he goes" (*bhutvā gacchati*), the word "having eaten" (*bhutvā*) is the term that indicates the action occurring at the prior time, while "he goes" (*gacchati*) indicates the action occurring at the subsequent time;
and these two terms share the same agent, meaning the actions belong to a single agent.
Because of being the agent. Thus, here, whoever is the agent of the action of going should be regarded as the very same one who has become the agent of the action of eating.
This method should be applied elsewhere in similar instances:
"Having destroyed the darkness, this sun has risen."
“Having illuminated with the radiance of wisdom, he has arisen”—
such expressions as these involve the use of the suffix *tvā* and others when the agents are the same and the times are the same. For here,
the word “having destroyed” (*nihantvānā*) is a word that indicates simultaneous action, whereas the word “arisen” (*udito*) is a word that indicates a subsequent action.
It should not be said [that this is an error], because here it is intended as having simultaneous action.
For that very reason, it should be understood as a phrase illustrating simultaneous action. This method should be applied elsewhere in similar instances as well.
Some, however, cite: "He sleeps with his mouth open; he looks with his eyes rolled back. Others...

“Sitting, he studies; standing, he speaks. In this context, the time subsequent to the opening of the mouth and the turning [of the words] is characterized by the act of seeing, which has the characteristic of the subsiding of the opening of the mouth. Furthermore, regarding the statement “sitting, he studies;
standing, he speaks,” although there is simultaneity, since sitting and standing can also exist prior to the study and the speaking, one may infer a temporal sequence of earlier and later.
Therefore, only the previous examples are appropriate. For the cessation of that which is to be ceased occurs at the very same time as its arising.
Expressions such as “having closed the door, he enters” involve the use of the suffix *tvā* and so forth when there is a single agent, but applied to a subsequent action.
Since, however, in this case the action of entering is prior and the action of closing is posterior, therefore [the word] “having closed” (*āvaritvā*)—this...

It should be understood that this is called a word indicating a subsequent action (*aparakālakriyādīpaka*). However, the word "enters" (*pavisati*) is a word indicating a prior action (*pubbakālakriyādīpaka*).
This method should be applied elsewhere as well in similar instances. Others say that "the staff fell with a 'dha' sound" is an example [of the former].
But in the case of the conjunction of the agent of striking and the object struck, there is simultaneity (*samānakālatā*) for the sound produced by the strike.
Regarding the phrase "it is found here," even in this context, the previous examples alone are appropriate.
The construction "Having seen a *pisāca*, fear arises in him; having seen with wisdom, his taints (*āsava*) are utterly destroyed" is an instance of a non-identical agent (*asamāne kattari*).
For in this case, having seen the *pisāca*, fear arises in the person, whereas having seen with wisdom, his [taints are destroyed].

The taints of the person are completely destroyed. Thus, it should be understood that grammatical coreferentiality (*samānakattukatā*) is not obtained for the verbal roots, because the action of seeing operates upon men, while the actions of being afraid and so forth operate upon fear and so on.
This method should be applied elsewhere in similar instances as well.

Furthermore, the following should be noted here: expressions such as "the mountain not having reached the river" (*appatvā nadiṃ pabbato*) and "having crossed the mountain, the river" (*atikkamma pabbataṃ nadī*) are examples of the construction involving priority and posteriority (*parāparayoga*).

Expressions such as "fear arises upon seeing a lion," "strength is born after drinking ghee," and "the stick fell because [one] made the sound 'dha'" are examples of the construction involving characteristic cause (*lakkhaṇahetu*) and so forth.
Examples include "going after bathing" (*nhatvā gamanaṃ*), "lying down after eating" (*bhutvā sayanaṃ*), and "depending upon" (*upādāya*).
The application of grammatical rules for the derivation of words such as *rūpaṃ* is also established through the principle of distinction (*byattaya*).
Thus, in every respect: there is the application of suffixes like *tvā* for verbal roots with a common agent in the prior time;

the application of suffixes like *tvā* for verbal roots with a common agent at the same time; the application of suffixes like *tvā* for verbal roots with a common agent in the subsequent time; and [the application] for those with different agents...

The application of words ending in *tvā* and so forth should be understood as sevenfold: the application of the word *tvā* and its variants; the application of successive connection (*parāparayoga*); the application of characteristics, causes, and so forth; and the application for the establishment of grammatical forms through their distinctness.
If this is so, why does the *Kaccāyana* [grammar] state, "For actions with a prior time and a single agent, [the suffixes] *tuna*, *tvāna*, or *tvā* [are used]," only in reference to the prior time?
Why was the term "single agent" (ekakattuka) included? Because it indicates that, for the most part, words beginning with *tvā* and so on denote an action performed at a prior time.
For in the *Kaccāyana*, it is stated—"of actions having a single agent at a prior time"—referring to their general usage.
However, since the ancient teachers have also explained the meaning of words such as "having done thus" (*iti katvā*) by way of the sense of cause (*hetu*), [the term was included].

Therefore, the causal sense (*hetu-attha*) should also be understood for words ending in suffixes such as *tvā* that are derived from the root *bhū*, such as “having been” (*bhavitvā*), as well as for others like “having cooked” (*pacitvā*), according to their respective applications—for instance, as “the cause of being” (*bhavana-hetu*) or “the cause of cooking” (*pacana-hetu*). Regarding this, it is said:
“Since there are words used in the sense of causality that convey a sense of urgency.”
Therefore, a wise person should also state the meaning by way of its cause.
For in the commentaries on the meaning of the word *iti katvā*,
the sense is grasped by the learned as "having thus made it the cause."
“I am now going to Nibbāna, where having gone one does not grieve.
Even in this reading, the sense of a cause is understood by those previously learned.
For it is said: “In that Nibbāna, for the sake of going.”
In this way, according to the circumstances, this method applies elsewhere as well.
Thus, the extraction of the meanings of the word *bhūta* and the categories of words ending in the suffix *-tuṃ* and those ending in *-tvā* and so forth—this triad of meanings has been analyzed.
Whoever [understands] this well-analyzed triad of meanings...
For those who have come to the tradition,
this elixir for the ears sustains them in existence,
free from doubt regarding the subtle meaning within the Teacher’s word that has been passed down.
Thus ends the section titled "The Analysis of the Fourfold Meaning" (*Atthattikavibhāga*) in the *Saddanīti*,

a treatise composed for the sake of the proficiency of the wise in the modes of expression within the Three Baskets (*Piṭakattaya*) together with their commentaries (*Sāṭṭhakatha*), which possess nine branches.
The Fourteenth Chapter.
Thus have the material phenomena of the earth element been shown in their various aspects.
The sequence of terms is concluded.
